title: Exporting Encoder Models
text:
Loading in WhiskerToolbox

Method 1: Widget UI

Open the Deep Learning widget (View → Deep Learning)
Select “General Encoder” from the model dropdown
Under the “image” slot, bind to your video data source
Click Load Weights and select the exported .pt or .pt2 file
Click Run to extract features



Method 2: JSON Specification
For more control, use the generated JSON specification file:

Open the Deep Learning widget
Click Load Model Spec and select the _spec.json file
The model will appear with the correct input/output shapes pre-configured

title: Exporting Encoder Models
Exporting Encoder Models
text:
Output Format
The encoder output is a spatial feature tensor of shape [B, C, H, W]:

B — batch size (number of frames processed simultaneously)
C — number of feature channels (depends on the encoder architecture)
H, W — spatial dimensions of the feature map

For ConvNeXt with 224×224 input, the output spatial size is 7×7 (224 / 32).
This feature tensor can be used as input to downstream processing such as global average pooling, spatial point extraction, or classification heads (see the Deep Learning roadmap for planned post-encoder modules).

title: ML Workflow Overview
text: The ML Workflow widget provides interactive machine learning directly in WhiskerToolbox. It supports two workflows:

title: ML Workflow Overview
text:
Opening the Widget
Open the ML Workflow widget from the menu: View → Analysis → ML Workflow.
The widget appears as a tabbed panel in the right dock area. The Classification tab is shown by default; switch to the Clustering tab for unsupervised workflows.

title: ML Workflow Overview
text:
General Workflow

Classification

Prepare features: Build a feature tensor using the TensorDesigner widget. Features are columns of numerical values (e.g., curvature, distance, angle) computed from your data.
Select features: Choose the feature tensor in the ML Workflow’s Feature panel.
Define training region (optional): Select a DigitalIntervalSeries that marks which frames to use for training.
Configure labels: Choose how frames are labeled — from interval annotations, entity groups, or data-entity groups.
Select model: Choose a classification algorithm (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, or Logistic Regression) and configure its parameters.
Train: Click “Train Model” to run the full pipeline. Training runs in the background and progress is shown in the status bar.
Review results: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and a confusion matrix are displayed in the Results panel.
Predict: Predictions are written as DigitalIntervalSeries and optional probability AnalogTimeSeries. Output appears in the DataManager and can be viewed in the DataViewer.



Clustering

Prepare features: Build a feature tensor as above.
Select data: Choose the tensor and optionally enable z-score normalization.
Select algorithm: Choose K-Means, DBSCAN, or Gaussian Mixture and set parameters.
Fit & Assign: Click “Fit & Assign” to run clustering. Results appear as putative entity groups with auto-assigned colors.
Review output: Cluster sizes, interval series, and optional probability series are created in the DataManager.

title: ML Workflow Overview
text:
Putative Group Output
Predictions and cluster assignments never overwrite your original labels. All outputs are written to new data keys and entity groups with a configurable prefix (e.g., "Predicted:Contact", "Cluster:0"). This lets you compare ML results against your manual annotations.

title: ML Workflow Overview
text:
Prediction Regions
You can restrict predictions to a specific frame range by selecting a DigitalIntervalSeries in the Prediction panel. This is especially useful when you have labeled some parts of a recording and want to predict just the unlabeled sections.
For the HMM, the pipeline automatically extends the prediction range to include training labels (for temporal context), then filters output back to your selected frames. A constrained decoding option (HMM only) uses the last known label at region boundaries to warm-start predictions.

title: ML Workflow Overview
text:
Available Models

Supervised (Classification Tab)



Model
Best For




Random Forest
General-purpose classification with many features


Naive Bayes
Fast training, works well with independent features


Logistic Regression
Binary classification with well-calibrated probabilities


Hidden Markov Model
Sequence-aware classification exploiting temporal continuity





Unsupervised (Clustering Tab)



Model
Best For




K-Means
Known number of clusters, spherical groups


DBSCAN
Unknown number of clusters, arbitrary shapes, noise detection


Gaussian Mixture
Soft cluster assignments, overlapping groups

title: Random Forest Classifier
text: Random Forest is an ensemble classifier that builds many decision trees during training and outputs the most common class prediction across all trees. It is a good general-purpose classifier that handles many features well and is resistant to overfitting.

title: Random Forest Classifier
text: Random Forest is an ensemble classifier that builds many decision trees during training and outputs the most common class prediction across all trees. It is a good general-purpose classifier that handles many features well and is resistant to overfitting.

title: Random Forest Classifier
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Number of Trees
10
More trees = better accuracy but slower training


Minimum Leaf Size
1
Minimum samples required in a leaf node. Larger values prevent overfitting.


Maximum Depth
0 (unlimited)
Limits tree depth. Set to prevent overfitting on noisy data.


Minimum Gain Split

Minimum information gain required to split a node

title: Random Forest Classifier
text:
When to Use

You have many features and are unsure which are important
You want a reliable baseline classifier
You need probability estimates (vote fractions across trees)
Your data may have non-linear decision boundaries

title: Random Forest Classifier
text:
Probability Output
Random Forest provides probability estimates based on the fraction of trees voting for each class. For example, if 73 out of 100 trees predict “Contact”, the probability output for that frame is 0.73.

title: Random Forest Classifier
text:
Tips

Start with the default parameters and increase num_trees if accuracy is insufficient
If the model overfits (high training accuracy, low prediction accuracy), increase minimum_leaf_size or set a maximum_depth
Training time scales linearly with num_trees

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a sequence-aware classifier that uses temporal continuity to improve predictions. Unlike frame-based classifiers (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression) that classify each frame independently, the HMM considers what state the system was in at the previous frame when predicting the current frame.
This makes HMMs ideal for detecting behavioral states that persist over time — for example, periods of whisker contact vs. non-contact, where transitions between states are rare relative to the frame rate.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is a sequence-aware classifier that uses temporal continuity to improve predictions. Unlike frame-based classifiers (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression) that classify each frame independently, the HMM considers what state the system was in at the previous frame when predicting the current frame.
This makes HMMs ideal for detecting behavioral states that persist over time — for example, periods of whisker contact vs. non-contact, where transitions between states are rare relative to the frame rate.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
How It Works
The HMM assumes your data is generated by a system that:

Has a fixed number of hidden states (e.g., “Contact” and “No Contact”)
Transitions between states according to learned probabilities (e.g., 95% chance of staying in the same state)
Emits observable features (e.g., curvature, distance) drawn from a Gaussian distribution specific to each state

Training learns these transition probabilities and per-state Gaussian distributions from labeled data. Prediction then finds the most likely sequence of hidden states given new observations.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Number of States
2
Number of hidden states. Use 2 for binary classification tasks.


Tolerance
1e-5
Convergence tolerance for parameter estimation


Diagonal Covariance
Off
Use diagonal covariance matrices for emissions (see below)




Diagonal Covariance
By default the HMM fits a full covariance matrix for each state’s Gaussian emission distribution. When diagonal covariance is enabled (checkbox in Model Configuration), each state stores only a variance per feature instead of a full covariance matrix. This:

Reduces parameters dramatically — from \(M(M+1)/2\) to \(M\) per state (where \(M\) is the number of features)
Improves numerical stability when training data is limited relative to the number of features
Assumes conditional independence of features given the hidden state

Enable this option when you have many features relative to your training data, or if training with full covariance fails or produces unstable results.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
When to Use

Your classification target is a temporal state that persists across consecutive frames
Frame-based classifiers produce “noisy” predictions with many rapid state switches
You have labeled event data (DigitalEventSeries) marking state occurrences
You want smoother predictions that respect temporal coherence

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Label Sources
The HMM supports all label sources available in the ML Workflow widget. The most natural pairing is From Events, which converts point events to binary state labels:







Label Source
How It Works




From Events (recommended for HMM)
Frames with a matching event → state 1; all others → state 0


From Intervals
Frames inside the interval → positive class; outside → negative class


From Groups
Each entity group maps to a class label


From Data Entity Groups
Like Groups, but scoped to a specific data key



To use event-based labels, select the “From Events” radio button in the Label Configuration panel and choose a DigitalEventSeries from the dropdown.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Sequence Segmentation
The HMM automatically detects temporal gaps in your feature data and splits it into contiguous sequences. For example, if your feature tensor covers frames 100–200 and 500–600, the HMM treats these as two separate sequences rather than assuming a continuous transition from frame 200 to frame 500.
Sequences shorter than 2 frames are discarded (a single frame carries no temporal information for an HMM).

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Output
The HMM produces the same outputs as other classifiers:








Output
Type
Description




State intervals
DigitalIntervalSeries
One series per state (e.g., "HMM:Contact", "HMM:NoContact")


State probabilities
AnalogTimeSeries
Per-frame probability of each state (if enabled)


Transition matrix
Displayed in Results panel
Learned state-to-state transition probabilities




Transition Matrix
After training, the Results panel shows the learned transition matrix. For a 2-state model:
         → State 0    → State 1
State 0:   0.97          0.03
State 1:   0.05          0.95
This means: if the system is in State 0, there is a 97% chance it stays in State 0 at the next frame, and a 3% chance it transitions to State 1. High diagonal values indicate states that persist over many frames.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Tips

Start with 2 states for binary classification. Only increase the state count if you know your data has more distinct behavioral modes.
The HMM works best when states are temporally persistent — if your target state changes every few frames, a frame-based classifier may perform equally well.
Z-score normalization is recommended, as Gaussian emissions are sensitive to feature scaling.
If training fails, ensure your training data contains examples of all states and includes at least a few state transitions.
Compare HMM predictions against Random Forest to see if temporal smoothing improves your results.
Enable diagonal covariance if you have many features but limited training data.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Prediction Regions
By default, the HMM predicts on all feature rows. You can restrict predictions to a specific frame range by selecting a DigitalIntervalSeries in the Prediction panel. When a prediction region is selected:

The HMM still runs on the full temporal range covering both your training labels and the prediction region (so it retains temporal context at boundaries)
Output is filtered to only write results for the frames you selected

This is useful when you’ve labeled parts of your recording and want to predict just the unlabeled gap, while still benefiting from the HMM’s awareness of the labeled regions on either side.

Constrained Decoding (Warm-Start)
When a prediction region is adjacent to labeled training data, the HMM can warm-start predictions using the known state at the boundary. For example, if your training labels end at frame 1000 with state “Contact”, the HMM starts predicting frame 1001 from that known state rather than guessing.
This is controlled by the “Constrained decoding” checkbox in the Prediction panel (visible only when using HMM). It is enabled by default and generally improves prediction accuracy at region boundaries.
Constrained decoding has no effect on frame-independent classifiers (Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression).

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian)
text:
Comparison with Frame-Based Classifiers








Aspect
Frame-Based (e.g., Random Forest)
HMM




Temporal context
None — each frame classified independently
Considers previous state via transition probabilities


Prediction smoothness
May produce rapid state switches
Naturally produces smooth state sequences


Training data
Shuffled, order does not matter
Order matters — sequences must be temporally contiguous


Speed
Fast (independent per frame)
Moderate (Viterbi decoding, Forward-Backward)


Best for
Features that are strongly discriminative on their own
States that persist over time with noisy features

title: Logistic Regression
text: Logistic Regression is a linear classifier that models the probability of class membership using the logistic (sigmoid) function. It is well-suited for binary classification tasks and produces naturally calibrated probability outputs.

title: Logistic Regression
text: Logistic Regression is a linear classifier that models the probability of class membership using the logistic (sigmoid) function. It is well-suited for binary classification tasks and produces naturally calibrated probability outputs.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Parameters








Parameter
Default
Description




Lambda
0.0
L2 regularization strength. Higher values penalize large weights and reduce overfitting.


Step Size
0.01
Optimizer step size for gradient descent


Max Iterations
10000
Maximum number of optimizer iterations (0 = unlimited)

title: Logistic Regression
text:
When to Use

You have a binary classification problem (two classes)
You want well-calibrated probability outputs
Your decision boundary is approximately linear in feature space
You need a simple, interpretable model

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Limitations
Logistic Regression supports binary classification only. For multi-class problems, use Random Forest or Naive Bayes.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Probability Output
Logistic Regression produces probability estimates via the sigmoid function, which are naturally calibrated — a predicted probability of 0.7 means roughly 70% of such frames truly belong to the positive class.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Tips

If the model underfits, decrease lambda (less regularization)
If the model overfits, increase lambda (more regularization)
The threshold for classification can be adjusted in the Prediction panel (default 0.5)

title: Python Console
text: The Python Console in Neuralyzer provides a powerful interface to interact with your data using Python 3.12. It allows you to run scripts, manipulate data structures, and perform custom analyses directly within the application.

title: Python Console
text:
Overview
Neuralyzer embeds a full Python 3.12 interpreter. This means you have access to the standard Python library as well as a specialized whiskertoolbox_python module that bridges the gap between the application’s C++ core and the Python environment.
Key features include: - Interactive Console (REPL): Test snippets and inspect data in real-time. - Script Editor: Write, save, and execute .py scripts. - Data Manager Integration: Seamless access to loaded data via the dm object. - Zero-Copy Access: Efficiently read large datasets (like analog signals and tensors) as NumPy arrays without copying memory.

title: Python Console
text:
Interface
The Python Widget is divided into three main areas:

Console Tab:

Output Area: Displays the results of your code, standard output (grey), and errors (red).
Input Area: A multi-line text editor for typing commands. Press Shift+Enter to execute.
History: Use Up/Down arrows to navigate through your command history.

Editor Tab:

A full-featured text editor for writing longer scripts.
Supports Open, Save, and Run functionalities.
Drag and drop .py files to open them.

Properties Panel (Right Side):

Environment: Displays the current Python version and active virtual environment (if any).
Settings: Configure font size, auto-scrolling, and line numbers.
Namespace: A live view of all variables in the current Python session.
Data Keys: A list of all data objects currently in the Data Manager. Click “Insert” to paste the code to retrieve an object into the console.

title: Python Console
text:
Accessing Data
The Data Manager is exposed to the Python environment as a pre-loaded object named dm. You can use dm to retrieve, modify, and create data.

Retrieving Data
Use dm.getData("key_name") to get a reference to a data object.
# Get the analog signal named 'whisker_angle'
angle_data = dm.getData("whisker_angle")

# Check if data was found
if angle_data:
    print(f"Loaded {angle_data.getNumSamples()} samples")


Creating and Registering Data
You can create new data objects using classes from the whiskertoolbox_python module and register them back to the Data Manager using dm.setData().

title: Python Console
text:
Example: Processing Point Data
This example demonstrates how to: 1. Retrieve a PointData object (e.g., tracked nose position). 2. Iterate through the time points. 3. Extract the X-coordinate for each point. 4. Create a new AnalogTimeSeries from these values. 5. Register the new series back to the Data Manager.
from whiskertoolbox_python import AnalogTimeSeries, Point2D

# 1. Retrieve the PointData object
# systematic_name: 'nose_tracking'
point_data = dm.getData("nose_tracking")

if point_data:
    # Prepare lists to store the processed data
    x_values = []
    times = []

    # 2. Iterate through all times that have data
    # getTimesWithData() returns a list of TimeFrameIndex
    for t in point_data.getTimesWithData():
        
        # getAtTime(t) returns a list of Point2D objects at that time
        points_at_t = point_data.getAtTime(t)
        
        # 3. Extract X coordinate (assuming one point per frame)
        if points_at_t:
            pt = points_at_t[0] 
            x_values.append(pt.x)
            times.append(t)

    # Convert to standard Python lists or NumPy arrays if needed
    # (The AnalogTimeSeries constructor accepts Python lists)
    
    # 4. Create a new AnalogTimeSeries
    # Constructor: AnalogTimeSeries(values, times)
    new_series = AnalogTimeSeries(x_values, times)
    
    # 5. Register back to the Data Manager
    # We use the same time base as the original data
    original_time_key = dm.getTimeKey("nose_tracking")
    dm.setData("nose_x_position", new_series, original_time_key)
    
    print("Successfully created 'nose_x_position'")

else:
    print("Error: 'nose_tracking' data not found.")

title: Python Console
text:
API Reference

DataManager (dm)

getData(key) -> object: Retrieve data by key. Returns None if not found.
setData(key, object, time_key): Register a new data object.
getAllKeys() -> list[str]: Get a list of all data keys.
deleteData(key) -> bool: Delete data by key.
getTimeKey(data_key) -> str: Get the time base name for a given data key.



PointData

getTimesWithData() -> list[int]: Get sorted list of time indices with data.
getAtTime(time_index) -> list[Point2D]: Get list of points at a specific time.
addAtTime(time_index, point): Add a point at a specific time.



Point2D

x: Float coordinate.
y: Float coordinate.



AnalogTimeSeries

AnalogTimeSeries(values, times): Constructor taking lists of floats and TimeFrameIndex values.
AnalogTimeSeries(values, num_samples): Constructor from a values list with a sample count (dense, regularly-spaced indices).
values: Read-only NumPy float32 array of the data values (zero-copy).
times: NumPy int64 array of the time index for every sample.
getNumSamples() -> int: Get the number of samples.
__len__() -> int: Same as getNumSamples().
toList() -> list[float]: Copy all values to a Python list.
getTimeSeries() -> list[TimeFrameIndex]: Get all time indices as a list of TimeFrameIndex objects.
toTimeValueArrays() -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: Return (times, values) as a (int64, float32) NumPy array pair.
getDataInRange(start, end) -> np.ndarray: Read-only NumPy view of values in [start, end] (zero-copy).
getAtTime(time) -> float | None: Value at a specific TimeFrameIndex, or None if not found.



MaskData

getTimesWithData() -> list[int]: Get sorted list of time indices with data.
getAtTime(time_index) -> list[Mask2D]: Get list of masks at a specific time.
addAtTime(time_index, mask): Add a mask at a specific time.
getDataByEntityId(entity_id) -> Mask2D: Get mask for a specific entity ID.



Mask2D

Mask2D(points): Constructor taking a list of Point2D.
size() -> int: Get the number of points in the mask.
points() -> list[Point2D]: Get the list of points.
__iter__(): Iterate over points in the mask.



LineData

getTimesWithData() -> list[int]: Get sorted list of time indices with data.
getAtTime(time_index) -> list[Line2D]: Get list of lines at a specific time.
addAtTime(time_index, line): Add a line at a specific time.
getDataByEntityId(entity_id) -> Line2D: Get line for a specific entity ID.



Line2D

Line2D(points): Constructor taking a list of Point2D.
size() -> int: Get the number of points in the line.
toList() -> list[Point2D]: Copy points to a Python list.
__iter__(): Iterate over points in the line.



DigitalEventSeries

addEvent(time_index): Add an event at the specified time index.
removeEvent(time_index): Remove an event at the specified time index.
clear(): Remove all events.
size() -> int: Get the number of events.
toList() -> list[int]: Get all event times as a list.
toListWithIds() -> list[tuple]: Get all events as (time, entity_id) tuples.



DigitalIntervalSeries

addEvent(interval): Add an interval object.
addInterval(start, end): Add an interval defined by start and end integers.
removeInterval(interval): Remove an interval.
clear(): Remove all intervals.
size() -> int: Get the number of intervals.
toList() -> list[Interval]: Get all intervals as a list.
toListWithIds() -> list[tuple]: Get all intervals as (Interval, entity_id) tuples.

For a full reference of the C++ classes and their Python bindings, refer to the Developer Documentation.

title: Lane Layout Profiles
text:
The Data Viewer can save and load lane layout profiles as JSON. A profile defines stable lane IDs, assigns data keys to those lanes, and places spike/event series relative to a lane without requiring you to calculate internal lane order values.
Use Save Lane Layout to write the current profile and Load Lane Layout to apply one. In Merge mode, only keys named in the file are added or updated. In Replace mode, the current displayed series and lane state are cleared first.
{
  "version": 2,
  "mode": "Merge",
  "lanes": [
    {
      "lane_id": "channel_11",
      "display_label": "11",
      "series": [
        { "key": "voltage_11", "type": "Analog", "color": "#FFFFFF", "visible": true },
        { "key": "voltage_raw_11", "type": "Analog", "color": "#888888", "visible": false }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "event_associations": [
    {
      "event_key": "spikes_11a",
      "target_lane_id": "channel_11",
      "placement": "Above",
      "glyph_shape": "Box"
    }
  ]
}
If a lane omits lane_order, the file order is used from top to bottom. When lane_order is present, it is treated as a relative rank: larger values appear higher, and the loader adds internal spacing so event lanes can be inserted between densely ranked lanes such as 31, 30, 29, and so on. Event associations use exact keys, so names such as spikes_11a and spikes_11b can be placed independently above, below, or over the same channel lane.
The event association array key must be named event_associations.


glyph_shape can be:

Tick: a standard vertical tick at the event time.
TopLine: a horizontal marker along the top of the lane.
Box: a box centered on the event time.

placement can be:

Above: place the event series in a lane immediately above target_lane_id.
Below: place the event series in a lane immediately below target_lane_id.
Overlay: draw the event series in the same lane as target_lane_id.

title: Lane Layout Profiles
text:
glyph_shape can be:

Tick: a standard vertical tick at the event time.
TopLine: a horizontal marker along the top of the lane.

placement can be:

text:
Loading in Python
All formats use # comment lines. Pass comment='#' to pd.read_csv() to skip them automatically.

Raster
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("event_plot.csv", comment="#")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.stripplot(
    data=df, x="relative_time", y="trial_index",
    hue="event_key", jitter=False, orient="h",
    size=2, ax=ax
)
ax.set_xlabel("Time relative to alignment (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Trial")
ax.invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


PSTH
df = pd.read_csv("psth.csv", comment="#")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
sns.lineplot(
    data=df, x="bin_center", y="value",
    hue="event_key", ax=ax
)
ax.set_xlabel("Time relative to alignment (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Heatmap

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.heatmap(df.astype(float), cmap="inferno", ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Unit")
plt.tight_layout()

title: Saving Back to Loaded Files
text:
When data is loaded from disk, WhiskerToolbox records the resolved source file path for that data key. If you later save the same key with the same format from a Data Inspector, the save target defaults to the original file instead of the global output directory.
Before writing, the existing file is moved to the same path with a .bak suffix. For example, saving back to points.csv first moves the previous file to points.csv.bak, then writes the new points.csv.
This behavior is currently applied to single-file exports. Directory-based exports still use the selected/export directory.

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
You have a pre-trained image encoder (e.g. ConvNeXt, ViT, ResNet) and want to export it as an AOT Inductor .pt2 package so it can be loaded in Neuralyzer’s Deep Learning widget. This guide walks through the process using ConvNeXt-Tiny from torchvision as a concrete example.
The exported encoder takes an RGB image and produces a spatial feature map — for ConvNeXt-Tiny with 224×224 input, this is a [B, 768, 7, 7] tensor. Post-encoder modules in Neuralyzer can then reduce this to a per-frame feature vector.

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
You have a pre-trained image encoder (e.g. ConvNeXt, ViT, ResNet) and want to export it as an AOT Inductor .pt2 package so it can be loaded in Neuralyzer’s Deep Learning widget. This guide walks through the process using ConvNeXt-Tiny from torchvision as a concrete example.
The exported encoder takes an RGB image and produces a spatial feature map — for ConvNeXt-Tiny with 224×224 input, this is a [B, 768, 7, 7] tensor. Post-encoder modules in Neuralyzer can then reduce this to a per-frame feature vector.

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Prerequisites

Python 3.10+
PyTorch 2.9+ (pip install torch torchvision)

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Step 1: Define the Encoder Wrapper
ConvNeXt (and most torchvision/timm models) includes a classification head that we don’t need. We wrap the model to return only the encoder’s spatial feature map, before any pooling or classification.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torchvision.models as models


class ConvNeXtEncoder(nn.Module):
    """
    Wraps ConvNeXt-Tiny to return the spatial feature map from the 
    final convolutional stage, before the classification head.

    Input:  [B, 3, 224, 224]   (RGB image, normalized)
    Output: [B, 768, 7, 7]     (spatial feature map)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        full_model = models.convnext_tiny(weights=models.ConvNeXt_Tiny_Weights.DEFAULT)
        # Keep only the feature extraction stages, discard avgpool + classifier
        self.features = full_model.features

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.features(x)






TipOther Encoders



The same pattern works for any encoder backbone. For timm models:
import timm

class TimmEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model_name: str = "convnext_tiny"):
        super().__init__()
        self.backbone = timm.create_model(model_name, pretrained=True, 
                                          num_classes=0, global_pool="")
    
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.backbone(x)
For a ViT that outputs [B, 197, 384] (patch tokens + CLS), you may want to reshape the patch tokens to a spatial grid (e.g. [B, 384, 14, 14]) so that spatial post-encoder modules work correctly:
class ViTEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.backbone = timm.create_model("vit_small_patch16_224", pretrained=True,
                                          num_classes=0, global_pool="")
    
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        tokens = self.backbone(x)          # [B, 197, 384]
        patches = tokens[:, 1:, :]         # drop CLS token -> [B, 196, 384]
        B, N, C = patches.shape
        H = W = int(N ** 0.5)              # 14 x 14
        return patches.permute(0, 2, 1).reshape(B, C, H, W)  # [B, 384, 14, 14]

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Step 2: Verify Output Shape
Before exporting, verify the encoder produces the expected output:
model = ConvNeXtEncoder()
model.eval()

example_input = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)

with torch.no_grad():
    output = model(example_input)
    print(f"Input shape:  {example_input.shape}")   # [1, 3, 224, 224]
    print(f"Output shape: {output.shape}")           # [1, 768, 7, 7]
    assert output.shape == (1, 768, 7, 7)

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Step 3: Export with AOT Inductor
import os

output_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

# IMPORTANT: use batch > 1 in the example input — batch=1 causes PyTorch
# to specialize the dimension as a constant and reject the dynamic annotation.
example_input_dynamic = torch.randn(2, 3, 224, 224)

# Dynamic batch dimension — allows variable batch sizes at inference time
batch_dim = torch.export.Dim("batch", min=1, max=32)
dynamic_shapes = {"x": {0: batch_dim}}

with torch.no_grad():
    exported = torch.export.export(
        model, (example_input_dynamic,), dynamic_shapes=dynamic_shapes
    )

    pt2_path = torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(
        exported,
        package_path=os.path.join(output_dir, "convnext_encoder.pt2"),
    )

print(f"Exported to: {pt2_path}")






NoteDynamic Shapes



The dynamic_shapes argument marks the batch dimension as dynamic, meaning the compiled model accepts any batch size between 1 and 32 at runtime. The spatial dimensions (224×224) remain fixed — the model was compiled for that resolution.
If you need multiple input resolutions, export separate .pt2 packages for each resolution and use the weights_variants field in the JSON spec (see below).

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
section: Step 4: Create the JSON Model Spec

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Step 5: (Optional) TorchScript Fallback
If AOT Inductor export fails for your encoder, fall back to TorchScript:
with torch.no_grad():
    traced = torch.jit.trace(model, example_input)
    traced.save(os.path.join(output_dir, "convnext_encoder.pt"))
Update weights_path in the JSON spec to "convnext_encoder.pt" — the backend auto-detects from the file extension.

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Step 6: Load in Neuralyzer

Open View → Tools → Deep Learning to open the widget.
Load the convnext_encoder.json model spec from the model selector.
The widget will show one input slot ("image") and one output slot ("features").
Bind "image" to your video media data.
Configure a post-encoder module if desired (e.g. Global Average Pooling to reduce [768, 7, 7] → [768]).
Bind the output to a TensorData key.
Run inference.

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Complete Export Script
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Export a ConvNeXt-Tiny encoder for Neuralyzer.
Produces both AOT Inductor (.pt2) and TorchScript (.pt) formats,
plus the JSON model spec.
"""

import json
import os

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torchvision.models as models


class ConvNeXtEncoder(nn.Module):
    """ConvNeXt-Tiny feature extractor (no classification head)."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        full_model = models.convnext_tiny(weights=models.ConvNeXt_Tiny_Weights.DEFAULT)
        self.features = full_model.features

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.features(x)


def main():
    output_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
    model = ConvNeXtEncoder()
    model.eval()

    example_input = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)

    # Verify
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model(example_input)
        print(f"Output shape: {out.shape}")  # [1, 768, 7, 7]
        assert out.shape == (1, 768, 7, 7)

    # --- AOT Inductor export (with dynamic batch) ---
    # IMPORTANT: use batch > 1 — batch=1 causes PyTorch to specialize it as constant.
    print("Exporting with AOT Inductor...")
    example_input_dynamic = torch.randn(2, 3, 224, 224)
    batch_dim = torch.export.Dim("batch", min=1, max=32)
    dynamic_shapes = {"x": {0: batch_dim}}

    with torch.no_grad():
        exported = torch.export.export(
            model, (example_input_dynamic,), dynamic_shapes=dynamic_shapes
        )
        pt2_path = torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(
            exported,
            package_path=os.path.join(output_dir, "convnext_encoder.pt2"),
        )
    print(f"  -> {pt2_path}")

    # --- TorchScript fallback ---
    print("Exporting with TorchScript...")
    with torch.no_grad():
        traced = torch.jit.trace(model, example_input)
        pt_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "convnext_encoder.pt")
        traced.save(pt_path)
    print(f"  -> {pt_path}")

    # --- JSON model spec ---
    spec = {
        "model_id": "convnext_encoder",
        "display_name": "ConvNeXt-Tiny Encoder",
        "description": "ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone producing spatial features",
        "weights_path": "convnext_encoder.pt2",
        "batch_mode": {"dynamic": {"min": 1, "max": 32}},
        "inputs": [
            {
                "name": "image",
                "shape": [3, 224, 224],
                "description": "Input RGB image",
                "recommended_encoder": "ImageEncoder",
            }
        ],
        "outputs": [
            {
                "name": "features",
                "shape": [768, 7, 7],
                "description": "Spatial feature map from last ConvNeXt stage",
            }
        ],
    }

    json_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "convnext_encoder.json")
    with open(json_path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(spec, f, indent=2)
    print(f"  -> {json_path}")

    print("\nDone! Files ready for Neuralyzer:")
    print(f"  Model (AOT Inductor): {pt2_path}")
    print(f"  Model (TorchScript):  {pt_path}")
    print(f"  JSON spec:            {json_path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

title: How-To: Exporting an AOTI Encoder Model
text:
Troubleshooting

torch.export.export() fails with ConvNeXt
Some ConvNeXt operations (e.g. LayerNorm with unusual shapes) may not trace cleanly. Try:

Update to the latest PyTorch — AOT Inductor coverage improves with each release.
Use the TorchScript fallback.
If using timm, ensure exportable=True is passed to create_model().



Wrong output shape
If your encoder returns a different shape than expected:

Check whether the model includes a global pooling layer. Many torchvision models have avgpool before the classifier — make sure you’re stopping before it.
For timm models, use global_pool="" and num_classes=0 to strip pooling and the classification head.



CUDA vs CPU
AOT Inductor compiles for the device present at export time. If you export on a GPU machine, the .pt2 will contain CUDA kernels. For CPU deployment, export on a CPU-only environment or call model.cpu() before export.

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
This guide walks through fitting a GLM-HMM (Generalized Linear Model–Hidden Markov Model) to classify whisker contact frames using deep-learning encoder features and the ssm library.
A standard HMM models contact/no-contact as hidden states emitting high-dimensional features from a Gaussian distribution. At high frame rates this struggles because (1) the transition matrix is overwhelmingly self-transitioning, (2) full covariance in 192 dimensions is underdetermined without enormous data, and (3) the transition dynamics cannot adapt to the feature context.
A GLM-HMM with input-driven observations (Ashwood et al., 2022) solves these problems. Instead of modelling the features as emissions, it treats them as inputs to a per-state logistic regression that predicts a binary contact label:
\[
P(y_t = \text{contact} \mid z_t = k,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\sigma(\mathbf{w}_k^\top \mathbf{u}_t)
\]
Each state \(k\) has its own weight vector \(\mathbf{w}_k\), so different states capture different feature→contact relationships (e.g., pole-present vs. pole-absent dynamics). The hidden states are discovered by EM.

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
This guide walks through fitting a GLM-HMM (Generalized Linear Model–Hidden Markov Model) to classify whisker contact frames using deep-learning encoder features and the ssm library.
A standard HMM models contact/no-contact as hidden states emitting high-dimensional features from a Gaussian distribution. At high frame rates this struggles because (1) the transition matrix is overwhelmingly self-transitioning, (2) full covariance in 192 dimensions is underdetermined without enormous data, and (3) the transition dynamics cannot adapt to the feature context.
A GLM-HMM with input-driven observations (Ashwood et al., 2022) solves these problems. Instead of modelling the features as emissions, it treats them as inputs to a per-state logistic regression that predicts a binary contact label:
\[
P(y_t = \text{contact} \mid z_t = k,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\sigma(\mathbf{w}_k^\top \mathbf{u}_t)
\]
Each state \(k\) has its own weight vector \(\mathbf{w}_k\), so different states capture different feature→contact relationships (e.g., pole-present vs. pole-absent dynamics). The hidden states are discovered by EM.

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Step 1: Extract Data from DataManager
import numpy as np
import whisker_toolbox as wt

dm = wt.DataManager()

# --- Encoder features: shape (T, D) ---
features_td = dm.getData("features")          # TensorData
X_all = np.array(features_td.values, copy=True)  # writable copy
T_total, D = X_all.shape
print(f"Feature matrix: {T_total} frames × {D} dimensions")

# --- Training block intervals ---
train_intervals = dm.getData("train").toList()
print(f"Training blocks: {len(train_intervals)}")
for iv in train_intervals:
    print(f"  [{iv.start}, {iv.end})")

# --- Contact intervals ---
contact_intervals = dm.getData("contact").toList()
print(f"Contact intervals: {len(contact_intervals)}")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
text:
Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
We need a frame-level binary label vector \(y_t \in \{0, 1\}\) for each training block. ssm expects a list of sessions (one array per training block).
def intervals_to_binary(total_frames, intervals):
    """Convert a list of Interval objects to a binary array of shape (total_frames,)."""
    labels = np.zeros(total_frames, dtype=int)
    for iv in intervals:
        labels[iv.start:iv.end] = 1
    return labels

# Build per-frame binary contact labels over the entire session
y_all = intervals_to_binary(T_total, contact_intervals)

# Split into per-block arrays (ssm expects a list of sessions)
X_blocks = []  # list of (T_block, D) arrays — inputs
y_blocks = []  # list of (T_block, 1) arrays — observations

for iv in train_intervals:
    s, e = int(iv.start), int(iv.end)
    X_blocks.append(X_all[s:e])
    # ssm requires observations shape (T, obs_dim) with obs_dim=1
    y_blocks.append(y_all[s:e].reshape(-1, 1))

print(f"Prepared {len(X_blocks)} training blocks")
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(zip(X_blocks, y_blocks)):
    n_contact = yb.sum()
    print(f"  Block {i}: {len(yb)} frames, {n_contact} contact ({100*n_contact/len(yb):.1f}%)")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Step 3: Create the GLM-HMM
import ssm

num_states = 3         # K: number of hidden behavioral states
obs_dim = 1            # y_t is scalar (binary contact label)
num_categories = 2     # binary outcome: contact / no-contact
input_dim = D          # encoder feature dimensionality

glmhmm = ssm.HMM(
    num_states,
    obs_dim,
    input_dim,
    observations="input_driven_obs",
    observation_kwargs=dict(C=num_categories),
    transitions="standard",
)
print(f"GLM-HMM: {num_states} states, {input_dim}-dim inputs, {num_categories} categories")

Choosing the number of states

K=2 is the minimum: one state for “contact-responsive” frames and one for “non-responsive”.
K=3 is recommended: adds a transition/ambiguous state that absorbs boundary uncertainty.
Higher K may overfit; use cross-validation (see Step 6) to select.



MAP estimation (optional)
If data is limited, add a prior to regularise the GLM weights:
prior_sigma = 2    # Gaussian prior σ on GLM weights
prior_alpha = 2    # Dirichlet prior α on transition rows

glmhmm_map = ssm.HMM(
    num_states,
    obs_dim,
    input_dim,
    observations="input_driven_obs",
    observation_kwargs=dict(C=num_categories, prior_sigma=prior_sigma),
    transitions="sticky",
    transition_kwargs=dict(alpha=prior_alpha, kappa=0),
)

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
text:
Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
N_iters = 200      # max EM iterations
tolerance = 1e-4   # stop early if LL improvement < tolerance

fit_ll = glmhmm.fit(
    y_blocks,
    inputs=X_blocks,
    method="em",
    num_iters=N_iters,
    tolerance=tolerance,
)
print(f"Final log-likelihood: {fit_ll[-1]:.2f}")

Multiple initialisations
EM finds a local optimum. Run several random initialisations and keep the best:
best_ll = -np.inf
best_model = None

for init in range(5):
    candidate = ssm.HMM(
        num_states, obs_dim, input_dim,
        observations="input_driven_obs",
        observation_kwargs=dict(C=num_categories),
        transitions="standard",
    )
    ll = candidate.fit(y_blocks, inputs=X_blocks, method="em",
                       num_iters=N_iters, tolerance=tolerance)
    if ll[-1] > best_ll:
        best_ll = ll[-1]
        best_model = candidate

glmhmm = best_model
print(f"Best log-likelihood across initialisations: {best_ll:.2f}")


Plot convergence
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.plot(fit_ll)
ax.set_xlabel("EM Iteration")
ax.set_ylabel("Log Probability")
ax.set_title("GLM-HMM Training Convergence")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Step 5: Decode and Inspect

Viterbi decoding (most likely state sequence)
# Decode each training block
for i, (yb, xb) in enumerate(zip(y_blocks, X_blocks)):
    states = glmhmm.most_likely_states(yb, input=xb)
    print(f"Block {i}: states = {np.unique(states, return_counts=True)}")


Posterior state probabilities
posterior_probs = [
    glmhmm.expected_states(data=yb, input=xb)[0]
    for yb, xb in zip(y_blocks, X_blocks)
]

# Plot posterior for the first block
fig, axes = plt.subplots(num_states + 1, 1, figsize=(10, 2 * (num_states + 1)),
                         sharex=True)
block_idx = 0
for k in range(num_states):
    axes[k].plot(posterior_probs[block_idx][:, k], label=f"State {k+1}")
    axes[k].set_ylabel(f"P(z={k+1})")
    axes[k].set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)

axes[-1].plot(y_blocks[block_idx], color="black", alpha=0.5)
axes[-1].set_ylabel("Contact label")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Frame (within block)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Inspect learned transition matrix
trans_mat = np.exp(glmhmm.transitions.log_Ps)
print("Transition matrix:")
print(np.around(trans_mat, decimals=3))


Inspect per-state GLM weights
weights = glmhmm.observations.params  # shape (K, C-1, input_dim)
for k in range(num_states):
    w = weights[k, 0, :]  # weight vector for state k (C-1 = 1 for binary)
    print(f"State {k+1}: ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, "
          f"top-5 features = {np.argsort(np.abs(w))[-5:][::-1]}")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 6: Predict Contact on Unlabeled Data
text:
Step 6: Predict Contact on Unlabeled Data
After training, we can predict frame-level contact probability on new data where labels are unavailable. The key insight is that the per-state GLM weights give \(P(y=1 \mid z_t=k,\; \mathbf{u}_t)\) and the transition model gives \(P(z_t \mid z_{t-1})\).
We use forward filtering to compute \(P(z_t \mid \mathbf{u}_{1:t})\) and then marginalise over states:
\[
P(y_t = 1 \mid \mathbf{u}_{1:t}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K}
P(y_t = 1 \mid z_t = k, \mathbf{u}_t)\;
P(z_t = k \mid \mathbf{u}_{1:t})
\]
from scipy.special import expit  # sigmoid function


def predict_contact(glmhmm, X_new):
    """Predict per-frame contact probability on unlabeled data.

    Parameters
    ----------
    glmhmm : ssm.HMM
        Fitted GLM-HMM with input_driven_obs observations.
    X_new : np.ndarray, shape (T, D)
        Encoder features for the prediction segment.

    Returns
    -------
    contact_prob : np.ndarray, shape (T,)
        P(contact) per frame.
    state_probs : np.ndarray, shape (T, K)
        Forward-filtered state probabilities.
    """
    K = glmhmm.K
    T_pred = X_new.shape[0]

    # Extract model parameters
    log_pi0 = glmhmm.init_state_distn.log_initial_state_distn(X_new)  # (K,)
    log_A = glmhmm.transitions.log_Ps  # (K, K)
    A = np.exp(log_A)
    weights = glmhmm.observations.params  # (K, C-1, D)

    # Per-state contact probability: P(y=1 | z=k, u_t) = sigmoid(w_k^T u_t)
    # weights shape: (K, 1, D) for binary case
    logits = X_new @ weights[:, 0, :].T  # (T, K)
    p_contact_given_state = expit(logits)  # (T, K)

    # Forward filtering (no observation updates — we don't have labels)
    alpha = np.exp(log_pi0)  # (K,)
    alpha = alpha / alpha.sum()

    state_probs = np.zeros((T_pred, K))
    state_probs[0] = alpha

    for t in range(1, T_pred):
        alpha = alpha @ A  # predict: (K,) @ (K,K) = (K,)
        alpha = alpha / alpha.sum()
        state_probs[t] = alpha

    # Marginalise: P(y=1 | u_{1:t}) = sum_k P(y=1|z=k, u_t) * P(z=k)
    contact_prob = np.sum(p_contact_given_state * state_probs, axis=1)

    return contact_prob, state_probs

Apply to a validation segment
# Use frames outside training blocks as validation
val_start = int(train_intervals[-1].end)  # after last training block
val_end = min(val_start + 5000, T_total)  # up to 5000 frames
X_val = X_all[val_start:val_end]

contact_prob, state_probs = predict_contact(glmhmm, X_val)

# Threshold to get binary predictions
threshold = 0.5
y_pred = (contact_prob >= threshold).astype(int)
print(f"Predicted {y_pred.sum()} contact frames out of {len(y_pred)}")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
section: Step 7: Convert Predictions to Intervals and Write Back
text:
Step 7: Convert Predictions to Intervals and Write Back
def binary_to_intervals(y_pred, offset=0):
    """Convert a binary prediction array to a list of (start, end) tuples.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y_pred : np.ndarray, shape (T,)
        Binary predictions (0 or 1).
    offset : int
        Frame offset to add (e.g., if y_pred starts from frame val_start).

    Returns
    -------
    intervals : list of (int, int)
        Each tuple is (start_frame, end_frame) of a contiguous contact block.
    """
    intervals = []
    in_interval = False
    start = 0
    for t in range(len(y_pred)):
        if y_pred[t] == 1 and not in_interval:
            start = t + offset
            in_interval = True
        elif y_pred[t] == 0 and in_interval:
            intervals.append((start, t + offset))
            in_interval = False
    if in_interval:
        intervals.append((start, len(y_pred) + offset))
    return intervals

# Convert to intervals
pred_intervals = binary_to_intervals(y_pred, offset=val_start)
print(f"Predicted {len(pred_intervals)} contact intervals")

# Write back to DataManager
result = wt.DigitalIntervalSeries()
for s, e in pred_intervals:
    result.addInterval(s, e)

time_key = dm.getTimeKey("features")
dm.setData("glm_hmm_contact", result, time_key)
print("Wrote 'glm_hmm_contact' to DataManager")

title: GLM-HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using ssm
text:
Cross-Validation
To select \(K\) and evaluate prediction quality, hold out one training block at a time:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score

def cross_validate(K, X_blocks, y_blocks, n_init=5, n_iters=200, tol=1e-4):
    """Leave-one-block-out cross-validation for GLM-HMM."""
    f1_scores = []
    for held_out in range(len(X_blocks)):
        X_train = [X_blocks[i] for i in range(len(X_blocks)) if i != held_out]
        y_train = [y_blocks[i] for i in range(len(y_blocks)) if i != held_out]

        best_ll = -np.inf
        best_m = None
        for _ in range(n_init):
            m = ssm.HMM(K, 1, D,
                        observations="input_driven_obs",
                        observation_kwargs=dict(C=2),
                        transitions="standard")
            ll = m.fit(y_train, inputs=X_train, method="em",
                       num_iters=n_iters, tolerance=tol)
            if ll[-1] > best_ll:
                best_ll = ll[-1]
                best_m = m

        # Predict on held-out block
        prob, _ = predict_contact(best_m, X_blocks[held_out])
        y_pred = (prob >= 0.5).astype(int)
        y_true = y_blocks[held_out].ravel()
        f1_scores.append(f1_score(y_true, y_pred))

    return np.mean(f1_scores), np.std(f1_scores)

for K in [2, 3, 4]:
    mean_f1, std_f1 = cross_validate(K, X_blocks, y_blocks)
    print(f"K={K}: F1 = {mean_f1:.3f} ± {std_f1:.3f}")

Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




EM converges but states are degenerate (one state used 99%)
Bad initialisation
Run more random initialisations (n_init ≥ 10)


Log-likelihood decreases
Numerical overflow in 192-dim logistic regression
Standardise features: X = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)


Fit is very slow
Too many features for the GLM
Reduce D via PCA before fitting


Poor F1 on held-out blocks
Too few/many states, or insufficient data
Try different K; use MAP estimation with prior_sigma=2

title: Tutorial: Using a Hidden Markov Model to Predict Behavioral Epochs with Deep Learning Features
text:
This tutorial walks through a complete workflow for classifying behavioral epochs in video data using deep learning feature extraction and a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). The pipeline is:

Extract per-frame features — Run a pre-trained encoder (e.g. ConvNeXt [paper]) over each video frame to produce a compact feature vector.
Reduce dimensionality — Apply post-encoder processing (global average pooling or spatial point extraction) to collapse the spatial feature map into a 1D feature vector per frame.
Train an HMM — Use the feature time series and a set of labeled epochs to fit a Hidden Markov Model that captures the temporal structure of behavioral states.
Predict epochs — Run the trained HMM on unlabeled frames to automatically segment the video into behavioral epochs.

By the end you will have a repeatable pipeline that turns raw video into labeled behavioral intervals stored as DigitalIntervalSeries in the DataManager.

title: Interval To Event Transform
text:
The IntervalToEvent transform extracts one event per interval from a DigitalIntervalSeries, producing a DigitalEventSeries with a 1:1 row mapping. This is the materialized counterpart to the alignment-point extraction in IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter used by GatherResult, and is the inverse of EventToInterval for point intervals.
Each interval produces one event at the selected alignment point:
Start  -> interval.start
End    -> interval.end
Center -> (interval.start + interval.end) / 2
Extraction is performed in TimeFrameIndex space (not absolute clock time). The output preserves the input TimeFrame.

TransformsV2 contributes commands to the shared CommandRegistry via an explicit dispatcher function, following the same pattern as DataSynthesizer. Transform algorithm registration (ElementRegistry) remains separate and uses static RAII registration with --whole-archive linking.

title: TensorWhitening
text:
TensorWhitening implements robust ZCA whitening for 2D TensorData interpreted as time x channels. Included channels are centered by their per-channel median, optionally filtered with a MAD-based clean-sample mask for covariance estimation, whitened with an epsilon-regularized ZCA matrix, and optionally rescaled back toward the original channel amplitude.
Excluded channels are copied through unchanged.

title: TensorWhitening
text:
Algorithm
For the included channels only:

Convert the input to LibTorch storage if needed.
Select the included channel subset.
Compute per-channel medians and median-center the data.
Estimate a robust scale per channel with:
\[\sigma_{robust} = \mathrm{median}(|x - \mathrm{median}(x)|) \cdot 1.4826\]
If mad_threshold_multiplier > 0, build a clean-sample mask that keeps rows whose included channels all remain below their channel-specific threshold.
Estimate covariance from the clean subset when at least two clean samples remain; otherwise fall back to all centered samples.
Compute the ZCA whitening matrix:
\[C = \frac{X^T X}{N - 1}\]
\[W = V \operatorname{diag}\left((\lambda + \epsilon)^{-1/2}\right) V^T\]
where \(C = V \operatorname{diag}(\lambda) V^T\).
Apply whitening with X_white = X_centered W.
If rescale_amplitude is enabled, multiply X_white by the mean robust channel amplitude.
Write the whitened values back into the included channels and leave excluded channels untouched.

title: TensorWhitening
text:
Backend And Storage
Unlike TensorCAR, this transform always executes on the LibTorch path for both CPU and GPU requests.

CPU input with non-LibTorch storage is converted with TensorData::toLibTorch().
GPU input is converted with TensorData::toLibTorchStrided() and moved to CUDA.
The final output tensor is materialized as contiguous float32 LibTorch storage.
CUDA results are copied back to CPU before constructing the output TensorData so the stored result remains portable in the wider application.

title: TensorCentralDifference
text:
TensorCentralDifference is a TransformsV2 container transform (TensorData → TensorData) that appends central-difference (delta) columns to a time-indexed tensor. For each original column, a new column is computed as:
\[\Delta_c[t] = \frac{\text{value}_c[t+1] - \text{value}_c[t-1]}{2}\]
This is useful for computing first-derivative approximations of features for downstream machine-learning pipelines.

title: TensorCentralDifference
text:
Time-Alignment Rule
Neighbors are determined by sorted row position in TimeIndexStorage, not by raw frame number ±1. For example, if rows exist at frames [10, 20, 50], the central difference at frame 20 uses frame 10 (previous row) and frame 50 (next row).

Columns are ordered as: [original cols (if include_original)] [delta_col0] [delta_col1] ...
Delta columns are named "{original_col}_delta", e.g. feat1_delta.
For an input with N columns, the output has 2*N columns (with include_original=true) or N columns (with include_original=false).

title: Architecture
text: TransformsV2 is built on a few core concepts that allow it to be both flexible and performant.

title: Architecture
text:
Concepts

1. Element Transforms
At the lowest level, most logic is defined as Element Transforms. These are functions that operate on a single unit of data, such as a Mask2D, Point2D, or float.

Stateless: They do not hold state between invocations.
Pure: f(x) -> y.



2. Lifting (ContainerTransform)
The system automatically “lifts” these element transforms to work on containers.

If you define Mask2D -> float (e.g., area calculation).
The system provides MaskData -> AnalogTimeSeries automatically.
This is done via ContainerTransform, which iterates over the input container, applies the element transform, and builds the output container.



3. Pipeline & Fusion
A TransformPipeline is a sequence of steps.

Naive Execution: Step 1 runs on all data -> Intermediate Result -> Step 2 runs on Intermediate Result -> …
Fused Execution: If multiple steps are element-wise, they are composed into a single function h(x) = g(f(x)).

The system iterates over the input container once.
Applies h(x) to each element.
Writes directly to the final output.
Benefit: Eliminates intermediate allocations and keeps data in CPU cache.




4. PipelineValueStore (V2 Context)
For operations that require global context (like normalization), we use a two-pass approach:

Pre-Reduction: Calculate global statistics (e.g., Mean) and store them in the PipelineValueStore.
Transformation: The transform step reads these values from the store (via parameter bindings) and applies them to each element.

This keeps the element transforms stateless and parallelizable, while still allowing global context dependencies.

title: Prune Overlapping Intervals Transform
text:
The PruneOverlappingIntervals transform applies greedy keep-first overlap pruning to a DigitalIntervalSeries, producing a disjoint (non-overlapping) DigitalIntervalSeries. This is the materialized counterpart to the overlap pruning in PlotAlignmentGather, applied directly to interval bounds rather than alignment-point windows.
The transform is parameterless and preserves the input TimeFrame.

title: Prune Overlapping Intervals Transform
Prune Overlapping Intervals Transform
text:
Algorithm

Collect all intervals from the input series (sorted by start time).
Greedy left-to-right scan:

Keep the first interval.
For each subsequent interval, keep it only if interval.start > last_kept.end.
Touching intervals (start == last_kept.end) are treated as overlapping and pruned.

Return a new DigitalIntervalSeries with IntervalLayout::Disjoint and the input TimeFrame.

This matches pruneOverlappingAlignmentTimes in PlotAlignmentGather.hpp with interval bounds used directly as the pruning window.

title: TensorCAR
text:
Phase 2.1 of the multi-channel storage roadmap. Applies Common Average Reference (CAR) to a multi-channel TensorData. For each time point, the transform subtracts a cross-channel reference signal (mean or median) from every channel:
\[\text{result}[t, c] = \text{input}[t, c] - r(t)\]
where \(r(t)\) is the mean or median across all non-excluded channels at time \(t\). This removes common-mode noise shared across channels — a standard preprocessing step in extracellular electrophysiology.

title: Media_Widget Refactoring Roadmap
text:
Media_Widget was the first visualization widget in WhiskerToolbox. It is built on a QGraphicsScene backend (Media_Window) with bespoke rendering, interaction, and configuration code for every data type it displays (media, lines, points, masks, tensors, intervals). Since its creation, the project has developed a mature, modular plotting stack:

CorePlotting — API-agnostic mappers, scene graph, hit testing, interaction controllers
PlottingOpenGL — GPU-accelerated batch renderers (glyphs, polylines, rectangles)
Plots/Common — Reusable Qt widgets (GlyphStyleControls, LineStyleControls, ColormapControls, PlotTooltipManager, axis widgets, PlotInteractionHelpers)
AutoParamWidget — Schema-driven auto-generated parameter forms
ParameterSchema — Compile-time schema extraction from reflect-cpp structs

Media_Widget duplicates significant portions of this infrastructure. Adding new features is difficult because the rendering pipeline, interaction handling, and UI controls are tightly coupled.


The motivating feature — plotting data (masks, lines, points) when no media is loaded — is blocked not by a hard technical limitation, but by entanglement. The canvas size is already independent of media resolution (driven by QGraphicsView widget size), and _clearMedia() just fills black. The real issues are:

The _plotMediaData() method has interleaved concerns: media rendering, transparency mask application, colormap processing, and multi-media compositing
The overlay rendering methods (_plotLineData, _plotMaskData, etc.) use aspect-ratio scaling factors derived from media dimensions for coordinate conversion
There’s no explicit “canvas-only mode” — the widget treats media absence as “nothing to show” rather than “show overlays on blank canvas”








These can be done independently, in any order, without touching the rendering pipeline.


Status: ✅ Complete
Replaced bespoke ColorPicker_Widget, point size slider/spinbox, and marker shape combo box with an embedded GlyphStyleControls + GlyphStyleState instance. PointMarkerShape enum was removed; PointDisplayOptions::marker_shape now uses CorePlotting::GlyphType directly. The rendering code in Media_Window::_plotPointData() was updated to switch on CorePlotting::GlyphType values. The Tick glyph type (vertical line) replaces the old X marker shape.



Status: ✅ Complete
Replaced bespoke ColorPicker_Widget, line thickness slider/spinbox with an embedded LineStyleControls + LineStyleState instance. The color, alpha, and thickness controls are now provided by the reusable LineStyleControls widget from Plots/Common/LineStyleControls/. Line-specific controls (show_points, edge_snapping, segment controls, position_marker) remain unchanged as domain-specific features.



What exists: - Bespoke color picker and alpha slider (same pattern as points/lines) - Mask-specific toggles: show_bounding_box, show_outline, use_as_transparency
Approach: - For color + alpha: embed LineStyleControls (it provides color + alpha, thickness can be hidden/ignored) or create a simpler ColorAlphaControls widget if that feels cleaner - The mask-specific checkboxes remain as-is



What exists (5 bespoke selection widgets):







Widget
Parameters




LineAddSelectionWidget
edge_snapping (bool), smoothing_mode (enum), polynomial_order (int), edge_threshold (double), edge_search_radius (double)


LineEraseSelectionWidget
eraser_radius (int), show_circle (bool)


LineSelectSelectionWidget

LineNoneSelectionWidget

Good candidates: LineAddSelectionWidget, LineEraseSelectionWidget, LineSelectSelectionWidget
These have simple scalar/bool/enum parameters that map directly to ParameterSchema + AutoParamWidget. The same pattern already works for media processing options.
Not a good candidate: LineDrawAllFramesSelectionWidget has a stateful workflow (start drawing → accumulate points → complete → apply). This is genuinely interactive, not just parameter configuration.
Approach: 1. Define reflect-cpp structs for each (e.g., LineAddParams, LineEraseParams, LineSelectParams) 2. Replace each widget body with AutoParamWidget + connect parametersChanged() to the existing signal emissions
Estimated scope per widget: ~40-60 lines removed, ~20 lines added



What exists: - BoxIntervalStyle_Widget — box_size (int), frame_range (int), location (enum) - BorderIntervalStyle_Widget — border_thickness (int)
Approach: Same as 1.4 — define reflect-cpp params structs, use AutoParamWidget.

Approach: Same as above. TensorDisplayOptions already has the reflect-cpp struct (display_channel); just need to wire AutoParamWidget to it.





These changes address the immediate pain point of rendering without media.


Current state:
The coordinate mapping has three interacting pieces:

Canvas pixel dimensions (_canvasWidth, _canvasHeight): fixed at 640×480 by default. This is the QGraphicsScene / QImage backing size. Media frames are scaled to this size.
Canvas coordinate system: the logical resolution that overlay data coordinates are interpreted against. Currently this is implicitly the active media’s native resolution (e.g., 640×480 for a 640×480 video). getXAspect() = _canvasWidth / media.getWidth() and getYAspect() = _canvasHeight / media.getHeight().
Per-data ImageSize: LineData, PointData, and MaskData each carry an ImageSize (from RaggedTimeSeries). If defined (not -1,‑1), the overlay rendering substitutes this for the media resolution, computing xAspect = _canvasWidth / data.getImageSize().width. If undefined (-1,‑1), the data trusts the media resolution.

Key behaviors to preserve (and formalize):

MediaData is always “correct”: its native resolution defines the authoritative canvas coordinate system when loaded. (Note: MediaData defaults to 640×480 when uninitialized — it never uses -1,‑1 — so an empty media object silently produces a coordinate system that may not match loaded overlay data.)
ImageSize -1,‑1 means “undefined”: data objects with undefined image size defer to the canvas coordinate system (currently media).
Scaling is “stretch to fill”, not “spatial subset”: when PointData has ImageSize 256×256 and media is 640×480, the points are scaled up so the 256×256 grid fills the full canvas. The implicit assumption is that the lower-resolution data represents the same spatial extent at coarser sampling, not a 256×256 crop of the 640×480 field of view. There is currently no way to express the alternative interpretation.

Problems this creates for no-media mode:

The program launches with empty MediaData whose size defaults to 640×480. If overlay data (e.g., masks at 512×512) is loaded without media, getXAspect() returns 1.0 (because no visible media → fallback), which silently misaligns data that expects coordinate mapping.
There is no explicit “canvas coordinate system” object — it is scattered across getXAspect(), getYAspect(), and per-overlay ad-hoc scaling logic, making it impossible for the user to inspect or override.
There is no mechanism for a data object to declare whether it should be stretched to fill the canvas or whether it represents a spatial subset (crop / ROI) of the canvas coordinates.

Approach:

Introduce CanvasCoordinateSystem — a small struct holding the logical { width, height } that defines the coordinate space overlays are plotted into. This replaces the implicit “ask the active media for its resolution” pattern.
Resolution priority chain — the canvas coordinate system should be determined by the first source that provides a valid (non -1,‑1) resolution, in this order:

User override (explicit manual setting via UI / state — highest priority)
Active media (MediaData::getImageSize(), if visible and not default-only)
First loaded data object with defined ImageSize (e.g., a MaskData at 512×512)
Fallback default (640×480, matching the current behavior)

When media is loaded/unloaded or data objects are added/removed, the coordinate system should be re-evaluated unless there is an active user override.
Per-data coordinate mapping mode — add a per-data-object setting (likely in the display options, e.g., PointDisplayOptions, LineDisplayOptions, MaskDisplayOptions) that controls how the data’s ImageSize relates to the canvas:








Mode
Meaning
Scaling




ScaleToCanvas (default)
Data covers the full canvas extent at its own resolution. Equivalent to current behavior.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / data.imageSize.width


SubsetOfCanvas
Data occupies a spatial sub-region. Coordinates are in canvas-coordinate-system units already.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / canvasCoordSystem.width (same as media-based scaling)



ScaleToCanvas preserves backward compatibility: data at 256×256 is stretched to fill a 640×480 canvas. SubsetOfCanvas allows, e.g., a 256×256 point cloud that lives in the top-left quadrant of a 640×480 canvas.
When ImageSize is -1,‑1, the mode is moot — the data uses the canvas coordinate system directly (equivalent to SubsetOfCanvas with matching dimensions).
Replace getXAspect() / getYAspect() — these methods currently encode the full priority chain in an ad-hoc way. Replace them with a single method (or free function) that takes CanvasCoordinateSystem, the data’s ImageSize, and the mapping mode, returning the x/y scale factors. All _plotXxxData() methods call this instead of computing their own scaling.
UI for canvas coordinate system — expose the resolved canvas coordinate system in the Media_Widget UI (read-only display showing source: “from media”, “from MaskData ‘whiskers’”, “manual override”). Provide width/height spinboxes for manual override. This can live in MediaWidgetState as a serializable field.

title: Media_Widget Refactoring Roadmap
text:
Media_Widget was the first visualization widget in WhiskerToolbox. It is built on a QGraphicsScene backend (Media_Window) with bespoke rendering, interaction, and configuration code for every data type it displays (media, lines, points, masks, tensors, intervals). Since its creation, the project has developed a mature, modular plotting stack:

CorePlotting — API-agnostic mappers, scene graph, hit testing, interaction controllers
PlottingOpenGL — GPU-accelerated batch renderers (glyphs, polylines, rectangles)
Plots/Common — Reusable Qt widgets (GlyphStyleControls, LineStyleControls, ColormapControls, PlotTooltipManager, axis widgets, PlotInteractionHelpers)
AutoParamWidget — Schema-driven auto-generated parameter forms
ParameterSchema — Compile-time schema extraction from reflect-cpp structs

Media_Widget duplicates significant portions of this infrastructure. Adding new features is difficult because the rendering pipeline, interaction handling, and UI controls are tightly coupled.


The motivating feature — plotting data (masks, lines, points) when no media is loaded — is blocked not by a hard technical limitation, but by entanglement. The canvas size is already independent of media resolution (driven by QGraphicsView widget size), and _clearMedia() just fills black. The real issues are:

The _plotMediaData() method has interleaved concerns: media rendering, transparency mask application, colormap processing, and multi-media compositing
The overlay rendering methods (_plotLineData, _plotMaskData, etc.) use aspect-ratio scaling factors derived from media dimensions for coordinate conversion
There’s no explicit “canvas-only mode” — the widget treats media absence as “nothing to show” rather than “show overlays on blank canvas”

These changes address the immediate pain point of rendering without media.


Current state:
The coordinate mapping has three interacting pieces:

Canvas pixel dimensions (_canvasWidth, _canvasHeight): fixed at 640×480 by default. This is the QGraphicsScene / QImage backing size. Media frames are scaled to this size.
Canvas coordinate system: the logical resolution that overlay data coordinates are interpreted against. Currently this is implicitly the active media’s native resolution (e.g., 640×480 for a 640×480 video). getXAspect() = _canvasWidth / media.getWidth() and getYAspect() = _canvasHeight / media.getHeight().
Per-data ImageSize: LineData, PointData, and MaskData each carry an ImageSize (from RaggedTimeSeries). If defined (not -1,‑1), the overlay rendering substitutes this for the media resolution, computing xAspect = _canvasWidth / data.getImageSize().width. If undefined (-1,‑1), the data trusts the media resolution.

Key behaviors to preserve (and formalize):

MediaData is always “correct”: its native resolution defines the authoritative canvas coordinate system when loaded. (Note: MediaData defaults to 640×480 when uninitialized — it never uses -1,‑1 — so an empty media object silently produces a coordinate system that may not match loaded overlay data.)
ImageSize -1,‑1 means “undefined”: data objects with undefined image size defer to the canvas coordinate system (currently media).
Scaling is “stretch to fill”, not “spatial subset”: when PointData has ImageSize 256×256 and media is 640×480, the points are scaled up so the 256×256 grid fills the full canvas. The implicit assumption is that the lower-resolution data represents the same spatial extent at coarser sampling, not a 256×256 crop of the 640×480 field of view. There is currently no way to express the alternative interpretation.

Problems this creates for no-media mode:

The program launches with empty MediaData whose size defaults to 640×480. If overlay data (e.g., masks at 512×512) is loaded without media, getXAspect() returns 1.0 (because no visible media → fallback), which silently misaligns data that expects coordinate mapping.
There is no explicit “canvas coordinate system” object — it is scattered across getXAspect(), getYAspect(), and per-overlay ad-hoc scaling logic, making it impossible for the user to inspect or override.
There is no mechanism for a data object to declare whether it should be stretched to fill the canvas or whether it represents a spatial subset (crop / ROI) of the canvas coordinates.

Approach:

Introduce CanvasCoordinateSystem — a small struct holding the logical { width, height } that defines the coordinate space overlays are plotted into. This replaces the implicit “ask the active media for its resolution” pattern.
Resolution priority chain — the canvas coordinate system should be determined by the first source that provides a valid (non -1,‑1) resolution, in this order:

User override (explicit manual setting via UI / state — highest priority)
Active media (MediaData::getImageSize(), if visible and not default-only)
First loaded data object with defined ImageSize (e.g., a MaskData at 512×512)
Fallback default (640×480, matching the current behavior)

When media is loaded/unloaded or data objects are added/removed, the coordinate system should be re-evaluated unless there is an active user override.
Per-data coordinate mapping mode — add a per-data-object setting (likely in the display options, e.g., PointDisplayOptions, LineDisplayOptions, MaskDisplayOptions) that controls how the data’s ImageSize relates to the canvas:








Mode
Meaning
Scaling




ScaleToCanvas (default)
Data covers the full canvas extent at its own resolution. Equivalent to current behavior.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / data.imageSize.width


SubsetOfCanvas
Data occupies a spatial sub-region. Coordinates are in canvas-coordinate-system units already.
xAspect = canvasPixelWidth / canvasCoordSystem.width (same as media-based scaling)



ScaleToCanvas preserves backward compatibility: data at 256×256 is stretched to fill a 640×480 canvas. SubsetOfCanvas allows, e.g., a 256×256 point cloud that lives in the top-left quadrant of a 640×480 canvas.
When ImageSize is -1,‑1, the mode is moot — the data uses the canvas coordinate system directly (equivalent to SubsetOfCanvas with matching dimensions).
Replace getXAspect() / getYAspect() — these methods currently encode the full priority chain in an ad-hoc way. Replace them with a single method (or free function) that takes CanvasCoordinateSystem, the data’s ImageSize, and the mapping mode, returning the x/y scale factors. All _plotXxxData() methods call this instead of computing their own scaling.
UI for canvas coordinate system — expose the resolved canvas coordinate system in the Media_Widget UI (read-only display showing source: “from media”, “from MaskData ‘whiskers’”, “manual override”). Provide width/height spinboxes for manual override. This can live in MediaWidgetState as a serializable field.

title: Registry Patterns
text:
WhiskerToolbox uses registries to make an operation discoverable at runtime while keeping its implementation in the library that owns it. The more recent registries also treat the operation’s parameter struct as a single source of truth for:
This guide compares the main patterns currently in the repository. It is a design guide for new work, not a replacement for the individual API references.
