text: This guide walks through the systems that a new widget in WhiskerToolbox should integrate with. Each section describes what the system does, when you need it, and how to wire it up. The goal is not to duplicate the detailed reference docs — those are linked throughout — but to give you a map of the landscape and a concrete checklist.

title: Widget Development Guide
text:
Overview: What Makes a Widget
A WhiskerToolbox widget is a Qt6 QWidget that lives inside the Qt6AdvancedDocking dock system. Unlike a traditional Qt application where you manually create widgets and add them to layouts, WhiskerToolbox widgets are registered as types with the EditorRegistry, which manages their lifecycle, placement, and serialization.
A fully-featured widget integrates with up to six systems:








System
Purpose
Required?




EditorRegistry
Type registration, factory functions, dock placement
Yes — every widget


DataManager + Observer
Reading/writing shared data, reacting to changes
Yes — nearly every widget


Command Architecture
Serializable, undoable data mutations
When widget mutates DataManager


ParameterSchema + AutoParamWidget
Auto-generated config forms from C++ structs
When widget has configurable parameters


Context Actions
Right-click actions that open/configure your widget
When widget can be a target for data


Keymap System
Configurable keyboard shortcuts
When widget has keyboard-driven actions



The following diagram shows how these systems relate at runtime:
  User types a key                   User right-clicks data
        │                                    │

title: Widget Development Guide
text:
Checklist: Creating a New Widget
Here is a step-by-step checklist for adding a new widget:

Minimum Viable Widget

Create MyWidgetState subclass of EditorState with reflect-cpp serializable data
Create MyWidget (the QWidget) and optionally MyWidgetProperties
Create MyWidgetRegistration.cpp with registerTypes() that registers EditorTypeInfo
Call registerTypes() from the application startup (where other widgets are registered)
Add CMakeLists.txt for the new widget and link required libraries



Data Integration

Accept std::shared_ptr<DataManager> in your factory/constructor
Register an observer callback to react to data changes
Store the CallbackID and remove the observer in the destructor
If the widget can be called from a background thread, use the QTimer::singleShot pattern



Optional: Command Integration

When the widget has “action buttons” that mutate DataManager, represent those as ICommands
Use commands::executeSequence() to dispatch
Consider undo support for destructive operations



Optional: Auto-Generated Parameter Forms

Define a reflect-cpp params struct for your algorithm/config
Optionally specialize ParameterUIHints<T> for tooltips and constraints
Create an AutoParamWidget from extractParameterSchema<T>()
Connect parametersChanged to your handler



Optional: Context Actions

Add a static void registerContextActions(EditorRegistry *, ...) helper in the anonymous namespace of your registration .cpp
Call it from registerTypes() before registry->registerType()
Implement is_applicable predicate based on data type/properties
Implement execute to open your widget and configure it with the selection
Use action IDs following <widget_domain>.<verb>_<noun> (e.g. my_widget.visualize_tensor)



Optional: Keyboard Shortcuts

Add a KeymapSystem::KeymapManager * parameter to registerTypes()
Add a static void registerEditorActions(KeymapSystem::KeymapManager *) helper in the anonymous namespace
Call it from registerTypes(), guarded by if (km)
Register KeyActionDescriptors with <widget_domain>.<verb>_<noun> action IDs
Create a KeyActionAdapter in the widget constructor with a handler lambda that dispatches by action_id
Remove the original keyPressEvent() / eventFilter() key handling once migrated



Optional: DataFocusAware

Inherit DataFocusAware and call connectToSelectionContext() if the widget should react to what the user has selected elsewhere



Optional: OperationContext

Implement consumer pattern if you need structured data from another widget
Implement producer pattern if other widgets should be able to request data from yours

title: DataManagerPipelineRunner
text:
DataManagerPipelineRunner is a Qt-free executable for running batch neural data workflows from a single JSON file. A typical pipeline loads data into a DataManager, runs legacy transformations and/or command-sequence operations, then saves selected outputs to disk.
The executable is a thin composition root around the reusable JsonPipelineRunner library in src/DataManager/JsonPipeline/. Tests and other headless tools can call runJsonPipeline() or runJsonPipelineFile() directly without linking the CLI target.
For end-user examples and CLI invocation, see the JSON Pipeline Runner user guide.

title: DataManagerPipelineRunner
text:
Execution Model
Pipelines run in up to three phases, controlled by JsonPipelineOptions:
┌─────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐
│ Load & Transform    │ ──► │ commands[]       │ ──► │ saves[]     │
│ (legacy JSON loader)│     │ (CommandSequence)│     │ (SaveData)  │
└─────────────────────┘     └──────────────────┘     └─────────────┘

Load and transform — Normalizes the config and delegates to load_data_from_json_config(). This reuses the existing DataManager JSON loader, including legacy transformation steps embedded in the data array.
Commands — Parses the root-level commands array into a commands::CommandSequenceDescriptor and executes it through commands::executeSequence().
Saves — Executes each root-level saves[] entry through commands::executeSingleCommand("SaveData", ...), with variable substitution and path resolution.

Phases can be skipped with CLI flags (--no-load-transform, --no-commands, --no-saves). Command and save phases can continue after individual failures when --continue-on-command-error or --continue-on-save-error is set.
On failure, JsonPipelineResult reports the failing phase (parse, normalize, load_and_transform, command, or save), a human-readable m_error_message, and — for command failures — m_failed_command_index.

JsonPipelineRunner is part of the DataManager library and is not thread-safe — callers must not invoke it concurrently on the same DataManager instance without external synchronization.

title: Post-Encoder Modules
text:
Post-encoder modules are optional torch-to-torch processing stages applied after ModelBase::forward() and before channel decoders. They transform a model’s raw output tensor (typically [B, C, H, W]) into a form suitable for decoding — most commonly collapsing spatial dimensions to [B, C].
Post-encoder modules are model-agnostic. They are not owned by GeneralEncoderModel or any other model subclass. SlotAssembler holds the active module as session configuration and applies it to the first output slot of whatever model is loaded — encoders, segmentation models, or JSON-defined RuntimeModel instances.
ModelBase::forward()  →  raw output [B, C, H, W]
        │
        ▼
PostEncoderModule::apply()   (optional — SlotAssembler session config)
        │
        ▼
ChannelDecoder::decode()     (e.g. TensorToFeatureVector, TensorToMask2D)
        │
        ▼
DataManager

title: Post-Encoder Modules
Post-Encoder Modules
text:
Implementations

GlobalAvgPoolModule
[B, C, H, W] → [B, C] via at::adaptive_avg_pool2d({1, 1}) with spatial squeeze.
Registry key: "global_avg_pool". Sets collapses_spatial_dims = true.
apply() validates 4D input with B, C, H, W >= 1. Invalid input throws std::invalid_argument after spdlog::debug logging.


SpatialPointExtractModule
Extracts the C-dimensional feature vector at a 2-D point in source-image coordinates. Registry key: "spatial_point". Also collapses spatial dims.







Mode
Mechanics




Nearest
Scale point to feature-map pixel, clamp, slice [B, C, iy, ix]


Bilinear
Normalise to [-1, 1], grid_sample with align_corners=true, border padding



The module is stateful: call setPoint(Point2D<float>) before each apply(). SlotAssembler::_updateSpatialPoint() reads the first point from SpatialPointModuleParams::point_key at the current frame.
Bilinear mode requires H >= 2 and W >= 2 (normalisation divides by H - 1, W - 1). Constructor requires positive source_image_size.
SpatialPointExtractModule forces single-frame batch inference (requiresSingleFrameBatch() returns true) because the query point is frame-specific.


PostEncoderPipeline
Ordered chain of modules. apply() threads the tensor through each stage. outputShape() propagates shape through all stages.

title: Post-Encoder Modules
text:
Integration with SlotAssembler
Post-encoder is owned by SlotAssembler::Impl::post_encoder_module, configured through:
void configurePostEncoderModule(
    dl::PostEncoderStepDescriptor const & params,
    ImageSize source_image_size = {});
PostEncoderStepDescriptor (SlotBindingTypes.hpp):
struct PostEncoderStepDescriptor {
    std::string module_key = "none";   // "none" or empty → no module
    std::string parameters_json = "{}";
};

Per-frame pipeline
Every inference mode follows the same pattern:
_updateSpatialPoint()          // spatial_point only
    → ModelBase::forward()
    → applyPostEncoderToFirstOutputSlot()   // first output slot only
    → decodeOutputs()
Free functions in PostEncoderOutputTransform.hpp:

applyPostEncoderToFirstOutputSlot() — transform first output tensor
effectiveOutputSlots() — propagate shapes for decoder UI and validation

ModelBase::outputSlots() always reports raw model shapes. SlotAssembler::currentModelInfo() uses effectiveOutputSlots() so output binding widgets reflect post-encoder shape changes.


Lifecycle

loadModel() and resetModel() clear post_encoder_module
PostEncoderWidget::syncToAssembler() re-applies saved params after weights load (_loadModelIfReady())
Parameter changes call configurePostEncoderModule() immediately when a model is loaded (weights not required for configuration)

Targeting: post-encoder applies to the first model output slot only. Per-slot targeting is planned.
Recurrent inference: recurrent tensor bindings cache the post-encoder output tensor (the same tensor passed to decoders) for the next frame’s input injection.


Decoder consistency
dl::constraints::validDecodersForPostEncoder() queries collapsesSpatialDims():







Post-encoder

"none" or spatial-preserving

Spatial-collapsing (global_avg_pool, spatial_point)

title: General Encoder Model
text:
GeneralEncoderModel is a reusable ModelBase subclass that wraps any image encoder backbone (e.g. ConvNeXt, ViT, ResNet) as a single-input, single-output model for spatial feature extraction. It maps an input image to a raw feature tensor without requiring a task-specific C++ wrapper for each architecture.
Post-encoder processing (global pooling, spatial point extraction, etc.) is not part of this model. Post-encoder modules are a separate, model-agnostic pipeline stage owned by SlotAssembler and configurable for any loaded model. See Post-Encoder Modules.
Source: src/DeepLearning/models_v2/general_encoder/

title: General Encoder Model
text:
Architecture
Input Image [B, C, H, W]  →  GeneralEncoderModel::forward()  →  Features [B, C_out, H_out, W_out]
         "image" slot              (any .pt/.pt2)                    "features" slot
                                                                    │
                                                                    ▼
                                              PostEncoderModule (optional, session config)
                                                                    │
                                                                    ▼
                                              Channel decoder (e.g. TensorToFeatureVector)

Design decisions
GeneralEncoderModel is intentionally minimal:

Single input slot ("image") — accepts any image tensor
Single output slot ("features") — produces the raw backbone output
Configurable shapes — input resolution and output feature shape are set at construction time or via registered model configuration
DynamicBatch — DynamicBatch{1, 0} (min 1, unlimited max)

For most users, defining an encoder via a RuntimeModelSpec JSON file (which creates a RuntimeModel) is sufficient and requires no C++ changes. GeneralEncoderModel provides a convenience wrapper with sensible defaults that auto-registers in ModelRegistry with a configuration schema.


Compile-time vs. runtime shapes
Input and output resolution do not need to be known at compile time:

TorchScript (.pt) accepts arbitrary dynamic shapes natively
AOT Inductor (.pt2) supports dynamic shapes via torch.export.Dim() — dimensions marked as dynamic can vary at runtime within declared bounds
RuntimeModel reads shapes from a JSON spec at runtime

The shapes declared in GeneralEncoderModel (or RuntimeModelSpec) are metadata for the UI and pre-allocation, not hard constraints enforced at the C++ level.


Post-encoder recommendation
GeneralEncoderModel::recommendedPostEncoderModule() returns "global_avg_pool". The output slot recommends TensorToFeatureVector as its decoder — appropriate after spatial collapse to [B, C].
On model selection, DeepLearningPropertiesWidget pre-populates DeepLearningState::postEncoderParams() from ModelInfo::recommended_post_encoder. The user can override the module for any model in PostEncoderWidget.

title: General Encoder Model
text:
Usage

Option 1: C++ GeneralEncoderModel (compiled)
The default constructor creates a model expecting 3×224×224 RGB input and 384×7×7 output:
auto model = std::make_unique<dl::GeneralEncoderModel>();
model->loadWeights("/path/to/convnext_tiny_encoder.pt");

auto image = torch::randn({1, 3, 224, 224});
std::unordered_map<std::string, torch::Tensor> inputs;
inputs["image"] = image;

auto outputs = model->forward(inputs);
auto features = outputs["features"];  // [1, 384, 7, 7]
For a different backbone, pass custom dimensions:
auto model = std::make_unique<dl::GeneralEncoderModel>(
    3, 224, 224, std::vector<int64_t>{768, 7, 7});


Option 2: RuntimeModelSpec JSON (no recompilation)
Create a JSON spec file (see examples/convnext_encoder_spec.json):
{
  "model_id": "convnext_tiny_encoder",
  "display_name": "ConvNeXt-Tiny Encoder",
  "weights_path": "convnext_tiny_encoder.pt",
  "batch_mode": { "dynamic": { "min": 1, "max": 32 } },
  "inputs": [
    { "name": "image", "shape": [3, 224, 224], "recommended_encoder": "ImageEncoder" }
  ],
  "outputs": [
    { "name": "features", "shape": [768, 7, 7], "recommended_decoder": "TensorToFeatureVector" }
  ],
  "recommended_post_encoder": "global_avg_pool"
}
Load via ModelRegistry:
dl::ModelRegistry::instance().loadFromJson("/path/to/spec.json");
auto model = dl::ModelRegistry::instance().create("convnext_tiny_encoder");


Option 3: Widget UI
GeneralEncoderModel appears in the Deep Learning widget model selector as General Encoder. The standard workflow:

Select the model
Configure input/output shapes in the Model Configuration section (EncoderShapeWidget) and click Apply Configuration
Load weights
Configure the image binding and optional post-encoder module
Run inference


Runtime shape configuration
Different backbones produce different output shapes and may require different input resolutions:



Backbone

Typical output

768×7×7

224×224

Field
Purpose

Configuration persists in DeepLearningStateData::model_configurations["general_encoder"] and is applied via SlotAssembler::applyModelConfiguration().
Weights loading is blocked until generalEncoderConfigurationComplete() returns true (shape_applied and positive height/width).






Important



AOT Inductor models compiled with fixed spatial dimensions will produce NaN output if fed the wrong input size. Match the input resolution to what was used during torch.export.export(). When using torch.export.Dim() for dynamic shapes, only the batch dimension is typically dynamic — spatial dimensions remain fixed.

auto model = std::make_unique<dl::GeneralEncoderModel>();
model->setInputResolution(256, 256);
model->setOutputShape({192, 16, 16});

title: Static Input Capture
text:
Cache invalidation
DataBank entries are invalidated when:

Explicit removal — dataBank().remove(id) or clearDataBank()
Re-capture — captureToBank() overwrites an existing entry with the same ID

resetModel() does not clear the DataBank (session-scoped across model switches).
Changing a static binding’s data_key or bank_entry_id in the UI does not automatically remove bank entries — stale entries remain until explicitly removed or overwritten.

title: Hybrid Sequence Inputs
text:
Hybrid sequence inputs let a single memory slot (e.g. memory_images with shape [5, 3, 256, 256] and sequence_dim = 0) mix static and recurrent sourcing across positions. Early positions hold reference frames from DataManager or pre-encoded DataBank tensors; later positions feed back the model’s previous output at that index.
This pattern is used by NeuroSAM-style models: user-selected reference frames occupy early sequence positions and the model’s own prediction at the final position is fed back recurrently.

Assembly: src/WhiskerToolbox/DeepLearning_Widget/Core/SlotAssembler.cpp
UI: src/WhiskerToolbox/DeepLearning_Widget/UI/Helpers/MemorySlotWidget.hpp

title: Hybrid Sequence Inputs
text:
Data model
Each sequence position is one MemoryFrameBinding with the same slot_name and a distinct memory_index. The frame tagged union selects static or recurrent for that position only — there is no separate recurrent panel or parallel recurrent_bindings vector.








Position kind
frame_kind
Source




Static
StaticFrameSource
DataManagerStaticSource (re-encode each run) or DataBankStaticSource (reuse cached tensor)


Recurrent
RecurrentFrameSource
Raw output tensor from output_slot_name, seeded at t=0 via init



See Memory Frame Bindings for the full type reference and DataBank for pre-encoded static tensors.

title: Hybrid Sequence Inputs
text:
Assembly logic

Per-position configuration
assembleInputs() groups memory_frames by slot_name and processes each static input slot:
Static positions (hasActiveStaticSource):

DataManager — channel-encode data_key at current_frame + time_offset into the slice at memory_index.
DataBank — copy the pre-encoded tensor from resolvedBankEntryId() into the slice. No re-encoding from source geometry.

Recurrent positions (hasActiveRecurrentBinding):

Skipped during static assembly (left zero-padded in the assembled tensor).
Filled later in runRecurrentSequence() by injecting the recurrent cache tensor at memory_index along sequence_dim.

Each memory_index is configured exactly once as either static or recurrent. There is no position-claiming map.


Hybrid injection in runRecurrentSequence()
During the frame loop:

assembleInputs() fills static positions (and leaves recurrent slices at zero).
For each active recurrent frame, the cached tensor is injected:

Sequence slots: tensor.select(sequence_dim + 1, memory_index).copy_(cache)
Non-sequence slots: the entire input tensor is replaced.

runModelAndPostEncoder() runs forward.
Output tensors are cached for the next frame (keyed by input slot name).

The recurrent cache key is recurrent:{input_slot_name} via recurrentCacheKey() — one cache entry per input slot, not per memory_index. Hybrid configurations typically use a single recurrent position per slot (e.g. the last index in a sequence).


t=0 initialization
Recurrent init modes (ZerosInit, StaticCaptureInit, FirstOutputInit) apply only to recurrent positions. Static positions are populated from their configured sources on every frame, including frame 0.
StaticCaptureInit resolution order at t=0:

If a static MemoryFrameBinding exists at the same slot_name + memory_index with DataBank source, use that bank entry’s encoded tensor.
Else try defaultBankEntryId(slot_name, memory_index) in the session DataBank.
Else if StaticCaptureInit specifies data_key and frame >= 0, call captureStaticInput() to encode into the default bank entry and use the result.
Else fall back to zeros (with a spdlog::warn).

title: Hybrid Sequence Inputs
text:
Batch constraint
Any active recurrent memory frame forces batch_size = 1 via dl::constraints::computeBatchSizeConstraint(). When all recurrent positions are removed or deactivated, the constraint relaxes to the model’s batch_mode.
See Session Constraints.

title: Hybrid Sequence Inputs
text:
Validation
At the start of runRecurrentSequence():

Throws if no active recurrent frames are configured.
Logs (does not throw) when memory_index exceeds sequence length.
Logs shape mismatches between the recurrent output slot and the per-element input shape at that position.

During assembleInputs(), unfilled sequence positions produce a stderr warning when filled_count < sequence_length.

title: Creating a C++ Model Wrapper
text:
This guide explains how to integrate a PyTorch model into Neuralyzer by creating a C++ wrapper. There are two approaches:

Runtime JSON model — define the model’s I/O in a JSON file (no C++ needed)
Compiled C++ model — create a ModelBase subclass with custom logic

Most models can use the JSON approach. The compiled approach is only needed when the model requires custom pre/post-processing logic in forward() that cannot be expressed through the standard encoder/decoder pipeline.

title: Creating a C++ Model Wrapper
text:
This guide explains how to integrate a PyTorch model into Neuralyzer by creating a C++ wrapper. There are two approaches:

Runtime JSON model — define the model’s I/O in a JSON file (no C++ needed)
Compiled C++ model — create a ModelBase subclass with custom logic

Most models can use the JSON approach. The compiled approach is only needed when the model requires custom pre/post-processing logic in forward() that cannot be expressed through the standard encoder/decoder pipeline.

title: Creating a C++ Model Wrapper
text:
Prerequisites

A trained PyTorch model exported as either:

AOT Inductor (.pt2) — recommended, see AOT Inductor Tutorial
TorchScript (.pt) — torch.jit.trace() or torch.jit.script()

Knowledge of the model’s input and output tensor shapes

title: Creating a C++ Model Wrapper
text:
Approach 1: Runtime JSON Model (Recommended)
For models with straightforward I/O (images in, masks/points/lines out), define a JSON specification file and register it at runtime. No recompilation needed.

Step 1: Determine Model I/O
Identify each input and output tensor:

Name — a unique identifier (e.g. "image", "heatmap")
Shape — dimensions excluding the batch axis (e.g. [3, 256, 256])
Data type — which Neuralyzer data type maps to this tensor
Encoder/Decoder — which conversion strategy to use



Step 2: Write the JSON Spec
Create a .json file alongside your model weights:
{
  "model_id": "whisker_detector",
  "display_name": "Whisker Detector",
  "description": "Detects whisker positions from video frames",
  "weights_path": "whisker_detector.pt2",
  "backend": "auto",
  "preferred_batch_size": 0,
  "max_batch_size": 0,
  "inputs": [
    {
      "name": "image",
      "shape": [3, 256, 256],

Batch-size constraint
computeBatchSizeConstraint() reads info.batch_mode and checks hasActiveRecurrentBindings(memory_frames).
A recurrent binding is active when hasActiveRecurrentBinding() is true: output_slot_name is non-empty and not "(None)" (see DeepLearningBindingData.hpp).
Implementation logic:

If any active recurrent binding OR isBatchLocked(batch_mode) (RecurrentOnlyBatch or FixedBatch{1}) → return {1, 1, has_recurrent}. forced_by_recurrent is true only when recurrent bindings caused the lock.
Else if FixedBatch{N>1} → {N, N, false}.
Else DynamicBatch → {minBatchSizeFromMode, maxBatchSizeFromMode, false}.

false



When both active recurrent bindings and FixedBatch{N>1} apply, recurrent wins (batch locked to 1 with forced_by_recurrent=true).

title: TensorToLine2D
text:
TensorToLine2D decodes a spatial model output channel into an ordered Line2D polyline by thresholding, skeletonizing with Zhang-Suen thinning, and tracing connected skeleton pixels.

Registry: DecoderFactory::create("TensorToLine2D") — outputTypeName() is "Line2D"
Dispatched via DecoderDispatch when OutputBindingData::decoder holds LineDecoderParams.

Dim

2

DecoderContext::height and DecoderContext::width must match tensor.size(2) and tensor.size(3) respectively.

title: TensorToLine2D
text:
Pipeline

Threshold channel activations using LineDecoderParams::threshold (strict >)
Skeletonize the binary mask to a 1-pixel-wide centerline (Zhang-Suen thinning)
Find a skeleton endpoint (pixel with one neighbor), or any skeleton pixel for closed loops
Trace connected skeleton pixels into an ordered polyline
Scale coordinates to DecoderContext::target_image_size when non-zero

Returns an empty Line2D when no pixels exceed the threshold or the skeleton is empty.

title: TensorToLine2D
text:
Coordinate scaling
When DecoderContext::target_image_size is non-zero, polyline vertices are scaled linearly from tensor space to the original image size.
When target_image_size is {0, 0}, coordinates are returned in tensor pixel space.

title: TensorToLine2D
text:
Validation
decode() validates at runtime:

Tensor is defined and 4-dimensional
batch_index and source_channel are in range
height and width are positive and match the tensor spatial dimensions

Invalid inputs throw std::invalid_argument or std::out_of_range after logging at spdlog::debug level.

Assembly
assembleInputs() fills static slots from memory-frame bindings:

DataBank — getBankCachedTensor() copies getEncoded() and expands batch dimension when batch_size > 1. Missing encoded data logs an error and leaves zeros.
DataManager — re-encodes at current_frame + time_offset each run.

At inference time, DataBank bindings use the cached encoded tensor, not a live re-encode from getSource() (source is retained for capture, encodeEntry(), and potential future refresh paths).


Recurrent StaticCapture init
At t=0, runRecurrentSequence() seeds recurrent cache by:

Matching static MemoryFrameBinding at the same slot/index with DataBank source → getBankCachedTensor()
Else getEncoded(defaultBankEntryId(slot, index))
Else capture from StaticCaptureInit data_key / frame into the default bank entry via captureStaticInput()
Else fall back to zeros

Post-encoder modules are not part of any ModelBase subclass. They are:

SlotAssembler (Core/SlotAssembler.hpp) is named after model tensor slots, not Qt slots. The widget uses a PIMPL pattern partly because Qt’s #define slots macro conflicts with libtorch’s slots() member function — an unrelated naming collision.

title: Observer Library
text: The Observer library provides a lightweight implementation of the observer pattern used throughout WhiskerToolbox to propagate data changes to dependent components. When data objects are modified, all registered observers are automatically notified, enabling reactive UI updates and derived data recalculation.

title: Observer Library
text: The Observer library provides a lightweight implementation of the observer pattern used throughout WhiskerToolbox to propagate data changes to dependent components. When data objects are modified, all registered observers are automatically notified, enabling reactive UI updates and derived data recalculation.

title: Observer Library
Observer Library
Observer Library
text:
Usage in WhiskerToolbox
The Observer library is fundamental to WhiskerToolbox’s reactive architecture:

DataManager: All data types (PointData, LineData, MaskData, etc.) use observers to notify the UI when data changes
Transforms: Output data objects observe their input sources to automatically recalculate when inputs change
TableView: Tables observe their source data and row/column selectors to update when dependencies change
UI Widgets: Qt widgets register observers on data objects to refresh their display

┌─────────────┐     notifies     ┌─────────────┐     notifies     ┌─────────────┐
│  Raw Data   │ ───────────────► │  Transform  │ ───────────────► │  UI Widget  │
│ (PointData) │                  │  (Output)   │                  │  (Display)  │
└─────────────┘                  └─────────────┘                  └─────────────┘

title: Observer Library
text:
Important Limitations






WarningNot Thread-Safe



The Observer library is not thread-safe. All operations (addObserver, removeObserver, notifyObservers) must be called from the same thread, or external synchronization must be provided.
Qt widgets that register observer callbacks must ensure those callbacks run on the main thread when data can be modified from background workers. See the Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap for audit status, fix patterns, and the task checklist.








NoteRe-entrant Modification During Notification



notifyObservers() copies the observer map to a snapshot before invoking callbacks. Adding or removing observers from within a callback is therefore safe for the current round — new registrations take effect on the next notifyObservers() call. This re-entrancy support does not provide thread safety across threads.








NoteException Behavior



If an observer callback throws an exception, remaining observers will not be notified. The exception propagates to the caller of notifyObservers(). Design callbacks to be exception-safe.

title: SkeletonizeMask (TransformsV2)
text:
Algorithm
For each input Mask2D:

Resolve canvas size from MaskSkeletonizeParams when both dimensions are positive (e.g. copied from MaskData::getImageSize()), otherwise size the canvas to the mask’s axis-aligned point extents via get_bounding_box, plus a one-pixel background border on each side so thinning is not biased at the raster edge.
Rasterize mask points to a binary image on the chosen canvas.
Apply the selected skeletonization method (see below).
Convert skeleton pixels back to absolute mask coordinates.
Return empty Mask2D if input is empty or skeletonization yields no pixels.


Methods








method
Algorithm
Best for




ZhangSuen (default)
Morphological thinning (fast_skeletonize, scikit-image)
Fast, general-purpose thinning


MedialAxis
Euclidean distance transform (Felzenszwalb) + single-pass medial-axis thinning (scikit-image)
Thick, staggered, or off-center masks where a geometric centerline is desired



Medial-axis skeletonization is typically more centered on thick bars than Zhang–Suen, which can hug the top edge of staggered rectangular shapes. For jagged whisker-like masks, chain with MedianFilterMask first (window_size: 3) to reduce boundary noise before skeletonizing. Note that medial axis may still produce short side branches; see scikit-image guidance to prefer ZhangSuen when fewer branches matter more than centering.

title: PointCoordinate
text: PointCoordinate is a TransformsV2 container transform that projects one coordinate component from PointData into RaggedAnalogTimeSeries.

title: PointCoordinate
PointCoordinate
text:
Semantics
For every time point in the input PointData, the transform emits one float value per point at that time:
PointData[t] = [(x1, y1), (x2, y2)]
PointCoordinate(X)[t] = [x1, x2]
PointCoordinate(Y)[t] = [y1, y2]
The output preserves the input TimeFrame.

title: PointCoordinate
text:
TensorDesign Use
For single-keypoint-per-time data, PointCoordinate can be sampled directly by timestamp or TimeFrame row providers:
{
  "name": "nose_x",
  "source_key": "Nose",
  "pipeline_json": "{\"steps\": [{\"step_id\": \"x\", \"transform_name\": \"PointCoordinate\", \"parameters\": {\"coordinate\": \"X\"}}]}"
}
For interval rows, use a terminal range reduction after coordinate projection:
{
  "name": "mean_nose_x",
  "source_key": "Nose",
  "pipeline_json": "{\"steps\": [{\"step_id\": \"x\", \"transform_name\": \"PointCoordinate\", \"parameters\": {\"coordinate\": \"X\"}}], \"range_reduction\": {\"reduction_name\": \"MeanValue\"}}"
}
Timestamp sampling of RaggedAnalogTimeSeries currently uses the first value at a time point. This is intended for single-keypoint-per-time PointData. Multi-point-per-time data should use an explicit reduction or future sampling policy before being treated as a single scalar column.

title: RunTransformsV2PipelineAtTime Command
RunTransformsV2PipelineAtTime Command
text:
Execution Flow

Validate input_key, output_key, and pipeline_path; require input_key in DataManager.
loadPipelineFromFile(pipeline_path) builds a typed TransformPipeline.
createTemporalSubset(input_key, [time, time]) extracts a single-frame input.
executePipeline(subset, pipeline) runs transforms off-DataManager (multi-step PipelineStepDescriptor chains are supported when types chain correctly).
Store output:

Inherit the input object’s TimeKey when creating a new key.
If output_key exists and the result type supports merge-overwrite (MaskData, LineData, PointData), call mergeOverwriteData. Transient pipeline results are assigned the target key’s identity context before merge so each frame gets a distinct registry-backed EntityId. Repeated runs at different time values therefore accumulate frames in a pre-existing empty output key; re-running the same time overwrites only that frame.
If output_key exists with an incompatible type, return an error.
Otherwise call setData to create or replace the output object.


Terminal range_reduction entries in the JSON are loaded but not applied by executePipeline (same behavior as the TransformsV2 widget).

title: Multi-Channel Storage Roadmap
text:
Completed

toLibTorch() zero-copy stride fix: TensorData::toLibTorch() uses torch::from_blob with column-major strides, eliminating \(O(n)\) virtual calls.
AnalogToTensor / TensorToAnalog transforms: Bridge between independent AnalogTimeSeries channels and unified TensorData. Registered, tested (12 cases).
Common Average Reference (CAR) transform: TensorData → TensorData, supports mean/median, channel exclusion, CPU/GPU via LibTorch. Registered, tested.
TensorColumnAnalogStorage: Zero-copy AnalogTimeSeries views backed by TensorData columns. TensorToAnalog uses this automatically. 17 test cases.
ParameterSchema std::vector<T> support: Multi-select lists and CSV line edits for vector parameters in AutoParamWidget.
Phase 4a — Eliminate Armadillo copy overhead (CPU): Removed matToFlat() helper from TensorCAR.cpp. All three output paths (TimeFrameIndex, Interval, Ordinal) now use std::move(result_mat) into arma::fmat factory overloads, reducing copies from 3 to 1. Added createFromIntervals(arma::fmat) overload to TensorData.
Phase 4b — LibTorch compute path for TensorCAR: Added conditional LibTorch backend to TensorCAR behind TENSOR_BACKEND_LIBTORCH. When use_gpu = true, uses toLibTorch() → device transfer → mean/median → subtract → download. TimeFrameIndex output path is zero-copy via LibTorchTensorStorage. TransformsV2 CMakeLists.txt links Torch privately with find_package(OpenCV) workaround for the protobuf target conflict.
Tensor-backed binary loading (Phase 1 — in-memory path): Added use_tensor_backed option to BinaryAnalogLoaderOptions. When enabled with num_channels > 1 and in-memory loading, reads interleaved binary → arma::fmat → TensorData → N TensorColumnAnalogStorage zero-copy views. BinaryFormatLoader, AnalogImport_Widget, and BinaryAnalogImport_Widget updated to register both the TensorData and per-channel views. Also fixed the hardcoded int16_t bug in the in-memory multi-channel path — now dispatches on binary_data_type. 9 test cases (764 assertions).
Shared block-cached mmap storage (Phase 2): Added SharedMmapBlockCache — a single mmap of an interleaved binary file with a FIFO circular buffer of decoded float32 blocks. When one channel loads a time window, all channels are decoded. BlockCachedMmapAnalogStorage provides per-channel AnalogTimeSeries views; MmapTensorStorage provides TensorData access. New TensorData::createTimeSeries2DFromStorage() factory method for custom storage backends. TensorStorageType::MemoryMapped added. loadTensorBacked() updated: use_tensor_backed + use_memory_mapped + num_channels > 1 takes the block-cached mmap path. 5 new test cases (540 assertions).

title: Multi-Channel Storage Roadmap
text:
Roadmap

1. Tensor-Backed Binary Loading






Note



Status: Complete (in-memory path). The mmap path is deferred to Phase 2 (Shared Block Cache).


Today the binary loader (src/IO/formats/Binary/analogtimeseries/Analog_Time_Series_Binary.cpp) returns independent AnalogTimeSeries objects — each channel with either VectorAnalogDataStorage (in-memory) or MemoryMappedAnalogDataStorage (mmap, per-channel stride). No TensorData is created and no channels share state.

Goals

Add use_tensor_backed option to BinaryAnalogLoaderOptions.
When enabled with num_channels > 1:

In-memory path: Read interleaved binary → arma::fmat → TensorData → N TensorColumnAnalogStorage views.
Mmap path: Deferred to shared block cache (see below).

Return BinaryAnalogLoadResult containing both the TensorData (memory owner) and per-channel AnalogTimeSeries views.
Update AnalogImport_Widget and BinaryFormatLoader to register both the TensorData and per-channel views in DataManager.
Expose use_tensor_backed in JSON loading configs (reflect-cpp automatic).
Fix the existing hardcoded int16_t bug in the in-memory multi-channel path (should dispatch on binary_data_type).



UI Changes
BinaryAnalogImport_Widget needs a “Tensor-backed (shared storage)” checkbox, enabled only when num_channels > 1.


Files to Modify

Files affected by tensor-backed binary loading






File
Change




src/IO/formats/Binary/analogtimeseries/Analog_Time_Series_Binary.hpp
Add use_tensor_backed option, BinaryAnalogLoadResult return type

Add checkbox





Tests

Load multi-channel binary with use_tensor_backed=true. Verify TensorData column count matches num_channels. Verify each view shares memory (pointer comparison). Verify values match legacy independent-channel path.
Data type dispatch fix: Load float32 binary files with legacy in-memory path.
JSON round-trip for BinaryAnalogLoaderOptions with use_tensor_backed=true.





2. Shared Block-Cached Mmap Storage






Note



Status: Complete. SharedMmapBlockCache, BlockCachedMmapAnalogStorage, and MmapTensorStorage are implemented and integrated into loadTensorBacked().


The current per-channel mmap storage (MemoryMappedAnalogDataStorage) reads the same file pages independently per channel. For 384 channels, each OS page is read ~384 times. Additionally, getSpanRangeImpl() always returns an empty span, forcing element-by-element virtual dispatch with per-element stride calculation, memcpy, type conversion, and scaling.

Design: SharedMmapBlockCache
A shared resource that memory-maps an interleaved binary file and maintains a circular buffer of decoded float blocks.
New files:

src/DataObjects/AnalogTimeSeries/storage/SharedMmapBlockCache.hpp
src/DataObjects/AnalogTimeSeries/storage/SharedMmapBlockCache.cpp
src/DataObjects/AnalogTimeSeries/storage/BlockCachedMmapAnalogStorage.hpp
src/DataObjects/Tensors/storage/MmapTensorStorage.hpp

Key properties:

Circular buffer of \(N\) decoded blocks (default 16).
Each block: block_size_samples × num_channels float32 values.
FIFO eviction (optimized for sequential temporal access).
Reader-writer lock for thread safety.
Bulk type conversion at block load time (single vectorized pass via LibTorch from_blob + .to(kFloat32) or plain C++ with SIMD).

Access pattern: When DataViewer renders a time window for one channel, all \(N\) channels’ data for that window is decoded into the cache. Subsequent channels hit the cache. The first channel pays the decode cost; the remaining \(N - 1\) are free lookups.
Cache sizing:
\[M = N_{\text{blocks}} \times B_{\text{samples}} \times N_{\text{channels}} \times 4 \;\text{bytes}\]

Tests & Benchmarks

Benchmark: block-cached vs element-by-element for 384-channel data.





3. Cross-Channel Transforms
Additional transforms that operate on multi-channel TensorData:

Spatial Whitening (ZCA): GitHub Issue #245 — Decorrelates channels and normalizes variances using eigendecomposition. Supports ZCA, PCA, and Cholesky methods.
Per-Channel IIR Filter: GitHub Issue #246 — Applies the same IIR filter to every column of a tensor. Operates on contiguous Armadillo columns for optimal cache utilization.

Both follow the TensorCAR transform pattern (container transform, TensorData → TensorData, LibTorch compute backend).



4. GPU-Accelerated Processing






Note



Status: Phase 4a and 4b complete. Ad-hoc benchmarks confirmed large GPU speedups for CAR transforms. See TensorCAR GPU vs CPU Benchmark Analysis for full results. Phase 4c (in-place transform support) remains.



Benchmark Summary
Ad-hoc benchmarks compared Armadillo CPU, LibTorch CPU, and LibTorch CUDA for mean-CAR and median-CAR across channel counts (32–384) and block sizes (1k–900k rows). Key findings at 384 channels:










Transform
Armadillo (30k rows)
Torch CPU
Torch CUDA
GPU speedup




Mean-CAR
11.4 ms
7.5 ms
0.5 ms
15×


Median-CAR
126.5 ms
32.3 ms
2.3 ms
14×




GPU crossover: Mean-CAR wins above ~5k rows. Median-CAR wins even at 1k rows because the per-row sort is compute-heavy.
Threading: Armadillo is single-threaded for these reductions. LibTorch CPU parallelizes across rows using its thread pool (4.2× speedup for median on 6 cores). LibTorch CUDA parallelizes most aggressively with one warp per row.
Transfer overhead: CPU↔︎GPU copies saturate PCIe at ~7 Gi/s. At 900k × 384 (1.4 GB), transfer takes ~467 ms vs 13 ms compute. GPU wins when data is already on-device or the compute exceeds the transfer cost.
Recommended gpu_block_hint: 100,000 rows (~3.3 s at 30 kHz, 153 MB at 384 channels). Achieves 80–95% peak GPU throughput.



Production Code Copy Overhead
The current Armadillo-based TensorCAR performs 2–3 unnecessary full-matrix copies per invocation:

arma::fmat result_mat = input_mat — full copy (\(N \times C \times 4\) bytes)
matToFlat(result_mat) — column-major to row-major conversion (another full copy)
TensorData::createTimeSeries2D(flat) — copy into new storage (third full copy)

For 384 channels × 100k rows (153 MB per copy), this wastes ~460 MB of memory bandwidth. The subtraction itself (each_col() -= ref) is in-place on the first copy — the overhead is entirely in format conversion and storage creation.


Implementation Plan
The GPU path decomposes into three sub-phases that can be landed independently.

Phase 4a: Eliminate Armadillo Copy Overhead (CPU-only improvement) ✅






Tip



Complete. Removed matToFlat() helper. All output paths use std::move(result_mat) into arma::fmat factory overloads. Added TensorData::createFromIntervals(arma::fmat). Copies reduced from 3 to 1.




Phase 4b: LibTorch Compute Path for TensorCAR ✅






Tip



Complete. Added tensorCARLibTorch() behind #ifdef TENSOR_BACKEND_LIBTORCH. Dispatched when use_gpu = true. Uses toLibTorch() → .to(device) → mean/median with index_select for excluded channels → subtract → .to(kCPU) → buildResultFromTorch(). TimeFrameIndex output wraps the result tensor in LibTorchTensorStorage (zero-copy). Interval and Ordinal paths materialize to flat/arma. TransformsV2 links Torch privately; find_package(OpenCV) before find_package(Torch) works around the protobuf target conflict.




Phase 4c: In-Place Transform Support
Eliminate the final storage copy by allowing transforms to mutate their input. This benefits both CPU and GPU paths.

Motivation: Container Transform Return-Type Redesign
Today, container transforms return std::shared_ptr<OutContainer>, which forces every invocation to heap-allocate a new data object — even when the transform could safely mutate the input. nullptr is overloaded to mean “failure,” so there is no way for a transform to signal “I mutated the input, reuse it.”
The fix changes the container transform signature to return a raw pointer and accept a non-const reference:
// Before (current)
auto tensorCAR(TensorData const& input, TensorCARParams const& params,
               ComputeContext const& ctx) -> std::shared_ptr<TensorData>;

// After
auto tensorCAR(TensorData& input, TensorCARParams const& params,
               ComputeContext const& ctx) -> TensorData*;
The raw pointer return encodes three unambiguous states:

Container transform return-value protocol







Return value
Meaning
Executor action




new TensorData(…)
New allocation (out-of-place)
Wrap in shared_ptr (takes ownership)


&input
In-place mutation (pointer identity with input)
Reuse original shared_ptr


nullptr
Failure
Throw / propagate error



The executor already holds the shared_ptr and can perform the address comparison:
auto* raw = transform->execute(*input_ptr, params, ctx);
if (!raw) {
    throw std::runtime_error("transform '" + name + "' failed");
}
if (raw == input_ptr.get()) {
    // In-place: reuse existing shared_ptr, no new allocation
    return DataTypeVariant{input_ptr};
} else {
    // New allocation: take ownership
    return DataTypeVariant{std::shared_ptr<OutContainer>(raw)};
}
Backward compatibility: Existing transforms that accept InContainer const& bind to InContainer& with no source changes. Transforms that currently return std::make_shared<Out>(…) need a mechanical change to new Out(…).


TransformsV2 Plumbing Changes

Files affected by container transform return-type redesign






File
Change




ContainerExecutor.hpp
TypedContainerTransform::FuncType: InContainer const& → InContainer&, shared_ptr<Out> → Out*. IContainerExecutor::execute(): DataTypeVariant const& → DataTypeVariant&, return unchanged.


ElementRegistry.hpp
registerContainerTransform(), executeContainerTransform(), RegisterContainerTransform RAII helper, TypedContainerExecutor::executeTyped() — same signature changes. Add pointer-identity check in TypedContainerExecutor::execute().


All container transform .cpp files
Mechanical: return std::make_shared<T>(…) → return new T(…); return nullptr unchanged. Input parameter const& → & (only for transforms that opt into mutation).





TensorCAR In-Place Path
Add bool in_place = false to TensorCARParams. When true, the transform mutates the input’s storage directly and returns &input:
Armadillo CPU path:
auto* arma_storage = input.storage().getMutableAsChecked<ArmadilloTensorStorage>(
        TensorStorageType::Armadillo);
arma::fmat& mat = arma_storage->mutableMatrix();
mat.each_col() -= ref_col;  // zero output allocation
return &input;
LibTorch CPU path:
auto& t = lt_storage->mutableTensor();
t.sub_(ref);  // PyTorch in-place subtraction
return &input;
LibTorch GPU path: Upload → compute → download → assign back to mutableTensor(). Eliminates CPU-side output TensorData allocation.
Savings: Eliminates the remaining storage copy from Phase 4b, bringing total copy overhead to: 1 upload + 1 download (GPU) or 0 copies (CPU in-place).




Temporal Block Processing for Large Datasets
When a dataset exceeds GPU memory, process it in temporal blocks:

Iterate over time in chunks of \(B\) samples (default \(B = 100{,}000\)).
For each chunk: toLibTorch() → .to(kCUDA) → compute → .to(kCPU) → write back.
Concatenate results (or write in-place per block).

This wraps any transform — no per-transform batching code needed.


Benchmarks Completed

✅ GPU vs CPU CAR on 384 channels × 1k–900k samples.
✅ Block upload/download overhead measurement (PCIe ~7 Gi/s).
✅ GPU crossover point determination (mean: ~5k rows, median: always).
✅ Threading analysis (Armadillo single-threaded, LibTorch multi-threaded).
✅ In-place vs out-of-place allocation overhead (negligible when original preserved).
⬚ GPU vs CPU whitening (requires §3 ZCA implementation).

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
This document describes the implemented infrastructure for representing multi-channel acquisition data (e.g. 32–384 channels from an analog-to-digital converter) using TensorData as the canonical owner, with zero-copy AnalogTimeSeries column views for compatibility with existing single-channel widgets and transforms.
See GitHub Issue #240 for the original feature request. For planned future work (spatial whitening, tensor IIR filtering, block-cached mmap, tensor-backed binary loading), see Multi-Channel Roadmap.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
Design Principles

TensorData is the canonical owner for multi-channel data. AnalogTimeSeries objects become lightweight column views.
LibTorch is the compute backend for cross-channel transforms. Armadillo remains the default storage backend for TensorData and provides zero-copy column access for AnalogTimeSeries views.
GPU acceleration is opt-in via device selection; the same LibTorch code runs on CPU or GPU.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
Compute Backend: Armadillo (Storage) + LibTorch (Compute)
Cross-channel transforms use LibTorch as the single compute backend, even on CPU-only systems. This avoids maintaining separate Armadillo and LibTorch code paths for the same operations.

Armadillo vs LibTorch comparison for cross-channel compute







Concern
Armadillo
LibTorch




CPU/GPU unification
Separate code paths
Same code, change torch::Device


Memory layout
Column-major
Row-major default (natural for row-wise cross-channel ops like CAR)


Median/mean
arma::median(mat, 1)
torch::median(t, 1)


Eigendecomposition
arma::eig_sym
torch::linalg::eigh


Bulk type conversion
Manual loop
tensor.to(torch::kFloat32) — fused, SIMD-friendly



The use_gpu parameter reduces to device selection rather than an entirely different algorithm:
auto t = tensor.toLibTorch();
if (use_gpu) {
    t = DeviceManager::instance().toDevice(t);
}
auto ref = torch::median(t, /*dim=*/1).values;
t = t - ref.unsqueeze(1);
Armadillo serves as the default storage backend for TensorData (ArmadilloTensorStorage). Its column-major layout is ideal for TensorColumnAnalogStorage because each column is contiguous — perfect for AnalogTimeSeries span access. The toLibTorch() conversion bridges storage to compute when transforms are applied.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
Storage Layout
A 32-channel, 1M-sample recording stored in-memory as a TensorData lives in an Armadillo arma::fmat(1000000, 32) — column-major. Each column is one channel, contiguous in memory. \(N\) AnalogTimeSeries objects (one per channel) reference this same matrix through TensorColumnAnalogStorage, which hands DataViewer a zero-copy std::span<float const> via fmat.colptr(c).
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          arma::fmat  (column-major in memory)        │
│                                                      │
│  col 0 (ch0)  col 1 (ch1)  col 2 (ch2)  …  col 31  │
│  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐     ┌──────┐ │
│  │ t0      │  │ t0      │  │ t0      │     │ t0   │ │
│  │ t1      │  │ t1      │  │ t1      │     │ t1   │ │
│  │ …       │  │ …       │  │ …       │     │ …    │ │
│  │ t999999 │  │ t999999 │  │ t999999 │     │ …    │ │
│  └─────────┘  └─────────┘  └─────────┘     └──────┘ │
│  ↑ contiguous  ↑ contiguous  ↑ contiguous            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │               │               │
        ▼               ▼               ▼
  AnalogTimeSeries  AnalogTimeSeries  AnalogTimeSeries
  (TensorColumn     (TensorColumn     (TensorColumn
   Storage, ch0)     Storage, ch1)     Storage, ch2)
This layout is the right canonical format for multi-channel data that fits in memory. Each AnalogTimeSeries is a lightweight view — no copies, no duplication, full compatibility with DataViewer_Widget and existing single-channel infrastructure.

Why not one flat AnalogTimeSeries?
An alternative would be concatenating all channels end-to-end in a single AnalogTimeSeries ([ch0_all_t, ch1_all_t, ...]). This is essentially what Armadillo column-major memory already is — a contiguous buffer of \(N_{\text{channels}} \times N_{\text{samples}}\) floats. But the matrix representation is strictly better: it carries shape, column names, TimeFrame metadata, and 2D indexing. Cross-channel transforms index mat.col(c) instead of manually computing offset + c * num_samples. And each TensorColumnAnalogStorage view is a first-class AnalogTimeSeries that plugs into DataViewer, transforms, and export without special-casing.


Armadillo ↔︎ LibTorch Conversion
When a cross-channel transform runs, data moves from Armadillo (storage) to LibTorch (compute) and back. TensorData::toLibTorch() uses torch::from_blob with column-major strides for a zero-copy view of Armadillo’s memory, followed by .contiguous() to produce a row-major tensor:
auto const & mat = arma_storage->matrix();
auto t = torch::from_blob(
    const_cast<float*>(mat.memptr()),
    {static_cast<int64_t>(mat.n_rows), static_cast<int64_t>(mat.n_cols)},
    {1, static_cast<int64_t>(mat.n_rows)},  // column-major strides
    torch::kFloat32
);
// t is a zero-copy strided view — no data movement
This eliminates the \(O(n)\) virtual calls from the old materializeFlat() path and reduces the conversion to a single contiguous memcpy.
The full round-trip cost for applying a transform is:

Round-trip cost for applying a cross-channel transform







Step
Operation
Copies




Storage
arma::fmat(time, channels) — column-major
canonical


View
\(N\) TensorColumnAnalogStorage views → DataViewer
0


To compute
toLibTorch() → strided view of Armadillo memory
0


Transform
e.g. whitening — allocates result tensor (row-major)
1 (result only)


Back to storage
result.toArmadillo() → new arma::fmat (col-major)
1 (layout convert)


New views
\(N\) new TensorColumnAnalogStorage on result
0



Total: one copy for the transform input (zero-copy via strides), one copy for the output (layout conversion). For 128 MB of data (32ch × 1M × 4B), the output copy is ~30ms — negligible compared to the eigendecomposition in whitening.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
Transform Responsibility: AnalogTimeSeries vs TensorData
A key architectural question arises when both single-channel and multi-channel data exist in the same system: where should per-channel transforms (like IIR filtering) live?
Principle: Single-channel transforms stay on AnalogTimeSeries. Multi-channel transforms — including “apply the same filter to all channels” — go on TensorData.

Transform responsibility by data origin







Data origin
Transform target
Why




Single-channel source (e.g. one sensor)
AnalogTimeSeries
Data is naturally a contiguous std::vector<float>. Existing filter code runs at full speed on a tight span.


Multi-channel source (e.g. 32-ch ADC)
TensorData
Data lives in a matrix. Per-column iteration on Armadillo columns is contiguous and fast. Cross-channel ops (CAR) need the full matrix.



Heavy compute (filtering, CAR, whitening) happens after materializing into a proper TensorData where columns are contiguous and LibTorch can operate on the full matrix. This avoids a problematic design where single-channel transforms need to be aware of their storage backend’s memory layout.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
AnalogToTensor & TensorToAnalog Transforms

AnalogToTensor Container Transform
Files:

src/TransformsV2/algorithms/AnalogToTensor/AnalogToTensor.hpp
src/TransformsV2/algorithms/AnalogToTensor/AnalogToTensor.cpp

Transform type: N-ary container (N AnalogTimeSeries → 1 TensorData).
Parameters struct (reflect-cpp):
struct AnalogToTensorParams {
    std::string channel_prefix;                // prefix to match AnalogTimeSeries keys
    std::vector<std::string> channel_keys;     // selected DataManager keys (populated from prefix)
};
The first-pass UI uses a hybrid prefix + multi-select approach:

channel_prefix is a dynamic_combo field populated with unique prefixes discovered from AnalogTimeSeries keys in DataManager (e.g. "voltage", "emg").
When a prefix is selected, channel_keys (a dynamic_combo std::vector<std::string> field) is populated with all matching keys and rendered as a multi-select QListWidget with all items checked by default. The user can uncheck individual channels to exclude them.

This is enabled by the std::vector<T> support in ParameterSchema and AutoParamWidget (see ParameterSchema developer docs).






Note



Infrastructure dependency resolved: ParameterSchema now detects std::vector<T> fields at compile time (is_vector, vector_element_type), and AutoParamWidget renders them as multi-select lists (for vector<string> + dynamic_combo) or CSV line edits (for vector<int>, vector<float>). All items are checked by default on first population. The list has a max height of 200px with scrolling for large channel counts.


Algorithm (implemented):

Validate all channels are non-null, share the same TimeFrame (pointer identity), and have identical sample counts.
Build flat row-major data by iterating each channel via viewValues() (mmap-safe; avoids the empty-span problem).
Return TensorData::createTimeSeries2D(...) preserving the shared TimeFrame and TimeIndexStorage. Column names come from channel_keys when sizes match, otherwise auto-generated as "ch0", "ch1", etc.



TensorToAnalog Container Transform
Files:

src/TransformsV2/algorithms/TensorToAnalog/TensorToAnalog.hpp
src/TransformsV2/algorithms/TensorToAnalog/TensorToAnalog.cpp

Parameters struct:
struct TensorToAnalogParams {
    std::string output_key_prefix; // prefix for generated AnalogTimeSeries keys
    std::vector<int> columns;      // which columns to extract (empty = all)
};
output_key_prefix uses a standard QLineEdit. columns uses a CSV QLineEdit (e.g. "0, 1, 2") via the std::vector<int> widget support. An empty list means “extract all columns”.
Algorithm (implemented):

For each selected column, extract data via TensorData::getColumn(i).
When the tensor has RowType::TimeFrameIndex, recover time indices via RowDescriptor::timeStoragePtr()->getAllTimeIndices() and construct the AnalogTimeSeries with those indices to preserve temporal alignment.
Set the source TimeFrame on each output series.

This transform creates zero-copy TensorColumnAnalogStorage views instead of owning copies (see TensorColumnAnalogStorage below).


Registration & Tests

Both transforms registered via registerPipelineStepFactoryFor in RegisteredTransforms.cpp.
12 Catch2 test cases (484 assertions) in src/TransformsV2/algorithms/AnalogToTensor/AnalogToTensor.test.cpp:

Round-trip: N AnalogTimeSeries → AnalogToTensor → TensorToAnalog → values match exactly.
Single channel, default column name generation.
Mismatched TimeFrames → nullptr (graceful failure).
Mismatched sample counts → nullptr (graceful failure).
Empty channels vector → nullptr.
TimeFrame and RowType::TimeFrameIndex preserved in output.
TensorToAnalog column selection, out-of-range index rejection.
Ordinal tensor extraction.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
Common Average Reference (CAR) Transform
See developer docs for full API reference.
Files:

src/TransformsV2/algorithms/TensorCAR/TensorCAR.hpp
src/TransformsV2/algorithms/TensorCAR/TensorCAR.cpp

Transform type: Container (TensorData → TensorData).
Parameters struct:
struct TensorCARParams {
    CARMethod method = CARMethod::Median; // Mean or Median
    std::vector<int> exclude_channels;    // channels excluded from reference
    bool use_gpu = false;
};
Algorithm (CPU via Armadillo):

auto t = tensor.toLibTorch() — convert from Armadillo storage.
If use_gpu: t = DeviceManager::instance().toDevice(t) — move to GPU.
Compute reference:

Mean: auto ref = torch::mean(t, /*dim=*/1).values
Median: auto ref = torch::median(t, /*dim=*/1).values

Subtract: t = t - ref.unsqueeze(1).
Return TensorData wrapping the result LibTorchTensorStorage.

The same code runs on CPU and GPU — the only difference is the device placement in step 2. See Section 3 for rationale.
Pattern reference: TensorPCA (container transform, TensorData → TensorData).

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
Zero-Copy TensorData Column Views
TensorToAnalog produces zero-copy AnalogTimeSeries views backed by TensorColumnAnalogStorage. This eliminates the data copy by creating an AnalogTimeSeries storage backend that directly references a TensorData column.

TensorColumnAnalogStorage Backend
New file: src/DataObjects/AnalogTimeSeries/storage/TensorColumnAnalogStorage.hpp
Members:
std::shared_ptr<TensorData const> _tensor; // shared ownership of source
std::size_t _column_index;
Key insight: Armadillo uses column-major layout. Each column of an arma::fmat is contiguous in memory. This means fmat.colptr(col_index) gives a float* to a contiguous block of num_rows floats — exactly what AnalogTimeSeries needs for span-based access.
CRTP implementation:

CRTP method implementations for TensorColumnAnalogStorage






Method
Implementation




getValueAtImpl(i)
_tensor->at({i, _column_index})


sizeImpl()
_tensor->numRows()


isContiguousImpl()
true if Armadillo backend (column-major)


tryGetCacheImpl()
Return {colptr, num_rows, true} if Armadillo


getSpanRangeImpl(s, e)
Return span{colptr + s, e - s} if Armadillo





Factory Method
Added a general-purpose createFromStorage factory to AnalogTimeSeries that accepts a pre-constructed AnalogDataStorageWrapper and TimeIndexStorage. This avoids adding a TensorData dependency to the AnalogTimeSeries library:
static std::shared_ptr<AnalogTimeSeries> createFromStorage(
    AnalogDataStorageWrapper storage,
    std::shared_ptr<TimeIndexStorage> time_storage);
The caller (e.g. TensorToAnalog.cpp) constructs the TensorColumnAnalogStorage, wraps it in an AnalogDataStorageWrapper, and passes it to this factory. This keeps the dependency on TensorData in the transform layer, not in the data object layer.


TensorToAnalog Integration
TensorToAnalog now copies the input TensorData into a shared_ptr (so views are self-contained), resolves time storage once, and creates a TensorColumnAnalogStorage for each selected column. Result: applying CAR → TensorToAnalog produces views that share the filtered TensorData memory with zero per-element copies.


Tests
17 Catch2 test cases in TensorColumnAnalogStorage.test.cpp:

Zero-copy verification: Pointer comparison confirms AnalogTimeSeries view shares memory with the source TensorData column.
Span access: getDataInTimeFrameIndexRange returns non-empty spans; full and range-based span access verified.
Element access: All elements match column * 1000 + row test pattern.
Edge cases: Single column, single row, span boundary conditions.
Round-trip: AnalogToTensor → TensorToAnalog produces zero-copy views matching the original data.
TimeFrame preservation: Output series carry the correct TimeFrame.

title: Multi-Channel Storage & Cross-Channel Transforms
text:
DataViewer Integration
DataViewer_Widget is the primary consumer of multi-channel AnalogTimeSeries data. It groups channels by naming convention (e.g. voltage_1, voltage_2, … under a voltage group) and plots them as stacked 1D temporal traces.
A critical design goal is that DataViewer_Widget does not need to change. The storage abstraction handles multi-channel efficiency transparently.

In-memory path
The loading path creates one TensorData (Armadillo) and \(N\) TensorColumnAnalogStorage-backed AnalogTimeSeries objects. Each one has a contiguous column span. When DataViewer calls getDataInTimeFrameIndexRange(), it receives a real std::span<float const> pointing into the Armadillo matrix column. This is exactly as fast as the VectorAnalogDataStorage path. DataViewer sees no difference.

title: TensorData Row Mutation
text: TensorData supports appending and inserting rows into 2D tensors. This enables incremental construction of tensors (e.g., adding new time points as data arrives) without rebuilding the entire tensor.

title: TensorData Row Mutation
text: TensorData supports appending and inserting rows into 2D tensors. This enables incremental construction of tensors (e.g., adding new time points as data arrives) without rebuilding the entire tensor.

title: TensorData Row Mutation
text:
Supported Backends
Row mutation is supported for:

ArmadilloTensorStorage (default 2D backend) — uses Armadillo’s native row insertion via insert_rows() and resize().
DenseTensorStorage — manipulates the flat std::vector<float> buffer directly.

Row mutation is not supported for:

LazyColumnTensorStorage — column providers have a fixed row count.
LibTorchTensorStorage — torch tensors are not resizable in-place.
1D or 3D+ tensors — only 2D tensors support row mutation.

title: TensorData Row Mutation
text:
API

appendRow(std::span<float const> row_data)
Appends a row at the end of the tensor. Works for Ordinal and Interval rows (see overloads below). Throws std::logic_error for TimeFrameIndex rows since TimeIndexStorage is immutable.


appendRow(std::span<float const> row_data, TimeFrameInterval interval)
Appends a row with an associated interval. Only valid for tensors with Interval row semantics.


insertRow(std::size_t index, std::span<float const> row_data)
Inserts a row before the given index. Index may equal numRows() to insert at the end.


insertRow(std::size_t index, std::span<float const> row_data, TimeFrameInterval interval)
Inserts a row with an associated interval at a specific position.


setRow(std::size_t index, std::span<float const> row_data)
Overwrites the data for an existing row. Works for all row types (Ordinal, TimeFrameIndex, Interval). Does not change the row descriptor or dimension descriptor — only replaces the float data. Throws if the tensor is not 2D, the index is out of range, or row_data.size() does not match the column count.


upsertRows(frame_rows, time_frame)
void upsertRows(
    std::vector<std::pair<int, std::vector<float>>> const & frame_rows,
    std::shared_ptr<TimeFrame> time_frame);
Frame-indexed merge operation for accumulating results across runs. Takes a vector of (frame_index, row_data) pairs and a TimeFrame reference. Semantics:

Reads the existing frame-to-row mapping (from TimeFrameIndex rows, or treats ordinal row indices as frame IDs).
Overlays the new rows using std::map for sorted-merge behavior: matching frames are overwritten, new frames are appended.
Rebuilds storage in-place with makeStorage() and TimeIndexStorageFactory::createFromTimeIndices().
Preserves column names.
Handles empty tensor (first initialization).

This is the primary API for deep learning inference output, where batch runs on overlapping frame ranges should merge rather than replace.

title: TensorData Row Mutation
text:
Orchestration
Each mutation method performs four steps:

Validate — checks 2D, supported backend, row type compatibility, and data size.
Storage mutation — delegates to ArmadilloTensorStorage::appendRow/insertRow or DenseTensorStorage::appendRow/insertRow.
RowDescriptor update — increments ordinal count or inserts an interval.
DimensionDescriptor update — resizes axis 0 via setAxisSize().
Observer notification — calls notifyObservers().

title: TensorData Row Mutation
text:
Row Descriptor Mutation
RowDescriptor exposes three mutation methods:








Method
Row Type
Effect




setOrdinalCount(n)
Ordinal
Sets the ordinal count


appendInterval(iv)
Interval
Appends an interval


insertInterval(i, iv)
Interval
Inserts an interval at position i



TimeFrameIndex rows cannot be mutated because TimeIndexStorage is an abstract interface with no insertion API.

title: Settings Widget — Design & Roadmap
text:
WhiskerToolbox has a growing number of application-level and widget-level preferences distributed across multiple widgets and systems:








Preference
Current Location
Issue




Output directory
DataManager_Widget (OutputDirectoryWidget)
Belongs in global settings, not the data manager


Python environment path
PythonPropertiesWidget reading AppPreferences
Discoverable only if user opens the Python widget


Default import/export directories
AppPreferences (no dedicated UI)
No centralized place to edit them


Default TimeFrame key
AppPreferences (no dedicated UI)
No centralized place to edit it


UI theme (dark/light)
Not implemented
Frequently requested


Font size / scaling
Not implemented
Accessibility concern


Keyboard shortcuts
Hardcoded per widget
No customization; scattered keyPressEvent overrides



Users have no single place to discover and configure these options. Settings that are logically application-global are hidden inside data-specific widgets. Additionally, the application lacks any customizable keyboard shortcut system — shortcuts are hardcoded in Media_Window::keyPressEvent(), Whisker_Widget::keyPressEvent(), and various eventFilter implementations with no way for users to change them.



Centralized settings access: One widget where users can discover and modify all application preferences.
Widget-contributed settings pages: Widgets can optionally contribute a settings panel rendered inside the Settings widget, following the same pattern as create_properties in the editor registry.
Appearance customization: Dark mode, light mode, system-follow, and font size.
Customizable keybindings: Users can remap keyboard shortcuts. The keybinding system integrates with the Command Architecture so command-based actions can be triggered by hotkeys.
Persistence: All settings persist in the existing AppPreferences JSON system with debounced auto-save.

title: Settings Widget — Design & Roadmap
text:
Settings widget zone placement. Is Zone::Center the right default? Some applications dock settings in a side panel. Given the potentially large keybinding table, Center seems appropriate for the view, but it could also work as a modal dialog instead of a docked widget.
Settings vs. Preferences naming. Qt conventions use “Preferences” (macOS) while Windows uses “Settings”. The codebase already uses AppPreferences for the data model. The widget can be called “Settings” in the UI (matching modern convention) while the data model remains AppPreferences.
Widget defaults granularity. Should the Settings widget allow configuring every property of an EditorState as a default, or just a curated subset? Recommendation: curated subset. Each widget author chooses which fields make sense as “defaults” by controlling what their create_settings factory exposes.
Keybinding conflict resolution. When a user assigns a key combo that conflicts with an existing binding: show a warning and require explicit override? Or automatically unbind the old action? Recommendation: show a warning with the conflicting action name and let the user choose.
Text input passthrough. The global event filter must not intercept keystrokes intended for text editing. Rule: if the focused widget is a QLineEdit, QTextEdit, QPlainTextEdit, QSpinBox, QDoubleSpinBox, or QComboBox (editable), only process key sequences that include Ctrl, Alt, or Meta modifiers. Bare keys (letters, digits) pass through to the text widget.

title: Planar angles and line tangents
text:
CoreGeometry/angle.hpp provides helpers used by line-angle transforms and polynomial fitting:

compute_sliding_secant_span — symmetric arc-length window around a midpoint, translated to stay inside ([0,1]) in fractional polyline length.
make_planar_orthonormal_basis — builds a right-handed orthonormal ((_x, _y)) from user-supplied “positive X” and “positive Y” directions (Gram–Schmidt on Y, with safe fallbacks).
calculate_direct_angle_secant — chord angle between point_at_fractional_position samples at the span ends, expressed in the basis via angle_degrees_vector_in_basis.
normalize_angle — legacy subtraction from a single reference direction (still used where a scalar reference angle is appropriate).

Fractional positions always resolve through cumulative arc length and linear edge interpolation (point_at_fractional_position with interpolation enabled).

title: Sequence Assembler
text:
The SequenceAssembler (pipelines/SequenceAssembler.hpp) segments a flat feature matrix and associated time indices into contiguous temporal sequences. This is essential for sequence models like HMMs that require observations grouped into runs of consecutive time steps.
TensorData may have gaps in its TimeFrameIndex rows (e.g., frames 100–200 then 500–600). The SequenceAssembler detects these gaps and splits the flat matrix into separate SequenceSegment objects, one per contiguous run.

title: Sequence Assembler
text:
Gap Detection
A gap occurs when consecutive TimeFrameIndex values differ by more than 1:
times[i+1] - times[i] > 1  →  new sequence starts at i+1
For example, given times {0, 1, 2, 10, 11, 12}:

Run 1: indices 0–2 (times 0, 1, 2)
Run 2: indices 3–5 (times 10, 11, 12)

title: Sequence Assembler
Sequence Assembler
text:
API
Two overloads are provided — one with labels (for training) and one without (for prediction):
// Labeled segmentation (training)
std::vector<SequenceSegment> SequenceAssembler::segment(
    arma::mat const & features,
    arma::Row<std::size_t> const & labels,
    std::vector<TimeFrameIndex> const & times,
    SequenceAssemblerConfig const & config = {});

// Unlabeled segmentation (prediction)
std::vector<SequenceSegment> SequenceAssembler::segment(
    arma::mat const & features,
    std::vector<TimeFrameIndex> const & times,
    SequenceAssemblerConfig const & config = {});

Preconditions

features.n_cols == times.size()
labels.n_elem == times.size() (labeled overload)
times must be sorted in ascending order

title: Sequence Assembler
Sequence Assembler
text:
Pipeline Integration
The SequenceAssembler slots into the ClassificationPipeline between label assembly and training when the selected model supports sequence-based training. The pipeline flow becomes:
ValidatingFeatures → ConvertingFeatures → AssemblingLabels →
SegmentingSequences → Training → Predicting → ComputingMetrics → WritingOutput
Models that implement trainSequences() / predictSequences() (e.g., HMM) receive the segmented sequences directly. Frame-based models skip the segmentation stage entirely.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
The classification pipeline implements ground-truth (GT) substitution: after Viterbi decoding, predictions for labeled frames are overwritten with their known labels. This ensures the final output is exact on training data, but it means train-set metrics are always 100% — which is useless for evaluation.
Additionally, the existing “validation” heuristic (frames outside the training region) is unreliable because many non-training frames have no labels at all, and unlabeled frames do not represent class 0.
Two features address this:

Explicit validation intervals — a dedicated DigitalIntervalSeries specifying regions with known labels for honest evaluation.
Leave-one-interval-out cross-validation — retrain the model multiple times, each time holding out one training interval, predict it with boundary constraints, and average per-fold metrics.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
The classification pipeline implements ground-truth (GT) substitution: after Viterbi decoding, predictions for labeled frames are overwritten with their known labels. This ensures the final output is exact on training data, but it means train-set metrics are always 100% — which is useless for evaluation.
Additionally, the existing “validation” heuristic (frames outside the training region) is unreliable because many non-training frames have no labels at all, and unlabeled frames do not represent class 0.
Two features address this:

Explicit validation intervals — a dedicated DigitalIntervalSeries specifying regions with known labels for honest evaluation.
Leave-one-interval-out cross-validation — retrain the model multiple times, each time holding out one training interval, predict it with boundary constraints, and average per-fold metrics.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
Architecture

Raw vs. GT-Substituted Predictions
The pipeline maintains two prediction vectors:

raw_predictions — the model’s actual Viterbi output, unmodified. Used for all metric computations.
predictions — after GT substitution (training frame labels overwrite model output). Used only for the final output writer (PredictionWriter), so downstream consumers get clean labeled data.

This split ensures metrics reflect true model performance while the output retains exact labels on known frames.


Validation Intervals
Config field: validation_interval_key (std::string)
When set, the pipeline partitions predicted frames into three buckets:








Bucket
Source
Metrics computed?




Training
Frames inside training_interval_key
Yes (train)


Validation
Frames inside validation_interval_key
Yes (validation)


Other
All remaining frames
No



Ground-truth labels for validation frames are assembled using the same label configuration as training (e.g., LabelFromIntervals with the same contact interval series). The key difference is that validation intervals are not used for training — the model has never seen these labels.
Validation intervals still benefit from boundary-constrained decoding: the first and last frames of a validation interval (which have known labels) serve as Viterbi bookends, just like training interval boundaries.


Leave-One-Interval-Out Cross-Validation
Config field: max_cv_folds (std::size_t, default 5; 0 = disabled)
Cross-validation runs as Stage 5c, after the main model is trained in Stage 5b. It does not affect the main model or its predictions — it is purely an evaluation mechanism.

Algorithm
For \(K\) training intervals (capped at max_cv_folds):

Hold out interval \(k\) from the training set.
Retrain a fresh model on the remaining \(K-1\) intervals.
Predict the held-out interval using the retrained model:

Segment the held-out interval’s features into contiguous sequences.
Apply bidirectional boundary constraints: the first and last frames of the held-out interval have known labels (from the full label assembly), which serve as initial and terminal Viterbi constraints.
Run predictSequencesBidirectionalConstrained().

Compute per-fold metrics by comparing raw predictions to ground truth on the held-out interval.
Average metrics across all \(K\) folds.

The main model (trained on ALL intervals) remains the one used for Stage 6 prediction. CV results are stored in separate result fields.


Why Full Retrain?
Each fold retrains from scratch rather than using the main model. This is because the HMM’s transition matrix, emission distributions, and initial state distribution are all estimated from training data. Removing one interval changes these parameters, and the difference is the signal we want to measure — how much does the model depend on each block of labeled data?


Boundary Constraints in CV
The held-out interval’s own first and last frame labels serve as bookends. These labels come from the label assembly (which covers all labeled frames), not from the training label_map (which excludes the held-out interval). This is realistic: in production, adjacent labeled blocks provide boundary constraints for unlabeled gaps between them.
