ValidatingFeatures → ConvertingFeatures → AssemblingLabels →
FilteringToTrainingRegion → BalancingClasses → SegmentingSequences →
Training → CrossValidation(5c) → Predicting → ComputingMetrics →
WritingOutput → Complete
Stage 5c (CrossValidation) is skipped when max_cv_folds == 0 or fewer than 2 training intervals exist.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
UI Integration

Validation Region Panel
A RegionSelectionPanel in RegionMode::Validation mode provides a combo box listing all DigitalIntervalSeries in the DataManager. The selected key populates config.validation_interval_key. An “All frames” checkbox is available but defaults to unchecked (no validation region).


Cross-Validation Controls
Located in ModelConfigPanel:

“Cross-validate” checkbox — enables/disables CV (max_cv_folds = 0 when unchecked).
“Max folds” spinbox (1–20, default 5) — caps the number of leave-one-out iterations.



Results Display
ResultsPanel shows three metric sections when available:

Training Metrics — computed on training-region frames using raw predictions (not 100%).
Validation Metrics — computed on validation-region frames if validation_interval_key is set.
Cross-Validation Metrics — averaged across folds, with per-fold accuracy detail.

title: Validation & Cross-Validation
text:
Example Workflow
TensorData: "features" (100,000 frames × 192 features)
Labels: "contact" DigitalIntervalSeries (contact events)
Training region: "train" DIS with intervals [1000–2000], [5000–6000], [8000–9000]
Validation region: "validate" DIS with intervals [3000–4000], [7000–7500]

Model trains on frames within [1000–2000] ∪ [5000–6000] ∪ [8000–9000].
CV holds out each training interval in turn (3 folds), retrains on the other 2, predicts the held-out interval with boundary constraints, and reports per-fold accuracy.
Main model predicts all 100k frames. Viterbi uses boundary constraints at labeled block boundaries.
Train metrics: raw predictions vs ground truth on training-region frames.
Validation metrics: raw predictions vs ground truth on validation-region frames.
Output: GT-substituted predictions + probabilities written to DataManager.

text:
Error Handling
Both pipelines use early-return on failure. The failed_stage field indicates where the problem occurred. Common failure modes:

ValidatingFeatures: Feature tensor not found, not 2D, or empty
ConvertingFeatures: All rows dropped due to NaN/Inf
AssemblingLabels: No labels found, incompatible row types
SegmentingSequences: No contiguous sequences meeting minimum length
Training/Fitting: Model failed internally (rare with valid data)
WritingOutput: DataManager write failure

title: Pipelines
text:
Bounding Span (Prediction Region Filtering)
See Prediction Regions for the full design of bounding span computation, output filtering, and constrained Viterbi warm-start.
Summary: BoundingSpan.hpp (pipelines/BoundingSpan.hpp) provides utilities for computing and applying temporal bounding spans when prediction is restricted to a specific interval. When prediction_interval_key is set, the pipeline computes the temporal union of training and prediction intervals, filters features to that range (preserving HMM context), runs prediction, then filters output back to the requested frames.







Function
Description




computeIntervalBounds(series)
Returns [min(start), max(end)] of all intervals


computeRowTimeBounds(times)
Returns [min, max] of a time vector


mergeSpans(a, b)
Returns the union span covering both inputs


filterRowsToSpan(features, times, span)
Filters columns and times to span


filterPredictionsToIntervals(preds, probs, times, intervals)
Keeps only frames within intervals

title: Pipelines
Pipelines
text:
Supervised Dimensionality Reduction Pipeline
SupervisedDimReductionPipeline (pipelines/SupervisedDimReductionPipeline.hpp) combines label assembly with supervised projection to produce a logit-space TensorData output.
The pipeline trains on labeled observations only, then transforms all valid rows (labeled and unlabeled) to produce a complete output tensor. This enables scatter visualization where both labeled clusters and unlabeled context points are visible.

Pipeline Stages
ValidatingFeatures → ConvertingFeatures → AssemblingLabels →
FilteringTrainingRegion → FittingAndTransforming → WritingOutput → Complete


Configuration
SupervisedDimReductionPipelineConfig config;

// Model
config.model_name = "Logit Projection";        // must be SupervisedDimensionalityReduction
config.model_params = &logit_params;            // or nullptr for defaults

// Features
config.feature_tensor_key = "encoder_features"; // must have RowType::TimeFrameIndex

// Labels (variant — choose one mode)
config.label_config = LabelFromIntervals{"Contact", "NoContact"};
config.label_interval_key = "contact_intervals";

// Conversion
config.conversion_config.drop_nan = true;
config.conversion_config.zscore_normalize = false;

// Training region (optional — restrict which labeled rows are used for fitting)
config.training_interval_key = "training_intervals"; // empty = use all labeled rows

// Output
config.output_key = "logit_projection";
config.time_key_str = "camera";
config.defer_dm_writes = false;                 // set true for background thread


Label Modes
The pipeline supports the same 4 label modes as ClassificationPipeline:








Mode
Type
Notes




LabelFromIntervals
DigitalIntervalSeries key
Binary: inside/outside interval


LabelFromTimeEntityGroups
EntityGroupManager group IDs
Per-group class assignment


LabelFromDataEntityGroups
EntityGroupManager group IDs
Per-entity group membership


LabelFromEvents
DigitalEventSeries key
Event proximity labeling



Group-based modes produce unlabeled rows (rows with no group assignment), marked with sentinel value num_classes. These rows are excluded from training but still projected by the fitted model into the output tensor.


Training Region
When training_interval_key is set (non-empty), the FilteringTrainingRegion stage restricts the labeled training rows to only those whose TimeFrameIndex falls within any interval of the specified DigitalIntervalSeries. This uses the same filterTrainingRowsToIntervals() utility from BoundingSpan.hpp as the classification pipeline.

If the key references a missing DigitalIntervalSeries, the pipeline fails at FilteringTrainingRegion with an error message.
If training_interval_key is empty, the stage is a no-op and all labeled rows are used.
The transform is still applied to all valid rows — only training (fitting) is restricted.
result.rows_excluded_by_training_region reports how many labeled rows were excluded.



Column Naming
Output columns are named "Logit:<ClassName>" using the actual class names from label assembly, not generic indices. For LabelFromIntervals{"Contact", "NoContact"}:

Class 0 (negative/outside) → "Logit:NoContact"
Class 1 (positive/inside) → "Logit:Contact"

Note: Class 0 is always the negative/outside class for interval-based labeling. Use the actual class names to identify columns — do not rely on column order.


Entry Point
auto result = runSupervisedDimReductionPipeline(dm, registry, config, progress_callback);

if (result.success) {
    // result.num_observations — all valid rows (NaN-dropped)
    // result.num_training_observations — labeled subset used for fitting
    // result.unlabeled_count — rows projected but excluded from training
    // result.num_classes, result.class_names
    // result.output_key — DataManager key of new TensorData
    // result.fitted_model — reusable for re-projection
}


Result Fields







Field
Description




success
Whether the pipeline completed


error_message
Human-readable error (if failed)


failed_stage
Which stage failed


num_observations
All valid rows after NaN dropping


num_training_observations
Labeled rows used for fitting


num_input_features
Number of input tensor columns


num_output_dimensions
Number of classes (output columns)


rows_dropped_nan
Rows dropped due to NaN/Inf


unlabeled_count
Rows excluded from training (group modes)


rows_excluded_by_training_region
Labeled rows excluded by training region filter


num_classes
Number of classes discovered


class_names
Class name per output column (no “Logit:” prefix)


output_key
Created TensorData DataManager key


deferred_output
shared_ptr<TensorData> for main-thread writing


fitted_model
Ownership transferred — reusable





Relationship to Other Pipelines









Pipeline
Labels
Transforms
Output




DimReductionPipeline
None (unsupervised)
All rows
TensorData: reduced space


ClassificationPipeline
Required
Labeled rows
Predictions + metrics


SupervisedDimReductionPipeline
Required for training
All rows
TensorData: logit space



The SupervisedDimReductionPipeline is unique in that it trains on a labeled subset but produces output that covers all valid inputs — filling in logit-space projections even for rows with no label.

Related documents: - Precondition Documentation Protocol — Step 8 applies this protocol to ML operation interfaces - src/MLCore/features/FeatureConverter.hpp — the single normalization entry point after this refactor


Feature scaling (z-score normalization) is currently handled inconsistently across MLCore algorithms. Some algorithms perform internal scaling silently, others don’t, and the pre-algorithm z-score checkbox interacts with per-algorithm scaling in confusing ways. This leads to:

Double-scaling risk: User checks “Z-score normalize” AND PCA/Supervised PCA default scale=true → data is standardized twice.
Inconsistent defaults: Switching from PCA (scales by default) to Robust PCA (no scaling) silently drops scaling.
Missing scaling option: Classification algorithms (Logistic Regression, Softmax, HMM) have no z-score option at all, despite being scale-sensitive.
Mixed normalization bases: When z-score uses all-data statistics but Supervised PCA uses labeled-subset statistics.

Single responsibility: Feature scaling is a precondition handled once at the pipeline input stage, not inside individual algorithms.

The z-score normalize checkbox becomes the sole scaling control.
Algorithms receive data that is either scaled or not, and do not re-scale.
All algorithms center (subtract mean) internally as needed — centering is mathematically distinct from scaling and is inherent to PCA/Robust PCA.

Serialized models: Existing saved PCA models (via PCAOperation::save()) store scaled and stddev fields. The load() method should handle legacy formats gracefully — if scaled=true is found in a saved model, transform() should still apply the stored stddev for backward compatibility. Consider a version field or try/catch during deserialization.
User-visible behavior change: PCA results will differ slightly if a user was running PCA with scale=true (default) but z-score checkbox unchecked. After this change, they would need to check the z-score box to get equivalent behavior. This should be noted in release notes.




Z-score normalization ((x - mean) / std) performs both centering (subtract mean) and scaling (divide by std). This means if z-score is applied pre-algorithm, the data arriving at PCA is already centered. PCA’s internal centering then computes mean ≈ 0 and subtracts it — a near no-op on already-centered data.
Why keep internal centering anyway:

Z-score is optional. The user can uncheck the z-score box. When they do, PCA’s internal centering is essential for correctness (PCA on un-centered data produces wrong eigenvectors).
Idempotent. Centering already-centered data is a no-op (subtracts ~0). It costs nothing and causes no harm.
Supervised methods have a different centering basis. Supervised PCA centers on the labeled subset, not all data. Even if z-score was computed on all data (making the global mean ≈ 0), the labeled subset’s mean may differ. This subset-specific centering is semantically meaningful for supervised algorithms.
Model serialization. The stored mean vector is needed for transform() on new data. Removing internal centering would break the projection pipeline.

Bottom line: Internal centering stays in all PCA-family algorithms. It is harmless when z-score is on, essential when z-score is off, and required for projection of new data.




Min-max normalization: Not currently offered; could be added as a future ConversionConfig option.
Per-feature selection of scaling: All features are scaled uniformly. Not needed for current use cases.

text:

title: MLCore Feature Scaling Roadmap
text:
Serialized models: Existing saved PCA models (via PCAOperation::save()) store scaled and stddev fields. The load() method should handle legacy formats gracefully — if scaled=true is found in a saved model, transform() should still apply the stored stddev for backward compatibility. Consider a version field or try/catch during deserialization.
User-visible behavior change: PCA results will differ slightly if a user was running PCA with scale=true (default) but z-score checkbox unchecked. After this change, they would need to check the z-score box to get equivalent behavior. This should be noted in release notes.

title: MLCore Feature Scaling Roadmap
text:
Z-score normalization ((x - mean) / std) performs both centering (subtract mean) and scaling (divide by std). This means if z-score is applied pre-algorithm, the data arriving at PCA is already centered. PCA’s internal centering then computes mean ≈ 0 and subtracts it — a near no-op on already-centered data.
Why keep internal centering anyway:

Z-score is optional. The user can uncheck the z-score box. When they do, PCA’s internal centering is essential for correctness (PCA on un-centered data produces wrong eigenvectors).
Idempotent. Centering already-centered data is a no-op (subtracts ~0). It costs nothing and causes no harm.
Supervised methods have a different centering basis. Supervised PCA centers on the labeled subset, not all data. Even if z-score was computed on all data (making the global mean ≈ 0), the labeled subset’s mean may differ. This subset-specific centering is semantically meaningful for supervised algorithms.
Model serialization. The stored mean vector is needed for transform() on new data. Removing internal centering would break the projection pipeline.

Bottom line: Internal centering stays in all PCA-family algorithms. It is harmless when z-score is on, essential when z-score is off, and required for projection of new data.

Provide two Quarto how-to guides demonstrating GLM-HMM fitting for whisker contact detection using the WhiskerToolbox Python bindings. One guide uses the ssm library; the other uses dynamax (JAX-based).
Both guides follow the same data contract: extract encoder features and labeled intervals from DataManager, fit a GLM-HMM, predict state sequences, and write results back as DigitalIntervalSeries.



See HMM_WhiskerContact_Analysis.md for the full problem analysis. The standard HMM’s fixed transition matrix cannot adapt to feature-dependent dynamics (e.g., pole position, whisking phase). A GLM-HMM replaces the static transition matrix with a softmax regression on observed features, solving this limitation without requiring separate models per condition.

title: LARS Projection Operation
text:
LARSProjectionOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that uses mlpack’s LARS (Least Angle Regression Stagewise) algorithm in a one-vs-all configuration to learn a linear projection from \(D\)-dimensional feature space into \(C\)-dimensional class space (one dimension per class).
The regularization mode controls which penalty terms are active:

LASSO (\(\lambda_1 > 0, \lambda_2 = 0\)): L1 penalty produces sparse coefficients, effectively performing feature selection
Ridge (\(\lambda_1 = 0, \lambda_2 > 0\)): L2 penalty produces dense, shrunken coefficients
Elastic Net (\(\lambda_1 > 0, \lambda_2 > 0\)): Combined L1+L2 for grouped sparsity

The objective minimized for each class \(c\) is:
\[\min_{\beta_c} \frac{1}{2} \| X \beta_c - y_c \|_2^2 + \lambda_1 \| \beta_c \|_1 + \frac{1}{2} \lambda_2 \| \beta_c \|_2^2\]
where \(y_c\) is a binary indicator (1 if observation belongs to class \(c\), 0 otherwise).
Task type: SupervisedDimensionalityReduction

title: LARS Projection Operation
text:
LARSProjectionOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that uses mlpack’s LARS (Least Angle Regression Stagewise) algorithm in a one-vs-all configuration to learn a linear projection from \(D\)-dimensional feature space into \(C\)-dimensional class space (one dimension per class).
The regularization mode controls which penalty terms are active:

LASSO (\(\lambda_1 > 0, \lambda_2 = 0\)): L1 penalty produces sparse coefficients, effectively performing feature selection
Ridge (\(\lambda_1 = 0, \lambda_2 > 0\)): L2 penalty produces dense, shrunken coefficients
Elastic Net (\(\lambda_1 > 0, \lambda_2 > 0\)): Combined L1+L2 for grouped sparsity

The objective minimized for each class \(c\) is:
\[\min_{\beta_c} \frac{1}{2} \| X \beta_c - y_c \|_2^2 + \lambda_1 \| \beta_c \|_1 + \frac{1}{2} \lambda_2 \| \beta_c \|_2^2\]
where \(y_c\) is a binary indicator (1 if observation belongs to class \(c\), 0 otherwise).
Task type: SupervisedDimensionalityReduction

Feature scaling (z-score normalization) is the caller’s responsibility via FeatureConverter. The operation sets normalizeData=false to avoid double-normalization.

title: LARS Projection Operation
text:
Architecture

Class Hierarchy
MLModelOperation (interface)
  └── MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (abstract base)
        └── LARSProjectionOperation (concrete)


Pimpl Pattern
LARSProjectionOperation.hpp  →  MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (public API)
LARSProjectionOperation.cpp  →  mlpack::LARS (hidden, used only during training)
The Impl struct holds:

arma::mat weight_matrix — \((C \times D)\) assembled from per-class regression coefficients
arma::vec bias — \((C)\) intercept per class
std::vector<std::size_t> active_features — union of non-zero coefficient indices
num_classes, num_features, col_names — metadata
trained — readiness flag

Unlike LogitProjectionOperation, the mlpack LARS objects are not retained after training. Only the extracted weight matrix and bias are kept for projection and serialization.


One-vs-All Training
For \(C\) classes, the operation trains \(C\) independent mlpack::LARS models:

For each class \(c \in [0, C)\):

Construct binary responses: \(y_c(i) = 1\) if label\((i) = c\), else \(0\)
Train mlpack::LARS with the resolved lambda1/lambda2
Extract lars.Beta() → row \(c\) of weight_matrix
Extract lars.Intercept() → bias(c)
Collect lars.ActiveSet() into the union of active features

Projection: \(\text{result} = W \cdot X + b\) (broadcast)



Projection
Both fitTransform() and transform() compute:
\[\text{result}_{c,i} = \sum_{d=0}^{D-1} W_{c,d} \cdot X_{d,i} + b_c\]
Output shape: \((C \times N)\), matching LogitProjectionOperation.

title: LARS Projection Operation
text:
Feature Selection
The activeFeatureIndices() method returns the sorted union of non-zero coefficient indices across all per-class models. In LASSO mode with a sufficiently large lambda1, many features will have zero coefficients. This provides a principled feature selection mechanism.

title: LARS Projection Operation
text:
Serialization
Save/load uses cereal binary archives, storing:

num_classes, num_features, col_names, active_features
weight_matrix (flattened C × D)
bias (C values)

This is identical to the pattern used by LogitProjectionOperation — no mlpack objects are serialized.

title: MLCore Widget
text:
Pipeline Execution
All three pipelines (four including supervised dim reduction) run asynchronously in a QThread background worker:

UI panels are disabled during execution
Progress callback updates a status label and indeterminate progress bar
On completion, results are displayed in the output panel
On failure, an error message is shown
Deferred writes are committed on the main thread for thread safety

The _runPipelineAsync() / _runClusteringPipelineAsync() / _runDimReductionPipelineAsync() / _runSupervisedDimReductionPipelineAsync() methods assemble the config from panel state, spawn a worker thread, and connect completion signals.

title: MLCore Widget

Incoming

Outgoing

Clicking an output data key in ResultsPanel or ClusterOutputPanel calls SelectionContext::setDataFocus so other widgets (DataViewer, DataInspector) navigate to that output.
Clicking a putative group entry calls SelectionContext::setSelectedEntities() to highlight the group’s entities across all widgets.

title: TriageSession
text: The TriageSession library provides a Mark/Commit/Recall state machine for triage workflows. It is a pure C++ library with no Qt dependency, designed as a consumer of the Command Architecture.

title: TriageSession
text: The TriageSession library provides a Mark/Commit/Recall state machine for triage workflows. It is a pure C++ library with no Qt dependency, designed as a consumer of the Command Architecture.

title: TriageSession
text:
Source Location
src/TriageSession/

title: TriageSession
text:
Library

CMake target: TriageSession (static library)
Alias: WhiskerToolbox::TriageSession
Dependencies: DataManager (for Commands API and data access)

title: TriageSession
text:
Architecture

State Machine
The triage session manages a two-state finite machine:
IDLE  ──[mark()]──►  MARKING  ──[commit()]──►  IDLE
                        │
                        └──[recall()]──►  IDLE

Idle: No triage in progress. mark() transitions to Marking.
Marking: A triage range has been started. commit() executes the pipeline and transitions to Idle on success. recall() aborts and returns to Idle.



Core Class: TriageSession







Method
Description




setPipeline(seq)
Configure the CommandSequenceDescriptor to execute on commit


pipeline()
Access the current pipeline


mark(frame)
Begin marking from the given TimeFrameIndex


recall()
Abort marking, return to Idle


commit(current_frame, dm)
Execute pipeline for [mark_frame, current_frame], transition to Idle on success


state()
Query current state (Idle or Marking)


markFrame()
The frame where marking started (only valid when Marking)


lastCommitCommands()
Commands from the last successful commit (for undo support)


takeLastCommitCommands()
Move ownership of last commit’s commands out





Commit Flow
On commit(), the session:

Validates preconditions (must be in Marking state, non-null DataManager, non-empty pipeline)
Creates a CommandContext with the DataManager and runtime variables:

mark_frame — the frame passed to mark()
current_frame — the frame passed to commit()

Calls executeSequence() from the Command Architecture
On success: transitions to Idle and retains executed commands for undo
On failure: remains in Marking state so the user can retry or recall



Relationship to Command Architecture
TriageSession has no knowledge of what commands are in its pipeline. It simply populates runtime variables and delegates to executeSequence(). Any valid CommandSequenceDescriptor can serve as a triage pipeline — move commands, interval tracking, save commands, or any combination.

title: KeymapSystem Library Reference
text: The KeymapSystem static library (src/WhiskerToolbox/KeymapSystem/) provides the core infrastructure for configurable, context-aware keyboard shortcuts. It implements action registration, scope-based resolution, user override management, and conflict detection.

title: KeymapSystem Library Reference
text:
Files

KeyAction.hpp
Defines the core action types:

KeyActionScopeKind — Enum: Global, EditorFocused, AlwaysRouted
KeyActionScope — Pairs a scope kind with an optional EditorTypeId. Factory methods: global(), editorFocused(type_id), alwaysRouted(type_id)
KeyActionDescriptor — Pure metadata for a bindable action: action_id, display_name, category, scope, and default_binding



Keymap.hpp
Defines binding types:

KeymapEntry — Runtime resolved binding (action → key sequence, enabled flag, override flag)
KeymapOverrideEntry — Serializable user override using std::string for reflect-cpp compatibility. Stored in AppPreferencesData for persistence.



KeyActionAdapter.hpp / KeyActionAdapter.cpp
Composition-based component for receiving keymap dispatches. Widgets create a KeyActionAdapter as a child QObject and install a handler lambda. No inheritance required.
Key API:

setHandler(Handler) — Install callback std::function<bool(QString const &)>
handleKeyAction(action_id) — Called by KeymapManager to dispatch
setInstanceId() / setTypeId() — Associate with an editor instance/type



KeymapManager.hpp / KeymapManager.cpp
Central manager class (owned by MainWindow). Inherits QObject.
Registration API:

registerAction(descriptor) — Register action metadata (returns false on duplicate)
unregisterAction(action_id) — Remove action and its override

Query API:

allActions() — All registered descriptors
action(action_id) — Lookup by ID
bindingFor(action_id) — Effective key (override > default)
isActionEnabled(action_id) — Check enabled state

Override API:

setUserOverride(action_id, key) — Override key binding
clearUserOverride(action_id) — Revert to default
clearAllOverrides() — Reset all customizations
setActionEnabled(action_id, enabled) — Enable/disable

Resolution API:

resolveKeyPress(key, focused_type_id) — Scope-priority resolution: EditorFocused > AlwaysRouted > Global
detectConflicts() — Find same-key/same-scope collisions

Adapter routing:

registerAdapter(adapter) — Register for dispatch (auto-deregisters on destruction)
dispatchAction(action_id, target_type, target_instance) — Route to matching adapter

Serialization:

exportOverrides() / importOverrides(overrides) — Round-trip persistence

Signal: bindingsChanged() — emitted on any binding modification.
Event filter (installed on QApplication by MainWindow):

eventFilter(obj, event) — Intercepts QEvent::KeyPress. Bypasses text-input widgets (QLineEdit, QTextEdit, QPlainTextEdit, QComboBox, QAbstractSpinBox). Resolves and dispatches through scope priority. Returns false (pass-through) when no action matches.
setEditorRegistry(registry) — Set the EditorRegistry used for focus tracking via SelectionContext::activeEditorId().

The goal was to determine whether adding a GPU (LibTorch CUDA) path to the existing Armadillo-based TensorCAR transform is worthwhile, and to identify the crossover points and optimal block sizes.

title: TensorCAR: GPU vs CPU Benchmark Analysis
text:
Transfer Overhead
Data must be copied between CPU and GPU memory. At 900k × 384 channels (1.4 GB):

CPU → GPU: ~192 ms
GPU → CPU: ~275 ms

Transfer saturates PCIe at ~7 Gi/s. For a single CAR operation, transfer dominates at large block sizes (e.g., 900k rows: 467 ms transfer vs 13 ms compute for mean-CAR). This means GPU acceleration is most effective when:

Data is already on the GPU (chained transforms), or
The compute cost exceeds transfer cost (always true for median-CAR, true for mean-CAR at 10k+ rows).

Recommended GPU Block Size
Based on throughput curves, 100,000 rows is the recommended default gpu_block_hint:

At 30 kHz sampling, this is ~3.3 seconds of data
Memory footprint: ~153 MB at 384 channels
Achieves 80–95% of peak GPU throughput for both mean and median
Large enough to amortize kernel launch overhead, small enough for reasonable memory use

title: TensorCAR: GPU vs CPU Benchmark Analysis
text:
Threading and Time-Domain Parallelism
CAR is embarrassingly parallel across time (rows). Each row’s reduction across channels is independent. Controlled experiments with OMP_NUM_THREADS confirmed:



Backend

Torch CPU Median
147 ms

Near-linear scaling



All measurements at 30k × 384.
Key findings:

Armadillo does not parallelize arma::mean(mat, 1) or arma::median(mat, 1) across rows. OMP_NUM_THREADS has no effect.
LibTorch CPU uses its internal thread pool (ATen parallel_for). The effect is dramatic for median (4.2× from 6 cores) because the per-row sort is expensive and independent. Mean shows modest gains because it is memory-bandwidth-bound.
LibTorch CUDA parallelizes most aggressively — every row gets its own warp(s). More rows = more thread blocks = better SM utilization, which is why throughput climbs with row count.
LibTorch auto-detects available cores. No environment variables need to be set at runtime. Use torch::set_num_threads(N) for programmatic control if needed.

title: TensorCAR: GPU vs CPU Benchmark Analysis
text:
In-Place vs Out-of-Place
Benchmarks comparing in-place (sub_()) vs out-of-place (input - ref) at 30k × 384:



Variant
Armadillo
Torch CPU
Torch CUDA




Out-of-place
11,419 µs
7,516 µs
502 µs


In-place (+clone)
11,303 µs
10,889 µs
801 µs



The in-place variants are not faster when the original must be preserved (both paths do one full copy). LibTorch out-of-place is actually faster because input - ref fuses allocation and write into a single streamed pass, while clone() + sub_() requires a read-modify-write on the same buffer.
The real savings are in the production code path, which currently performs 2–3 unnecessary full-matrix copies:

result_mat = input_mat — copy entire matrix (153 MB)
matToFlat(result_mat) — column-major to row-major conversion (153 MB)
TensorData::createTimeSeries2D(flat) — copy into new storage (153 MB)

A LibTorch-native path where TensorData operates directly on torch::Tensor would eliminate all of these copies. Combined with in-place transform support in the pipeline (where the original doesn’t need to be preserved), this would reduce memory traffic from ~460 MB to near zero for a 384ch × 100k block.
crumbs: TensorCAR: GPU vs CPU Benchmark Analysis

title: TensorCAR: GPU vs CPU Benchmark Analysis
text:
Architecture Implications
Adding GPU support to TensorCAR does not require coupling TransformsV2 to the DeepLearning module. The recommended approach:

Add conditional find_package(Torch QUIET) directly to the TransformsV2 CMakeLists.txt
Use torch::cuda::is_available() inline — no DeviceManager sharing needed
Both TransformsV2 and DeepLearning submit to the same CUDA context, which handles concurrent kernels correctly

For in-place transform support, the TransformsV2 pipeline would need:

A parallel registration path accepting (Container&, Params, Context) → void
A supports_in_place metadata flag on ContainerTransformMetadata
Pipeline executor logic: when output_key == input_key and the transform supports in-place, pass a mutable reference and skip reallocation

title: Contact-Aligned Spikes Performance Analysis

Background
In neural data analysis, we often need to: 1. Align spike events to behavioral events (e.g., contact onsets) 2. Extract normalized time values relative to the alignment point 3. Pass these values to OpenGL for rendering raster plots
This benchmark measures the performance of this pipeline using real ground truth data with ~5,338 contact intervals and ~3,031 spikes.

Key Findings

✅ Normalized Time Extraction: 0.167 ms (Well Under Target!)
The RasterMapper::mapEventsInWindow approach used by EventPlotWidget is extremely efficient: - Target: < 50 ms - Actual: 0.167 ms - Performance: ~300x faster than target
This confirms that the rendering pipeline is highly optimized and suitable for real-time updates.


⚠️ GatherResult Creation Bottleneck Identified

Method

Root Cause: The IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter used by gatherWithIntervalAlignment adds significant overhead: - Iterator wrapper overhead (accessing intervals through adapter) - Per-interval alignment time computation - Time conversion checks (getTimeConverter()) even when not needed - Additional vector allocations for _alignment_times
Impact: The adapter adds ~5.4 ms of overhead (4.8x slower) compared to basic gather().

title: Contact-Aligned Spikes Performance Analysis
text:
Detailed Analysis

Phase-by-Phase Breakdown

1. GatherResult Creation
With Adapter (gatherWithIntervalAlignment): - Time: 6.80 ms - Creates IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter wrapper - Stores alignment times for each interval - Performs time conversion checks - Recommendation: Use basic gather() when alignment metadata isn’t needed
Without Adapter (gather()): - Time: 1.43 ms - Direct interval iteration - Only stores interval bounds - 4.8x faster than adapter version
Direct View Creation: - Time: 1.24 ms - Baseline performance - No GatherResult overhead - 5.5x faster than adapter version


2. Normalized Time Extraction
RasterMapper Approach: - Time: 0.167 ms - Uses RasterMapper::mapEventsInWindow - Filters events within ±500 window - Converts to relative time coordinates - Materializes normalized float values
This phase is extremely efficient and not a bottleneck.


3. Full Pipeline
Combined Performance: - GatherResult creation: 6.80 ms (with adapter) or 1.43 ms (basic) - Normalized extraction: 0.167 ms - Total: ~7.0 ms (with adapter) or ~1.6 ms (basic)
Note: FullPipeline benchmark shows 5.93 ms, which is slightly faster than CreateGatherResult alone, likely due to caching/optimization effects.



Bottleneck Identification
The primary bottleneck is GatherResult creation with adapter (6.80 ms), specifically:

Adapter Iterator Overhead (~3-4 ms)

Wrapper indirection when accessing intervals
Alignment time computation per interval
Iterator state management

Time Conversion Checks (~1-2 ms)

getTimeConverter() called for every interval
Even when timeframes match (no conversion needed)

Additional Metadata Storage (~0.5-1 ms)

Storing _alignment_times vector
Extra allocations and memory operations

title: Contact-Aligned Spikes Performance Analysis
text:
Recommendations

1. Use Basic gather() When Possible
If you only need interval starts for alignment, use:
auto gathered = gather(_spikes, _contacts);  // 1.43 ms instead of 6.80 ms
Then compute alignment times manually if needed:
for (size_t i = 0; i < gathered.size(); ++i) {
    auto alignment_time = gathered.intervalAt(i).start;
    // Use alignment_time for normalization
}
Performance gain: 4.8x faster (1.43 ms vs 6.80 ms)


2. Cache GatherResult
Since GatherResult creation takes 1.43-6.80 ms depending on method: - Cache the GatherResult when contacts don’t change - Only recreate when contact data is modified - This is especially important for interactive visualization


3. Optimize the Adapter (Future Work)
If gatherWithIntervalAlignment is required, potential optimizations: - Lazy alignment computation: Only compute alignment times when accessed - Skip time conversion checks: Cache timeframe comparison result - Batch processing: Process intervals in batches to improve cache locality - Specialized path: Fast path when timeframes match (no conversion needed)


4. Current Performance is Excellent
With basic gather(): - GatherResult creation: 1.43 ms - Normalized extraction: 0.167 ms - Total: ~1.6 ms
This is 31x faster than the 50 ms target, making it suitable for: - Real-time rendering updates - Interactive visualization - Frequent data refreshes

Key Finding: RasterMapper Mapping is the Bottleneck
The RasterMapper mapping phase takes 27.7 ms (84% of total time), which is significantly slower than the earlier isolated benchmark (0.167 ms). This discrepancy suggests:

Materialization overhead: Converting lazy ranges to vectors for each trial
Per-trial overhead: Setting up RasterMapper for each of 5,338 contacts
Window filtering: The mapEventsInWindow filter operation for each trial

Performance per contact: 27.7 ms / 5,338 contacts = 5.2 µs per contact, which is reasonable but accumulates to a significant total.

Batch Materialization: Instead of materializing each trial separately, consider batching
Lazy Evaluation: Keep ranges lazy until absolutely necessary
Pre-compute Windows: If window sizes are constant, pre-compute window bounds
Reduce Per-Trial Overhead: Minimize setup costs in the mapping loop

The benchmark results demonstrate:

✅ Normalized time extraction is highly optimized (0.167 ms isolated)
⚠️ Adapter overhead is significant (5.4 ms overhead)
✅ Basic gather() is efficient (1.43 ms, only 15% overhead)
⚠️ RasterMapper materialization is the bottleneck (27.7 ms in full workflow)
✅ Layout and SceneBuilding are fast (<1 ms each)

Recommendations: - Use basic gather() when alignment metadata isn’t needed - Optimize RasterMapper materialization (consider batch processing or lazy evaluation) - Cache GatherResult when contacts don’t change - Profile the RasterMapper mapping loop to identify specific bottlenecks

title: Min–max polyline decimation

CorePlotting::decimatePolyLineBatchMinMax() reduces the number of vertices in each line strip of a RenderablePolyLineBatch by uniform x-binning and keeping the minimum and maximum y in each bin (plus the first and last original vertices). title: Building Custom Plot Widgets with CorePlotting
text:
The CorePlotting library is a framework-agnostic plotting engine designed for high-performance time-series and spatial data visualization. It separates the concerns of Data Processing, Layout Calculation, and Rendering to ensure testability and flexibility.
When building a Qt widget (like DataViewer_Widget or OpenGLWidget), you act as the Integrator, connecting these distinct layers.


The rendering pipeline follows a unidirectional data flow:
graph TD
Data[Data Source] -->|LayoutRequest| Layout[Layout Engine]
Layout -->|LayoutResponse| Mapper[Coordinate Mappers]
Data --> Mapper
Mapper -->|Mapped Elements| Builder[Scene Builder]
Builder -->|RenderableScene| Renderer[Scene Renderer]
Renderer -->|OpenGL| Screen[QOpenGLWidget]

Layout Engine: Determines where series should appear (vertical stacking, row layouts).

Mappers: Transforms domain data (e.g., AnalogTimeSeries) into world-space geometry.

Scene Builder: Batches geometry into optimization-friendly structures.

Scene Renderer: Handles the actual OpenGL draw calls (via PlottingOpenGL).

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

title: Threaded Loading Roadmap
section: Why This Is a Simple Concurrency Case
text:
Why This Is a Simple Concurrency Case
Data loading is a pure producer: the worker reads from a file (no DataManager dependency), builds a complete data object, and hands it off. There is no shared mutable state during the work.
Deep Learning:  Worker ↔ DataManager (reads frames, writes results)
Data Loading:   Worker ← File system only → returns finished data object
The existing IFormatLoader::load() is already a pure function: file path in, LoadResult out. Moving it to a worker thread is mechanical. This uses the fork-join pattern described in the Concurrency Architecture — no write reservations needed because the data object doesn’t exist in DataManager until the worker is done.

title: Threaded Loading Roadmap
text:
Implementation Plan

Phase 1: Loader Progress Infrastructure
Goal: Enable loaders to report progress so users see feedback during loading, even before threading is added.

Add progress callback to IFormatLoader::load() — Optional parameter: LoadProgressCallback progress = nullptr where using LoadProgressCallback = std::function<void(int percent)>.
Implement progress in CSV loaders — CSV loaders can report bytes_read / file_size * 100 periodically (e.g., every 10,000 rows).
Implement progress in binary loaders — Report per-channel progress for multi-channel batch loads.
Add progress bar to import widgets — Each type-specific import widget gets a QProgressBar that updates during loading.

At this point loading is still synchronous, but users see progress.


Phase 2: Worker Thread for Single-Object Loading
Goal: Move file parsing off the main thread for single-object imports.

Create DataLoadWorker : QThread — Define in a shared header or in the import widget. Constructor takes: loader reference, filepath, data type, config, output key name. run() calls loader.load(filepath, type, config, progress). Emits progressChanged(int percent) signal. Stores LoadResult for harvest.
Add cancellation support — std::atomic<bool> _cancel_requested checked by the loader progress callback. CSV loader checks between row batches; binary loader checks between channels.
Wire import widgets to use DataLoadWorker — On “Load” click: disable UI, create worker, connect signals, start. On finished: harvest result, call _data_manager->setData() on main thread, re-enable UI, show success/error message.
Handle errors — If LoadResult::success is false, show error dialog on main thread. If cancelled, show cancellation message.



Phase 3: Batch Loading and Polish
Goal: Support multi-channel binary imports and general robustness.

Extend DataLoadWorker for batch loads — Worker calls loadBatch(), stores BatchLoadResult. Main thread loops results and calls setData() for each.
Suppress intermediate notifications — When writing N results from a batch, use a bulk-write pattern: write all with notification suppressed, then call _notifyObservers() once. This may require a small DataManager enhancement (a setData overload with NotifyObservers parameter).
Prevent concurrent loads — If a load is already in progress, disable the Load button across all import widgets. Only one DataLoadWorker active at a time.
Cancel button — Wire the progress bar’s cancel button (or repurpose the Load button) to call worker->requestCancel().



Phase 4: Testing and Documentation

Unit test loader progress — Verify CSV loader reports monotonically increasing progress. Verify cancellation returns partial result or empty result.
Integration test — Load a large CSV via DataLoadWorker, verify the resulting data matches a synchronous load.
Developer documentation — Create docs/developer/DataManager/threaded_loading.qmd after implementation, documenting the pattern and how to extend to new loaders.

title: Data Manager
text: The DataManager has 3 core functionalities

title: Data Manager
section: Time Frame Structure for Multi-Rate Data Visualization
text:
Time Frame Structure for Multi-Rate Data Visualization
An important feature of the program is being able to simultaneously visualize data that was collected at different sampling rates. The time frame structure is designed to indicate when time events occur at a particular sampling frequency. The data manager is responsible for keeping track of which data is located in what time frame. Multiple data objects can belong to one time frame, but one data object can only belong to a single time frame. However, if the relationship between time frame objects is specified, then data requested in one coordinate system can be converted to another.

Illustrative Example: Electrophysiology and Video Data
Consider the following example: an NI-DAQ box samples at 30000 Hz for electrophysiology. This results in analog data with 30000 samples per second as well as event data for sorted spikes at 30000 Hz resolution. The experiment may have also had a high-speed video camera collecting frames at 500 Hz. A digital event for each frame was recorded with the same NI-DAQ. The user may have processed the video frames to categorize behavior, which would also be at the 500 Hz resolution and be interval data.


Default Time Frame and Customization
The default time frame is simply called “time” and defaults to numbers between 1 and the number of frames in a loaded video. The scroll bar operates in this time frame and consequently sends signals in this time frame. The user can override this default time frame and replace it with an event structure with the same number of samples but where each event corresponds to the 30000 Hz resolution digitized camera frame exposures. The user can then create a new clock called “master” that again counts from 1,2,3,… up to the total number of samples collected by the NI-DAQ.


Data Indexing within Time Frames
All data manager data types have a notion of “index,” and these correspond to the time frame they are associated with. This index property is important because data may be sparsely labeled and not have the same number of samples as their time frame.


Widget Considerations for Data Synchronization
Widgets that represent different data simultaneously must be aware of accounting for these differences.


Performance Notes
The user should also be aware that pointer indirections sample by sample for large vectors will be quite inefficient. If the user needs to find a series of values in a range in a different coordinate system it is most likely important to.

Data Types

Point
A Point represents a 2 dimensional (x, y) coordinate, which may vary in time. The PointData structure can hold multiple points per unit time.



Examples of Point Data
















Line
A Line represents a 2 dimensional (x,y) collection of points, which may vary with time. The collection of points is ordered, meaning that each point is positioned relative to its neighbors. The LineData structure can hold multiple lines per unit time.



Examples of Line Data














Currently, lines are represented by a raw list of points. One could imagine lines being parameterized in different ways, such as the coefficients of a polynomial fit. For many calculations, the parameterized version of a line may be less memory intensive and more efficient.


Mask
A mask represents a 2 dimensional collection of points, which may vary with time. Compared to a Line, the points in a Mask are not ordered. These would correspond to something like a binary segmentation mask over an image. The MaskData structure can hold multiple masks per unit time.



Examples of Mask Data




Binary Semantic Segmentation Labels









A mask may just be thought as a raw pixel, by pixel definition of a shape. Shapes could be defined as bounding boxes, circles, polygons, etc. It may one day be useful to describe shapes in other ways compared to the raw pixel-by-pixel definition.


Tensors
Tensors are N-Dimensional data structures, and consequently very flexible containers for complex data. A concrete use would be to store a Height x Width x Channel array for different timepoints during an experiment. These may be the features output from an encoder neural network that processes a video.

text:
Profiling: Middle Insertion Performance
The following benchmark compares insertion performance across different data types and storage strategies.

Results
=============================================================================
RaggedTimeSeries Storage Benchmark
=============================================================================

Configuration:
  Initial elements: 200000
  Middle insertions: 1000
  Average elements moved: 100000

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
MIDDLE INSERTION PERFORMANCE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Type                              Size    Per Insert    Bytes Moved
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- Trivially Copyable Types (uses memmove) --
Point2D<float>                  8 bytes        18.6 µs        800000 bytes
EntityId                        8 bytes        18.7 µs        800000 bytes
TimeFrameIndex                  8 bytes        19.2 µs        800000 bytes
SoAKey (composite)             24 bytes        65.0 µs       2400000 bytes

-- Non-Trivially Copyable Types (move constructor per element) --
Mask2D (empty)                 24 bytes       190.7 µs       2400000 bytes
Mask2D (100 bytes)             24 bytes       210.9 µs       2400000 bytes
Mask2D (1KB)                   24 bytes       155.7 µs       2400000 bytes
Line2D (empty)                 24 bytes       159.6 µs       2400000 bytes
Line2D (50 points)             24 bytes       169.0 µs       2400000 bytes

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
APPEND PERFORMANCE (for comparison)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Type                        Per Append
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Point2D<float>                 1.38 ns
SoAKey (composite)             5.14 ns
Mask2D (empty)                 2.66 ns
Mask2D (1KB)                 245.80 ns


Analysis
Key findings:

Trivially copyable types are 3-10× faster for middle insertion:

Point2D (8 bytes): 18.6 µs per insert
SoAKey (24 bytes): 65.0 µs per insert

Mask2D (24 bytes, non-trivial): 155-210 µs per insert

Data size inside containers doesn’t matter for moves:

Mask2D with 0 bytes: 190.7 µs
Mask2D with 1KB: 155.7 µs (within noise)

This is because std::vector’s move constructor just swaps 3 pointers.
Append is dramatically faster than middle insertion:

Point2D append: 1.38 ns (13,000× faster than insert)
Mask2D append: 2.66 ns (60,000× faster than insert)

For SoA with views: Keep metadata (TimeFrameIndex, EntityId) in trivially copyable arrays; keep actual data (Mask2D) in append-only storage.

This benchmark compares the current map-based implementation against the SoA approach.

Storage Strategy Benchmark: Map-Based vs Structure of Arrays

SoA (hash, indices only): 0.1 ms, 998 results
Speedup (hash vs map):    75x

SoA:        0.5 ms

Analysis



Operation
Map-Based
SoA

Key findings:

EntityId operations are dramatically faster with SoA:

Single lookup: 13,120× faster (910 µs → 69 ns)
Filtering 1000 EntityIds: 75× faster (8.1 ms → 0.1 ms)

This is because SoA maintains an unordered_map<EntityId, size_t> for O(1) lookup, while map-based requires O(n) full scan.
TimeFrameIndex lookup is slightly faster with Map:

Both are O(log m) where m = unique time points
Map wins by ~1.4× due to direct access vs indirection

Construction favors Map:

Map: 35.3 ms
SoA: 85.5 ms (2.4× slower)

This is because SoA maintains additional acceleration structures.
Iteration strongly favors SoA:

5× faster due to cache-friendly sequential memory access
Map traverses fragmented memory (many small vectors)

For view-based filtering, the SoA approach returns indices only (8 bytes each), while map-based must copy the entire DataEntry<TData> including the data.

title: Data Structure Performance
Data Structure Performance
text:
Recommendations
Based on the profiling results:

Append-only data: SoA storage is highly efficient for data that arrives chronologically. With 200,000 entries, iteration is 5× faster due to cache-friendly memory layout.
Frequent EntityId lookups: The current map-based implementation is O(n) per lookup (910 µs with 200k entries). Adding an entity_to_index map provides O(1) access (69 ns), a 13,000× improvement.
View-based filtering: Use index vectors rather than copying data. Filtering 1000 EntityIds takes 8.1 ms with copy vs 0.1 ms with indices only (75× faster).
Middle insertions: Avoid when possible; batch operations and sort. A single middle insertion into 200k Mask2D elements costs ~170 µs, while append costs ~3 ns.
TimeFrameIndex operations: The current map-based approach is already optimal for time-based lookup (O(log m)). SoA provides similar performance.
Hybrid approach: For best overall performance:

Keep Mask2D/Line2D data in append-only storage (arena)
Maintain parallel vectors of trivially-copyable metadata (TimeFrameIndex, EntityId)
Use hash maps for O(1) EntityId lookup
Views hold index vectors referencing the source data

title: Data Structure Performance
text:
CRTP + Variant vs Virtual Inheritance
An alternative to virtual inheritance for polymorphic storage is the CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) combined with std::variant for type erasure. This pattern is already used in AnalogDataStorage.hpp.

The Two Approaches
Virtual Inheritance (Classic OOP):
template<typename TData>
class IRaggedStorage {
public:
    virtual ~IRaggedStorage() = default;
    virtual size_t size() const = 0;
    virtual TData const& getData(size_t idx) const = 0;
    // ... other pure virtual methods
};

class SourceStorage : public IRaggedStorage<Mask2D> { /* ... */ };
class DerivedStorage : public IRaggedStorage<Mask2D> { /* ... */ };

// Usage via base pointer
std::shared_ptr<IRaggedStorage<Mask2D>> storage = /*...*/;
auto& data = storage->getData(i);  // vtable dispatch
CRTP + Variant (Modern C++):
template<typename Derived, typename TData>
class StorageBase {
public:
    // Static dispatch via CRTP
    size_t size() const { 
        return static_cast<Derived const*>(this)->sizeImpl(); 
    }
    // ...
};

class SourceStorage : public StorageBase<SourceStorage, Mask2D> { /* ... */ };
class DerivedStorage : public StorageBase<DerivedStorage, Mask2D> { /* ... */ };

// Type erasure via variant
using StorageVariant = std::variant<
    std::shared_ptr<SourceStorage>,
    std::shared_ptr<DerivedStorage>
>;

StorageVariant storage = /*...*/;
auto& data = std::visit([i](auto& ptr) -> auto& { 
    return ptr->getData(i); 
}, storage);  // std::visit dispatch


Results
=============================================================================
CRTP + Variant vs Virtual Inheritance Benchmark
=============================================================================

Configuration:
  Entries: 200000
  View size: 10000
  Iterations: 100

=============================================================================
PART 1: Point2D (trivially copyable) - Isolating Dispatch Overhead
=============================================================================

POINT2D: SEQUENTIAL ITERATION (dispatch overhead visible)
Virtual (base ptr):      691.7 µs  (3.5 ns/elem)
CRTP (direct):           332.3 µs  (1.7 ns/elem)
CRTP (variant):          320.8 µs  (1.6 ns/elem)

Speedup vs Virtual:
  CRTP direct:  2.08x
  CRTP variant: 2.16x

=============================================================================
PART 2: Mask2D (non-trivially copyable) - Data Access Dominates
=============================================================================

SOURCE STORAGE: SEQUENTIAL ITERATION
Virtual (base ptr):      7366.7 µs  (36.8 ns/elem)
CRTP (direct):           6635.9 µs  (33.2 ns/elem)
CRTP (variant):          7000.2 µs  (35.0 ns/elem)

Speedup vs Virtual:
  CRTP direct:  1.11x
  CRTP variant: 1.05x

ENTITY ID LOOKUP (10000 lookups)
Virtual:                 4406.9 µs  (440.7 ns/lookup)
CRTP (direct):           3778.3 µs  (377.8 ns/lookup)
CRTP (variant):          2993.7 µs  (299.4 ns/lookup)

Speedup vs Virtual:
  CRTP direct:  1.17x
  CRTP variant: 1.47x


Analysis Summary



Access Pattern
Virtual
CRTP Direct
CRTP Variant




Point2D iteration
3.5 ns/elem
1.7 ns
1.6 ns


Mask2D iteration
36.8 ns/elem
33.2 ns
35.0 ns


EntityId lookup
440.7 ns
377.8 ns
299.4 ns



Key insights:

CRTP is 2× faster for lightweight data (Point2D):

Dispatch overhead becomes visible when data access is cheap
Both direct and variant approaches eliminate vtable lookup

When data access dominates, dispatch doesn’t matter:

For Mask2D (vector-backed), virtual vs CRTP vs variant are within 10%
The CPU spends most time chasing pointers, not dispatching

CRTP Variant wins on hash lookups (1.47× faster):

std::visit can be faster than virtual when compiler can see all types
Better inlining opportunities

When to use each approach:



Approach
Best For




Virtual
Open extension (plugins), external libraries


CRTP Direct
Maximum performance, type known at compile time


CRTP Variant
Closed type set, value semantics, pattern matching



CRTP + Variant advantages:

No heap allocation for small types (in-place storage)
Exhaustive handling enforced by compiler (std::visit)
No virtual destructor overhead
Better optimization across type boundaries

CRTP + Variant disadvantages:

More complex code
All types must be known at compile time
Larger object size (variant stores largest type + discriminant)
Recompile required to add new types

title: File IO
text:
Overview of File IO Requirements
Because Neuralizer is compatible with a wide range of data, its file IO needs to support a wide range of file formats. Some of these file formats will be pre-subscribed, such as data acquisition-specific formats for electrophysiology. Others are more specific to this package, such as for line data that varies over time. We must also be aware from the start that some electrophysiology file sizes can be expected to be larger than easy to work with on a regular desktop machine. For instance, Neuropixel probes record almost 400 channels at 20 kHz and are becoming more routine for use. Consequently, multiple file formats should have the ability to be easily memory-mapped and loaded from disk rather than loading the entire file into RAM.

title: File IO
section: Incremental Data Adjustments and Key-Value Stores
text:
Incremental Data Adjustments and Key-Value Stores
Another important consideration from the start is that many of these data types will be incrementally adjusted. For instance, processing a video sequence frame by frame or manually adjusting the output of an automated algorithm requires changing some subset of data in a much larger scheme. For some of these file types that are greater than hundreds of megabytes, resaving an entire file for point manipulations could be onerous and time-consuming. Consequently, for some file types, it would be advantageous to use a key-value database type structure that allows us to easily make incremental adjustments and only save those changes, consequently saving data much more quickly. To my knowledge, this process is quite common in the wild but uncommon in neuroscience.

title: File IO
text:
Serialization with Captain Proto
The process of data serialization and deserialization will be accomplished with the Captain Proto library. This is able to easily create binary files from more complex data structures, such as those that hold multiple lines of varying size per unit time. This library can define output file structures that are purely binary and would be saved and loaded as entire objects. Alternatively, different definitions can be used to save objects as key-value pairs; for instance, each time point can be the key and the data at that time can be the value.

title: File IO
text:
Memory Mapping Implementation
Captain Proto does not perform memory mapping itself. Memory mapping is different across different types of file systems, so to maintain cross-platform use, we will need to either specify different interfaces for interacting with Captain Proto or we could use another third-party library that does this for us. Boost.Interprocess is commonly cited for this purpose, but there are others.

title: File IO
text:
Key-Value Database Libraries
For key-value database structures, there are multiple libraries available. Many of these are mature and designed to work with servers of extremely large datasets, and some have been developed by very large companies. One of the most popular is called LMDB, but in my test cases, this appears to be not as great with Windows. Using this library requires specifying some maximum file size; on Linux, the resulting file size is only the size of the data, but with my testing on Windows, this large maximum file size seems to persist. An alternative database is RocksDB. This software is developed by Facebook, seems to be quite mature, and should also be able to save as a key-value pair across platforms.

title: File IO
text:
Prioritization and Future Considerations
Currently, the data that would benefit from key-value updates is only theoretical. Having a line for whiskers for each frame in a high-speed video of up to 200,000 frames results in a file size that is almost 300 MB. However, saving a binary file in its entirety when making whisker-specific updates through manual curation still takes less than a second to save and is not noticeable to the user. Consequently, I think prioritizing having binary outputs to save entire files and memory mapping of those binary file types that are read-only, such as for Neuropixel analog traces, may be the most desirable next feature. Key-value pairs with something like RocksDB should be remembered for the future, but I am going to make that less of a priority until I see a clear use case that would benefit.

title: File IO
text:
Loop expansion ({loop_var})
When using the extended object format, a top-level "loops" object defines iteration values that expand templated data entries before ${variable} substitution runs.







Syntax
Meaning




{whisker_id} in string fields
Replaced once per loop iteration (single-brace; distinct from ${name})


"loops": { "whisker_id": { "from": 0, "to": 4 } }
Inclusive integer range (step optional, default 1)


"loops": { "whisker_id": [0, 1, 2] }
Explicit iteration values (numbers or strings)



Each data entry that contains {...} placeholders must reference exactly one loop variable name defined in "loops". Entries without placeholders load once. Embedded "transformations" objects are not expanded.
Processing order: loops → ${variables} / environment → load.
Plain JSON arrays (no root object) do not support "loops"; use { "loops", "data" } or a pipeline JSON file.
{
  "variables": { "session_root": "/data/session1" },
  "loops": { "whisker_id": { "from": 0, "to": 4 } },
  "data": [
    {
      "filepath": "whiskers/whisker_{whisker_id}.csv",
      "data_type": "line",
      "name": "whisker_{whisker_id}",
      "format": "csv"
    }
  ]
}

title: File IO
text:
Default time TimeFrame fallback (JSON load)
After all JSON entries are processed (including clock remapping and transformation pipelines), load_data_from_json_config calls ensureDefaultTimeFrameFallback once as a last resort:

Runs only when TimeKey("time") still has zero samples (explicit data_type: "time" entries are respected).
If any loaded MediaData has a positive frame count, builds an identity TimeFrame [0, N-1] on time.
Media selection: prefer key "media" if it has frames; else prefer video over image stacks; else largest frame count (with a warning when ambiguous).
Does not infer time from point, line, or other non-media data. Points-only configs should include an explicit data_type: "time" entry (e.g. format: "max_value" from an analog or event series).

The same helper is used from MainWindow::_updateFrameCount for File → Load Video / Load Images.

title: File IO
text:
Digital event multi-file loading
When spike timestamps are stored as one file per channel (e.g. 23a.txt, 24a.txt, 25a.txt), set multi_file: true and point filepath at the containing directory. Each matching file becomes one DigitalEventSeries registered as {name}_0, {name}_1, … (or {name}_{file_stem} when append_filename: true) in alphabetical filename order. Optional file_pattern (glob) filters files; default extensions are .csv and .txt.
{
    "filepath": "spikes",
    "data_type": "digital_event",
    "name": "spikes",
    "format": "csv",
    "multi_file": true,
    "append_filename": true,
    "scale": 30000,
    "event_column": 0,
    "clock": "master"
}
With append_filename: true, keys are {name}_{file_stem} (e.g. spikes_23a from 23a.txt).
See CSV Digital Event I/O for full loader options.

title: SaverInfo & AtomicWrite
text:
The command persistence layer introduces two pieces of core infrastructure for uniform data saving:

SaverInfo — a metadata struct describing a registered saver’s capabilities.
AtomicWrite — a utility for crash-safe file writes.

title: SaverInfo & AtomicWrite
SaverInfo & AtomicWrite
text:
AtomicWrite
atomicWriteFile() (src/DataManager/IO/core/AtomicWrite.hpp) provides crash-safe file writing:
bool atomicWriteFile(
    std::filesystem::path const & target_path,
    std::function<bool(std::ostream &)> const & write_callback);
Algorithm:

Create parent directories if they don’t exist.
Write to target_path.tmp via the callback.
If the callback succeeds and the stream is good, rename .tmp → target.
On any failure, remove the .tmp file and leave the target untouched.

This ensures that a crash mid-write cannot corrupt an existing file.

title: OpenCV Binary Image Mask I/O
text:
The OpenCV binary image mask saver and loader handle reading and writing MaskData objects to/from directories of binary (black and white) image files. Each frame produces a separate image file where mask pixels are drawn with a configurable intensity value.
This format involves pixel-level rasterization — mask coordinates are drawn onto a fixed-size image canvas, so the save/load round-trip is not exact. Coordinates may shift slightly due to image resize operations when the source mask’s image size differs from the output dimensions.

text:
This document summarizes a performance investigation into loading multi-channel binary analog data in WhiskerToolbox. The goal was to identify bottlenecks in the current loading approach and evaluate alternative strategies.

title: Binary Multi-Channel Loading Performance Analysis
text:
Root Cause Analysis
The bottleneck is NOT: - Disk I/O speed (SSDs can easily sustain 5+ GB/s) - int16 → float conversion (~1.6 GB/s throughput)
The bottleneck IS: 1. Syscall overhead: Reading 64 bytes at a time causes millions of syscalls for a 5GB file 2. Cache thrashing: Strided writes across 32 different vectors have poor locality 3. Double handling: Current approach reads + distributes in same loop, can’t overlap I/O

title: Binary Multi-Channel Loading Performance Analysis
Binary Multi-Channel Loading Performance Analysis
text:
Benchmark Code Location
Ad-hoc benchmarks are in benchmark/adhoc/:

disk_read_benchmark.cpp - Raw disk read patterns
int16_to_float_benchmark.cpp - Conversion overhead
multichannel_loading_benchmark.cpp - End-to-end loading strategies

To build and run:
cd benchmark/adhoc
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
make -j
./benchmark_multichannel_loading
These are temporary benchmarks for this investigation. They can be deleted once the fix is implemented and verified.

title: Binary Multi-Channel Loading Performance Analysis
text:
Memory-Mapped Alternative
For extremely large files where even chunked reading is slow, the memory-mapped path (MmapStorageConfig) in Analog_Time_Series_Binary.cpp already provides an excellent solution:

No explicit I/O - OS handles paging
Lazy loading - only pages actually accessed are read
Can handle files larger than RAM
Already implemented for single-channel strided access

For multi-channel memory-mapped loading, each channel gets its own MemoryMappedAnalogDataStorage with appropriate stride and offset, which works well for sequential access patterns.

title: Binary Multi-Channel Loading Performance Analysis
text:
Conclusion
The current multi-channel loading performance issue is caused by excessive syscalls from reading one time-slice (64 bytes for 32-channel int16) at a time. Switching to a chunked reading strategy with ~10,000 time samples per chunk should improve performance by approximately 20-25×, bringing 5 GB file loading time from over a minute down to ~3 seconds.

title: TensorDesign Library
text: The TensorDesign library (src/TensorDesign/) provides Qt-free DataManager operations for tensor workflows. It is the headless counterpart to the TensorDesigner UI panel and TensorInspector column-view actions.

title: TensorDesign Library
text:
Motivation
TensorColumnBuilders can build individual column providers from ColumnRecipe + pipeline JSON, but assembling a full tensor (row source, RowDescriptor, invalidation wiring, optional DataManager registration) was previously duplicated in TensorDesigner::_buildTensor(). Similarly, tensor↔︎analog DataManager glue lived in TensorColumnViewCreator inside the UI library. Extracting both enables:

Integration tests that exercise production code without linking DataInspector_Widget

Each pipeline_json string is a PipelineDescriptor fragment. Interval-row columns require a terminal range_reduction.
Current interval-row tensor columns gather over the full row interval when row_pipeline_json is omitted, empty, or an explicit identity descriptor such as {"steps": []}. Non-identity row pipelines may run against the original interval row source when they produce a DigitalIntervalSeries with the same row count; the output is used as prepared gather windows for that column. Row pipelines that produce DigitalEventSeries with the same row count are routed to timestamp/sample provider behavior when the column pipeline has no terminal range reduction. Per-row normalization markers should be bound into the column TransformPipeline through TransformsV2 PipelineValueStore parameter bindings rather than through row_pipeline_json; GatherResult remains only the row container and direct gather executor.
TimeFrame row sources use row_source.time_key and build one row per index in the selected TimeFrame. The previous temporary compatibility path that detected a top-level "offset" field inside pipeline_json has been removed; offsets should be expressed as row-pipeline transforms such as ShiftDigitalEventSeries.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Status: Partially implemented. GatherResult, interval-window primitives, ColumnRecipe::row_pipeline_json, TensorDesign JSON round-trip, identity row-pipeline dispatch, DigitalIntervalSeries row-pipeline gather windows, pipeline_value_bindings for row-specific PipelineValueStore values, DigitalEventSeries sample-time row-pipeline dispatch, TimeFrame row sources, PointCoordinate keypoint coordinate projection, and Phase 9c column presets with TensorDesigner Add Preset… support are implemented. Phase 9g polymorphic preset refactoring is implemented, paving the way for file-based presets and dynamic UI generation. The broader preset file library and user/bundled preset catalog (Phase 10) remain planned.
This document describes the target architecture for per-column gather geometry in lazy-column tensors. The implementation sequence is tracked separately in Column Row Pipeline Roadmap.
See also:

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Goal
TensorDesign should support feature tables where every row comes from one row source, but each column can choose a different row-aligned temporal geometry before gathering its source data.
The motivating table is:

One row per whisker Contact interval.
A curvature column reduced over the full contact interval.
A spike column reduced over a short window around contact onset.
An angle column sampled at contact onset.
Downstream analysis, such as binning angle and estimating P(spike | bin), remains outside tensor building.

The design should use existing project primitives instead of tensor-specific interval abstractions:

DataObjects carry TimeFrame and entity identity.
TransformPipelines mutate or derive DataObjects.
GatherResult stores gathered row DataObjects plus prepared window metadata when direct gathering is needed.
TensorDesign assembles the row source, column recipes, lazy providers, and output TensorData.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Current State
Implemented today:

TensorDesign can build lazy-column tensors from interval, timestamp, TimeFrame, and derived timestamp row sources.
Interval-row columns gather over the full row interval.
ColumnRecipe::pipeline_json describes source processing and interval range reductions.
ColumnRecipe::row_pipeline_json is parsed, serialized, and used for interval-row gather geometry.
ColumnRecipe::pipeline_value_bindings is parsed, serialized, and used to bind one row-aligned DigitalEventSeries value into PipelineValueStore per tensor row.
ColumnRecipe::interval_property provides row metadata columns such as interval start, end, and duration.
Empty or whitespace row_pipeline_json and explicit empty-step descriptors are treated as identity row geometry.
Non-identity interval-row pipelines may produce row-aligned DigitalIntervalSeries prepared windows.
TensorDesign verifies row-pipeline window output preserves the original row count.
Digital event/interval iteration exposes ClockTicks API-facing values, so cross-timeframe temporal math should happen in clock-tick coordinates rather than raw TimeFrameIndex coordinates.
PipelineValueStore can store ClockTicks, and NormalizeTimeParamsV2::alignment_time is a ClockTicks value.
Direct binding sources from DataManager keys and derived binding sources using source_pipeline_json are supported when they resolve to row-aligned DigitalEventSeries objects.
NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative normalizes gathered DigitalEventSeries rows to relative ClockTicks storage before reductions such as EventCountInWindow.
gatherAndExecutePipeline() can execute JSON-loaded container steps before the terminal range reduction, and can apply a per-row bound pipeline copy when row stores are supplied.
DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline outputs are routed to timestamp/sample providers for interval-row columns without terminal range reductions.
ShiftDigitalEventSeries expresses sample offsets as a normal TransformPipeline step.
Angle-at-contact-onset point sampling is tested through TensorDesign JSON in the whisker-contact scenario.
row_source.time_key with row_type: "timeframe" builds one row per index in a registered TimeFrame.
PointCoordinate converts PointData to RaggedAnalogTimeSeries for x/y keypoint columns.
GatherResult consumes prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows and can hold companion alignment events, but TensorDesign should not rely on that metadata path for column transformations.
GatherResult converts prepared window bounds to the gathered source TimeFrame with convertTimeFrameRange().
DigitalIntervalSeries supports IntervalLayout::Overlapping through createOverlapping().
IntervalToEvent, EventToInterval, and PruneOverlappingIntervals are registered TransformsV2 algorithms.

Not implemented yet:

Row-pipeline caching across columns.
Broader preset catalog and bundled/user preset file library.
UI support for configuring row pipelines.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Problem
Original interval-row tensor columns always gathered source data over the full row interval. With the implemented DigitalIntervalSeries row-pipeline path, onset-window event reductions are now expressible in TensorDesign JSON. With pipeline_value_bindings, per-row normalization context is also expressible for row-aligned DigitalEventSeries markers. With DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline dispatch, point sampling is expressible in row-pipeline JSON. Phase 9c presets cover common authoring patterns; remaining gaps are row-pipeline caching, preset libraries, and richer UI for manually configuring row pipelines.
The full design addresses these common per-row features:

Spike presence within [-W, +W] of contact onset.
Analog value sampled at contact onset.
Statistics over a lagged or shifted version of the row interval.
Statistics aligned to a data-derived point inside a row, such as a peak curvature time.

Adding tensor-specific fields such as lag, window_start, or gather_mode would duplicate the TransformPipeline and DataObject systems. Those systems already handle TimeFrame conversion and entity identity, which are core requirements for correct scientific analysis.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Core Model
The target per-column data flow is:
flowchart LR
    RowSource["row_source DataObject"]
    RowDesc["RowDescriptor"]
    RowPipeline["row_pipeline_json\nTransformPipeline"]
    Metadata["row-aligned gather geometry\nDIS windows or DES sample times"]
    Gather["GatherResult<SourceT>"]
    Context["iterable bindings\noptional marker per row"]
    SourcePipeline["pipeline_json\nper-row transform + reduction"]
    Value["one value per row"]

    RowSource --> RowDesc
    RowSource --> RowPipeline --> Metadata --> Gather --> SourcePipeline --> Value
    RowSource --> Context --> SourcePipeline
row_source defines row identity. row_pipeline_json defines where a column looks for data. pipeline_json defines how the gathered source data becomes a column value.
The invariant is that row i remains row i. A row pipeline may change the gather bounds or sample time for row i, but it must not silently reorder rows, merge rows, or create extra rows unless the column builder explicitly supports that behavior.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Responsibilities







Component
Responsibility




DataObjects
Store data, TimeFrame, entity IDs, view/copy semantics, and materialization behavior.


TransformsV2 row pipeline
Derive row-aligned gather inputs from the row source, such as windows or sample times.


GatherResult
Gather source rows from prepared windows. It does not execute TransformPipelines or own per-row column context.


TransformsV2 iterable binding
Maps one element per row from a DataObject iterable into PipelineValueStore keys.


pipeline_json
Processes gathered source rows with PipelineValueStore parameter bindings and produces a scalar column value or supported DataObject output.


TensorDesign
Parse recipes, build row descriptors, connect row pipelines to column providers, and assemble TensorData.



TensorData materialization stops at scalar float. pipeline_json may produce a gathered DataObject (for example a relative DigitalEventSeries after NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative), but LazyColumnTensorStorage column providers must collapse each row to a single float. Gather-layer DataObject output is valid for intermediate transforms and future GatherResult tooling; only aggregators with ColumnOutputKind::ScalarFloat are exposed as tensor column presets.
This keeps the dependency direction aligned with the GatherResult refactor:
TensorDesign / TransformsV2 extensions -> GatherResult -> DataObjects
not:
GatherResult -> TensorDesign or TransformPipeline execution

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Row Identity And Gather Inputs








Concept
Defined by
Example




Row identity
TensorDesignSpec::row_source
Contact interval i


Row descriptor
Original row source
Contact start/end metadata


Gather windows
row_pipeline_json output or identity row source
Trial window or onset window around contact i


Sample times
row_pipeline_json output, when sampling
Contact onset event for row i


Iterable binding values
DataManager object or row-pipeline output
ClockTicks for raster/PSTH row i


Feature value
pipeline_json over gathered source rows
Spike presence, mean curvature, angle sample



Prepared windows should be represented as DigitalIntervalSeries. Per-row sample times should be represented as DigitalEventSeries. These are normal DataObjects, not tensor-specific side channels.
When a column needs to normalize gathered data relative to a marker that is not the gather window start, that marker should be supplied through PipelineValueStore parameter binding for pipeline_json, not encoded as a second output of row_pipeline_json.
For example, a spike raster column may gather spikes inside each trial window, then run a normalize-time transform with the contact onset event for that row supplied through the value store as ClockTicks.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Transform Composition
TensorDesign should express per-column geometry through composed registered transforms rather than new tensor enums.
TransformPipeline execution and iterable bindings both use the DataObject view() contract. For example, a DigitalEventSeries contributes ClockTicksWithId elements. Users should not need to choose between entity-carrying and bare-time implementation types; presets and generated raw JSON should select the appropriate registered transform for the pipeline execution mode.
For value projections, bindValueProjectionV2() operates on ElementVariant types. ElementVariant contains ClockTicks but not ClockTicksWithId; when the source view element is ClockTicksWithId, the projection helper passes element.time() into the TransformPipeline. Therefore the canonical normalize transform for DigitalEventSeries event times is NormalizeClockTicksValueV2. The EntityId remains available from the original ClockTicksWithId view element outside the TransformPipeline.








Intent
Row pipeline output
Source pipeline




Mean over full contact
Identity row DigitalIntervalSeries
Range reduction such as MeanValue


Spike near onset
