title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Row Source Extensions
The implemented row sources include interval rows from DigitalIntervalSeries, timestamp rows from DigitalEventSeries, TimeFrame rows from registered TimeKeys, and derived timestamp rows from timestamp-bearing data objects through extractTimeIndices().
TimeFrame rows let a tensor have one row per index in a named TimeFrame without requiring a synthetic data object:
{
  "row_source": {
    "time_key": "Time",
    "row_type": "timeframe"
  }
}
This is distinct from row_source.data_key, because timeframes are DataManager time metadata addressed by TimeKey, not normal data object keys. In the TensorDesigner UI this appears as a separate TimeFrame Rows option populated from DataManager::getTimeFrameKeys(). This makes the row-source distinction clearer:








UI row mode
Source list
Row identity




Interval Rows
DigitalIntervalSeries data keys
one row per interval


Timestamp Rows
DigitalEventSeries data keys
one row per event


TimeFrame Rows
TimeKey entries
one row per TimeFrame index


Derived from Source
timestamp-bearing data object keys
one row per timestamp extracted from the data object



Derived from Source should remain available for objects such as AnalogTimeSeries, PointData, LineData, MaskData, DigitalEventSeries, and DigitalIntervalSeries, but the UI should describe it as “derive rows from timestamps in a data object” rather than implying a row TransformPipeline.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Point And Keypoint Columns
Point/keypoint tables are a motivating case for presets because the low-level representation is simple but verbose. For example, a PointData object representing one tracked keypoint often needs two scalar tensor columns, x and y, at each row time.
The preferred low-level building block is a parameterized TransformsV2 container transform rather than tensor-specific column enums or two separate element transforms:
PointCoordinate: PointData -> RaggedAnalogTimeSeries
parameters: coordinate = "x" | "y"
This keeps the implementation in one registry entry with a small coordinate switch, preserves PointData as the input object, and produces an analog-family output that existing timestamp sampling and interval reductions can consume.
A one-keypoint tensor column group would expand to two ColumnRecipes:
[
  {
    "name": "nose_x",
    "source_key": "Nose",
    "pipeline_json": "{\"steps\": [{\"step_id\": \"x\", \"transform_name\": \"PointCoordinate\", \"parameters\": {\"coordinate\": \"x\"}}]}"
  },
  {
    "name": "nose_y",
    "source_key": "Nose",
    "pipeline_json": "{\"steps\": [{\"step_id\": \"y\", \"transform_name\": \"PointCoordinate\", \"parameters\": {\"coordinate\": \"y\"}}]}"
  }
]
For multiple keypoints, the same idea expands one source key into two columns. For example Nose and Paw become Nose_x, Nose_y, Paw_x, and Paw_y. Users should not need to manually author those four raw pipelines; this should be handled by multi-column presets.
For interval-row analyses, the row pipeline can still determine when the point is sampled. For example, point x/y at contact onset uses Contact -> IntervalToEvent(start) as row_pipeline_json, then applies PointCoordinate to the sampled PointData source.
PointCoordinate should preserve all point entries as a RaggedAnalogTimeSeries: if a PointData time contains multiple points, the corresponding ragged analog time contains multiple x or y values. Tensor timestamp sampling currently consumes the first value at a time point, which is appropriate for single-keypoint-per-time data and should be documented or made configurable before using multi-point-per-time data. Interval-row workflows can use normal range reductions such as MeanValue, SumValue, or MaxValue over the coordinate values.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
Column Row Pipeline Design
Column Row Pipeline Design
Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
PipelineValueStore Iterable Binding
TransformsV2 already has the mechanism needed to inject runtime values into a TransformPipeline: PipelineValueStore plus parameter bindings loaded from pipeline JSON. GatherResult previously used this mechanism through TransformsV2 gather extension helpers such as buildGatherRowStore().
The row-pipeline refactor reuses that mechanism rather than adding TensorData-specific context plumbing. The implemented iterable binding layer lives in the TensorColumnBuilders/TransformsV2 integration and is exposed through ColumnRecipe::pipeline_value_bindings.
The core contract is:

A column recipe identifies an iterable context source through pipeline_value_bindings.
The source is a DataObject in DataManager or a DataObject produced by a row TransformPipeline.
The source has one row-aligned element per tensor row.
For row i, the iterable binding converts element i into the DataObject’s default binding value and writes it into PipelineValueStore under the declared key.
pipeline_json parameter bindings map those store keys onto transform parameters.

This is conceptually equivalent to how the GatherResult extension previously created a per-row store, but the values are no longer limited to GatherResult metadata. Any row-aligned iterable DataObject can supply bound values.
Binding declarations live on ColumnRecipe, beside pipeline_json. They are not embedded in PipelineDescriptor, because the descriptor remains a reusable transform pipeline that does not know about DataManager keys, tensor rows, or external iterable sources. All pipeline-valued fields, including row_pipeline_json, source_pipeline_json, and pipeline_json, use the same PipelineDescriptor schema.

Binding Source Options
There are two useful source forms.
Direct DataManager source:
{
  "source_key": "ContactOnset",
  "store_key": "row_alignment_time"
}
DataManager source plus transform pipeline:
{
  "source_key": "Contact",
  "source_pipeline_json": "{\"steps\": [{\"transform_name\": \"IntervalToEvent\", \"parameters\": {\"point\": \"start\"}}]}",
  "store_key": "row_alignment_time"
}
The second form covers the case where the iterable does not already exist as a DataManager object. The implicit default is identity: if source_pipeline_json is omitted or empty, use the DataObject referenced by source_key directly.
This keeps every binding grounded in a DataManager key while still allowing the iterable to be derived. It also makes testing straightforward: a direct-key test and a key-plus-transform test should produce the same PipelineValueStore values when the derived object is equivalent to a precomputed object.


Binding Value Semantics
The user should not need to specify an extractor for the initial Phase 5 use case. Instead, each supported DataObject type should define a default binding value for one row element.
Initial support should be deliberately narrow:








Source DataObject
Row element
Default binding value




DigitalEventSeries
ClockTicksWithId event row i
event.time() as ClockTicks



If a caller needs interval start, end, or center as the bound value, it should first derive a DigitalEventSeries with IntervalToEvent. This avoids requiring users to choose coordinate extractors and keeps start/end/center selection in the TransformPipeline where it already belongs.
The ClockTicks refactor removes the need for binding declarations to carry TimeFrame pointers. DigitalEventSeries::view() and DigitalIntervalSeries::view() expose API-facing elements in clock ticks (ClockTicksWithId and ClockTicksIntervalWithId) while storage/persistence APIs can still expose TimeFrameIndex through explicit stored-value accessors.
Phase 5 binds temporal iterable values as ClockTicks. NormalizeTimeParamsV2::alignment_time receives ClockTicks, not raw TimeFrameIndex values.
This also means IntervalToEvent and EventToInterval should compose in clock-tick coordinates at the API boundary. If a transform still uses TimeFrameIndex internally, that should be treated as an implementation detail hidden behind the DataObject view/storage boundary.
For NormalizeTime, the user-facing intent is simply “normalize event time by a row-specific clock tick”. The raw transform name for DigitalEventSeries value projections is NormalizeClockTicksValueV2 because the projection helper extracts ClockTicks from ClockTicksWithId view elements before transform execution. When the gathered row should remain a DigitalEventSeries, use the container transform NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative, which writes relative ClockTicks storage and preserves event EntityIds. Presets should hide these raw transform names when possible.


Execution Shape
For a gathered source and one binding source:
windows_i = row_pipeline(row_source)[i]
row_i = gather(source_key, windows_i)

iterable = source_pipeline(source_key_for_binding)
store_i = buildGatherRowStore(gathered, i) or empty PipelineValueStore
store_i[store_key] = defaultBindingValue(iterable, i)

pipeline_i = pipeline_json with param_bindings applied from store_i
value_i = execute/reduce pipeline_i(row_i)
buildGatherRowStore() may still be useful as a base store for generic row metadata such as trial_index and trial_duration, but TensorDesign should not depend on GatherResult::alignmentTimeAt() for normalization markers. Iterable bindings should override or add store keys explicitly.


Validation Rules
Phase 5 enforces these rules:

Binding source DataObject must exist or the binding source pipeline must produce a supported DataObject.
Binding source row count must equal the GatherResult row count.
store_key must be unique within the column and must not collide with base row-store keys; reject duplicates rather than silently overwriting.
Produced DataObject type must have a default binding value implementation.
Binding value construction must be deterministic and must not mutate the source object.
If row filtering is introduced later, filtering must be applied consistently to gather windows and binding sources.

Failure occurs at provider construction when possible. If a lazy source can only be evaluated at provider invocation time, fail with a message that identifies the column, binding source, and store key.


Motivating Test Cases
Phase 5 has tests using the raster/PSTH normalization pattern.
Direct iterable source:
row_source: Contact intervals
source_key: Spikes
row_pipeline_json: identity or trial window pipeline
pipeline_value_bindings: ContactOnset DigitalEventSeries[i] -> ClockTicks -> row_alignment_time
pipeline_json: NormalizeTime(alignment_time bound to row_alignment_time) + event/bin reduction
Derived iterable source:
row_source: Contact intervals
source_key: Spikes
row_pipeline_json: identity or trial window pipeline
pipeline_value_bindings: Contact -> IntervalToEvent(start) -> ClockTicks -> row_alignment_time
pipeline_json: NormalizeTime(alignment_time bound to row_alignment_time) + event/bin reduction
The tests assert that normalized event times are relative to the bound marker, not to the gather window start. They also assert row-count mismatch rejection by using a binding source with a missing event.
Example binding shape, shown as design intent rather than final JSON:
{
  "pipeline_json": "{\"steps\": [{\"step_id\": \"normalize\", \"transform_name\": \"NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative\", \"parameters\": {\"alignment_time\": 0}, \"param_bindings\": {\"alignment_time\": \"row_alignment_time\"}}], \"range_reduction\": {\"reduction_name\": \"EventCountInWindow\", \"parameters\": {\"window_start\": 0.0, \"window_end\": 15.0}}}",
  "pipeline_value_bindings": [
    {
      "source_key": "ContactOnset",
      "store_key": "row_alignment_time"
    }
  ]
}
The ownership is clear: TransformsV2 binds row-specific values into PipelineValueStore; TensorDesign selects the row source, gather/sample input, and column recipe; TensorData stores the resulting column values.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Raster/PSTH Example
A raster or PSTH-like tensor column illustrates the separation between gather input and transform context:

The row source defines trials, such as one DigitalIntervalSeries interval per contact or behavioral trial.
row_pipeline_json defines which spikes are gathered for each row. This can be identity for full-trial windows or a window-producing transform for a restricted interval.
The gathered row DataObject is a DigitalEventSeries subset in source coordinates.
pipeline_json runs per row and includes a normalize-time transform, such as NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative for event-series rows.
The normalize-time transform needs one marker for the current row, such as contact onset or cue time.
That marker is supplied through PipelineValueStore when executing pipeline_json, not through GatherResult row metadata and not as a paired output of row_pipeline_json.

Conceptually:
row_pipeline_json: trial interval -> spike gather window
gather:            Spikes + window_i -> spikes_i
iterable binding:  ContactOnset[i] -> ClockTicks -> PipelineValueStore["row_alignment_time"]
pipeline_json:     NormalizeTime(spikes_i, row_alignment_time) -> PSTH/bin/reduction output
This keeps row_pipeline_json focused on selecting rows of source data and keeps transformations such as normalization inside the column pipeline where they belong.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Provider Dispatch
The implemented dispatch for interval-row columns is:

If interval_property is present, use the existing row metadata provider and ignore source gather.
Resolve row_pipeline_json.
If row_pipeline_json is empty, use the current full-interval gather path.
If the row pipeline produces DigitalIntervalSeries windows, verify row count and gather the column source through GatherResult.
Build any iterable PipelineValueStore bindings requested by pipeline_value_bindings, such as one normalization marker per row. Initial support binds one ClockTicks value per row from a direct or derived DigitalEventSeries.
Run pipeline_json over gathered rows with the row store to produce one value per tensor row.
If the row pipeline produces DigitalEventSeries sample times and the column pipeline has no terminal range reduction, route those sample times to timestamp/sample provider behavior.

Planned dispatch extensions are:

Optional future expansion may allow recipes to choose whether DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline output should sample directly or be expanded to windows with EventToInterval.

The dispatch should reject row-pipeline outputs that do not preserve row count unless the recipe explicitly opts into row filtering.
Implemented behavior rejects DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline output only when the interval-row column also declares a terminal range reduction, because sample-time output is point geometry rather than gather-window geometry.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
TimeFrame Semantics
Window-producing transforms operate in their input DataObject’s TimeFrame. They should not need a hidden tensor-specific output-timeframe parameter.
GatherResult handles source query conversion at gather time:
prepared window TimeFrame -> source DataObject TimeFrame
Projection and trial-relative transforms should use ClockTicks values supplied through PipelineValueStore. TimeFrame conversion should happen at DataObject boundaries, not in TensorDesign JSON.
The row descriptor should continue to describe the original row source, not the per-column gather window. Per-column geometry is column metadata used to produce a value; it does not redefine tensor row identity.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Overlapping Windows
Gather geometry can overlap even when the semantic row source is disjoint.








Role
Layout
Example




Row source
Usually Disjoint
Contact intervals or trial epochs.


Gather geometry
Usually Overlapping
Onset windows around nearby contacts.



Window-producing row pipelines should use DigitalIntervalSeries::createOverlapping() when overlap is possible. They should not rely on default disjoint insertion behavior because disjoint series merge overlapping intervals and destroy row identity.
Overlap pruning is not a tensor default. It drops rows and changes the analysis question. Use PruneOverlappingIntervals only when a recipe or caller explicitly requests this behavior, and apply the same kept-row selection to any iterable context sources.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Relationship To Plot Alignment
PlotAlignmentGather already follows the core prepared-window model for UI plotting:

Build DigitalIntervalSeries windows.
Build or reuse companion DigitalEventSeries alignment events.
Call GatherResult::create(source, windows, alignment_events).

Tensor row pipelines should use the same DataObject vocabulary for windows and events, but column normalization should be modeled as PipelineValueStore parameter binding rather than inherited from GatherResult alignment metadata. Plot code may later share descriptor-building helpers with TensorDesign, but the TensorDesign row-pipeline design does not require a plot refactor.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Out Of Scope

Binned or grouped downstream analysis such as P(spike | angle bin).
Nonlinear time warping.
Persisting gather windows as a new DataManager object type.
UI affordances for editing row-pipeline JSON or presets.
Backward compatibility for removed GatherResult interval adapters.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Open Questions

Should row pipelines be allowed to use additional_input_keys, and if so should those keys be declared per column or at the tensor level?
Should identical row pipelines be cached across columns during one tensor build?
How should DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline output choose between point sampling, window expansion, or rejection?
Should row filtering ever be supported, or should row pipelines always be required to preserve row count?
Should raw JSON expose low-level transform names such as NormalizeClockTicksValueV2, or should TensorDesign provide friendlier aliases/presets for common column workflows?

Settled for Phase 5:

Temporal iterable values bind as ClockTicks.
NormalizeTimeParamsV2::alignment_time is ClockTicks.
PipelineValueStore supports ClockTicks storage and JSON binding through ClockTicksReflector.
Binding declarations live on ColumnRecipe, not inside PipelineDescriptor.
source_pipeline_json uses the same PipelineDescriptor schema as row_pipeline_json and pipeline_json.
Duplicate binding store_key values should be rejected rather than overwritten.
Direct-key bindings and key-plus-source_pipeline_json bindings are implemented for DigitalEventSeries sources.

title: Column Row Pipeline Design
text:
Tests
Current coverage is split by architectural layer:








Test file
Layer
Coverage

resolveIntervalGatherWindows(), identity row pipelines, DigitalIntervalSeries row-pipeline output, overlapping windows, row-count rejection, interval-property bypass, provider dispatch, JSON-loaded container steps before reduction, direct/derived pipeline_value_bindings, and binding row-count rejection.

Parse/serialize row_pipeline_json, parse/serialize pipeline_value_bindings, identity behavior, Phase 4 JSON builds, Phase 5 bound-normalization JSON builds, mixed interval-property/gather columns, cross-timeframe gather windows, and offset compatibility characterization.

Builds the whisker-contact JSON design with mean curvature, full-contact spike count, contact-onset spike presence, and angle-at-onset point sampling through row_pipeline_json.

The two whisker-contact test files intentionally cover different levels. The TransformsV2 test validates the lower-level provider/lazy tensor path. The TensorDesign test validates the JSON-to-tensor path, including the new contact-aligned spike column. If test runtime becomes a concern, keep both layers but reduce duplicate statistical assertions rather than deleting one file.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
This document provides a phased implementation plan for migrating gather-window generation from gather-specific interval adapters to DigitalIntervalSeries-based TransformsV2 algorithms.
The companion design document is digital_interval_series_migration_design.qmd. Read that first for the rationale, affected libraries, and open design decisions.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
This document provides a phased implementation plan for migrating gather-window generation from gather-specific interval adapters to DigitalIntervalSeries-based TransformsV2 algorithms.
The companion design document is digital_interval_series_migration_design.qmd. Read that first for the rationale, affected libraries, and open design decisions.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Desired End State
The migration is complete when:

Event and interval alignment windows are produced as DigitalIntervalSeries objects with IntervalLayout::Overlapping.
Alignment points are represented as companion DigitalEventSeries objects, not raw vectors.
GatherResult primarily accepts prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows for direct gather creation.
GatherResult<T> is positioned as a row-aligned collection of supported DataObject instances plus row metadata; it should not care whether each row DataObject is view-backed, owning, lazy, or transform-produced.
PSTH, event plot, event-rate estimation, interval reduction, and export paths no longer depend on EventExpanderAdapter or IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter.
Trial alignment metadata remains available through alignmentTimeAt() and TransformsV2 gather-extension row stores.
Cross-timeframe gather uses the existing TimeFrame conversion primitives (convertTimeFrameRange() for interval edges and convert_time_index() for single alignment/event indices) in one gather/query path.
Future DataObject-producing per-row transforms can return another GatherResult<OutputDataObject> through external TransformsV2 helpers rather than introducing a parallel row-collection container.
Tests cover overlapping windows, cross-timeframe alignment, overlap pruning (via PruneOverlappingIntervals), reordering, and plot-facing gather behavior.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Phase 0: Baseline And Test Inventory

Goals
Establish current behavior before changing APIs.


Tasks

Identify existing tests that cover GatherResult, PSTH/event plot alignment, interval reduction, and range reductions.
Add characterization tests for current behavior if coverage is missing.
Record expected behavior for event alignment, interval alignment, overlap prevention, and reordering.



Suggested Tests

Gathering event data around event alignment points with overlapping windows preserves one gathered view per event.
Gathering around interval starts and interval ends produces expected alignment times.
Centered event windows report alignment time equal to the original event time, not the window start.
prevent_overlap keeps the first candidate under the existing greedy behavior.
GatherResult::reorder() preserves originalIndex(), intervalAtReordered(), and alignmentTimeAt().
Cross-timeframe gather converts alignment windows into source coordinates correctly.



Exit Criteria

Current behavior is covered by tests or documented with explicit manual checks.
The tests can be run through the appropriate CMake preset and ctest filters.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Phase 1: Add Window-Producing TransformsV2 Algorithms

Goals
Introduce reusable TransformsV2 algorithms that materialize gather windows and alignment points as DigitalIntervalSeries and DigitalEventSeries objects.


Status
Largely complete. Event window expansion, interval alignment-point extraction, and overlap pruning are implemented. Remaining migration work is to use the existing TimeFrame conversion primitives consistently at gather/query and projection boundaries.
Done (partial): EventToInterval is implemented and registered. It expands DigitalEventSeries events into overlapping DigitalIntervalSeries windows using EventToIntervalParams (pre_expansion, post_expansion as TimeFrameIndex). See src/TransformsV2/algorithms/EventToInterval/ for the source and tests.
Done (partial): IntervalToEvent is implemented and registered. It extracts one DigitalEventSeries event per interval at start, end, or center using IntervalToEventParams (point as IntervalEventPoint). See src/TransformsV2/algorithms/IntervalToEvent/ for the source and tests.
Done (partial): PruneOverlappingIntervals is implemented and registered. It applies greedy keep-first overlap pruning to a DigitalIntervalSeries, producing a disjoint output series. See src/TransformsV2/algorithms/PruneOverlappingIntervals/ for the source and tests.
Remaining: optional companion alignment-point filtering helper for paired window/event pruning at gather call sites, and consistent use of convertTimeFrameRange() / convert_time_index() where windows or alignment points cross TimeFrame boundaries.


Tasks

Add event window algorithm under src/TransformsV2/algorithms/. Done: EventToInterval/.
Define parameter struct for event windows. Done: EventToIntervalParams.
Add interval-to-event extraction for interval start/end/center alignment points. Done: IntervalToEvent/.
Implement event-to-interval expansion. Done: eventToInterval() via EventToInterval.
Use composition for fixed windows around interval-derived points: intervalToEvent() followed by EventToInterval.
Ensure window algorithms return output created with DigitalIntervalSeries::createOverlapping(...). Done for EventToInterval.
Use normal data-object composition for alignment points: existing event series for event alignment, and IntervalToEvent output for interval alignment.
Add overlap pruning as a TransformsV2 container transform. Done: PruneOverlappingIntervals/.
Use the existing TimeFrame conversion primitives when source/output TimeFrame conversion is required.
Register pipeline-addressable transforms. Done for EventToInterval, IntervalToEvent, and PruneOverlappingIntervals.
Add unit tests for event window edge cases. Done: EventToInterval.test.cpp.
Add unit tests for interval-to-event edge cases. Done: IntervalToEvent.test.cpp.
Add unit tests for overlap pruning edge cases. Done: PruneOverlappingIntervals.test.cpp.



Event Window Cases (EventToInterval)
These cases are covered by EventToInterval.test.cpp unless noted:

Empty event series returns an empty overlapping interval series.
Zero pre/post expansion creates point interval [T, T].
Negative expansion values are rejected via debug assert() on pre_expansion and post_expansion.
Input TimeFrame is propagated to the output (no cross-timeframe conversion yet).
Overlapping windows remain separate.
Not yet covered by EventToInterval: cross-timeframe output. Companion alignment points are supplied by the original event series for event alignment.



Interval To Event Cases (IntervalToEvent)
These cases are covered by IntervalToEvent.test.cpp unless noted:

Empty interval series returns an empty event series with preserved TimeFrame.
IntervalEventPoint::start uses interval start.
IntervalEventPoint::end uses interval end.
IntervalEventPoint::center uses integer midpoint behavior matching the current adapter.
The output DigitalEventSeries preserves the input interval series TimeFrame.
The output does not inherit interval entity IDs; provenance should use lineage tracing if needed later.
Overlapping input intervals produce one event per row (not merged).
Round-trip with EventToInterval at zero expansion recovers original event times.
If callers need fixed windows around these points, they compose the result with EventToInterval.
Not yet covered by IntervalToEvent: cross-timeframe output.



Overlap Pruning Cases (PruneOverlappingIntervals)
These cases are covered by PruneOverlappingIntervals.test.cpp unless noted:

Empty interval series returns an empty disjoint interval series.
Single interval is kept unchanged.
Well-separated intervals are all kept.
Overlapping intervals are pruned with greedy keep-first behavior.
Touching intervals (start == last_kept.end) are treated as overlapping and pruned.
Chain pruning keeps non-overlapping survivors after earlier rows are dropped.
Input TimeFrame is propagated to the output.
Overlapping input layout (IntervalLayout::Overlapping) produces disjoint output.
Not yet covered by PruneOverlappingIntervals: paired filtering of a companion DigitalEventSeries alignment-point series to the same kept row indices. Plot code still uses local helpers for alignment-point + window pruning until Phase 4.



Exit Criteria

Event window algorithm compiles and passes focused unit tests. Done: EventToInterval.
Interval-to-event algorithm compiles and passes focused unit tests. Done: IntervalToEvent.
Overlap pruning algorithm compiles and passes focused unit tests. Done: PruneOverlappingIntervals.
Output windows are represented as DigitalIntervalSeries, not std::vector<Interval>.
Output alignment points are represented as DigitalEventSeries where required by the migration design.
The algorithms can be used without checking the result into DataManager.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
section: Phase 2: Centralize Use Of TimeFrame Conversion Primitives
text:
Phase 2: Centralize Use Of TimeFrame Conversion Primitives

Goals
Centralize interval conversion between alignment/window timeframe and source-data timeframe by reusing the existing primitives in src/TimeFrame/TimeFrame.hpp:

convertTimeFrameRange(start, stop, from_time_frame, to_time_frame) for one interval’s edges.
convert_time_index(time, source_timeframe, target_timeframe) for one event or alignment index.



Status
Complete for gather-window query bounds. GatherResult now converts prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows to the source data TimeFrame at view-creation time with convertTimeFrameRange(). The duplicate prepareIntervalsForGather() materialization helpers in IntervalReduction.cpp and GatherPipelineExecutor.cpp have been removed.
Prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows are expected to carry a non-null TimeFrame; missing window/source TimeFrame values are treated as invalid input for the prepared-window path. Legacy adapter null-TimeFrame behavior is isolated in the deprecated adapter compatibility path until Phase 3/4 removes the adapters.


Tasks

Update the refactored gather path so source view creation converts each window interval with convertTimeFrameRange() when querying source data. Done.
Update trial-relative projection code to use convert_time_index() or physical time values from the relevant TimeFrame objects when gathered events and alignment points have different TimeFrame objects.
Keep EventToInterval, IntervalToEvent, and PruneOverlappingIntervals in their input TimeFrame; do not add a transform parameter solely to target the gathered source timeframe.
Preserve interval and event order during gather and projection.
If a call site still needs a materialized converted DigitalIntervalSeries or DigitalEventSeries, implement that materialization as a thin wrapper around convertTimeFrameRange() or convert_time_index().
Do not inherit entity IDs for generated or converted temporary windows/alignment points. If provenance is required later, use lineage tracing rather than entity ID copying.
Replace or remove the private prepareIntervalsForGather() implementation in IntervalReduction.cpp; if materialization remains necessary, it should delegate to convertTimeFrameRange(). Done: the helper is removed and IntervalReduction passes original row intervals directly to GatherResult.
Add tests for same-timeframe, different-timeframe, and invalid missing-TimeFrame prepared-window cases.



Gather-Time Conversion Shape
auto [query_start, query_stop] = convertTimeFrameRange(
        window.start,
        window.end,
        *window_time_frame,
        *source_time_frame);
Prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows should carry a non-null TimeFrame. Null-TimeFrame behavior is legacy adapter compatibility only and should not be documented as a supported prepared-window convention.


Exit Criteria

Gather-window interval conversion uses convertTimeFrameRange() rather than duplicate edge-conversion logic.
Gather alignment/projection conversion uses convert_time_index() or direct physical-time lookup through TimeFrame rather than duplicate index-conversion logic.
IntervalReduction.cpp and GatherPipelineExecutor.cpp no longer carry independent interval conversion implementations.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Phase 3: Refactor GatherResult Around DigitalIntervalSeries

Goals
Make DigitalIntervalSeries the internal window representation for direct gather results while keeping GatherResult<T> compatible with the broader row-aligned DataObject model.
GatherResult should store row DataObjects and row metadata. It should not distinguish whether a row T is a view, owning copy, lazy object, or transform output; those storage details belong to the DataObject implementation.


Status
Complete. GatherResult<T> now accepts prepared std::shared_ptr<DigitalIntervalSeries const> windows with optional companion std::shared_ptr<DigitalEventSeries const> alignment points. Prepared windows and alignment points are retained as row metadata while intervalAt() continues to expose source-coordinate query intervals for existing plot/export consumers.
The adapter overloads and IntervalAdapters.hpp have been removed. Window and alignment construction now belongs to TransformsV2 algorithms or call-site preparation helpers, not to GatherResult.


Tasks

Add an overload that accepts std::shared_ptr<DigitalIntervalSeries const>. Done.
Add the companion parameter std::shared_ptr<DigitalEventSeries const> alignment_points. Done.
Store the window series in GatherResult as _windows. Done.
Store the companion event series in GatherResult as _alignment_points. Done.
Assert in debug builds that _windows->size() == _alignment_points->size(). Done.
Keep row storage as a vector of std::shared_ptr<T>; optionally rename _views to _rows if it can be done without obscuring the interval-storage refactor. Done: _views was kept to limit churn.
Treat _source as direct-gather provenance. Do not make future row-transformed results depend on having a single non-null source object of type T. Done for current storage; fromRows() remains deferred.
Replace _intervals reads with iteration over _windows->view() where practical, or keep a clearly named compatibility cache if callers still need source-query intervals. Done: _query_intervals is the compatibility cache.
Keep intervalAt() and intervalAtReordered() behavior stable. If new accessors are added, distinguish prepared window intervals from source-query intervals by name. Done: windows() exposes prepared windows.
Implement alignmentTimeAt() from _alignment_points and row ordering. Done for prepared-window gathers.
Collapse the duplicated row DataObject creation logic into one helper path. The helper may call createView() or createTimeRangeCopy(), but after construction the row is just a T. Done.
Update materialize() and reorder() to copy or share _windows, _alignment_points, row objects, and order metadata. Done.
Consider adding fromRows() and fromRowsLike(parent, rows) if it is low-risk. These are optional for adapter migration but are the preferred future API for DataObject-producing per-row transforms. Done in Phase 5.5.
Do not expand the TransformsV2 responsibility inside GatherResult during this phase. Preserve existing methods if needed for compatibility, but design the storage/accessors so they can move to extension helpers later. Done.



Exit Criteria

The primary gather path is GatherResult<T>::create(source, windows, alignment_points).
Internally, gather windows are stored as DigitalIntervalSeries.
Internally, alignment points are stored as DigitalEventSeries.
Row storage is independent of whether each row DataObject is view-backed, owning, lazy, or transform-produced.
source() is not required to be meaningful for every future GatherResult<T> construction path; only direct gather results must have direct source provenance.
Existing public accessors used by plot/export code still work.
Tests from Phase 0 still pass.



Deferred Follow-Up
After the interval storage refactor is stable, move TransformsV2-specific row processing toward extension helpers:

DataObject-producing per-row pipelines should consume GatherResult<InputT> and return GatherResult<OutputT>.
Scalar reductions should return ordinary vectors such as std::vector<int> or std::vector<float>.
PipelineValueStore construction should be externalized from core GatherResult once callers are migrated.

See row_aligned_dataobject_container_design.qmd for the follow-on design.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
section: Phase 4: Replace Adapter-Based Plot Alignment Paths
text:
Phase 4: Replace Adapter-Based Plot Alignment Paths

Goals
Move PSTH, event plot, and event-rate code from adapter-based window generation to TransformsV2 window generation.


Status
Complete for plot-facing alignment preparation. PlotAlignmentGather.hpp now prepares DigitalIntervalSeries windows and companion DigitalEventSeries alignment points before calling the prepared GatherResult path. EventRateEstimation.cpp uses the same Qt-free preparation helper instead of keeping a local adapter/pruning copy. LineBatchBuilder has a preferred overload that reads alignment metadata directly from GatherResult<AnalogTimeSeries>.
The implementation preserves the legacy plot contract that UI window sizes are physical display-time widths. The new PlotAlignmentWindowPreparation.hpp helper materializes display windows in the gathered source TimeFrame so cross-timeframe plot behavior remains stable while alignmentTimeAt() continues to expose physical alignment time for trial-relative rendering.


Tasks

Update PlotAlignmentGather.hpp to build windows through TransformsV2 algorithms. Done: plot alignment now uses prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows plus companion DigitalEventSeries alignment points.
Update event alignment to call EventToInterval (registry name "EventToInterval") instead of expandEvents(). Adapted: plot event windows preserve physical display-time semantics through PlotAlignmentWindowPreparation.hpp; index-space EventToInterval remains available for transform pipelines where its parameter contract matches the requested operation.
Update interval alignment to call IntervalToEvent (registry name "IntervalToEvent") instead of withAlignment(). Done.
Replace local pruneOverlappingAlignmentTimes / createFilteredIntervalSeries usage with PruneOverlappingIntervals (registry name "PruneOverlappingIntervals") when pruning interval bounds directly, or compose window expansion + pruning as appropriate for event/interval alignment paths. Done for prepared windows: paired pruning uses the shared helper and PruneOverlappingIntervals for the window series.
Apply the same kept-row selection to the companion alignment-point event series (may require a small shared helper until a paired transform exists). Done.
Call gather(source, windows, alignment_points) after window preparation. Done.
Update EventRateEstimation.cpp to reuse the same window-preparation path instead of duplicating filtering and adapter logic. Done.
Update plot-facing consumers to prefer GatherResult::alignmentTimeAt() over caller-managed raw alignment-time vectors when constructing relative display coordinates. Done for the standard line batch path.
Update CorePlotting::buildLineBatchFromGatherResult() so the preferred overload reads alignment metadata from GatherResult<AnalogTimeSeries> directly. Keep a two-argument alignment-vector overload only if an explicit override is still needed. Done.
Update LinePlotOpenGLWidget.cpp to call the preferred LineBatchBuilder overload. It may still cache alignment times for double-click relative-to-absolute conversion and group-color behavior. Done.
Verify PSTH, event plot, line plot, and event-rate rendering behavior manually or with available widget tests. Automated focused tests cover the gather and line-batch paths; manual rendering remains recommended.



Affected Files

src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/Common/PlotAlignmentGather.hpp
src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/Common/EventRateEstimation/EventRateEstimation.cpp
src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/PSTHWidget/Rendering/PSTHPlotOpenGLWidget.cpp
src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/EventPlotWidget/Rendering/EventPlotOpenGLWidget.cpp
src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/LinePlotWidget/Rendering/LinePlotOpenGLWidget.cpp
src/CorePlotting/LineBatch/LineBatchBuilder.hpp
src/CorePlotting/LineBatch/LineBatchBuilder.cpp



Exit Criteria

Plot alignment helpers do not call expandEvents() or withAlignment().
Overlap prevention uses PruneOverlappingIntervals or an equivalent shared composition path rather than local pruneOverlappingAlignmentTimes copies where interval bounds are pruned directly.
PSTH/event plot code continues to receive valid GatherResult<DigitalEventSeries> objects.
Line plot code continues to receive valid GatherResult<AnalogTimeSeries> objects with alignment metadata suitable for relative x-coordinate construction.
LineBatchBuilder no longer requires a separately maintained alignment-time vector for the standard line plot path.
Trial-relative time projections remain unchanged.
Start/end/center selection is not part of the GatherResult API.

section: Phase 5: Update Transform And Export Consumers
text:
Phase 5: Update Transform And Export Consumers

Goals
Move remaining non-UI consumers to the new prepared-window and companion-alignment-event model.


Status
Complete for transform/export consumers. GatherPipelineExecutor, TensorColumnBuilders, and TensorDesignBuilder now pass prepared row windows as std::shared_ptr<DigitalIntervalSeries const>. IntervalReduction uses a const non-owning alias for row-defining windows before delegating to GatherResult, while source aliases remain constrained by the current non-const DataObject view APIs.
Export and line-batch consumers were verified to depend only on stable public GatherResult accessors such as alignmentTimeAt() and row access. Remaining adapter APIs are isolated to the legacy GatherResult compatibility path until Phase 6.

Update IntervalReduction.cpp to use the refactored GatherResult and the existing TimeFrame conversion primitives. Done.
Update IntervalReduction.cpp to pass row intervals as std::shared_ptr<DigitalIntervalSeries const> where possible. Avoid mutable aliasing for prepared windows; source aliases may remain constrained by current DataObject view APIs. Done.
Update GatherPipelineExecutor.hpp and GatherPipelineExecutor.cpp to accept std::shared_ptr<DigitalIntervalSeries const> for prepared row windows. Done.
Verify TransformsV2 tensor-column and interval-row consumers can operate on row DataObjects and stable row metadata without depending on _intervals internals. Done.
Verify RasterCSVExport.hpp only depends on stable public accessors. Confirm callers pass a TimeFrame compatible with the gathered event rows/source series when computing exported relative times. Done.
Verify LineBatchBuilder only depends on stable public accessors after the Phase 4 alignment-metadata update. Done.
Remove any temporary call-site conversions to std::vector<Interval>. Done: no Phase 5 production call site materializes row windows as std::vector<Interval>.



Exit Criteria

Transform and export paths compile against the new GatherResult API. Done.
GatherPipelineExecutor exposes prepared row windows as std::shared_ptr<DigitalIntervalSeries const>. Done.
IntervalReduction does not materialize converted row intervals or mutate row-defining windows. Done.
Raster export continues to compute relative event times from alignmentTimeAt() and a compatible event/source TimeFrame. Verified.
No production call site needs IntervalAdapters.hpp. Done outside the legacy GatherResult compatibility API.
No production call site needs to know whether a GatherResult row DataObject is view-backed or owning. Done.

section: Phase 5.5: Decouple TransformsV2 Row Processing From Core GatherResult
text:
Phase 5.5: Decouple TransformsV2 Row Processing From Core GatherResult

Goals
Move TransformsV2-specific per-row projection/reduction concerns out of the core gather container while preserving the ability to return GatherResult<OutputDataObject> for DataObject-producing row transforms.
This phase can occur after adapter migration if moving the methods earlier would create unnecessary churn.


Status
Complete. Core GatherResult now provides fromRows() and fromRowsLike(parent, rows) for synthesized row DataObjects without requiring a direct source pointer. TransformsV2 row stores, projection helpers, reduction helpers, sort helpers, and DataObject-producing row pipeline execution live in src/TransformsV2/extension/gatherResult/GatherResultRowContext.hpp. GatherResult no longer exposes PipelineValueStore or value-projection APIs and no longer links to TransformsV2.


Tasks

Add or finalize GatherResult::fromRows() for row-aligned DataObjects and fromRowsLike(parent, rows) for preserving parent row metadata. Done.
Add TransformsV2 extension helpers that consume GatherResult<InputT> and run a pipeline per row. Done.
Return GatherResult<OutputT> when the per-row pipeline output is a supported DataObject type. Done.
Return std::vector<Scalar> for scalar reductions such as spike counts. Done.
Move PipelineValueStore construction for trial-specific parameters into the TransformsV2 extension helper or caller-provided row-context function. Done.
Deprecate or remove core GatherResult methods that directly expose TransformsV2 types, such as buildTrialStore(), project(), reduce(), and sortIndicesBy(), once callers have migrated. Done.
Drop TransformsV2 includes from GatherResult.hpp when no core API uses them. Done.



Exit Criteria

Core GatherResult depends on DataObject and TimeFrame concepts, not TransformsV2 pipeline types.
TransformsV2 extension code depends on GatherResult, not the other way around.
DataObject-producing per-row transforms can synthesize new GatherResult<OutputT> values.
Scalar row reductions return plain vectors.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Phase 6: Deprecate And Remove IntervalAdapters

Goals
Remove the gather-specific interval source abstraction after all call sites migrate.


Status
Complete. IntervalAdapters.hpp has been removed, GatherResult.hpp no longer includes it, and the adapter-backed GatherResult::create() / gather() overloads have been deleted. Former adapter tests now use prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows plus companion DigitalEventSeries alignment points.
Searches for expandEvents, withAlignment, EventExpanderAdapter, IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter, AlignedInterval, and IntervalSource no longer find production or test call sites. Remaining IntervalSourceIndex / IIntervalSource matches refer to unrelated range-reduction and table-view terminology.


Tasks

Grep for expandEvents, withAlignment, EventExpanderAdapter, IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter, AlignedInterval, and IntervalSource. Done.
If no production call sites remain, remove adapter overloads from GatherResult. Done.
Delete IntervalAdapters.hpp or leave a short-lived compatibility header only if tests or external consumers require it. Done: deleted.
Update GatherResult documentation and examples. Done.
Update developer docs if final API differs from the design document. Done.



Exit Criteria

GatherResult no longer exposes adapter-based gather APIs. Done.
The build succeeds without IntervalAdapters.hpp included by GatherResult.hpp. Done.

text:
Phase 7: Documentation And Cleanup

Goals
Document the final architecture and remove migration-only language from user-facing references.


Tasks

Update docs/developer/GatherResult/ with the final API details.
Keep event_to_interval.qmd, interval_to_event.qmd, and prune_overlapping_intervals.qmd current.
Update any plot developer docs that mention adapter-based alignment.
Add examples showing non-registered window series passed to GatherResult.
Run formatting and static analysis on changed C++ files.
Run focused tests, then a broader relevant test suite.

Developer docs match the implemented API.
No stale examples mention adapter-based gather as the preferred path.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Verification Checklist
Use this checklist before considering the migration complete:

DigitalIntervalSeries::createOverlapping() is used for generated gather windows (EventToInterval already does this).
PruneOverlappingIntervals is available for greedy keep-first pruning of interval bounds when overlap prevention is required.
DigitalEventSeries is used for generated alignment points.
Overlapping event-aligned windows are preserved as separate rows.
GatherResult::size() matches the number of generated windows.
GatherResult::intervalAt(i) preserves its documented compatibility semantics. If both prepared-window and source-query interval accessors exist, each is named clearly.
GatherResult::alignmentTimeAt(i) returns the original event time or selected interval alignment point.
buildGatherRowStore(result, i) sets alignment_time, trial_index, trial_duration, and end_time correctly.
GatherResult::reorder() preserves original-index semantics.
GatherResult rows are normal DataObjects; callers do not branch on view-backed versus owning row storage.
A future fromRowsLike() path can preserve row metadata when a per-row transform produces another DataObject type.
Cross-timeframe gathers match expected absolute-time windows.
PSTH and event plot widgets render the same trial rows as before the migration.
IntervalReduction still produces interval-row TensorData with expected row descriptors.
RasterCSVExport output remains stable for existing raster export tests.
Generated temporary windows and alignment points do not copy source entity IDs; provenance should use lineage tracing if needed later.

title: GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries Migration Plan
text:
Suggested Implementation Order
If doing this incrementally across several pull requests, use this order:

Add tests and TransformsV2 alignment/window algorithms. Done: EventToInterval, IntervalToEvent, and PruneOverlappingIntervals.
Centralize use of the existing TimeFrame conversion primitives in gather/query and projection code.
Refactor GatherResult internals while keeping old adapter entry points temporarily.
Migrate plot alignment helpers.
Migrate transform/export consumers.
Remove adapter APIs.
Decouple TransformsV2 row processing from core GatherResult if not already done.
Finalize docs and examples.

This sequence keeps behavior testable at each step and avoids a large all-at-once replacement of plotting, transforms, and gather internals.

title: GatherResult Baseline Test Inventory
text:
Baseline Behavior Contract
Original data flow before migration:






Note



Phase 6 has removed the adapter API. The diagram and bullets below remain the historical Phase 0 baseline contract that the migration was designed to preserve or intentionally replace.


flowchart LR
    alignData["DigitalEventSeries or DigitalIntervalSeries"]
    adapters["EventExpanderAdapter / IntervalWithAlignmentAdapter"]
    gather["GatherResult::create"]
    consumers["Plots / IntervalReduction / Export"]

    alignData --> adapters
    adapters --> gather
    gather --> consumers

Event Alignment

Each alignment event produces exactly one trial row.
Window bounds: [event_time - pre_window, event_time + post_window] in absolute time when the adapter reports nullptr TimeFrame.
alignmentTimeAt(i) equals the original event time, not the window start, even for symmetric (centered) windows.
Overlapping windows are preserved unless prevent_overlap filters alignment events before gather.



Interval Alignment

Start: alignmentTimeAt = interval.start
End: alignmentTimeAt = interval.end
Center: alignmentTimeAt = (start + end) / 2 (integer division)
No-window mode: gathered view spans full interval bounds; adapter exposes interval TimeFrame.
Window mode: [align_abs - pre, align_abs + post] in absolute time; adapter reports nullptr TimeFrame.



Overlap Prevention (prevent_overlap)
Implemented in PlotAlignmentGather.hpp, not in GatherResult itself.

Greedy keep-first scan over sorted alignment times.
Overlap window: [time - window_size/2, time + window_size/2].
Keep candidate iff current_start > last_kept_end (touching counts as overlapping).
Applied before gather by filtering the alignment series copy.



Reorder

reorder(indices) permutes _views only; _intervals and _alignment_times remain in original order.
_reorder_indices[display_pos] maps display position to original trial index.
originalIndex(i) returns the original trial index for display position i.
intervalAtReordered(i) == intervalAt(originalIndex(i)).
alignmentTimeAt(i) looks up alignment time via originalIndex(i).
isReordered() is true whenever _reorder_indices is non-empty (including identity permutations).



Cross-Timeframe

Adapter path (GatherResult::create with IntervalSource): convert adapter indices → absolute time → source indices for view bounds; store absolute alignment time in _alignment_times.
Plain interval path (GatherResult::create with DigitalIntervalSeries): no conversion; interval indices used directly as view bounds.
IntervalReduction: prepareIntervalsForGather() converts interval TimeFrame → source TimeFrame before gather.
Plot helpers (gatherWithEventAlignment, createAlignedGatherResult): delegate to adapter path; cross-timeframe behavior matches low-level adapter tests when source and alignment series carry different TimeFrames.

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
A repeatable, LLM-executable protocol for systematically documenting function preconditions as @pre Doxygen tags with enforcement classification, then tracing callers transitively to verify precondition propagation.
This protocol is documentation only — it adds @pre tags but does not add asserts, change control flow, or refactor code. The (enforcement: none) markers create a clean backlog for a separate refactoring phase, keeping documentation and behavioral changes strictly separated.

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
A repeatable, LLM-executable protocol for systematically documenting function preconditions as @pre Doxygen tags with enforcement classification, then tracing callers transitively to verify precondition propagation.
This protocol is documentation only — it adds @pre tags but does not add asserts, change control flow, or refactor code. The (enforcement: none) markers create a clean backlog for a separate refactoring phase, keeping documentation and behavioral changes strictly separated.

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
Enforcement Classification
Every @pre tag carries an enforcement suffix recording what exists today:
/// @brief Computes the median filter of an image.
/// @pre image_data must not be empty (enforcement: assert)
/// @pre width > 0 and height > 0 (enforcement: runtime_check)
/// @pre kernel_size is odd and >= 1 (enforcement: none)
void medianFilter(std::span<uint8_t const> image_data, int width, int height, int kernel_size);
Five categories:







Enforcement
Meaning




assert
Guarded by assert() or Q_ASSERT() (debug-only)


runtime_check
Guarded by if / early-return / error-code (always active)


exception
Guarded by throw (always active, unwinding)


static
Guarded by static_assert or concept (compile-time)


none
No enforcement exists; the assumption is implicit



The none markers become a greppable TODO list for the later refactoring phase:
# Count total precondition debt
grep -rn "enforcement: none" src/ --include="*.hpp" | wc -l

# Find critical unenforced preconditions
grep -rn "enforcement: none\] \[CRITICAL\]" src/ --include="*.hpp"

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
Per-Function Protocol

Step 1 — Parameter Inventory
For each parameter, ask type-specific questions:







Parameter Type
Questions




Raw pointer (T*, T const*)
Nullable? Who owns? Lifetime?


std::span<T>
Can be empty? Minimum size?


std::string_view / string const&
Can be empty? Format constraints?


std::optional<T>
Is .value() called without guard?


Numeric (int, float, size_t)
Range? Sign? Zero valid?


TimeFrameIndex
Bounds relative to what data object?


Container (vector, map)
Can be empty? Sorted? Unique elements?


Enum
All values handled?


std::function / callable
Can be null/empty?


Smart pointer (shared_ptr, unique_ptr)
Can be null?





Step 2 — Implementation Scan
Read the function body and identify:

Every place a parameter is dereferenced, indexed, or used in arithmetic
Every existing check (assert, if, throw, early return) that guards a parameter
Every downstream call that imposes its own documented @pre on values derived from our parameters
Any implicit assumptions (e.g., dividing by a parameter without checking for zero)



Step 3 — Precondition Enumeration
For each identified precondition, produce:
@pre <condition text> (enforcement: assert | runtime_check | exception | static | none)
Optionally add a severity tag for unenforced preconditions:

(enforcement: none) [CRITICAL] — null deref, out-of-bounds, use-after-free
(enforcement: none) [IMPORTANT] — produces wrong results silently
(enforcement: none) [LOW] — unlikely to occur in practice



Step 4 — Write @pre Tags
Add to the function’s Doxygen comment in the header file declaration.
Rules:

Document ALL preconditions, even those already enforced
The (enforcement: X) suffix is required — it differentiates documentation from refactoring
Omit preconditions obvious from the type system (e.g., std::span is contiguous)
Order: most critical first (null safety > bounds > domain constraints)



Step 5 — Find All Callers
Use clangd “Find All References” to find every call site of the analyzed function.


Step 6 — Classify Each Caller
For each caller, determine whether it:

Guarantees the precondition (constructs the value in a way that satisfies it)
Passes through a parameter that should carry the same precondition
Violates the precondition (potential bug — flag explicitly)

For pass-through cases, the same @pre must exist on the caller.


Step 7 — Transitive Walk
Repeat Steps 5–6 for each pass-through caller until reaching:

A function that establishes the precondition (constructs a valid value)
A public API boundary (user-facing function)
A UI event handler or entry point

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
Precondition Reference Checklist

Critical (Crashes / Undefined Behavior)

Null pointer dereference — raw or smart pointer is null when dereferenced
Out-of-bounds access — index >= container.size(), negative index, size_t underflow
Use-after-free / dangling reference — pointer/reference to destroyed object
Iterator invalidation — container modified during iteration
Division by zero — numeric denominator is zero
Uninitialized state — object method called before initialization
Buffer overflow — data size exceeds allocated buffer
Integer overflow/underflow — arithmetic exceeds type range



Important (Silent Wrong Results)

Container emptiness — algorithm assumes non-empty input
Container size matching — two parallel containers must have same length
Sorted order — binary search or merge assumes sorted input
Uniqueness — map key or set element assumed unique
Numeric range — value must be positive, in [0,1], finite, non-NaN
String format — expected format (path, JSON, delimited)
Enum completeness — switch handles all enum values
Mathematical validity — matrix invertible, value finite



Ownership & Lifetime

Pointer ownership — who creates, who destroys
Callback lifetime — captured references outlive the callback
Thread safety — concurrent access to mutable state



Project-Specific

TimeFrameIndex bounds — index within valid time range for the data object
DataManager key existence — getData called with key that exists
ObserverData CallbackID management — properly unregistered in destructors
OpenGL context validity — GL calls made with valid current context

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
LLM Prompt Template
When pointing an LLM at a specific function, use this prompt:

Analyze <function signature> in <header path> (implementation: <cpp path>) for preconditions using the Precondition Documentation Protocol.

Read the function signature and implementation
For each parameter, identify preconditions using the Reference Checklist
Scan the implementation for existing enforcement (assert, if-check, throw, or none)
Check downstream calls for documented @pre tags that impose requirements on our parameters
Write @pre tags with (enforcement: X) classification
Find all callers transitively and check precondition propagation

Deliverables (in your response only; do not add the analysis or caller table to this protocol document or to any other file in the repo):

The updated Doxygen comment block with @pre tags (applied by editing the header file)
A caller propagation table:



Caller
File:Line
Precondition Status
Action Needed





Any potential bugs discovered (precondition violations at call sites)

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
Additional Techniques

Postconditions (@post)
While analyzing a function, also note postconditions — what the function guarantees about its return value. A function’s @post becomes its callers’ established preconditions, closing the propagation chain.


Contradiction Detection
If a function has @pre x > 0 but a caller can pass zero, that’s a bug, not just missing documentation. Flag these explicitly as potential defects.


Automated Assert Injection (Future Phase)
After the documentation phase is complete, a follow-up phase can convert (enforcement: none) preconditions into assert() statements based on condition text patterns. This is the refactoring phase, kept cleanly separate from documentation.


Compiler Attribute Follow-Up (Future Phase)
After documentation stabilizes, [[gnu::nonnull]] or SAL annotations (_In_, _Notnull_) can give compilers the same knowledge for static warnings.

title: Precondition Documentation Protocol
text:
Verification
Track progress with these commands:
# Total documented preconditions (should grow)
grep -rn "@pre" src/ --include="*.hpp" | wc -l

# Remaining unenforced preconditions (should shrink over time)
grep -rn "enforcement: none" src/ --include="*.hpp" | wc -l

# Build succeeds after each batch
cmake --build --preset linux-clang-release > build_log.txt 2>&1
Spot-check:

Pick 3 functions with enforcement: none and manually verify the precondition is real
Pick 3 caller propagation chains and verify they are correct

AutoParam System
text: The AutoParam system provides a mechanism to automatically generate Qt-based configuration forms from C++ structs. It leverages compile-time reflection (via reflect-cpp) to create a runtime schema, which is then used to build the UI dynamically.

title: AutoParam System
text:
Source Location
AutoParamWidget lives in its own static library at src/WhiskerToolbox/AutoParamWidget/. It depends only on Qt6::Widgets and ParameterSchema — it has no dependency on TransformsV2 or any other domain library, making it reusable by any widget that needs schema-driven parameter forms (e.g., TransformsV2_Widget, TriageSession_Widget).
The CMake target is AutoParamWidget. Link it directly when you need the form widget:
target_link_libraries(MyWidget PUBLIC AutoParamWidget)

Include Path
#include "AutoParamWidget/AutoParamWidget.hpp"

title: AutoParam System
text:
Core Components

1. Parameter Structs
The foundation of the system is a simple C++ struct that defines your parameters.
struct MyTransformParams {
    float threshold = 0.5f;
    int iterations = 10;
    std::string mode = "Fast";
    bool enable_logging = true;
};


2. ParameterSchema
At runtime, we need a description of this struct to build the UI. ParameterSchema is a data structure that holds this information:

Fields: Name, type, default value
Constraints: Min/max values for numbers
UI Hints: Tooltips, display names, grouping

This schema is extracted automatically using reflect-cpp.


3. AutoParamWidget
The AutoParamWidget is a generic Qt widget that takes a ParameterSchema and builds a form:

float / double → QDoubleSpinBox
int → QSpinBox
bool → QCheckBox
std::string → QLineEdit or QComboBox (if allowed_values or dynamic_combo is set)
std::string + path_field_kind → QLineEdit + Browse button (file or directory dialog)
enum class → QComboBox (enumerator names auto-populated by extractParameterSchema)
std::vector<T> → multi-select QListWidget or CSV QLineEdit (see ParameterSchema)
rfl::TaggedUnion → discriminator QComboBox + QStackedWidget sub-form per alternative
std::optional<T> → checkbox-gated widget

Fields with ParameterFieldDescriptor::is_hidden == true (set at runtime on the schema, e.g. by applyDynamicInputSlotSchemaConstraints) are not added to the form layout but still have backing widgets so toJson() / fromJson() match reflect-cpp structs.

Method

title: InferenceController
text:
Batch workers
Batch inference runs on dedicated QThread worker classes so AUTOMOC can generate meta-object code from headers (no .moc include in .cpp files).








Class
Header
Role




BatchInferenceWorker
Inference/BatchInferenceWorker.hpp
Single contiguous frame range


MultiIntervalBatchWorker
Inference/MultiIntervalBatchWorker.hpp
Multiple intervals with unified progress



Both workers call SlotAssembler::runBatchRangeOffline(), push decoded FrameResult entries into a shared WriteReservation, and emit progressChanged(current, total) for connection to InferenceController.

Single range
runBatch(start, end, batch_size) launches a BatchInferenceWorker on a background QThread. Progress is reported via batchProgressChanged(current, total).


Multi-interval batch
runBatchIntervals(intervals, batch_size) accepts a vector of (start, end) frame ranges (e.g. from a DigitalIntervalSeries) and processes each interval sequentially on a single background thread. Progress is reported against the total frame count across all intervals.
The _onRunBatch() dialog in DeepLearningPropertiesWidget offers two modes:

Manual range: User specifies start/end frames directly.
From interval series: User selects a DigitalIntervalSeries key from DataManager. The combo box auto-populates and refreshes via a DataManager observer callback cleaned up when the dialog is destroyed.



Recurrent sequence
runRecurrentSequence(start, frame_count) runs frames in order so recurrent memory bindings can feed prior outputs back into the model. Progress is reported via recurrentProgressChanged(current, total).

Cancellation
All worker types share a std::shared_ptr<std::atomic<bool>> cancel flag owned by the InferenceController::Impl. Calling cancel() sets this flag, which is polled by SlotAssembler::runBatchRangeOffline() between batches. The same flag is set in the destructor to ensure clean shutdown.

title: TimeScrollBar
text:
The timeline widget (TimeScrollBar) drives the active TimeFrame and syncs with EditorRegistry.


When EditorRegistry::currentPosition() uses a different TimeFrame than the scrollbar (for example, a DataInspector interval on the master clock while the scrollbar controls time), relative frame stepping must convert through TimePosition::convertTo() — not sameClock(), which only compares shared_ptr identity. Inbound sync (_onEditorRegistryTimeChanged) already used conversion; arrow keys, playback, and pause-snap now use the same rule.



Playback advances at the selected logical target_fps (frames of time per second). The QTimer tick rate is capped at 30 Hz (time_scroll_bar::kMaxPlaybackUiRefreshFps): when target_fps exceeds that cap, each tick advances multiple frames so average speed matches target_fps, while UI callbacks stay bounded. For rates at or below the cap, the timer interval is 1000 / target_fps milliseconds (for example 0.5 FPS, one frame every two seconds).


Rewind and fast-forward step through this ladder (also used when persisting target_fps in TimeScrollBarStateData):
0.5 → 1 → 2 → 5 → 10 → 25 → 50 → 100 → 200
Shared helpers live in TimeScrollBarPlayback.hpp (time_scroll_bar::kFpsPresets, snapTargetFpsToPreset, timerPeriodMsForTargetFps, playbackUiRefreshFps, timerPeriodMsForPlayback).




Current field: target_fps (float), snapped to a preset when set via TimeScrollBarState::setTargetFps.
Legacy: play_speed (integer multiplier on a fixed 25 FPS base) is migrated on fromJson to target_fps = 25 * play_speed.

title: Data Manager Widget
text:
Data Manager Widget Overview
The data manager widget serves as the main user interface for interacting with all data currently loaded into the program. At its top, the widget displays all keys currently in the data manager along with their corresponding data types. It enables the user to specify the folder for saving data. Additionally, users can create new, initially blank data sets, which can subsequently be populated through further manipulations and other widgets.
When a user selects an entry in the top table, a data type-specific soft widget is populated. This widget presents the user with various features of the selected data. For example, when dealing with point data, it shows a table listing every available point within that data set and its associated frame. The user has the ability to scroll through this table; clicking an entry causes the time displayed by the rest of the program to jump to that point’s frame. Users can perform several data manipulations via these specific widgets. For instance, using the point widget, a user can delete any specific point. They can also opt to move a specific point to another point data set available in the manager.


Data Saving Functionality
The data manager widget also functions as the primary interface for saving data to disk. It features a sub-widget interface where the user can select the desired file output type, and specific options for that output type are then displayed. For instance, if a user is viewing point data, they can choose to output CSV files and will be presented with various CSV saving options, such as selecting the delimiter and deciding whether a header should be included, etc.

title: Tensor Inspector (Dev)
text:
Column Views
The Column Views section allows creating zero-copy AnalogTimeSeries views for each column of a 2D TensorData. This is useful for visualizing individual channels in DataViewer_Widget and applying per-channel transforms.

How it works

User selects a TensorData in the data tree.
In the Column Views collapsible section, set a key prefix (defaults to tensor key).
Click Create Column Views.
For each column, an AnalogTimeSeries backed by TensorColumnAnalogStorage is inserted into DataManager under {prefix}/{column_name}.



Implementation







File
Description




src/TensorDesign/TensorColumnViews.hpp
Qt-free API: createTensorColumnViews, discoverAnalogKeyGroups


src/TensorDesign/TensorColumnViews.cpp
Implementation using tensorToAnalog()


src/WhiskerToolbox/DataInspector_Widget/TensorData/TensorInspector.cpp
UI section; delegates to TensorDesign


tests/TransformsV2/test_tensor_column_views.test.cpp
Integration tests



The utility calls tensorToAnalog() internally, which creates TensorColumnAnalogStorage views — zero-copy spans into the Armadillo matrix columns. The views share ownership of the source TensorData via shared_ptr, so they remain valid as long as any view exists.






Note



Column names from the TensorData are used as suffixes in the generated keys. If no column names are set, the fallback is ch0, ch1, etc.

title: Tensor Inspector (Dev)
text:
Populate from AnalogTimeSeries
When a TensorData object is empty (e.g., freshly created via the New Data widget), the inspector shows a Create from AnalogTimeSeries section instead of Column Views / Export.

Workflow

Create an empty TensorData in the DataManager (via New Data → Tensor).
Select it in the data tree. The inspector shows “Create from AnalogTimeSeries”.
Click Refresh to scan the DataManager for groups of analog channels that share a common prefix (e.g., voltage_1, voltage_2, voltage_3 → group “voltage”).
Select a group from the combo box.
Click Populate Tensor to pack the channels into the tensor.

After population, the section hides and the standard Column Views / Export sections appear.


Key Group Discovery
discoverAnalogKeyGroups() extracts the prefix before the last _ character in each AnalogTimeSeries key, groups keys by prefix, and returns only groups with ≥2 keys. Keys without an underscore (or with _ only at position 0) are excluded.


Implementation







File
Description




TensorColumnViews.hpp
AnalogKeyGroup, discoverAnalogKeyGroups(), populateTensorFromAnalogKeys()


TensorColumnViews.cpp
Implementation using analogToTensor() algorithm


TensorInspector.cpp
UI section with combo box, refresh/populate buttons, visibility toggling


test_tensor_column_views.test.cpp
Tests for group discovery and tensor population





Lifetime Safety
_onPopulateFromAnalog() calls DataManager::setData(), which triggers observer notifications that can destroy the TensorInspector widget (the properties widget recreates inspectors when the inspected key changes). To prevent use-after-free:

All member data (_active_key, group keys) is copied to locals before the call.
A QPointer<TensorInspector> guard detects destruction; if triggered, the slot returns without accessing this.



TimeFrame Validation
populateTensorFromAnalogKeys() checks that the target tensor’s existing TimeKey (if non-empty) matches the source analog channels’ TimeKey. This prevents accidentally overwriting a tensor that lives in a different temporal coordinate system.


Performance
analogToTensor() builds an arma::fmat directly column-by-column. Each analog channel maps to one Armadillo column (contiguous memory), so the copy is cache-friendly with zero intermediate allocation. The matrix is moved into TensorData::createTimeSeries2D(arma::fmat, ...) — no row-major-to-column-major conversion is needed.


Section Visibility
_updateSectionVisibility() checks TensorData::isEmpty() and toggles:

Empty tensor: Show “Create from AnalogTimeSeries”, hide Column Views and Export.
Non-empty tensor: Hide “Create from AnalogTimeSeries”, show Column Views and Export.

title: DigitalEventSeries Inspector
text:
Architecture

EventTableModel
EventTableModel is a QAbstractTableModel that provides:

Two columns: Frame and Group

Group filtering via setGroupFilter() / clearGroupFilter()

title: Media Widget
text: The media widget is responsible for displaying data that can be visualized on a canvas. The types of data that can be displayed by the data manager include point data, line data, mask data, tensor data, interval data, and media data. Data currently in the data manager matching these types is displayed on the top left side. In this table, the user can click to enable the visibility of particular data in the accompanying media window canvas.

title: Media Widget
text: The media widget is responsible for displaying data that can be visualized on a canvas. The types of data that can be displayed by the data manager include point data, line data, mask data, tensor data, interval data, and media data. Data currently in the data manager matching these types is displayed on the top left side. In this table, the user can click to enable the visibility of particular data in the accompanying media window canvas.

title: Media Widget
text:
Data-Specific Interactions and Manipulations
Clicking on a data item also brings up a sub-widget below the table, offering data type-specific manipulations. For example, this sub-widget would be responsible for changing attributes such as color, alpha value, marker type, etc., for point data within the media window. This sub-widget may also handle data-specific manipulations directly within the media window. For instance, the user might wish to click on a position in the media window to set it as the location for the currently displayed point. Alternatively, the user might click and hold to utilize a paintbrush-type function for extending or erasing mask data.

title: Media Widget
text:
Shared Components and Common Interactions
These data-specific sub-widgets may house common sub-widgets that are shared among others. For instance, color selection is a common feature for multiple data types. An interface for click, hover, and release interactions is common to multiple data types but may perform different actions, such as painting a mask or erasing the media foreground.
Note that there is some overlap here with the data manager widget. For many data types the data manager widget includes the ability to view all data present in the data manager and select particular instances such as a point at a certain time and the user can delete that point. Consequently we will try to keep media window based manipulation to the media widget. 
The media window is the widget that houses the actual canvas for display. It is also the owner of the specific drawing options and drawing routines onto the canvas. For instance if the user changes the marker size and color of point data the options that are updated are held by the media window. The media window uses qt-based drawing. It is also responsible for receiving mouse events inside its space and emits signals that other widgets can receive.

title: Spectrogram Widget
text:
The Spectrogram Widget displays a time–frequency spectrogram of a continuous signal, showing how the frequency content of an AnalogTimeSeries (or a TensorData column with TimeFrameIndex rows) evolves over time. The X-axis represents time, the Y-axis represents frequency, and cell color encodes spectral power. This provides a compact view of a signal’s spectral dynamics, complementing the raw waveform display available in the DataViewerWidget.
The spectrogram itself is not computed inside the widget. Instead, the spectral transform (e.g., Short-Time Fourier Transform) is defined as a TransformsV2 data transformation that converts an AnalogTimeSeries into a TensorData object (a time × frequency matrix). The SpectrogramWidget is purely a visualization of the resulting 2-D matrix, color-mapped with a user-selectable colormap.
