Opens QColorDialog; stores as hex string


Alpha
QDoubleSpinBox
Transparency (0.0 – 1.0, step 0.05)



The controls use the anti-recursion _updating_ui guard pattern to avoid feedback loops when the state updates the UI.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Zoom and Pan
The widget supports separated X/Y zoom for independent axis exploration, using the shared PlotInteractionHelpers:



Input
Action




Mouse wheel
X-zoom only


Shift + wheel
Y-zoom only


Ctrl + wheel
Uniform zoom (both axes)


Click + drag
Pan in both axes



Zoom and pan update only the view projection (no scene rebuild), providing smooth interactive performance. The PlotInteractionHelpers are shared across all OpenGL plot widgets — see Plot Widget Guide.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Double-Click-to-Navigate
Double-clicking on a scatter point navigates other time-synced widgets to that point’s TimeFrameIndex. Hit testing uses the shared SceneHitTester (CorePlotting/Interaction/SceneHitTester.hpp), which queries the QuadTree<EntityId> spatial index built automatically by SceneBuilder::addGlyphs() during scene construction. This is the same infrastructure used by EventPlotWidget for double-click navigation and click-to-select.
The implementation:

On mouseDoubleClickEvent, converts screen position to world coordinates via screenToWorld()
Converts an 8-pixel tolerance to world units (using the max of X and Y to handle non-uniform aspect ratios)
Calls _hit_tester.queryQuadTree(world_x, world_y, _scene) for O(log n) nearest-neighbor lookup
Maps the returned EntityId back to a TimeFrameIndex via the cached ScatterPointData
Emits pointDoubleClicked(TimePosition), which is forwarded as timePositionSelected and wired to EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime() in the registration

The most recently navigated-to point is highlighted with a larger yellow glyph (size 9, rendered as a second addGlyphs() batch on top of the main point batch). The highlight is cleared when data sources change.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Hover Highlight
When the cursor dwells over a scatter point, the nearest point is highlighted to give visual feedback before a double-click or selection action.
Visual style: The hovered point is drawn at the same color it already has (preserving any feature-based or fixed coloring) but at a larger size, making it visually distinct without changing its semantic meaning.
Hit testing: Uses the same SceneHitTester/QuadTree infrastructure as double-click navigation. A single-shot QTimer (~400 ms) debounces rapid mouse movement; the hit test fires only when the cursor stops moving. The timer is cancelled and any visible highlight is cleared immediately when a pan or zoom gesture begins.
Rendering: Because GlyphRenderer uses u_point_size as a per-batch uniform (not per-instance), the hovered point must be issued as a separate addGlyphs() call at the desired larger size. Per-instance color is handled directly in the shader (a_instance_color attribute on the instanced VBO), so the hover batch re-uses the original point color without any additional CPU-side logic. This results in one extra GPU draw call for the single hovered point.
See roadmap Phase 8 for the complete dwell-timer and tooltip implementation plan.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Hover Tooltip
When the cursor dwells over a scatter point (~500 ms), a tooltip appears showing the point’s X and Y coordinates and its TimeFrameIndex. The tooltip uses the shared PlotTooltipManager (Plots/Common/TooltipManager/), the same infrastructure used by EventPlotWidget.
Hit test provider: Reuses the existing hitTestPointAt() method (which queries the QuadTree<EntityId> via SceneHitTester) and passes the scatter data index as user_data.
Text provider: Formats the tooltip as:
X: 1.234
Y: 5.678
Index: 42
Suppression: Tooltips are automatically suppressed during pan and polygon interaction by passing _is_panning || _polygon_controller->isActive() to onMouseMove(). The tooltip is also hidden when the mouse leaves the widget via leaveEvent().

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Point Selection
Points can be selected via polygon (lasso) drawing. Selected points are visually distinguished from unselected points and can be added to an entity group.
Visual style: Selected points are drawn at the same size as normal points but with a distinct selection color (e.g., red). Keeping the same size means no per-batch size change is needed — only color differs.
Rendering: Since color is stored as a per-instance attribute in the shader (a_instance_color on the instanced VBO), selected points can be rendered with any color without rebuilding the main point batch. The selected subset is issued as a separate addGlyphs() call with the selection color, rendering on top of the unselected points. This results in one extra GPU draw call for the entire selected set, regardless of how many points are selected.
The polygon drawing interaction uses the shared PolygonInteractionController from CorePlotting/Interaction/. After the polygon is closed, selectPointsInPolygon() (a pure geometry function in CorePlotting/Selection/) identifies which points fall inside the polygon. Selected point indices are stored in ScatterPlotStateData::selected_indices and cleared when the data source changes.
See roadmap Phase 3 for the full polygon selection and group integration implementation plan.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
ContextAction Integration
The scatter plot’s right-click context menu dynamically populates ContextActions from the SelectionContext system. When a SelectionContext is available (set via setSelectionContext() during registration), contextMenuEvent() queries SelectionContext::applicableActions() and appends matching actions to the menu below the group management actions.
This enables cross-widget workflows: for example, right-clicking in the scatter plot can trigger the “Cluster with ML Workflow” action registered by MLCoreWidgetRegistration, which sets the scatter’s data source as the clustering input and switches to the Clustering tab.

Selective Clustering (“Cluster Selection…”)
A dedicated “Cluster Selection…” action appears in the context menu when:

Points are currently selected (via polygon selection)
The scatter data source is a TensorData key (not AnalogTimeSeries)

When triggered, _executeClusterSelection():

Extracts the selected point indices from ScatterPlotState
Reads the corresponding rows from the source TensorData via TensorData::row(idx)
Creates a new TensorData with TensorData::createOrdinal2D() containing only the selected rows
Stores it in DataManager with key "<source_key>_selection"
Sets data focus via SelectionContext::setDataFocus() so DataFocusAware widgets pick it up
Programmatically triggers the mlcore.cluster_tensor ContextAction to open the ML Workflow Clustering tab with the filtered data pre-loaded

This provides a workflow where users can visually identify a cluster of interest in the scatter plot, select it with a polygon, and immediately run clustering on just those points.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Cluster Label Overlay
When ScatterPlotState::showClusterLabels() is enabled, drawClusterLabels() renders text labels at group centroids using a QPainter overlay on top of the OpenGL rendering.
Implementation: After all OpenGL draw calls complete in paintGL(), a QPainter is constructed on the widget. For each group in the GroupManager, the method:

Accumulates the screen-space centroid (average X, average Y) of all scatter points belonging to that group
Converts world coordinates to screen coordinates via worldToScreen()
Renders "GroupName (n=count)" at the centroid position using the group’s assigned color with a dark outline for readability

State: The show_cluster_labels field is part of ScatterPlotStateData (serialized via reflect-cpp). A checkbox in the “Glyph Options” section of ScatterPlotPropertiesWidget toggles it. The clusterLabelsChanged signal triggers a repaint.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Horizontal Axis (X)
Uses the shared HorizontalAxisWidget with HorizontalAxisState. The axis uses identityAxis("X", 0) mapping. Range is synchronized bidirectionally with the view state using setRangeSilent().
This is the same axis type used by ACFWidget, TemporalProjectionViewWidget, and OnionSkinViewWidget. See Plot Widget Guide for full axis integration details.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Vertical Axis (Y)
Uses VerticalAxisWidget with VerticalAxisState. Range is auto-adjusted when data bounds are computed, and synchronized bidirectionally with the view state.
Both axis widgets provide collapsible range control sections (HorizontalAxisRangeControls and VerticalAxisRangeControls) that are inserted into the properties panel when setPlotWidget() is called.

title: Scatter Plot Widget
text:
Data Source Selection
A “Data Sources” collapsible section contains controls for both X and Y axes:
Per axis (X and Y):

Key combo box — lists all AnalogTimeSeries keys (prefixed [ATS]) and TensorData keys (prefixed [Tensor]) from DataManager
Column combo box — visible only when a TensorData key is selected; populated with column names from TensorData::getColumnNames(), falling back to numeric indices (0, 1, 2, …) if no names are set
Offset spinbox — integer spinbox for temporal offset in TimeFrameIndex steps (default: 0, range: -10000 to 10000)
Compatibility label — shows “Sources are compatible” (green) or a descriptive warning (red) based on checkSourceCompatibility() result

The combo boxes are kept in sync with DataManager via the observer pattern: an observer is registered in the constructor (_data_manager->addObserver()) and removed in the destructor (_data_manager->removeObserver()). When the observer fires, all key combo boxes are repopulated while preserving the current selection.

title: Event Plot Widget
text: The Event Plot Widget renders neuroscience-style raster plots showing discrete events (spikes, behavioral markers) across multiple trials, aligned to a user-selected reference event or interval. Users can overlay multiple DigitalEventSeries, configure glyph appearance per series, sort trials by built-in or external features, and interact with the plot via zoom, pan, and single-click selection.

title: Event Plot Widget

GatherResult Integration
Trial alignment uses the shared GatherResult infrastructure from DataManager. The gatherTrialData() method creates aligned views of each DigitalEventSeries using the alignment settings from state:

The alignment event key selects a DigitalEventSeries or DigitalIntervalSeries from the DataManager
Each event/interval defines a trial center point
The window size determines how much data is gathered around each trial center
The result is a GatherResult<DigitalEventSeries> containing per-trial views

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Scene Building
The EventPlotOpenGLWidget manages the full rendering lifecycle:

Scene rebuild (on stateChanged): Gathers trial data, applies sorting, maps events to glyphs via RasterMapper, and builds a RenderableScene
View update (on viewStateChanged): Updates only the projection matrix — no data re-gathering
Paint (on paintGL): Renders the cached scene through PlottingOpenGL::SceneRenderer

The widget also renders a center line at t=0 and axis labels/tick marks.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Row Layout
Trials are laid out vertically using CorePlotting::RowLayoutStrategy. Each trial occupies a row of equal height. The LayoutResponse is cached for use by the hit tester during interaction.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Zoom and Pan
The widget supports separated X/Y zoom for independent exploration of time and trial dimensions:



Input
Action




Mouse wheel
X-zoom only (time axis)


Shift + wheel
Y-zoom only (trial axis)


Ctrl + wheel
Uniform zoom (both axes)


Click + drag
Pan in both axes



Zoom and pan update only the view projection (no scene rebuild), providing smooth interactive performance even with large datasets.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Hit Testing and Selection
Single-click selection uses CorePlotting::SceneHitTester for point queries against the rendered scene:

Single click: Select event → emits eventSelected(trial_index, relative_time_ms, series_key)
Double click: Navigate to event time → emits eventDoubleClicked(time_frame_index, series_key)
Click vs. drag detection: 5-pixel threshold prevents accidental selections during panning

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Tooltips
Hover tooltips display trial index and relative time position. The tooltip timer prevents excessive updates during mouse movement.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Built-in Modes
Three sorting modes are available via a combo box in the properties panel:







Mode
Behavior




TrialIndex
Original trial order (default)


FirstEventLatency
Sort by latency to first event at or after t=0 (ascending). Trials with no positive events are placed at the end.


EventCount
Sort by total number of events in each trial’s window (descending)



Sorting is applied after data gathering by computing sort indices and calling GatherResult::reorder():
auto sorting_mode = _state->getSortingMode();
if (sorting_mode != TrialSortMode::TrialIndex) {
    gathered = applySorting(gathered, sorting_mode);
}

External Feature Sorting
External sorting via TensorData objects is planned. See the EventPlot Roadmap for the design.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Time Axis (X)
Uses the shared RelativeTimeAxisWidget with RelativeTimeAxisState. The axis is synchronized bidirectionally with the view state:

User changes axis range → view state updates → scene rebuilds
User zooms/pans → axis range updates silently (no feedback loop)

See Plot Widget Guide for full axis integration details.

title: Event Plot Widget

Trial Axis (Y)
Uses a VerticalAxisWidget with VerticalAxisState managed locally (not serialized in EventPlotStateData, since Y bounds are derived from trial count). The axis uses CorePlotting::trialIndexAxis() mapping for integer trial labels.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
SelectionContext Integration
The Event Plot Widget participates in the project’s SelectionContext system for inter-widget communication. When a DigitalEventSeries is selected in another widget (e.g., clicking a row in HeatmapWidget), the Event Plot Widget can automatically update to display that series — unless pinned.

title: Event Plot Widget
text:
Pinning
The pinned flag in state controls whether the widget responds to SelectionContext changes:

Unpinned (default): Widget updates when a compatible data key is selected elsewhere
Pinned: Widget ignores external selection changes, preserving its current view

This enables workflows where one Event Plot is locked to a specific unit while another follows the user’s selection across a HeatmapWidget or PSTHWidget.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
The Data Viewer Widget visualizes time series data — analog time series, digital event series, and digital interval series — on a shared OpenGL canvas. Users select data series by key from a feature tree, configure display options per series, and view synchronized plots that scroll with the application’s global time bar.
For planned features and refactoring work, see the roadmap.






NoteLocation Note



The Data Viewer Widget predates the unified Plots/ directory structure and currently lives at src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/ rather than src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/DataViewerWidget/. A future refactoring may relocate it for consistency with other plot widgets. Several of its components could be refactored to use shared infrastructure from Plots/Common/ — see the roadmap for details.

title: Data Viewer Widget
Data Viewer Widget
text:
Signal Flow
The state drives a unidirectional data flow:
User action (UI)
    → Modify DataViewerState
        → State emits signal (viewStateChanged, themeChanged, etc.)
            → OpenGLWidget reacts → calls update()
Key principle: UI modifies state directly; OpenGLWidget never has pass-through setter methods. All rendering configuration flows through the state object.

title: Data Viewer Widget
Data Viewer Widget
Data Viewer Widget
Data Viewer Widget
text:
Layered Architecture
The rendering system is organized into five layers:

Data Storage (TimeSeriesDataStore): Series data in typed maps with layout transforms and caches
View State (DataViewerState): Time window, Y bounds, zoom, pan — the “camera”
Layout (CorePlotting::LayoutEngine): Computes vertical positioning via StackedLayoutStrategy; produces a LayoutResponse with per-series SeriesLayout
Scene Building (SceneBuildingHelpers): Converts series data + layout into RenderableBatch primitives (polylines for analog, glyphs for events, rectangles for intervals)
Rendering (PlottingOpenGL::SceneRenderer): Uploads and draws batches via OpenGL shaders

title: Data Viewer Widget
Data Viewer Widget
text:
X-Axis: Global Time-Yoked
Unlike other plot widgets that allow independent X panning (see Plot Widget Guide for RelativeTimeAxis and HorizontalAxis), the Data Viewer’s X-axis is yoked to the application’s global time position. The visible time window is always centered on the current playback position. The user can zoom the X-axis (changing how much time is visible), but there is no independent X panning — the view follows the global time bar.
This is distinct from the RelativeTimeAxis used by event-aligned widgets (LinePlotWidget, EventPlotWidget, PSTHWidget, HeatmapWidget) where X represents time relative to alignment events, and from the HorizontalAxis used by spatial widgets (ScatterPlotWidget, ACFWidget).






TipRefactoring Opportunity



A CenteredTimeAxis variant of the Common Axis System could formalize this behavior: zoom-only with no pan, always centered on the global time position. This would bring the DataViewer in line with the shared axis architecture. See roadmap Phase 1.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Y-Axis: Stacked Lane Layout
Multiple series are arranged vertically in stacked lanes, with each series occupying its own vertical band. The CorePlotting::LayoutEngine with StackedLayoutStrategy computes the lane positions. This is conceptually similar to the trial-row layout in EventPlotWidget, but with several key differences:








Aspect
DataViewer
EventPlotWidget




Lane contents
Each lane holds a different data series (analog, event, or interval)
Each lane holds one trial of the same event series


Data types
Mixed: AnalogTimeSeries, DigitalEventSeries, DigitalIntervalSeries
Homogeneous: DigitalEventSeries only


Lane height
All lanes currently shrink equally as more are added
Fixed per-trial height with Y pan/zoom to navigate


Y pan/zoom
Y pan is available; lanes shrink as more are added
Full Y pan and zoom — can zoom into a subset of trials



Currently, when many series are added (e.g., 32 electrophysiology channels), each lane shrinks proportionally. This becomes impractical for analog signals where detail matters. The roadmap proposes adopting EventPlotWidget-style Y pan/zoom so users can zoom into a subset of channels even when many are loaded.
Mixed-lane placement is now wired through state overrides (series_lane_overrides and lane_overrides). Ordering precedence for stackable lanes is:

Explicit lane_order overrides (per-series)
Analog spike-sorter ordering fallback (analog-only, no explicit lane order)
Legacy type-based fallback (analog before stacked digital events)

Shared lane overlays (same lane_id) are aggregated to a single axis lane descriptor, with lane labels resolved from lane_overrides[lane_id].display_label when provided, otherwise from deterministic series-derived fallback labels.
OpenGLWidget::buildLayoutRequest() now delegates to DataViewer::buildLayoutRequest(...) in DataViewer_Widget/Core/LayoutRequestBuilder.cpp, which isolates ordering policy rules (explicit lane order, optional spike-sorter fallback, and deterministic type/key fallback) from rendering code.

text:
Series Types
Three data types can be visualized simultaneously:



Type
Visual Representation
Current Style Options

—

Adjustable glyph type (circle, square, diamond, cross, triangle), glyph size (roadmap Phase 3)

Per-series display options are managed through the SeriesOptionsRegistry and the CorePlotting::SeriesStyle base struct. See roadmap Phases 3–4 for planned enhancements to align with the shared PointGlyphOptions infrastructure planned for OnionSkinViewWidget, EventPlotWidget, and ScatterPlotWidget.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Multi-Series Display
Multiple series can be drawn on the same canvas with individual or overlapping positioning. Both X and Y axes are zoomable, and per-series amplitude scaling allows data of different magnitudes to be visualized simultaneously. Drawing is synced to the global time scroll bar, enabling simultaneous visualization across widgets (e.g., video + electrophysiology).
The viewer handles different sampling rates transparently. For instance, camera-frame events at 500 Hz plot correctly alongside electrophysiology at 30 kHz. The TimeFrame system in DataManager handles coordinate conversions, and the viewer plots data appropriately in the master time frame.

text:
Interaction Modes
The DataViewerInteractionManager implements a state machine with four modes:



Mode
Behavior




Normal
Pan, select entities, hover tooltips


CreateInterval
Click-drag to create a new digital interval


ModifyInterval
Edge-drag to resize an existing interval

Click-drag to draw a selection line



Switching modes cancels any active interaction. Completed interactions emit interactionCompleted with DataCoordinates containing all information needed to update the DataManager.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Entity Selection
DataViewerSelectionManager provides multi-select support (Ctrl+click). Selection state is tracked via EntityId and emits selectionChanged signals.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Coordinate Conversions
DataViewerCoordinates provides a unified interface for converting between:

Canvas coordinates (pixels, origin at top-left)
World coordinates (normalized space used by scene/layout)
Time coordinates (data time values)
Data values (analog series values via inverse transform)

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Interactive Interval Editing
The widget supports editing digital interval series through mouse-based dragging:

Click-to-Select: Click on intervals to select them; selected intervals get enhanced borders
Edge Dragging: Hover near boundaries (within 10px) shows resize cursor; drag to modify start/end times
Real-time Preview: Original position shown dimmed alongside new position during drag
Collision Prevention: Automatic constraints prevent overlap with neighboring intervals
Multi-Timeframe: Mouse coordinates in master time frame are automatically converted to the series’ native time frame; boundary constraints are enforced in native time frame for accuracy
Cancel: ESC key restores original boundaries

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Event Viewer Features
The EventViewer_Widget provides display mode controls:

Stacked Mode (Default): Each event series gets a horizontal lane with configurable spacing and height; auto-calculated when groups are loaded
Full Canvas Mode: Events stretch top-to-bottom

Auto-spacing uses 80% of canvas height with 60% of spacing allocated to event height to prevent overlap.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Analog Vertex Cache
The AnalogVertexCache provides a ring buffer-based caching strategy for scrolling analog time series. Instead of regenerating all vertices each frame, it maintains a cache and only generates new edge data:

Without cache: ~1.3ms to regenerate all vertices (100K visible points)
With cache: ~10–50µs for incremental updates (26–130x faster)

This is critical for smooth scrolling with dense electrophysiology data.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Viewport Visibility Culling
When many channels are loaded but only a few are visible in the Y viewport (e.g., viewing 4 of 32 channels after Y zooming in), the rendering pipeline uses additive culling to avoid building batches for off-screen series while ensuring that panning never permanently loses rendered data.

Design Principles

Y-panning is a view matrix operation — it does NOT set scene_dirty. This means a scene rebuild is never triggered by panning alone.
Culling is additive, never subtractive — once a series is built into the scene, it stays there until a full data change (time window, layout config, or global Y scale) triggers a reset.
Vertex caches are never invalidated — off-screen series retain their cached vertex data so they render instantly when panned back into view.



Mechanism
SceneCacheState maintains a series_in_scene set tracking which series have been built into the current scene. The set accumulates across additive rebuilds and is only cleared on full data changes.
Render loop (renderWithSceneRenderer):

computeAndApplyLayout() — recomputes lane positions if layout is dirty.
hasNewVisibleSeries() — checks if any enabled, viewport-visible series is not in series_in_scene. If so, sets scene_dirty = true to trigger an additive rebuild.
If scene_dirty: rebuildScene() builds batches for all series that are either viewport-visible OR already in series_in_scene (additive). Each built series is inserted into series_in_scene.
Render with current view/projection matrices.

Full reset triggers (clear series_in_scene):

timeWindowChanged — new temporal data range
layoutConfigChanged — lane sizing policy/height/gap change
global_y_scale change — vertex data is rebaked

Key files: LayoutEngine.hpp (isSeriesVisible, visibleSeriesIds), OpenGLWidget.hpp (SceneCacheState::series_in_scene, hasNewVisibleSeries), OpenGLWidget.cpp (additive culling in batch builders).

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
SVG Export
The SVGExporter generates publication-quality SVG output from the current view by building the same RenderableScene used for OpenGL rendering. It uses a fixed 1920×1080 canvas with viewBox for clean scaling, and preserves all visual styles (colors, transparency, line thickness).

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Motivation
When a group of analog time series (e.g., voltage_0, voltage_1, …, voltage_N) is added to the Data Viewer, each series receives its own standard deviation for Y-axis normalization via forStdDevRange(mean, std_dev, 3.0f). This causes each channel to fill its lane regardless of actual amplitude, making it impossible to visually compare signal magnitudes across channels within the group.

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Mechanism
When a group of analog series is added (via batch add from the feature tree), the system:

Computes each series’ individual std_dev (stored in SeriesDataCache::individual_std_dev)
Takes the maximum std_dev across the group
Applies the max std_dev as cached_std_dev and recomputes intrinsic_scale = 1/(3*max_std_dev) for all series in the group

This ensures that the channel with the largest amplitude fills its lane fully, while quieter channels appear proportionally smaller — enabling fair visual comparison.

title: Data Viewer Widget
Data Viewer Widget
text:
User Controls

Enabled by default: When a group with 2+ analog series is added, unified scaling is applied automatically
Toggle: Right-click a group node in the feature tree → “Unified Std Dev Scaling” checkbox
Display: The AnalogViewer_Widget shows per-series Std Dev and Group Std Dev (with active/disabled status)
Reversible: Toggling off reverts each series to its individual_std_dev

title: Data Viewer Widget
text:
Group Name Derivation
Group names are derived from series keys by stripping the trailing _N suffix (where N is one or more digits). For example, voltage_3 belongs to group voltage. This matches the grouping pattern used by Feature_Tree_Widget.

title: Data Viewer Widget Roadmap
text:
This document tracks remaining development tasks for the Data Viewer Widget. For documentation of completed features and current architecture, see the main developer documentation.
For the mixed-lane ordering refactor that precedes interactive lane drag-and-drop, see ordering abstractions implementation roadmap.






NotePre-Architecture Widget



The Data Viewer Widget was the first plot widget developed, before the unified Plots/ directory structure and common axis/interaction infrastructure. Several refactoring items below extract DataViewer-specific code into shared components or adopt existing shared components from Plots/Common/. These refactoring tasks are ordered by priority and can be interleaved with feature work.








TipRelated GitHub Issues



Open issues tracking remaining feature work:

#223 — Extract reusable temporal X-axis (CenteredTimeAxis widget)
#227 — Mouse-wheel modifiers for Y scaling (global, per-lane, viewport zoom)
#247 — Y-axis scalebars and lane labels

Closed issues:

#248 — Viewport culling and configurable lane sizing (completed in Phases 1 + 2)





The following features are complete and documented in index.qmd:

EditorState pattern: DataViewerState with DataViewerStateData serialization via reflect-cpp
SeriesOptionsRegistry: Generic type-safe per-series options for analog, event, and interval types
Rendering pipeline: SceneBuildingHelpers → RenderableBatch → PlottingOpenGL::SceneRenderer
Layout system: CorePlotting::LayoutEngine with StackedLayoutStrategy; spike sorter configuration for custom channel ordering; FitToViewport lane sizing with configurable margin_factor
Y-axis transform pipeline: TransformComposers composing data normalization, user adjustments, layout positioning, global scaling

When many channels are loaded but only a few are visible (e.g., viewing 4 of 32 channels), non-visible series are culled from the rendering pipeline using additive culling:

Layout query: LayoutResponse::isSeriesVisible() and visibleSeriesIds() determine which lanes overlap the effective Y viewport (accounting for y_pan).
Additive tracking: SceneCacheState::series_in_scene tracks which series have been built into the current scene. The set accumulates across pan-triggered rebuilds and is only cleared on full data changes (time window, layout config, global Y scale).
Pan-triggered rebuild: hasNewVisibleSeries() checks if any enabled, viewport-visible series is not yet in series_in_scene. If so, an additive rebuild is triggered that builds the new series plus all previously-built series.
Additive batch building: add*BatchesToBuilder methods skip a series only if it is both off-screen AND not in series_in_scene. This ensures panning never removes already-rendered series from the scene.

Non-stackable series (full-canvas intervals, full-canvas events) always pass the visibility check because their layout spans the entire viewport.

Global Y scale (Alt+Scroll): Adjusts global_y_scale, which amplifies all series uniformly within their lanes. This is a data gain factor baked into vertices, so it triggers a scene rebuild.
Per-lane Y scale (Alt+Shift+Scroll): Adjusts the user_scale_factor for the analog series under the cursor. Uses OpenGLWidget::findSeriesAtPosition() for hit testing. No-op if the cursor is not over an analog lane. The per-series scale is already serialized and shown in the properties panel, so this provides a mouse-driven shortcut for an existing feature. Shift narrows the scope from global to local.
Y viewport zoom (Alt+Ctrl+Scroll): Adjusts y_zoom in ViewStateData, which scales the view matrix — making lane heights appear larger or smaller without changing the data gain. This is a cheap matrix-only update (no scene rebuild). Cursor-anchored: the focal point under the mouse remains stable during zoom. Define min/max span clamps so projection and hit testing never degenerate.

CenteredTimeAxis scope: Should the new axis variant handle the time-following logic itself (receiving timeChanged signals), or should it remain a pure zoom widget with the center set externally? The external approach is more flexible but requires the parent widget to manually update the center on every time change.
Lane height policy: Should lane height be fixed across all series types, or should analog channels get taller lanes than event/interval channels by default? A configurable policy (uniform vs. type-weighted) could address both preferences.
Viewport culling granularity: Should culling operate at the series level (skip entire series) or could it operate at the sample level (skip analog samples outside the viewport)? Sample-level culling is already partially handled by the AnalogVertexCache time range queries.
Hatching renderer: Fragment shader stipple vs. additional geometry — the shader approach is more performant but adds shader complexity. Is the interval count high enough to warrant shader-based hatching, or would geometry-based hatching suffice?
SeriesOptionsRegistry scope: If extracted to Plots/Common/, should it remain specific to the three DataViewer series types (analog, event, interval), or should it be generalized to support arbitrary option types via a compile-time type list?
Y-axis wheel modifier chords: Which modifier combinations should be used for Y-axis operations? Alt+Scroll is a natural candidate but may conflict with Linux window manager defaults (Alt+click is often window move). Alternatives include right-click+scroll or other combinations.




Multi-lane VerticalAxisWidget design (was Q6): Decision — new separate widget. MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget will be a standalone widget in Plots/Common/, not a subclass or extension of the existing VerticalAxisWidget. The single-range widget remains unchanged for consumers that need a uniform Y range.
CenteredTimeAxis state representation (was Q8): Decision — time_start/time_end. Consistent with TimeSeriesViewState. The State class provides halfWindow() and center() convenience accessors computed from time_start/time_end.

Goal: Establish the lane sizing model that all subsequent Y-axis features depend on.


Merged global_zoom and global_vertical_scale into a single global_y_scale field. Exposed as “Global Y Scale” in the UI and used consistently in all TransformComposers functions.



StackedLayoutStrategy uses FitToViewport (equal division of viewport among stackable lanes). Layout config persisted in DataViewerLayoutConfig via reflect-cpp with a user-configurable margin_factor (fraction of allocated lane height used for data rendering, default 0.8). State API: setMarginFactor(), marginFactor(), layoutConfigChanged() signal.






Note



The former FixedHeight lane sizing policy (with lane_height and lane_gap parameters) was removed because Y viewport zoom (y_zoom + y_pan in ViewStateData) provides the same functionality — users zoom into the viewport to see a subset of channels at larger resolution, rather than setting a fixed pixel height per lane.


Key files: StackedLayoutStrategy.hpp/.cpp, DataViewerStateData.hpp, DataViewerState.hpp/.cpp

title: Data Viewer Widget Roadmap
text:
Status: Complete. Depends on: Phase 1.
Goal: Migrate from TimeSeriesViewState to shared ViewStateData zoom/pan model. Eliminate the performance bottleneck where Y-axis panning triggered full scene rebuild + GPU re-upload every frame.


ViewStateData adoption (1B.1): DataViewerStateData::view is now CorePlotting::ViewStateData (x_min/x_max as double, y_min/y_max, y_pan, y_zoom). global_y_scale remains a separate field in DataViewerStateData (data amplitude gain, not a view transform). DataViewer defaults: x_min=0, x_max=1000, y_min=-1, y_max=1. Convenience methods on DataViewerState: timeStart(), timeEnd(), timeWidth(), timeCenter().
Scene dirty guard (1B.3, 1B.6): OpenGLWidget uses separate signal handlers:

timeWindowChanged → scene_dirty = true (scene rebuild needed)
viewStateChanged → matrix update only (Y pan/zoom is instant)
layoutConfigChanged → scene_dirty = true (layout transforms baked into vertices)
global_y_scale changes detected via cached comparison → scene_dirty = true

Scene rebuilds (rebuildScene()) only occur when _cache_state.scene_dirty is set. Y-axis panning updates only the projection/view matrices.
Caller migration (1B.7): All files across DataViewer_Widget/ updated to use ViewStateData field names (x_min/x_max/y_pan with appropriate casts). DataViewerCoordinates, DataViewerInputHandler, DataViewerInteractionManager, DataViewerDebugPanel, DataViewerPropertiesWidget, SVGExporter, and all test files migrated.
Key architectural decisions:

x_zoom fixed at 1.0, x_pan at 0.0 (DataViewer X-axis controlled externally via time bar)
Lane sizing policy changes reset y_pan to 0 to prevent stranded viewport on mode switch
double precision for time bounds sufficient for indices up to ~9×10¹⁵

title: Data Viewer Widget Roadmap
text:
Status: In progress (Phase 2.1 completed). Issues: #227 (wheel modifiers, per-lane scaling), #248 (viewport culling), #247 (axis synchronization) Depends on: Phase 1 (layout foundation must exist), Phase 1B (pan/zoom must be performant before adding more interaction modes).
Goal: Allow users to pan and zoom the Y-axis so they can view a subset of channels at readable resolution, inspired by EventPlotWidget’s trial Y navigation.


Create a new MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget in Plots/Common/ and integrate it into DataViewer. This is a standalone widget — not a subclass of the existing single-range VerticalAxisWidget, which continues to serve ScatterPlotWidget and EventPlotWidget unchanged.
The existing VerticalAxisWidget manages a single y_min/y_max range with uniform tick marks. DataViewer lanes have independent amplitude scales (each series has its own user_scale_factor, data range, and normalization), so a single-range axis cannot meaningfully represent per-lane amplitudes. Building the multi-lane widget from the start avoids a throwaway integration cycle.
New files:
Plots/Common/MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget/
├── Core/
│   ├── MultiLaneVerticalAxisStateData.hpp   # LaneAxisDescriptor + vector, serializable
│   └── MultiLaneVerticalAxisState.hpp       # QObject with lane update signals
├── MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget.hpp/.cpp     # QPainter rendering: labels + separators
└── CMakeLists.txt
The widget follows the standard four-layer pattern (StateData → State → Widget → optional WithControls) and is driven by a std::vector<LaneAxisDescriptor>:
struct LaneAxisDescriptor {
    std::string lane_id;        ///< Series key in DataManager
    std::string label;          ///< Display name (channel name or series key)
    float y_center;             ///< Center Y position in world coordinates
    float y_half_height;        ///< Half-height of the lane in world coordinates
};
Minimal rendering scope (Phase 2 only):

Channel name labels painted at each lane’s center Y position
Lane boundary separators (horizontal lines between lanes)
Viewport-aware: only renders labels for lanes visible in the current Y viewport
Fixed 50px width (matching existing VerticalAxisWidget sizeHint)

Scalebars, visibility toggles, and per-lane range annotations are deferred to Phase 3, which adds them incrementally to this same widget.
Layout: Place MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget in a QHBoxLayout to the left of OpenGLWidget:
DataViewer_Widget (QWidget)
├── QVBoxLayout
│   ├── QHBoxLayout [stretch 1]
│   │   ├── MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget (50px fixed width)
│   │   └── OpenGLWidget [stretch 1]
│   └── (future: CenteredTimeAxisWidget — Phase 4)
State integration:
// In DataViewerState
_multi_lane_axis_state = std::make_unique<MultiLaneVerticalAxisState>(this);
Data flow (one-directional — labels are read-only display):

After each layout computation, DataViewer extracts LaneAxisDescriptor entries from LayoutResponse and pushes them to MultiLaneVerticalAxisState
DataViewerState::viewStateChanged → widget repaint (for Y pan/zoom tracking)
No bidirectional range sync is needed (Y pan/zoom originates from wheel events on OpenGLWidget, not from the axis widget)

Files: src/WhiskerToolbox/Plots/Common/MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget/ (new), src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/DataViewerState.hpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/DataViewerState.cpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/DataViewerStateData.hpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/UI/DataViewer_Widget.cpp



When many channels are loaded but only a few are visible (e.g., viewing 4 of 32 channels), non-visible series are culled from the rendering pipeline using additive culling:

Layout query: LayoutResponse::isSeriesVisible() and visibleSeriesIds() determine which lanes overlap the effective Y viewport (accounting for y_pan).
Additive tracking: SceneCacheState::series_in_scene tracks which series have been built into the current scene. The set accumulates across pan-triggered rebuilds and is only cleared on full data changes (time window, layout config, global Y scale).
Pan-triggered rebuild: hasNewVisibleSeries() checks if any enabled, viewport-visible series is not yet in series_in_scene. If so, an additive rebuild is triggered that builds the new series plus all previously-built series.
Additive batch building: add*BatchesToBuilder methods skip a series only if it is both off-screen AND not in series_in_scene. This ensures panning never removes already-rendered series from the scene.

Non-stackable series (full-canvas intervals, full-canvas events) always pass the visibility check because their layout spans the entire viewport.
Key files: src/CorePlotting/Layout/LayoutEngine.hpp (isSeriesVisible, visibleSeriesIds), src/CorePlotting/Layout/LayoutEngine.cpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Rendering/OpenGLWidget.hpp (SceneCacheState::series_in_scene, hasNewVisibleSeries), src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Rendering/OpenGLWidget.cpp









ImportantPreserving Existing Behavior



The current default mouse wheel behavior (time-axis zoom) must be preserved. Users who do not use modifiers should see no change. Y-axis panning is already handled by left-click drag (via DataViewerInputHandler) and does not need a wheel chord.








WarningKnown Limitation — Y Viewport Zoom Not Yet Rendered



The Alt+Ctrl+Scroll chord correctly updates y_zoom and y_pan in ViewStateData, but the DataViewer rendering pipeline does not yet incorporate y_zoom into the projection or view matrices. As a result, the gesture currently appears as a pan rather than a zoom. See Phase 2.7 for the rendering refactoring plan.

Action

Shift
Time-axis zoom (fine sensitivity)


Ctrl

New chords — all Y-axis wheel actions share Alt as the common prefix, distinguishing them from X-axis zoom (no Alt):









Modifier
Action
Scope
State Field




Alt+Scroll
Global Y scale
All lanes
global_y_scale


Alt+Shift+Scroll

y_zoom in ViewStateData



Global Y scale (Alt+Scroll): Adjusts global_y_scale, which amplifies all series uniformly within their lanes. This is a data gain factor baked into vertices, so it triggers a scene rebuild.
Per-lane Y scale (Alt+Shift+Scroll): Adjusts the user_scale_factor for the analog series under the cursor. Uses OpenGLWidget::findSeriesAtPosition() for hit testing. No-op if the cursor is not over an analog lane. The per-series scale is already serialized and shown in the properties panel, so this provides a mouse-driven shortcut for an existing feature. Shift narrows the scope from global to local.
Y viewport zoom (Alt+Ctrl+Scroll): Adjusts y_zoom in ViewStateData, which scales the view matrix — making lane heights appear larger or smaller without changing the data gain. This is a cheap matrix-only update (no scene rebuild). Cursor-anchored: the focal point under the mouse remains stable during zoom. Define min/max span clamps so projection and hit testing never degenerate.
Implementation notes:

Alt+click is window-move on some Linux WMs, but Alt+Scroll is generally safe
Respect OpenGLWidget::isInteractionActive() (no zoom while creating/editing intervals)
When multiple modifiers match (e.g., Alt+Ctrl+Shift), the most specific chord wins: per-lane (Alt+Shift) > viewport zoom (Alt+Ctrl) > global scale (Alt)
Document chords in a user-facing summary (tooltip, status bar, or User Guide stub)

Spinbox synchronization: The properties panel already has spinboxes for global_y_scale and per-series user_scale_factor. Wheel-driven changes update these spinboxes without triggering feedback loops by leveraging the existing _updating_from_state guard in DataViewerPropertiesWidget::_connectStateSignals():

Global Y scale: _handleGlobalYScaleWheel() calls setGlobalYScale() on the state, which emits viewStateChanged. The properties widget’s viewStateChanged handler sets _updating_from_state = true, updates the spinbox value, then clears the guard — preventing the spinbox’s valueChanged signal from re-entering the state setter.
Per-lane Y scale: _handlePerLaneYScaleWheel() uses the same getMutable() + update() pattern as AnalogViewer_Widget::_setAnalogScaleFactor(). No spinbox sync is needed because the AnalogViewer_Widget sub-panel only shows when the user explicitly selects a series in the feature tree, and the spinbox value is set when setActiveKey() is called.

Key implementation details:

Three new private helper methods in DataViewer_Widget: _handleGlobalYScaleWheel(), _handlePerLaneYScaleWheel(), _handleYViewportZoomWheel()
OpenGLWidget::findSeriesAtPosition() moved from private to public for hit testing
All wheel handlers use multiplicative 5% steps with std::clamp for bounds
Y viewport zoom is cursor-anchored: computes world-Y under cursor before zoom, then adjusts y_pan so the same world-Y maps back to the same screen position after zoom

Files: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/UI/DataViewer_Widget.cpp (wheelEvent), src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/DataViewerState.cpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/SeriesOptionsRegistry.cpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/UI/DataViewerPropertiesWidget.cpp



A read-only “Visible lanes: N of M” label in DataViewerPropertiesWidget updates whenever the viewport or lane count changes. Added to the Layout Settings group in the properties panel UI. The update is driven by two signal connections wired in DataViewerWidgetRegistration::create_editor_custom:

OpenGLWidget::sceneRebuilt → recomputes visible/total from layout response
DataViewerState::viewStateChanged → recomputes when Y pan/zoom changes

The effective viewport is computed as [y_min + y_pan, y_max + y_pan] and passed to LayoutResponse::visibleSeriesIds() to count visible lanes.
Files: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/UI/DataViewerPropertiesWidget.cpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/UI/DataViewerPropertiesWidget.hpp, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/UI/DataViewerPropertiesWidget.ui, src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/DataViewerWidgetRegistration.cpp




Load 32+ channels.
Y pan scrolls through lanes; Y zoom narrows the visible range.
Viewport culling skips off-screen series (verify via Developer Debug Panel rendering stats).
Per-lane hover scaling adjusts the hovered series only.
Channel name labels appear on the MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget at correct Y positions.

Workspace save/restore roundtrips all new state.
Existing DataViewer_Widget tests that assert time window changes after wheel remain green.
Existing VerticalAxisWidget consumers (ScatterPlot, EventPlot) are unaffected.




Status: Complete.


y_zoom in ViewStateData now affects rendered output in DataViewer so that Alt+Ctrl+Scroll produces true cursor-anchored Y viewport zoom.
The implementation folds both y_zoom and y_pan into the projection matrix via a new computeEffectiveYViewport() helper in ViewStateData.hpp. The view matrix is now identity — all vertical camera state lives in the projection. Every location that previously computed effective_y_min = y_min + y_pan now calls the helper instead.

Added EffectiveYViewport struct and computeEffectiveYViewport() inline helper

Goal: Extract the DataViewer’s temporal X-axis behavior into a reusable CenteredTimeAxisWidget in Plots/Common/, following the established four-layer axis widget pattern (StateData → State → Widget → WithRangeControls). The SpectrogramWidget (currently a stub with time-axis state defined but no axis widget) is the primary second consumer.


The DataViewer’s X-axis behavior is unique among the plot widgets: it is always centered on the global time position with zoom but no independent X panning. Neither the existing RelativeTimeAxis (event-relative, symmetric window) nor HorizontalAxis (arbitrary range with pan) match this pattern exactly.
A new CenteredTimeAxis variant should be added to Plots/Common/:
Plots/Common/CenteredTimeAxisWidget/
├── Core/
│   ├── CenteredTimeAxisStateData.hpp   # half_window (zoom level), serializable
│   └── CenteredTimeAxisState.hpp       # QObject with zoom math + signals
├── CenteredTimeAxisWidget.hpp          # Axis display (tick marks, labels) via QPainter
└── CenteredTimeAxisWithRangeControls.hpp  # Factory with zoom spinbox
State fields:
struct CenteredTimeAxisStateData {
    double time_start = 0.0;   ///< Visible window start in time units
    double time_end = 10000.0; ///< Visible window end in time units
};
The state uses time_start/time_end rather than half_window for consistency with the existing TimeSeriesViewState representation. The State class provides convenience accessors for halfWindow() and center() computed from these fields.

Signals: rangeChanged (user action), rangeUpdated (silent sync — matches bidirectional sync pattern used by all axis widgets)
The axis widget receives the current time position from an external source (the application’s global time bar emits timeChanged). On each time change, the parent widget recenters the window: time_start = current_time - half_window; time_end = current_time + half_window.
Sharing potential: This axis variant could also be useful for any future widget that needs a time-following view (e.g., a real-time signal monitor).



The wheel-zoom math currently lives in DataViewer_Widget::wheelEvent and DataViewerState::adjustTimeWidth. This logic should be extracted into CenteredTimeAxisState as reusable methods:

applyWheelZoom(int angle_delta, ZoomScalingMode mode, Qt::KeyboardModifiers mods, int64_t total_frames)

title: Data Viewer Widget Roadmap
text:
CenteredTimeAxis scope: Should the new axis variant handle the time-following logic itself (receiving timeChanged signals), or should it remain a pure zoom widget with the center set externally? The external approach is more flexible but requires the parent widget to manually update the center on every time change.
Lane height policy: Should lane height be fixed across all series types, or should analog channels get taller lanes than event/interval channels by default? A configurable policy (uniform vs. type-weighted) could address both preferences.
Viewport culling granularity: Should culling operate at the series level (skip entire series) or could it operate at the sample level (skip analog samples outside the viewport)? Sample-level culling is already partially handled by the AnalogVertexCache time range queries.
Hatching renderer: Fragment shader stipple vs. additional geometry — the shader approach is more performant but adds shader complexity. Is the interval count high enough to warrant shader-based hatching, or would geometry-based hatching suffice?
SeriesOptionsRegistry scope: If extracted to Plots/Common/, should it remain specific to the three DataViewer series types (analog, event, interval), or should it be generalized to support arbitrary option types via a compile-time type list?
Y-axis wheel modifier chords: Which modifier combinations should be used for Y-axis operations? Alt+Scroll is a natural candidate but may conflict with Linux window manager defaults (Alt+click is often window move). Alternatives include right-click+scroll or other combinations.




Multi-lane VerticalAxisWidget design (was Q6): Decision — new separate widget. MultiLaneVerticalAxisWidget will be a standalone widget in Plots/Common/, not a subclass or extension of the existing VerticalAxisWidget. The single-range widget remains unchanged for consumers that need a uniform Y range.
CenteredTimeAxis state representation (was Q8): Decision — time_start/time_end. Consistent with TimeSeriesViewState. The State class provides halfWindow() and center() convenience accessors computed from time_start/time_end.

Whitespace- or comma-delimited; three columns: timestamp (ignored), digital_channel (1-based), analog_channel (1-based). Example:

0.01670, 24,  6
0.04320, 24,  6
For each unique digital_channel, the analog_channel that appears most often (mode) is the pairing. Both channel numbers are converted to 0-based before lookup.

title: DataViewer Rendering Performance Audit
text:
An in-depth code and architecture audit of DataViewer_Widget, SceneBuildingHelpers, AnalogVertexCache, and PlottingOpenGL was conducted to diagnose interactive rendering lag during time series visualization and scrolling.
The audit identified five critical bottlenecks:

Origin Baking & Full Buffer Re-Uploads: Relative X coordinates are subtracted per vertex on the CPU on every frame. Because all vertex X coordinates change when the viewport scrolls by even 1 sample, 100% of the vertex data is invalidated every frame, forcing a full glBufferData VBO allocation and upload over PCIe.
Failure of Incremental Streaming Caches: The existing AnalogVertexCache on the CPU still materializes and extracts all \(N\) visible vertices on every frame. The GPU-side StreamingPolyLineRenderer compares relative-X floats; because all X values shift during scrolling, dirty region detection flags 100% of the buffer as dirty, falling back to full re-uploads.
Geometry Shader Primitive Expansion: wide_line.geom converts every line segment into a 4-vertex triangle strip on the GPU. On modern GPUs, geometry shaders introduce significant primitive-assembly bottlenecks even for 1.0px lines.
Disabled-by-Default Min-Max Decimation: enable_min_max_line_decimation is false by default. Zooming out over \(10^5\) to \(10^7\) samples causes millions of triangles to be rasterized to a \(\sim 1920\)-pixel viewport. Even when enabled, decimation occurs after full vertex extraction.
Continuous Heap Allocations: Rebuilding std::vector<float> vertices and batch structures creates gigabytes of transient heap churn during active scrolling.







Timestamps in neural data acquisition (e.g., sample indices represented by strongly typed TimeFrameIndex or ClockTicks) are discrete 64-bit integers (int64_t).
Standard IEEE 754 32-bit single-precision floating-point numbers (float) allocate only 24 bits to the significand (1 sign bit + 23 mantissa bits). This provides exact integer representation only up to:
\[2^{24} = 16,777,216 \text{ integers}\]
When absolute sample timestamps exceed \(\sim 16.7\text{ million}\) (which occurs in under 10 minutes of recording at 30 kHz sampling rates), converting raw absolute timestamps to float results in loss of resolution. For example, at sample \(50,000,000\), the spacing between representable floats is \(4.0\):
Absolute timestamp: 50,000,000  -->  (float)  -->  50,000,000.0f
Absolute timestamp: 50,000,001  -->  (float)  -->  50,000,000.0f  (Lost lower 2 bits!)
Absolute timestamp: 50,000,002  -->  (float)  -->  50,000,000.0f
Absolute timestamp: 50,000,003  -->  (float)  -->  50,000,000.0f
Absolute timestamp: 50,000,004  -->  (float)  -->  50,000,004.0f
Neighboring samples snap to the same float value, leading to severe visual stutter, non-monotonic X coordinates, and waveform distortion.



To avoid rounding artifacts, the codebase currently subtracts the view window’s starting position (x_origin_master_absolute_time) on the CPU before casting to float:
In AnalogVertexCache::getVerticesForRange:
double const rel_x = static_cast<double>(v.x - x_origin_master_absolute_time);
result.push_back(static_cast<float>(rel_x));
result.push_back(v.y);
While this eliminates sub-pixel rounding errors (since \(t - t_{\text{origin}}\) is small), it introduces a severe architectural side effect:

Every time the view window scrolls by even a single sample, x_origin_master_absolute_time changes, altering the float value of every single vertex currently visible.

Because the vertex values themselves change, GPU VBOs cannot be reused, dirty region checks detect 100% invalidation, and the entire vertex buffer must be reallocated and re-uploaded over PCIe via glBufferData.



Because time is fundamentally a discrete, strongly typed integer index (TimeFrameIndex), the proper architectural solution is to treat time as an integer primitive in the shader pipeline:

VBO Format: Store sample indices as 32-bit signed/unsigned integers (int32_t / uint32_t) alongside float Y values:
struct AnalogVertex {
    int32_t time_index; // 4 bytes (exact up to 2.14 billion samples)
    float value;        // 4 bytes
};
Attribute Configuration: Use glVertexAttribIPointer (OpenGL 3.0+ / GLSL 1.30+) to bind the integer attribute without automatic float conversion:
gl->glVertexAttribIPointer(0, 1, GL_INT, sizeof(AnalogVertex), (void*)0);
gl->glVertexAttribPointer(1, 1, GL_FLOAT, GL_FALSE, sizeof(AnalogVertex), (void*)offsetof(AnalogVertex, value));
Integer Uniform: Pass the view window’s starting index as an integer uniform:
shader->setUniform("u_view_start_sample", static_cast<int32_t>(start_time.getValue()));
Vertex Shader:
#version 410 core
layout(location = 0) in int a_time_index;
layout(location = 1) in float a_y_val;

uniform int u_view_start_sample;
uniform mat4 u_projection_matrix;
uniform float u_y_gain;
uniform float u_y_offset;

void main() {
    // 1. Bit-exact integer subtraction on GPU hardware:
    int rel_idx = a_time_index - u_view_start_sample;

    // 2. Cast to float only after subtraction (rel_idx is small: 0 .. viewport_width):
    float rel_x = float(rel_idx);
    float rel_y = a_y_val * u_y_gain + u_y_offset;

    gl_Position = u_projection_matrix * vec4(rel_x, rel_y, 0.0, 1.0);
}




Precision: Integer subtraction on the GPU hardware is exact with zero floating-point error. Converting rel_idx to float operates on values within \([0, \text{visible\_window}]\), well within the 24-bit mantissa limit.
Static VBOs: The stored sample index in the VBO is invariant (sample 50,000,000 is always stored as 50000000). Scrolling updates only the integer uniform, leaving the VBO intact.
Persistent Streaming: Because VBO values are static, streaming updates only require appending new edge samples via glBufferSubData.









When the user pans or playback advances from window [1, 1000] to [2, 1001]:
User scrolls by 1 tick
  └── DataViewerState::timeWindowChanged
        └── OpenGLWidget::renderWithSceneRenderer()
              └── OpenGLWidget::rebuildScene()
                    └── SceneBuildingHelpers::buildAnalogSeriesBatchCached()
                          ├── AnalogVertexCache::needsUpdate() (Ring buffer appends 1 sample)
                          └── AnalogVertexCache::getVerticesForRange() (Full O(N) extraction loop!)
                                └── Allocates std::vector<float>(2N)
                                └── Computes rel_x for all N samples
              └── SceneRenderer::uploadScene()
                    └── PolyLineRenderer::uploadData()
                          └── m_vbo.allocate() -> glBufferData(GL_ARRAY_BUFFER, ...)
                                └── Discards old GPU buffer
                                └── Allocates new VBO memory in VRAM
                                └── Transfers 2N floats over PCIe
              └── SceneRenderer::render()
                    └── PolyLineRenderer::render()
                          └── Geometry shader expands all N segments to quads




AnalogVertexCache (CPU): AnalogVertexCache uses a boost::circular_buffer<CachedAnalogVertex> to avoid querying AnalogTimeSeries for points already in memory. However, getVerticesForRange() performs a linear scan over all \(N\) visible vertices to compute rel_x relative to the current frame’s origin. It then allocates and populates a new std::vector<float> on every frame.
StreamingPolyLineRenderer (GPU): StreamingPolyLineRenderer was designed to use glBufferSubData for incremental GPU updates. But because batch.vertices contains window-relative X coordinates, comparing incoming vertices with cached vertices in computeDirtyRegions finds that 100% of floats have changed. The incremental path aborts, triggering a full re-upload.
Renderer Disconnect: SceneRenderer instantiates and calls PolyLineRenderer, which unconditionally calls glBufferData on every frame, bypassing streaming entirely.








PolyLineRenderer compiles and binds wide_line.geom for all polyline rendering:
#version 410 core
layout(lines) in;
layout(triangle_strip, max_vertices = 4) out;

uniform float u_line_width;
uniform vec2 u_viewport_size;

void main() {
    // Computes screen-space perpendiculars
    // Emits 4 vertices (triangle strip) per segment
    ...
}

Default Line Width: The default line thickness in AnalogSeriesOptionsData is 1.0px.
Cost: On desktop GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel), geometry shaders cannot utilize the hardware rasterizer’s fast primitive assembly paths. For \(100\text{K}\) samples, the geometry shader must generate \(400\text{K}\) vertices and \(200\text{K}\) triangles per frame.
Fast Path Available: Standard OpenGL GL_LINE_STRIP without a geometry shader renders 1.0px lines with an order of magnitude higher primitive throughput.








In DataViewerStateData.hpp, enable_min_max_line_decimation is initialized to false:
bool enable_min_max_line_decimation = false;



When viewing a time window containing \(10^6\) samples on a 1920-pixel monitor: * The renderer attempts to draw \(>500\) vertices per horizontal pixel column. * \(99.8\%\) of line segments land on sub-pixel coordinates already covered by other segments in the same column, causing extreme GPU fragment overdraw and visual aliasing. * When decimation is enabled via user checkbox, decimatePolyLineBatchMinMax is executed after all \(10^6\) vertices have already been extracted, converted, and assembled into RenderablePolyLineBatch.

Phase 1: Integer Vertex Attribute & Shader Pipeline — Completed:

Bound integer vertex attribute at location 0 using glVertexAttribIPointer(0, 1, GL_INT, ...) and float attribute at location 1.
Updated wide_line.vert and embedded shader fallbacks to perform bit-exact GPU integer subtraction rel_sample = a_time_index - u_view_start_sample; before casting to float.
Updated AnalogVertexCache and SceneBuildingHelpers to pack static integer coordinates via std::bit_cast<float>(int32_t) without CPU origin baking during scrolling.
Enabled SVG polyline export decoding for integer time series batches.






Implement GPU Ring Buffer Streaming (Phase 2): With fixed integer coordinates in the VBO, scrolling right by \(K\) samples only requires uploading \(K\) new points via glBufferSubData. Existing samples remain valid in VRAM. Adjust glDrawArrays(GL_LINE_STRIP, start_index, count) dynamically.
Fast-Path 1.0px Lines (Phase 3): Bypass the geometry shader when line thickness is 1.0px, routing directly through a minimal vertex/fragment shader pair.
Adaptive Min-Max Decimation (Phase 4): Automatically enable min-max decimation when visible samples exceed \(2 \times \text{canvas\_width}\), and perform decimation during raw storage read rather than post-extraction.
Memory Reuse (Phase 5): Scratch buffer reuse in SceneCacheState to eliminate per-frame allocations.

For the step-by-step implementation plan, see the companion document: Rendering Optimization Refactoring Guide.

title: DataViewer Rendering Performance Audit
text:
An in-depth code and architecture audit of DataViewer_Widget, SceneBuildingHelpers, AnalogVertexCache, and PlottingOpenGL was conducted to diagnose interactive rendering lag during time series visualization and scrolling.
The audit identified five critical bottlenecks:

Origin Baking & Full Buffer Re-Uploads: Relative X coordinates are subtracted per vertex on the CPU on every frame. Because all vertex X coordinates change when the viewport scrolls by even 1 sample, 100% of the vertex data is invalidated every frame, forcing a full glBufferData VBO allocation and upload over PCIe.
Failure of Incremental Streaming Caches: The existing AnalogVertexCache on the CPU still materializes and extracts all \(N\) visible vertices on every frame. The GPU-side StreamingPolyLineRenderer compares relative-X floats; because all X values shift during scrolling, dirty region detection flags 100% of the buffer as dirty, falling back to full re-uploads.
Geometry Shader Primitive Expansion: wide_line.geom converts every line segment into a 4-vertex triangle strip on the GPU. On modern GPUs, geometry shaders introduce significant primitive-assembly bottlenecks even for 1.0px lines.
Disabled-by-Default Min-Max Decimation: enable_min_max_line_decimation is false by default. Zooming out over \(10^5\) to \(10^7\) samples causes millions of triangles to be rasterized to a \(\sim 1920\)-pixel viewport. Even when enabled, decimation occurs after full vertex extraction.
Continuous Heap Allocations: Rebuilding std::vector<float> vertices and batch structures creates gigabytes of transient heap churn during active scrolling.

title: Ordering Policy Resolver
text:
OrderingPolicyResolver centralizes stackable-series ordering precedence for DataViewer_Widget and returns deterministic diagnostics for each resolved position.



Source: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/OrderingPolicyResolver.hpp
Source: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Core/OrderingPolicyResolver.cpp




resolveOrdering(...) consumes a vector of normalized ordering items and a fallback sortable-rank map.
Input fields include:

series key
series type
normalized identity (group, optional channel_id)
optional explicit lane order
insertion index

It returns an OrderingResolution with:

ordered_input_indices: stable resolved order as original input indices
diagnostics: per-series reason metadata (ExplicitLaneOrder, FallbackSortableRank, or DeterministicTieBreak)




Resolver precedence is:

explicit lane_order
fallback sortable provider rank
deterministic tie-breaks: group, channel, series-type precedence, key, insertion index




LayoutRequestBuilder constructs OrderingInputItem entries from stackable candidates, delegates ordering to the resolver, then rebuilds candidate order using ordered_input_indices.
This keeps policy decisions out of the layout assembly path while preserving deterministic behavior.

title: Swindale SpikeSorter Loader
text:
SwindaleSpikeSorterLoader parses SpikeSorter electrode configuration files and converts electrode Y positions into stackable-series lane ranks for DataViewer_Widget.



Source: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Ordering/SwindaleSpikeSorterLoader.hpp
Source: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Ordering/SwindaleSpikeSorterLoader.cpp
Channel identity helpers: src/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/Ordering/ChannelPositionMetadata.hpp




SpikeSorter .cfg files are whitespace-separated with columns:

Row index (ignored)
Channel number (1-based in file, converted to 0-based internally)
X position (micrometers)
Y position (micrometers)

The first line is treated as a header and skipped.



SpikeSorter channel numbers in the file are always 1-based. Series key suffixes in the data manager may be either:

1-based (voltage_1 = first channel), or
0-based (voltage_0 = first channel)

buildSwindaleSpikeSorterRanks(..., key_one_based) controls this mapping via extractChannelFromSeriesKey. When loading through the UI, SpikeSorterKeyNumberingDialog offers auto-detect (suffix 0 implies 0-based), with manual override.



Within a group, ranks are assigned by:

Ascending electrode Y (bottom = lowest Y)
Channel ID tie-break when Y values are equal
Lexicographic key tie-break

Ranks are written to DataViewerState as explicit lane_order overrides and consumed by OrderingPolicyResolver / StackedLayoutStrategy.



lane_order overrides are keyed by series name and persist in DataViewerState when a group is hidden in the feature tree (unchecked). Re-enabling the same group restores the saved spikesorter ordering without reloading the configuration file.
lane_order deduplication in DataViewerState::normalizeAllLaneOverrides is scoped per probe group (parseSeriesIdentity(series_key).group). Independent groups such as voltage_* and voltage_raw_* may both use ranks 0..N without colliding.
clearSpikeSorterConfiguration clears overrides from state by group identity, including series that are not currently displayed in the viewer.



Unit tests live in tests/WhiskerToolbox/DataViewer_Widget/SwindaleSpikeSorterLoader.test.cpp, including a full poly2 fixture with 0-based voltage_0..voltage_31 keys.

title: Onion Skin View Widget Roadmap
text:
This document tracks remaining development tasks for the Onion Skin View Widget. For documentation of completed features and current architecture, see the main developer documentation.


The following features are complete and documented in index.qmd:

Widget skeleton: EditorState pattern, registration, state/view/properties factories
State management: OnionSkinViewState with HorizontalAxisState, VerticalAxisState composition; OnionSkinViewStateData serializable struct with rfl::json
Three data type support: Add/remove multiple PointData, LineData, and MaskData keys via properties panel
Temporal window: Configurable window_behind / window_ahead (frames before/after current time)
Alpha curve: Linear, Exponential, Gaussian curves with configurable min/max alpha
Rendering pipeline: SceneRenderer for points (glyphs), lines (polylines), and mask contours (polylines), all with per-element temporal alpha
Spatial mapping: SpatialMapper::mapPointsInWindow(), mapLinesInWindow(), mapMaskContoursInWindow() for windowed data retrieval
Back-to-front rendering: Depth-sorted by temporal distance for correct alpha blending
Current-frame highlight: Distinct colors for current-frame elements (orange-red vs blue/green/orange)
Auto-fit bounds: Bounding box computation from all windowed point, line, and mask contour data
Axis system: HorizontalAxisWidget (X) and VerticalAxisWidget (Y) with bidirectional sync, including the “silent update” pattern
Interaction: Separated X/Y zoom, pan via shared PlotInteractionHelpers
Entity selection: Click-to-select point at current frame (15px tolerance), double-click for navigation
Properties panel: Data key tables + combo boxes for all 3 types, temporal window controls, alpha curve controls, rendering controls (point size, line width, highlight current), axis range controls in collapsible sections
DataManager observer: Combo box population (point, line, mask), cleanup in destructor, and stale key purging when data keys are deleted from DataManager; tested in OnionSkinViewPropertiesWidget.test.cpp
State serialization: Full round-trip JSON via rfl::json
Registration wiring: timeChanged → _onTimeChanged(), timePositionSelected → EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime()
Per-key line style: Each LineData key has its own CorePlotting::LineStyleData (color, thickness, alpha) stored in OnionSkinViewStateData::line_key_line_styles; managed at runtime via LineStyleState QObject wrappers; editable in a collapsible “Line Style Options” section in the properties panel via LineStyleControls; `alpha` field sets the maximum alpha before temporal decay; serialized/deserialized as part of the JSON state
Per-key mask contour style: Each MaskData key has its own CorePlotting::LineStyleData (color, thickness, alpha) stored in OnionSkinViewStateData::mask_key_line_styles; managed at runtime via LineStyleState QObject wrappers; editable in a collapsible “Mask Style Options” section in the properties panel via LineStyleControls; alpha field sets the maximum alpha before temporal decay; serialized/deserialized as part of the JSON state

Not yet implemented: SVG export.



Status: Not started. No export infrastructure exists in the current widget.
Goal: Allow the user to export the current onion skin view as an SVG file, preserving vector quality for publication.


SVG export requires converting the OpenGL scene to vector graphics. Two approaches:
Option A — Scene-to-SVG serialization (recommended): Walk the RenderableScene primitives (glyphs, polylines) and emit SVG <circle>, <polygon>, and <polyline> elements with the same colors and alpha values computed during rebuildScene(). This avoids OpenGL framebuffer capture and produces clean, resolution-independent output.
Option B — QPainter-based rendering: Use QSvgGenerator + QPainter to re-render the scene data using Qt’s 2D drawing API. This provides more mature vector rendering but requires duplicating the rendering logic outside OpenGL.



Because SVG export will be needed by multiple widgets (see cross-widget export below), the export logic should be implemented as a shared utility rather than per-widget code:

Location
Purpose

Scene-to-SVG conversion


ExportButton

Shared “Export SVG” button + file dialog

Trial-aligned lines + axes

Full spatial overlay

Medium

        ↓
File dialog → choose output path
        ↓

        ↓
For each glyph: emit SVG element with position, size, fill color + opacity
For each polyline: emit SVG <polyline> with stroke color + opacity + width
        ↓
Add axis labels, tick marks, bounds metadata
        ↓
Write SVG file

Export SVG button — opens file dialog and triggers export
Include axes checkbox — whether to render axis labels and ticks in the SVG

Entity selection: Click-to-select point at current frame (15px tolerance), double-click for navigation
Properties panel: Data key tables + combo boxes for all 3 types, temporal window controls, alpha curve controls, rendering controls (point size, line width, highlight current), axis range controls in collapsible sections
DataManager observer: Combo box population (point, line, mask), cleanup in destructor, and stale key purging when data keys are deleted from DataManager; tested in OnionSkinViewPropertiesWidget.test.cpp
State serialization: Full round-trip JSON via rfl::json
Registration wiring: timeChanged → _onTimeChanged(), timePositionSelected → EditorRegistry::setCurrentTime()
Per-key line style: Each LineData key has its own CorePlotting::LineStyleData (color, thickness, alpha) stored in OnionSkinViewStateData::line_key_line_styles; managed at runtime via LineStyleState QObject wrappers; editable in a collapsible “Line Style Options” section in the properties panel via LineStyleControls; `alpha` field sets the maximum alpha before temporal decay; serialized/deserialized as part of the JSON state
Per-key mask contour style: Each MaskData key has its own CorePlotting::LineStyleData (color, thickness, alpha) stored in OnionSkinViewStateData::mask_key_line_styles; managed at runtime via LineStyleState QObject wrappers; editable in a collapsible “Mask Style Options” section in the properties panel via LineStyleControls; alpha field sets the maximum alpha before temporal decay; serialized/deserialized as part of the JSON state

title: Onion Skin View Widget Roadmap
text:
Status: Not started. No export infrastructure exists in the current widget.
Goal: Allow the user to export the current onion skin view as an SVG file, preserving vector quality for publication.


SVG export requires converting the OpenGL scene to vector graphics. Two approaches:
Option A — Scene-to-SVG serialization (recommended): Walk the RenderableScene primitives (glyphs, polylines) and emit SVG <circle>, <polygon>, and <polyline> elements with the same colors and alpha values computed during rebuildScene(). This avoids OpenGL framebuffer capture and produces clean, resolution-independent output.
Option B — QPainter-based rendering: Use QSvgGenerator + QPainter to re-render the scene data using Qt’s 2D drawing API. This provides more mature vector rendering but requires duplicating the rendering logic outside OpenGL.



Because SVG export will be needed by multiple widgets (see cross-widget export below), the export logic should be implemented as a shared utility rather than per-widget code:








Component
Location
Purpose




SvgExporter

Scene-to-SVG conversion


ExportButton

Shared “Export SVG” button + file dialog

Notes

Full spatial overlay

Windowed spatial + alpha fading

        ↓
File dialog → choose output path

        ↓
For each glyph: emit SVG element with position, size, fill color + opacity
For each polyline: emit SVG <polyline> with stroke color + opacity + width
        ↓
Add axis labels, tick marks, bounds metadata
        ↓
Write SVG file



Add an “Export” section to the properties panel:

Export SVG button — opens file dialog and triggers export
Include axes checkbox — whether to render axis labels and ticks in the SVG
Background color — whether to include the dark background or use transparent
