title: Column Recipe Preset Registry
text:
Test Coverage
tests/TensorDesign/test_column_recipe_preset_registry.cpp verifies that:

The built-in registry exposes mean_over_interval metadata and parameter schema fields.
Expanding each initial built-in preset produces the expected raw ColumnRecipe fields.
Duplicate preset ids are rejected.

tests/TensorDesign/test_tensor_design_builder.cpp includes end-to-end checks that expanded preset recipes can be serialized as ordinary TensorDesign JSON and then executed through buildTensorFromDesignJson().
It also verifies direct preset-authored JSON, such as columns[].preset = "point_xy", through both parseDesignJson() and buildTensorFromDesignJson().
tests/fuzz/integration/TensorDesign/fuzz_tensor_design_registry.cpp adds an allowlisted scalar-composition fuzz target. Each fuzz input selects one explicit (row_modifier, column_aggregator) pair from a curated table rather than the full registry Cartesian product. The allowlist is organized in tiers that mirror the former monolithic presets:

Tier 0: no modifier + mean_value, event_count, or event_presence over full row intervals.
Tier 1: interval_start + analog_sample, point_xy, or multi_point_xy.
Tier 2: window_around_interval_start + interval reducers, with fuzzed pre/post.
Tier 3: bind_interval_start + trial_relative_event_count.

raster_events_relative is intentionally excluded because it produces per-row DigitalEventSeries output (relative spike times) rather than scalar float tensor columns. Add new allowlist entries incrementally as deterministic Catch2 coverage lands for each composition.

title: Column Recipe Preset Registry
text:
TensorDesigner UI
TensorDesigner exposes Add Preset… next to Add Column. The dialog lists built-in registry presets, shows each preset description and parameter field names, collects the shared preset parameters, expands the selected preset through ColumnRecipePresetRegistry, and appends all generated raw ColumnRecipes to the current design.
Saving from TensorDesigner uses serializeDesignJson() on the expanded recipes. The saved JSON contains ordinary columns[] entries and does not require the preset registry for execution.

title: Column Recipe Preset Registry
text:
Planned Follow-Up
Phase 10 should add preset file/library support, including bundled and user preset catalogs. Later UI refinements may replace the shared-argument form with per-preset generated forms, but the Phase 9c path is functional and saves expanded raw recipes.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Status: Implementation roadmap for Column Row Pipeline Design.
Phases 1-6 and 9a-9g are implemented. Phase 7 and preset-library work (Phase 10) remain planned.
This roadmap breaks the per-column row-pipeline refactor into small, testable steps. The design goal is to let each tensor column derive its own row-aligned gather inputs through TransformPipelines while keeping GatherResult a container/direct-gather executor rather than a pipeline runner.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
End State
The refactor is complete when:

ColumnRecipe has an optional row_pipeline_json field.
TensorDesign JSON parse/serialize round-trips row_pipeline_json.
Empty row_pipeline_json preserves the current full-interval behavior.
A row pipeline can produce DigitalIntervalSeries windows that are passed to GatherResult as prepared windows.
A column pipeline can receive row-specific values through PipelineValueStore, such as one normalization event per row.
Per-column gather geometry can differ across columns while row identity and RowDescriptor remain tied to the original row source.
Onset-window spike presence and onset-sampled analog covariates are expressible in JSON.
Common workflows are available through discoverable presets so users do not need to remember raw transform or binding keywords.
The temporary pipeline_json "offset" sample-at-offset path is removed or replaced by row-pipeline behavior.
Tests cover identity behavior, onset windows, point sampling, overlapping windows, cross-timeframe gather, and invalid row-count changes.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Current Inventory
Implemented foundations:

GatherResult::create(source, windows, alignment_points) accepts prepared windows and optional alignment events for existing direct-gather consumers.
GatherResult::fromRows() and fromRowsLike() support row-aligned DataObject results from external pipeline helpers.
DigitalIntervalSeries::createOverlapping() preserves overlapping gather windows.
IntervalToEvent converts interval rows to events.
EventToInterval converts events to overlapping windows.
PruneOverlappingIntervals provides explicit keep-first overlap pruning.
buildIntervalPipelineProvider() gathers over interval rows and applies range reductions.
buildPipelineColumnProvider() handles timestamp-row columns.
TensorDesignBuilder builds lazy-column tensors from JSON.
ColumnRecipe::row_pipeline_json is parsed and serialized.
resolveIntervalGatherWindows() resolves identity and DigitalIntervalSeries row-pipeline output.
buildProviderFromRecipe() uses row-pipeline windows for interval-row columns.
Digital event/interval views expose ClockTicks-based API-facing elements.
PipelineValueStore stores ClockTicks, and NormalizeTimeParamsV2::alignment_time is ClockTicks.
gatherAndExecutePipeline() executes JSON-loaded pipeline steps, including container steps, on each gathered row before applying the terminal range reduction.
NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative normalizes a gathered DigitalEventSeries into relative ClockTicks storage while preserving event EntityIds.
ColumnRecipe::pipeline_value_bindings is parsed, serialized, and used to bind one row-aligned DigitalEventSeries value into PipelineValueStore per tensor row.
Direct binding sources from DataManager keys and derived binding sources using source_pipeline_json are supported when they resolve to row-aligned DigitalEventSeries objects.
Interval-row columns can dispatch DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline output as sample times for timestamp-style providers.
ShiftDigitalEventSeries shifts DigitalEventSeries sample times and replaces the temporary top-level pipeline_json "offset" compatibility path.
Angle-at-contact-onset point sampling is tested through TensorDesign JSON in the whisker-contact scenario.
Contact-aligned spike presence is tested through TensorDesign JSON in the whisker-contact scenario.

Known gaps:

There is no row-pipeline caching.
UI does not expose row-pipeline configuration.
The Phase 9c column recipe preset registry exists with a compiled preset set and TensorDesigner Add Preset… support.
The Phase 9d design authoring preset registry exists with a compiled whisker_contact_feature_table preset and TensorDesigner Apply Table Preset… support.
There is no broader preset JSON/file library yet.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 1: Baseline Tests — Done
Goal: lock down current behavior before adding row-pipeline dispatch.
Tasks:

Add or verify tests for interval-row tensors gathering over the full row interval.
Add or verify tests for interval_property columns.
Add or verify tests for timestamp row columns.
Add a characterization test for the current pipeline_json "offset" behavior if it must remain during the transition.
Confirm cross-timeframe interval-row gather behavior through GatherResult query conversion.

Exit criteria:

Existing JSON without row_pipeline_json is covered.
Current behavior can be compared against the post-refactor identity path.

Suggested test areas:

tests/TensorDesign/
tests/TransformsV2/ TensorColumnBuilders tests
Whisker-contact scenario tests

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 2: Add Recipe Field And JSON Round Trip — Done
text:
Phase 2: Add Recipe Field And JSON Round Trip — Done
Goal: make row_pipeline_json part of the data model without changing provider behavior.
Tasks:

Add std::string row_pipeline_json to ColumnRecipe.
Parse columns[].row_pipeline_json in TensorDesignBuilder.
Serialize row_pipeline_json only when non-empty, unless existing conventions prefer explicit empty fields.
Update docs for TensorDesignBuilder.qmd and TensorColumnBuilders.qmd.
Add JSON parse/serialize tests.

Exit criteria:

Existing JSON remains valid.
New JSON round-trips row_pipeline_json.
No provider behavior changes yet.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 3: Row Pipeline Execution Skeleton — Done
text:
Phase 3: Row Pipeline Execution Skeleton — Done
Goal: execute an empty or identity row pipeline and route through existing providers.
Tasks:

Define the row-pipeline execution boundary in TensorColumnBuilders or a small helper.
Treat empty row_pipeline_json as identity.
For interval row sources, identity returns the original DigitalIntervalSeries as prepared windows.
Verify row count matches the original row source.
Keep interval_property columns on their current no-gather path.

Exit criteria:

Identity row-pipeline output produces exactly the same values as current full-interval gather.
No new transform requirements are introduced.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 4: DigitalIntervalSeries Output Dispatch — Done
Goal: support row pipelines that output prepared DigitalIntervalSeries windows.
Tasks:

Execute row pipelines that return DigitalIntervalSeries.
Require output size to match original row count.
Pass the output as prepared windows to the existing interval gather provider path.
Preserve the original RowDescriptor from the row source.
Ensure overlapping output windows are not merged.
Add tests using EventToInterval over event row sources or IntervalToEvent followed by EventToInterval where possible.

Exit criteria:

A column can gather over row-pipeline-produced windows.
Overlapping windows produce one tensor row per original row.
Cross-timeframe gather still passes through GatherResult conversion.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 5: Iterable PipelineValueStore Bindings
Status: done. The gathered-row execution path supports container-step pipelines before terminal range reduction, NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative provides container-level DigitalEventSeries -> DigitalEventSeries normalization, and pipeline_value_bindings supplies row-specific ClockTicks values through PipelineValueStore.
Goal: supply per-row values to pipeline_json transforms through the existing TransformsV2 PipelineValueStore mechanism without making row_pipeline_json responsible for normalization markers.
Motivating example: gather Spikes into one DigitalEventSeries per trial/contact interval, then execute a TransformPipeline containing NormalizeTime on each gathered row. The normalization time comes from a row-aligned DigitalEventSeries, such as ContactOnset, or from Contact -> IntervalToEvent(start). The event for row i is written into PipelineValueStore as ClockTicks and bound to the NormalizeTime parameter for row i.
Tasks:
Completed tasks:

Allow gathered row execution to run JSON-loaded container steps before terminal range reduction.
Add NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative as the container-level normalize transform for gathered DigitalEventSeries rows.
Cover container-step-before-reduction behavior with a TensorColumnBuilders test using EventCountInWindow after normalization.
Define a JSON schema for iterable bindings from DataObjects into PipelineValueStore keys: pipeline_value_bindings[] with source_key, optional source_pipeline_json, and store_key.
Support direct iterable sources from DataManager keys with implicit identity source pipeline.
Support derived iterable sources from a DataManager key plus source_pipeline_json.
Start with DigitalEventSeries binding into PipelineValueStore as ClockTicks from the event returned by DigitalEventSeries::view().
Defer DigitalIntervalSeries binding. Use IntervalToEvent in source_pipeline_json for start/end/center selection.
Build one store value per tensor row from the resolved iterable DataObject.
Inject the current row’s values into PipelineValueStore before applying pipeline_json parameter bindings.
Verify a normalize-time transform uses the bound store value, not the gather window start.
Add raster/PSTH-style tests where spikes are gathered in trial windows and normalized to a separate event per row.
Add row-count mismatch tests for direct iterable sources.

Exit criteria:

Per-row transforms can consume a marker that is outside the gathered DataObject through parameter bindings.
Trial-relative transforms can consume correct marker times.
Iterable binding sources are explicit and row-count checked.
Direct-key iterable bindings and key-plus-pipeline iterable bindings are both covered by tests.
NormalizeTime accepts a ClockTicks binding and subtracts in clock-tick coordinates.
Phase 5 tests use the same DataObject view() element types that normal TransformPipeline execution uses.

Settled design choices:

Iterable binding declarations live on ColumnRecipe, beside pipeline_json.
source_pipeline_json uses the same PipelineDescriptor schema as row_pipeline_json and pipeline_json.
Iterable binding store_key values must not overwrite other keys; duplicates are rejected.
Temporal iterable values should be bound as ClockTicks, not raw TimeFrameIndex values.
PipelineValueStore stores ClockTicks directly.
NormalizeTimeParamsV2::alignment_time is ClockTicks and binds through ClockTicksReflector.
NormalizeClockTicksValueV2 is the canonical pipeline transform for DigitalEventSeries value projections; ClockTicksWithId is reduced to ClockTicks by the projection helper before pipeline execution.
NormalizeDigitalEventSeriesRelative is the canonical container-level transform when the gathered row should remain a DigitalEventSeries with relative ClockTicks values before reduction or export.
Existing PipelineValueStore, parameter bindings, and gather extension helpers should be reused or generalized to bind iterable values per row.
User-facing presets should hide the distinction between ClockTicksWithId and ClockTicks normalize transforms whenever possible.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 6: Timestamp And Point Sampling — Done
text:
Phase 6: Timestamp And Point Sampling — Done
Goal: replace the temporary "offset" sample-at-offset path with row-pipeline-driven point sampling.
Tasks:

Support row pipelines that produce DigitalEventSeries sample times without interval windows.
Route event output to timestamp/sample provider behavior.
Define how optional offsets are expressed as transforms rather than top-level ad hoc JSON.
Remove the pipeline_json.find("\"offset\"") compatibility path from TensorDesignBuilder::buildColumnProvider() once tests cover the replacement.
Add angle-at-onset tests for the whisker-contact scenario.

Exit criteria:

Point sampling is expressible through row-pipeline JSON.
The offset string-search path is gone.
Existing sample-at-offset behavior is preserved where intended.

Implemented notes:

resolveIntervalRowPipelineGeometry() resolves interval-row pipelines to either DigitalIntervalSeries gather windows or DigitalEventSeries sample times.
buildProviderFromRecipe() routes DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline output to timestamp/sample provider behavior when the column pipeline has no terminal range reduction.
ShiftDigitalEventSeries expresses sample offsets as a regular TransformPipeline step.
The old top-level pipeline_json "offset" detection path has been removed.
Tests cover provider-level analog sampling at interval starts, shifted sample times, and TensorDesign JSON replacing the old offset behavior.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 7: Optional Additional Row Transforms
Goal: add only the transforms needed by concrete analyses.
Candidate transforms:

IntervalShift for lag/lead interval windows.
Data-derived event transforms that produce one event per row from a row interval plus another source object.
Optional fused convenience transforms if repeated JSON patterns become too verbose.

Tasks:

Add one transform at a time under src/TransformsV2/algorithms/.
Ensure output DataObjects preserve or intentionally set TimeFrame.
Use DigitalIntervalSeries::createOverlapping() for window-like interval outputs.
Add focused transform tests.
Add one TensorDesign integration test per new analysis pattern.

Exit criteria:

New transforms are generally useful outside TensorDesign.
TensorDesign does not gain tensor-specific geometry enums.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 8: Whisker-Contact Integration — Done
Goal: prove the design on the motivating analysis table.
Status: done for the motivating whisker-contact feature table. TensorDesign JSON covers full-contact curvature, full-contact spike count, contact-onset spike presence, and angle-at-onset point sampling. Trial-relative raster/PSTH examples are now tracked as preset/example-library work in later phases rather than as a blocker for this integration phase.
Tasks:

Extend the whisker-contact scenario with contact onset features. Done for onset spike presence.
Add a full-contact curvature column. Done.
Add a spike-in-onset-window column. Done.
Add an angle-at-onset column after timestamp/sample row-pipeline dispatch is implemented. Done.
Verify row count, row descriptors, and expected values. Done.
Update scenario documentation with valid JSON. Done.

Exit criteria:

Contact-aligned spike presence is built through production TensorDesign code.
Angle-at-contact-onset point sampling is built through production TensorDesign code.
The JSON example in the whisker-contact scenario documentation is a working example of the motivating feature table.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Test Coverage Notes
Current row-pipeline coverage is split across four files:

tests/TransformsV2/test_tensor_column_builders.test.cpp covers the TransformsV2 provider layer, resolveIntervalGatherWindows() behavior, and Phase 5 direct/derived pipeline_value_bindings execution.
tests/TensorDesign/test_tensor_design_builder.cpp covers TensorDesign JSON parsing, serialization, JSON-to-tensor builds, and Phase 5 end-to-end bound normalization through fully specified JSON.
tests/TransformsV2/test_tensor_whisker_contact_scenario.cpp covers programmatic provider/lazy tensor construction over the whisker-contact fixture.
tests/TensorDesign/test_tensor_whisker_contact_scenario.cpp covers the TensorDesign JSON path over the same fixture, including contact-aligned spikes.

The two whisker-contact files are not exact duplicates. They exercise different architectural layers. The older TransformsV2 file does not validate row_pipeline_json; it remains useful as lower-level integration coverage, though it may be a candidate for reduced assertions if runtime becomes an issue.
Potential stale or missing coverage after Phase 8:

DigitalEventSeries row-pipeline output rejection is covered at the row-geometry/helper layer; add a TensorDesign JSON-level rejection test if error messages become part of the user contract.
Add explicit tests for malformed but non-empty row_pipeline_json at the TensorDesign JSON build layer if not already covered by provider tests.
Add a derived binding row-count mismatch test if direct mismatch coverage is not considered sufficient.
Add cache behavior tests when row-pipeline caching is introduced.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 9a: TimeFrame Row Source — Done
Goal: allow tensors with one row per index in a named TimeFrame, without requiring a synthetic data object.
Status: done. TensorDesign supports row_type: "timeframe" with row_source.time_key, and TensorDesigner exposes a TimeFrame Rows mode populated from DataManager::getTimeFrameKeys().
Tasks:

Add RowType::TimeFrame or equivalent to TensorDesign row source parsing.
Extend row-source JSON with a time_key field distinct from data_key.
Build row descriptors from every index in the selected TimeFrame.
Add TensorDesigner UI support for a TimeFrame Rows mode populated from DataManager::getTimeFrameKeys().
Keep Timestamp Rows data-object based (DigitalEventSeries) and clarify Derived from Source as “derive rows from timestamps in a data object”.
Add tests for TimeFrame rows sampling analog data.
Add UI tests that TimeFrame row sources appear separately from timestamp-event row sources.

Implemented notes:

TensorDesign JSON uses row_source.time_key for TimeFrame rows.
serializeDesignJson() omits data_key for TimeFrame row sources.
Backend tests cover parsing, serialization, and analog sampling over all TimeFrame rows.
TensorDesigner load-config tests cover building a tensor from TimeFrame rows.

Exit criteria:

Users can build frame-aligned tensors directly from a TimeFrame key.
TensorDesigner no longer implies that a DigitalEventSeries is the only way to create timestamp-like rows.
Existing timestamp and derived-from-source behavior is unchanged.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 9b: Point And Keypoint Column Primitives — Done
text:
Phase 9b: Point And Keypoint Column Primitives — Done
Goal: support common keypoint feature tables without tensor-specific geometry enums.
Status: done. PointCoordinate converts PointData to RaggedAnalogTimeSeries using a coordinate parameter, and TensorDesign JSON can build x/y keypoint columns over TimeFrame rows.
Tasks:

Add PointCoordinate as a parameterized container transform (PointData -> RaggedAnalogTimeSeries) with coordinate = x | y.
Register the transform with TransformsV2 JSON loading and parameter schema infrastructure.
Add transform tests for point coordinate extraction.
Document timestamp sampling semantics for RaggedAnalogTimeSeries output: single-keypoint data uses the first/only value; multi-point-per-time data needs an explicit policy before broad use.
Add TensorDesign tests for PointData rows from DerivedFromSource producing x/y columns.
Add TensorDesign tests for TimeFrame rows sampling PointData into x/y columns after Phase 9a.
Add interval-row tests reducing point coordinate values with a standard range reduction.
Add TensorDesigner UI/load-config tests for a PointData x/y tensor once TimeFrame rows are available.

Implemented notes:

PointCoordinate is implemented as one container transform with coordinate = X | Y.
TensorDesign tests cover TimeFrame rows sampling one-keypoint-per-time PointData into x/y columns.
Sparse TimeFrame sampling is covered for analog data and produces NaN where no source sample exists.
Additional DerivedFromSource, interval-reduction, and TensorDesigner UI tests remain useful follow-up coverage but are not required to prove the primitive path.

Exit criteria:

A PointData keypoint can produce scalar x and y tensor columns through normal TransformPipeline JSON using one parameterized transform.
Multiple keypoint tables can be represented by repeating the same primitive column recipes.
The primitive transforms remain useful outside TensorDesign.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 9c: Column Preset Registry And Expansion
text:
Phase 9c: Column Preset Registry And Expansion
Goal: provide friendly recipe generators that expand user-supplied parameters into raw ColumnRecipe objects, avoiding manual embedded JSON authoring. Presets are for authoring convenience; saved designs remain expanded raw TensorDesign JSON.
Status: done. ColumnRecipePresetRegistry is implemented in src/TensorDesign with the Phase 9c compiled preset set. Focused expansion tests cover raw recipe output, TensorDesign JSON tests verify both JSON-authored preset invocations and selected expanded presets through buildTensorFromDesignJson(), and TensorDesigner exposes Add Preset… to append expanded raw recipes. This phase does not add preset files or user/bundled preset catalogs; those are Phase 10.
Tasks:

Add a ColumnRecipePresetRegistry or equivalent registry in the TensorDesign/TransformsV2 boundary. Started with a TensorDesign-side registry.
Define preset descriptors with name, display name, description, parameter schema, source (Built-in or User), and expansion function/template. Started for compiled presets.
Preset expansion must return a list of ColumnRecipes, not a single recipe, so grouped features can be appended atomically. Done in the expansion type.
Add presets for the initial common workflows: Done.

mean over interval Done.
event count over interval Done.
event presence around interval start Done.
analog sample at interval start Done.
point x/y for one keypoint Done.
point x/y for multiple keypoints Done.
point x/y sampled at interval start Done.
raster events relative to interval start Done.
trial-relative event times using NormalizeTime with row-specific ClockTicks bindings Done as trial_relative_event_count_from_interval_start.

Expand preset JSON into raw ColumnRecipe fields before provider construction. Done for compiled built-in presets in parseDesignJson().
Add tests that preset expansion produces the same tensor values as equivalent raw recipes. Done through focused expansion tests and TensorDesign JSON build tests.
Add TensorDesigner UI support for Add Preset… that appends all expanded columns. Done.
Save expanded raw recipes only after presets are applied; preset invocations are not required for execution. Done through TensorDesigner::toJson() / serializeDesignJson().
Reject duplicate preset IDs across built-in and user presets for the initial implementation. Done for registry registration.

Exit criteria:

Users can express the whisker-contact examples without raw transform names.
Users can add keypoint x/y column groups without manually authoring repeated PointCoordinate pipelines.
Presets are discoverable from a registry that can be reused by documentation and UI.
Raw JSON remains available for advanced workflows.
Saved designs remain reproducible expanded TensorDesign JSON and do not depend on the preset registry at load time.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 9d: Design Authoring Presets
Status: done for the initial compiled design authoring preset registry and motivating whisker-contact table preset.
Goal: support reusable whole-table authoring templates that set row source and add multiple related column groups, while preserving expanded raw TensorDesign JSON as the executable and saved-analysis format.
Design authoring presets are a higher-level convenience layer than Phase 9c column presets. A column preset expands to one or more ColumnRecipes and appends them to the current design. A design authoring preset expands to a row source plus a set of raw ColumnRecipes, producing an ordinary TensorDesignSpec immediately after application.
Design preset invocations should not become the single source of truth for reproducible analysis. They are authoring shortcuts only. After applying a design preset, saving should write the expanded row_source and columns fields, not the preset invocation. Loading and executing a saved design should not require the design preset registry.
Tasks:

Define a DesignPresetExpansion shape containing row-source fields plus multiple raw ColumnRecipes. Done.
Add a compiled whisker_contact_feature_table authoring preset covering curvature, spike count, onset spike presence, angle at onset, and optional keypoint x/y columns. Done.
Add tests comparing design preset expansion to the equivalent raw TensorDesign JSON. Done.
Prefer compiled expansion functions initially for design presets that need loops or complex defaults. Done.
Ensure applying a design preset produces an ordinary TensorDesignSpec and that serializeDesignJson() writes expanded raw fields only. Done.
Add TensorDesigner UI affordance such as New From Preset… or Apply Table Preset…. Because this changes the row source, the UI should confirm replacement when the current design already has a row source or columns. Done.

Exit criteria:

A complete motivating analysis table can be authored from one preset plus a small parameter form.
Column presets remain useful for incremental table editing.
Applying a design preset produces ordinary row-source and column recipe JSON that can be saved and executed independently of the preset registry.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 9e: Decoupling Row Modifiers and Column Aggregators
text:
Phase 9e: Decoupling Row Modifiers and Column Aggregators
Status: done.
Goal: Prevent combinatorial explosion of monolithic presets (e.g., analog_sample_at_interval_start, event_presence_around_interval_start) by splitting the registry into two composable domains: Row Modifiers and Column Aggregators.
Tasks:

Introduce RowModifierRegistry. This registry provides descriptors that output row_pipeline_json and declare the resulting Effective Row Type (e.g., Interval -> Event, Interval -> Interval). Done. RowModifiers also support emitting pipeline_value_bindings.
Introduce ColumnAggregatorRegistry. This registry provides descriptors that output pipeline_json and optional pipeline_value_bindings. These are filtered based on the Effective Row Type and Target Data Type. Done.
Refactor ColumnRecipePresetRegistry (or create a UI “Stitcher” equivalent) to seamlessly combine a selected Row Modifier and a Column Aggregator into one or more ColumnRecipes. Done. Handled natively in TensorDesignBuilder json parsing.
Carefully untangle multi-input presets (like multi_point_xy_at_interval_start): Done.

The UI Stitcher must handle cases where the Column Aggregator accepts a list of source_keys (e.g., multiple keypoints).
For each input key, the Stitcher generates a distinct ColumnRecipe, applying the same row_pipeline_json (from the Row Modifier) to each.

Create a two-step UX flow in TensorDesigner: (Deferred to UI layer)

Step A (Optional): Select a Row Modifier (filtered by top-level row strategy).
Step B (Required): Select a Target Data Series and Column Aggregator (filtered by the Effective Row Type from Step A).

Write tests ensuring that a composed Modifier + Aggregator yields the exact same JSON as the older monolithic presets. Done.

Exit criteria:

Users can independently mix and match row gather geometry (like “Onset Window”) with data extraction logic (like “Mean”, “Event Count”) without requiring a custom C++ preset for every combination.
Multi-input workflows (like expanding 5 keypoints at interval onset) remain fully supported and generate the correct Nx2 ColumnRecipes.
The UI successfully hides the complexity of building two coordinated JSON pipelines.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 9f: Two-Step UI Column Stitcher
Status: planned.
Goal: Provide an intuitive UI in TensorDesigner for building modular columns without requiring users to write raw JSON or use monolithic presets. This phase implements the frontend encapsulation of Phase 9e’s decoupled backend.
Tasks:

Backend Registry Metadata (UI-Independent):

Introduce an EffectiveRowType enum (e.g., Interval, Event) in the C++ backend.
Update RowModifierDescriptor to declare its output_row_type.
Update ColumnAggregatorDescriptor to declare its supported_row_types (e.g., Event Rate only supports Interval).
Add query methods to the registries (e.g., ColumnAggregatorRegistry::getAggregatorsFor(AggregatorQueryContext)) so the UI remains stateless and driven purely by the backend composition rules.

Create a Two-Step Column Builder Dialog (replacing or augmenting the existing ColumnConfigDialog).

Step A: Row Modification (Optional). Prompt: “Do you want to modify the row before extracting data?”

Populate a dropdown from the RowModifierRegistry.
Internally track the Effective Row Type resulting from this modifier (queried from the backend descriptor).

Step B: Data Aggregation (Required). Prompt: “What data do you want to extract?”

Populate a dropdown from the ColumnAggregatorRegistry, dynamically filtered by querying the backend with the Effective Row Type from Step A.


The “Custom/Raw” Escape Hatch:

In Step B (or as a top-level toggle), include an “Advanced / Custom Pipeline” option.
When selected, instead of showing a preset AutoParamWidget, the UI embeds the full TransformPipelineEditor (or a raw JSON text box).
This allows users to author completely novel aggregations block-by-block without needing a preset to exist.

Implement the UI Stitcher logic. When the user confirms the dialog, generate the ColumnRecipe by:

Calling expand() on the selected descriptors.
Stitching them together into a final set of ColumnRecipes, just as the JSON backend does, and appending them to the TensorDesigner column list.

Add frontend tests for the UI Stitcher logic to ensure that selecting specific combinations yields the exact same raw ColumnRecipes as the JSON backend.

Exit criteria:

Users can mix and match row geometries (Step A) with data extraction logic (Step B) using a guided, wizard-like UI.
The UI safely prevents illegal combinations (e.g., Range Reduction on an Event row) by filtering Step B options based on Step A’s output.
Combinatorial explosion of UI presets is completely eliminated; the UI is highly composable.
The TensorDesigner list view accurately displays the generated columns.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 9g: Polymorphic Preset Architecture and JSON DTOs
text:
Phase 9g: Polymorphic Preset Architecture and JSON DTOs
Status: done.
Goal: Refactor the monolithic ColumnRecipePresetRegistry into a modular architecture that separates behavioral execution (the Strategy pattern) from serialization (Flat DTOs for reflect-cpp). This allows complex presets to be defined in their own C++ files with custom UI callbacks, while enabling simple presets to be data-driven.
Tasks:

Define Polymorphic Interfaces:

Create IRowModifier and IColumnAggregator base classes replacing the std::function structs.
Include standard metadata methods (id(), parameters(), expand()).
Include optional UI hook methods (e.g., virtual std::vector<std::string> getDynamicOptions(std::string const& field_name) const) to support dynamic AutoParam combo boxes without hardcoding UI logic into the registry.

Refactor Existing Complex Presets:

Extract complex presets (like MultiPointXyAggregator) into their own .hpp/.cpp files implementing the new interfaces.
Update the registry to store std::unique_ptr<IColumnAggregator> and std::unique_ptr<IRowModifier>.

Define Flat DTOs for JSON Presets:

Create JsonColumnPresetDto (and a Row Modifier equivalent) as flat, inheritance-free structs designed specifically for reflect-cpp parsing. These structs will hold id, ParameterSchema, and raw JSON template strings (e.g., pipeline_json_template).

Implement the JSON Preset Strategy:

Create a JsonColumnAggregator : public IColumnAggregator class that accepts a parsed JsonColumnPresetDto in its constructor.
Implement expand() to perform simple string replacement, injecting user-provided parameters into the DTO’s JSON templates.


Exit criteria:

The registry monolithic file is eliminated; presets are modularized into independent files.
reflect-cpp serialization boundaries are strictly separated from C++ behavioral polymorphism.
Custom C++ presets can provide specialized UI behaviors (like populating data keys) via interface methods.
The foundation is laid to load simple presets from JSON files (Phase 10).

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
section: Phase 10: Preset Library Files and User Authoring
text:
Phase 10: Preset Library Files and User Authoring
Goal: Distribute Neuralyzer with useful built-in JSON recipe generators and let users author, save, and import their own preset definitions using a library pattern.
Tasks:

Add Qt-free helpers for tensor column preset files, scanning default directories ({config_dir}/presets/tensor_design/columns/ for users and resources/... for bundled).
Implement catalog initialization that parses JSON files into JsonColumnPresetDto via reflect-cpp, wraps them in JsonColumnAggregator classes (from Phase 9g), and registers them.
Implement load/save/delete for user preset JSON files.
UI Save Workflow: Add a “Save as Custom Preset…” action in the TensorDesigner Advanced Pipeline editor.
In the Save dialog, allow users to name the preset and declare simple parameters (e.g., exposing a window offset as an int).
Serialize the resulting JsonColumnPresetDto to the user’s config directory so it appears in the “Add Preset” dialog in future sessions.
Reject duplicate preset IDs across bundled and user entries in the initial implementation.
Add tests for path helpers, catalog merge behavior, load/save/delete, duplicate ID policy, and template expansion.

Exit criteria:

A fresh Neuralyzer install has useful TensorDesign JSON column presets without user setup.
Users can parameterize and save custom JSON pipelines directly from the UI, generating reusable template files.
The preset library correctly loads and seamlessly integrates User JSON presets alongside complex C++ Built-in presets.
User presets do not silently override bundled presets; lab-specific variants use unique IDs until explicit namespacing is introduced.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Phase 11: Documentation And UI Follow-Up
Goal: update public developer docs and decide how users configure row pipelines.
Tasks:

Update TensorDesignBuilder.qmd with the implemented row_pipeline_json contract.
Update TensorColumnBuilders.qmd with provider dispatch behavior.
Update tensor_stack.qmd status language.
Update test scenario docs.
Add UI support for browsing bundled and user column presets in TensorDesigner, with raw JSON available as an advanced option.

Exit criteria:

Docs clearly distinguish implemented behavior from future work.
UI work can proceed without changing the core data model.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Verification Checklist

Existing JSON without row_pipeline_json produces unchanged tensors.
Empty row_pipeline_json is identity.
row_pipeline_json round-trips through parse and serialize.
DIS row-pipeline output must match source row count.
DES sample-time output must match source row count.
Iterable binding sources must match source row count.
Overlapping windows remain separate rows.
Generated gather windows use IntervalLayout::Overlapping where needed.
PipelineValueStore-backed normalization uses the marker for the current row, not the gather window start.
Cross-timeframe gathers match expected source query bounds.
interval_property columns remain source-gather-free.
The offset string-search compatibility path is removed after replacement.
Preset expansion and equivalent raw recipes produce the same values.
Bundled and user preset library entries load and expand correctly.

title: Column Row Pipeline Roadmap
text:
Suggested Build And Test Commands
Determine the configured CMake preset from out/build/ before running these commands.
List candidate tests:
ctest --preset linux-clang-release -N | grep -i "tensor"
Run focused TensorDesign tests:
ctest --preset linux-clang-release --output-on-failure -R "TensorDesign|TensorColumnBuilders|whisker_contact" > test_log.txt 2>&1
After C++ changes, run clang-format and clang-tidy on touched C++ files following the repository development workflow.

title: Design Preset Registry
text: Status: Phase 9d implemented for compiled design authoring presets. The built-in registry currently provides whisker_contact_feature_table. Preset file catalogs remain Phase 10 work.

title: Design Preset Registry
text:
Purpose
DesignPresetRegistry provides Qt-free TensorDesign table-level authoring presets. A design preset accepts friendly parameters and expands to an ordinary TensorDesignSpec: row source fields plus raw ColumnRecipe entries.
Design presets are authoring shortcuts, not the canonical saved-analysis representation. parseDesignJson() accepts a design preset invocation and expands it before returning a TensorDesignSpec. serializeDesignJson() writes expanded row_source and columns fields only, so saved designs remain executable without loading the design preset registry.

title: Design Preset Registry
text:
Current API
The registry lives in src/TensorDesign/DesignPresetRegistry.hpp and exposes:

DesignPresetDescriptor: preset id, display name, description, parameter schema, source, and expansion function.
DesignPresetArgs: shared arguments for the initial compiled table preset.
DesignPresetExpansion: an expanded TensorDesignSpec.
DesignPresetRegistry: register, find, list, and expand operations.
createBuiltInDesignPresetRegistry(): constructs the built-in compiled registry.

Duplicate preset ids are rejected by registerPreset().

title: Design Preset Registry
text:
JSON Authoring
A TensorDesign JSON envelope can invoke a design preset:
{
  "tensor_key": "contact_features",
  "preset": "whisker_contact_feature_table",
  "parameters": {
    "row_source_key": "contacts",
    "curvature_source_key": "curvature",
    "spike_source_key": "spikes",
    "angle_source_key": "angle",
    "keypoint_source_keys": ["tip"],
    "onset_pre": 2,
    "onset_post": 3
  }
}
Parsing expands this into raw row_source and columns. Serializing the parsed spec does not preserve the preset invocation.

title: Design Preset Registry
text:
Built-In Presets

whisker_contact_feature_table
Parameters:







Field
Meaning




row_source_key
DigitalIntervalSeries key defining contact rows.


curvature_source_key
Analog-like source reduced with MeanValue over each contact interval.


spike_source_key
DigitalEventSeries source counted over intervals and queried near contact onset.


angle_source_key
Analog-like source sampled at contact onset.


keypoint_source_keys
Optional PointData keys sampled at contact onset and expanded into x/y columns.


onset_pre
Clock ticks before contact onset for spike presence.


onset_post
Clock ticks after contact onset for spike presence.



Expansion:

Row source: row_type = interval, data_key = row_source_key.
mean_curvature: mean_over_interval(curvature_source_key).
spike_count: event_count_over_interval(spike_source_key).
spike_presence_at_onset: event_presence_around_interval_start(spike_source_key, onset_pre, onset_post).
angle_at_onset: analog_sample_at_interval_start(angle_source_key).
For each keypoint source: point_xy_at_interval_start(source_key, name_prefix = source_key).

The implementation composes Phase 9c column presets internally so the generated columns stay consistent with incremental authoring behavior.

title: Design Preset Registry
text:
TensorDesigner UI
TensorDesigner exposes the built-in registry through Apply Table Preset…. Applying a design preset replaces the current row source and columns after confirmation when the current design is non-empty. The in-memory design is immediately expanded to raw fields, so Save Config continues to write normal TensorDesign JSON rather than preset invocations.

title: Wide Line Rendering
text: glLineWidth() is clamped to 1.0 on many OpenGL 3.3+ Core profile drivers, making the line thickness spinbox in the DataViewer have no visible effect for analog time series.

title: Wide Line Rendering
text: glLineWidth() is clamped to 1.0 on many OpenGL 3.3+ Core profile drivers, making the line thickness spinbox in the DataViewer have no visible effect for analog time series.

title: Wide Line Rendering
text:
Solution
Both PolyLineRenderer and StreamingPolyLineRenderer use a geometry shader (wide_line.geom) to expand each line segment into a screen-space quad (triangle strip). The geometry shader receives GL_LINE_STRIP primitives and emits 4-vertex triangle strips per segment.

Shader Pipeline

wide_line.vert — Transforms a_position (vec2) by u_mvp_matrix to clip space.
wide_line.geom — Converts each line segment to a quad. Width is specified in pixels via u_line_width and converted to NDC using u_viewport_size.
wide_line.frag — Outputs u_color (vec4 uniform).



Uniforms



Uniform
Type
Description




u_mvp_matrix
mat4
Model-View-Projection matrix


u_color
vec4
Line color (RGBA)


u_line_width
float
Line width in pixels


u_viewport_size
vec2
Viewport dimensions in pixels





Viewport Size
The renderers query GL_VIEWPORT via glGetIntegerv at render time to pass the current viewport dimensions to the geometry shader. This ensures correct pixel-to-NDC conversion regardless of widget resize.


Embedded Fallback
Both renderers include embedded shader source strings (PolyLineShaders::VERTEX_SHADER, GEOMETRY_SHADER, FRAGMENT_SHADER) as fallback when shader files cannot be loaded from disk.

title: CapnProto Binary Line Data I/O
text: The CapnProto binary line data saver and loader handle reading and writing LineData objects to/from a binary Cap’n Proto serialization format. This format is lossless — floating-point values survive the round-trip without precision loss, unlike CSV formats.

title: CapnProto Binary Line Data I/O
text: The CapnProto binary line data saver and loader handle reading and writing LineData objects to/from a binary Cap’n Proto serialization format. This format is lossless — floating-point values survive the round-trip without precision loss, unlike CSV formats.

title: CapnProto Binary Line Data I/O
text:
File Location
src/DataManager/IO/formats/CapnProto/
├── linedata/
│   ├── Line_Data_Binary.hpp   # Option structs, function declarations, ParameterUIHints
│   ├── Line_Data_Binary.cpp   # Implementation (save with atomicWriteFile, load)
│   └── line_data.capnp        # Cap'n Proto schema definition
├── common/

title: CapnProto Binary Line Data I/O
CapnProto Binary Line Data I/O
text:
Atomic Writes
The save() function uses atomicWriteFile() to ensure crash safety. The binary data is first serialized to memory via IO::CapnProto::serializeLineData(), then written to a temporary file, and atomically renamed over the target path.

title: CapnProto Binary Line Data I/O
text:
Registry Integration

title: Concurrency Architecture
text: This document describes the concurrency architecture for WhiskerToolbox: what problems need concurrency, what design patterns fit the existing single-threaded DataManager-centric architecture, and a staged plan for introducing safe concurrency without rewriting the core.

title: Concurrency Architecture
text: This document describes the concurrency architecture for WhiskerToolbox: what problems need concurrency, what design patterns fit the existing single-threaded DataManager-centric architecture, and a staged plan for introducing safe concurrency without rewriting the core.

title: Concurrency Architecture
section: Context: How the System Works Today
text:
Context: How the System Works Today
WhiskerToolbox runs entirely on the Qt main thread. A shared DataManager instance holds all data objects (MaskData, LineData, PointData, AnalogTimeSeries, VideoData, etc.) in a std::map<std::string, DataTypeVariant> map. Consumers call getData<T>(key) to get a shared_ptr<T> — always mutable, always unsynchronized. The ObserverData callback system is synchronous and explicitly not thread-safe.
For immediate fixes when background workers trigger observer callbacks (deferred writes, main-thread marshaling, and the widget audit checklist), see the Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap.
This is simple and correct for a single-threaded program. The concurrency challenge is to keep this core model intact while moving expensive work off the main thread.

title: Concurrency Architecture
text:
Where Concurrency Is Needed









Use Case
Nature
Duration
Current State




Data loading (CSV, binary, HDF5)
Pure producer — reads file, builds object
Seconds
Blocks main thread


Deep learning inference (batch)
Reads media frames, runs model, writes results
Minutes
Blocks main thread


Data transforms (TransformsV2)
Reads input data, computes, writes output
ms–seconds
Blocks main thread


OpenMP within transforms
Embarrassingly parallel inner loops
ms
Works but GUI still hangs


Interactive editing (masks, points)
User modifies data at one frame
μs
Works, main thread only


Display / rendering
Reads data for visualization
μs
Works, main thread only



The pattern: 95% of operations are microsecond-scale and single-threaded. The remaining 5% are seconds-to-minutes and need to run in the background.

title: Concurrency Architecture
text:
Why Not Locks on DataManager?
DataManager, ObserverData, and all data types (MaskData, PointData, LineData, RaggedTimeSeries, AnalogTimeSeries) are entirely unsynchronized. Adding mutexes would mean:

Every getData() call acquires a lock — overhead on every widget interaction (~100 call sites across the codebase).
Every addAtTime() call acquires a lock — overhead on every data mutation.
notifyObservers() fires synchronous callbacks while holding a lock — deadlock risk if any callback accesses DataManager.
Every consumer must reason about lock ordering to avoid deadlocks.

This would be a massive, error-prone refactor for marginal benefit. The system’s access pattern (grab data, compute, release) doesn’t match the mutex model (short critical sections with immediate release).

title: Concurrency Architecture
text:
Why Not Per-Key Reader-Writer Locks?
A reader-writer lock per DataManager key ("masks", "points", etc.) seems attractive: multiple readers, exclusive writer, scoped to each data object.
The problem is that writes are not scoped to DataManager. Consumers call getData<MaskData>("masks") once and then call addAtTime() on the returned object many times across many frames. The “write” is a long-lived mutable reference, not a single atomic operation. A reader-writer lock would either:

Lock for the entire duration the mutable reference is held — blocking all readers for seconds/minutes during a transform.
Require lock-per-mutation — locking every addAtTime() call, even for microsecond operations. This adds overhead everywhere and changes every consumer.

Neither is practical.

title: Concurrency Architecture
section: Why Not Per-Frame Locks on Time Series?
text:
Why Not Per-Frame Locks on Time Series?
Since nearly all data is time series, locking individual time elements seems natural: a DL transform writes frame 100 while the UI reads frame 42.
This fails because of the underlying storage layout. RaggedTimeSeries stores data in contiguous SoA arrays (std::vector<TimeFrameIndex>, std::vector<TData>, std::vector<EntityId>). addAtTime() can trigger vector reallocation, which invalidates all pointers and iterators — not just those for the written frame. A per-frame lock cannot protect against reallocation.
Additionally, for microsecond transforms, the cost of acquiring and releasing a lock per frame would dominate the actual computation time.

title: Concurrency Architecture
section: The Right Model: Thread Confinement + Merge
text:
The Right Model: Thread Confinement + Merge
The design that fits this system is:

DataManager stays single-threaded. All reads and writes happen on the main (Qt) thread. No synchronization added.
Workers use private data. Background threads work with either independent data (file I/O) or private buffer objects (transform outputs).
Results merge on the main thread. Workers produce results in private buffers. The main thread absorbs those results into DataManager, either all-at-once (simple) or periodically (for progressive visibility).
Qt signals provide the communication channel. Cross-thread signals use Qt::QueuedConnection automatically — no manual synchronization needed.

This requires zero synchronization primitives on data objects. Safety comes from: (a) the type system (shared_ptr<T const> prevents mutation), (b) thread isolation (workers write to private buffers), and (c) temporal separation (merges happen on the main thread between event loop iterations).

title: Concurrency Architecture
Concurrency Architecture
Concurrency Architecture
section: How Threaded Scenarios Map to This Design
text:
How Threaded Scenarios Map to This Design

Data Loading (Simple: Fork-Join)
Worker reads a file, builds a complete data object, returns it. No DataManager contact during work. Main thread calls setData() once after worker finishes. Uses no reservations or borrows — the data object doesn’t exist in DataManager until the worker is done.
See Threaded Loading Roadmap.


Deep Learning Batch Inference (Merge Pattern)
Worker runs model inference over a frame range, producing mask/point/line data. Worker clones VideoData for independent frame access. Writes to a private buffer (write reservation). Main thread merges periodically for progressive visibility. User can simultaneously interact with the media widget and existing data.
See Batch Range Inference.


Data Transforms (Fork-Join or Merge)
Short transforms (< 100ms): run synchronously on the main thread, no threading needed.
Long transforms (seconds+): use the merge pattern. Worker computes into a private buffer, main thread merges after completion (or periodically for very long transforms).


Interactive Editing During Background Work
User edits mask at frame 42 while a DL transform populates frames 100-500:

Worker writes to a private buffer, not the real MaskData.
User’s edit goes through getData<MaskData>("masks") → addAtTime(42, ...) on the real object, on the main thread.
Next merge absorbs the worker’s new frames into the real object, alongside the user’s edit.
No conflict — worker and user operate on different objects.

title: Concurrency Architecture
text:
The Full Progression
Today:          getData<T>() → shared_ptr<T>           (mutable, untracked)

Stage 1:      + getConstData<T>() → shared_ptr<T const> (immutable, untracked)
                Most consumers migrate to this.
                No threading yet — just better API hygiene.

Stage 2:      + createWriteReservation<T>(key) → WriteReservation<T>
                Returns a private buffer + merge handle.
                Used when spawning background workers.
                getConstData() still works during reservation.
                getData() flagged in debug builds during reservation.

Stage 3:      + Borrow tracking (debug-only)
                DataManager tracks per-key BorrowState.
                Asserts on protocol violations.
Each stage is independently useful and doesn’t break previous consumers.

title: Concurrency Architecture
text:
Concepts for the Reader

Thread Confinement
Designate that certain objects are only ever accessed from one specific thread. DataManager is main-thread-confined. Workers operate on private data only. Communication happens through Qt signals (automatically queued across thread boundaries) and result harvesting after QThread::finished.


The Fork-Join Pattern
Main thread forks a worker, worker runs independently, main thread joins (via finished signal) to collect results. During the fork phase, main thread and worker share nothing. Used by data loading.


The Merge Pattern
Extension of fork-join with incremental result delivery. Worker produces data continuously into a private buffer. Main thread periodically merges buffer contents into the real data object. Provides progressive visibility and allows interactive editing during background work. Used by DL inference and long transforms.


Value Types vs Reference Types in Concurrency

Value types (returned by value): inherently safe — each thread has its own copy.
Reference types (shared_ptr, raw pointers): create aliasing — two threads with shared_ptr<MaskData> point to the same object.
shared_ptr<T const>: shared immutable reference — safe for concurrent reads when no mutable reference exists simultaneously.



const as a Concurrency Contract
When data types are correctly designed — const methods truly only read, mutable is only used for thread-safe caches — then shared_ptr<T const> acts as a contract: “I will not modify this object, and I expect no one else to modify it while I hold this reference.”
The existing RaggedTimeSeries API already respects this: addAtTime() and clearAtTime() are non-const, so they cannot be called through a const reference. See the caveat about mutable caches in Stage 1.


Type Traits as Compile-Time Documentation
ConcurrencyTraits<T>::supports_concurrent_read is a constexpr bool that enables static_assert at API boundaries, if constexpr for compile-time code path selection, and self-documenting code. No runtime overhead.

title: Concurrency Architecture
text:
Design Decisions

No synchronization primitives on data objects. Safety comes from thread isolation and temporal separation, not locks.
QThread (not std::jthread) for background work. Consistent with existing MLCoreWidget pattern; integrates with Qt signal/slot.
Merge, not lock, for progressive results. Avoids mutex contention, allows interactive editing, has zero overhead for fast operations.
Staged rollout. Each stage is useful alone. No big-bang migration.
DataManager stays single-threaded indefinitely. Workers return or buffer results; main thread writes.

title: Storage Backend Architecture
text:
DigitalEventSeries & DigitalIntervalSeries
These types keep events/intervals sorted, enabling binary search for time-range queries. The digital interval type provides two distinct range query modes:

Overlapping: Returns intervals where [start, end] overlaps the query range
Contained: Returns intervals fully within the query range

Both storage types use shared_ptr for the wrapper, enabling the aliasing constructor pattern for zero-copy view creation from the owning storage.

title: Storage Backend Architecture
text:
RaggedTimeSeries
Ragged types use std::map<TimeFrameIndex, std::pair<size_t, size_t>> for time-range acceleration — mapping each timestamp to (start_index, end_index) in the SoA arrays. This provides O(log n) time lookup without scanning.
View storage detects contiguous index ranges automatically, enabling the cache fast-path even for filtered subsets when the filter selects a consecutive block.

title: Data Object Merge
text: WhiskerToolbox provides utilities for copying or merging data between objects of the same type. Merge semantics are type-specific; v1 exposes overwrite-merge for ragged spatial types (LineData, MaskData, PointData).

title: Data Object Merge
text:
Preconditions

Source and target must not be the same object.
getTimeFrame() on both objects must be non-null and refer to the same TimeFrame instance (shared_ptr identity).
The target is materialized to owning storage if it currently uses a view or lazy backend.

title: Data Object Merge
text:
EntityId collision handling
Before appending, the target removes:

Any entries whose EntityIds appear anywhere in the source (cross-time collision safety).
Any remaining entries at each source time (per-time overwrite).

title: Tensor Transform Library — Design Roadmap
text:
Last updated: 2026-03-29


TensorData is the richest numeric container in WhiskerToolbox, supporting 2D matrices, 3D cubes, and N-dimensional arrays across multiple storage backends (Armadillo, Dense, LibTorch). Many scientific workflows require tensor-in → tensor-out operations: dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP), spectral decomposition (SVD, NMF), normalization, slicing, and reshaping. These transforms differ from element-level transforms because:

Shape-dependence — A PCA requires 2D; a conv-filter might need 3D.
Whole-container semantics — Operates on the entire matrix, not element-by-element.
Output shape differs from input — PCA(N×D) → (N×K) where K < D.
Shared state — Some algorithms produce fitted models reusable for projection.





The primary motivating use case is the encoder → embedding → visualization → interaction loop:
Video (frames)
  │  DeepLearning_Widget: encoder + global average pooling
  ▼
TensorData  (N×192, TimeFrameIndex rows, "encoder_features")
  │  DataTransform_Widget or MLCore Dim Reduction tab
  ▼
TensorData  (N×2, TimeFrameIndex rows, columns "PC1"/"PC2")
  │  ScatterPlotWidget: X=PC1, Y=PC2, color-by-group
  ▼
Scatter visualization with interactive selection
  │  User selects cluster → entity group created
  ▼
EntityGroupManager → downstream analysis

Goal: Supervised linear projection via softmax regression, treating the logit space as a C-dimensional embedding optimized for class discrimination. Developer documentation: docs/developer/MLCore/softmax_regression.qmd.

Implementation note: mlpack::SoftmaxRegression requires template argument <arma::mat>. The constructor argument order is (data, labels, numClasses, optimizer, lambda, fitIntercept) — optimizer precedes lambda.



Delivered: Abstract base class MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation and concrete LogitProjectionOperation, with LogitProjectionParameters and SupervisedDimensionalityReduction task type. 9 test cases, 79 assertions.

MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation — new abstract base in src/MLCore/models/MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation.hpp. Adds fitTransform(), transform(), outputDimensions(), outputColumnNames() pure virtuals. Routes train() to fitTransform() for registry compatibility.
LogitProjectionOperation — concrete implementation in src/MLCore/models/supervised/LogitProjectionOperation.hpp/.cpp. Uses mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat> with fitIntercept=true. Extracts weight matrix \(W\) (C×D) and bias \(b\) (C) from Parameters() (column 0 = bias, columns 1..D = weights). Inference: result = W * X; result.each_col() += b.
LogitProjectionParameters — lambda (0.0001), max_iterations (10000), scale_features (false). When scale_features=true, scaling is absorbed into \(W\) and \(b\) at training time for transparent inference.

title: Architecture and Data Flow
text: CorePlotting allows different visualization types (DataViewer, SpatialOverlay, Raster Plots) to share a common rendering and interaction backend.

title: Architecture and Data Flow
text:
The Three-Layer Model
The architecture separates visualization-specific logic from generic scene composition.

1. Visualization Layer (Mappers)
This layer understands specific data types (AnalogTimeSeries, PointData) and how they map to space.

Input: Data Objects + TimeFrame + Layout
Output: Ranges of MappedElement (x, y, entity_id)



2. Generic Layer (SceneBuilder)
This layer knows nothing about time series or biological data. It only knows about geometry.

Input: Ranges of positions and IDs.
Output: RenderableScene



3. Rendering Layer (PlottingOpenGL)
This layer consumes the scene and issues draw calls.

Input: RenderableScene
Output: Pixels on screen.

title: Architecture and Data Flow
text:
Core Abstractions

ViewState
The single source of truth for the camera.

ViewStateData: Serializable camera state for time-series plots (x_min/x_max as master frame indices, Y bounds, zoom/pan). Used by DataViewer via DataViewerState.
ViewState: Full runtime 2D camera (includes viewport pixels). Used for spatial 2D plots.



LayoutTransform
A purely geometric affine transform (output = input * gain + offset).

Used to convert data units (volts, classes) into world coordinates.
Composes data normalization (Z-score) with layout positioning (Stacking).



RenderableScene
A snapshot of a frame. It contains:

Batches: poly_line_batches, glyph_batches, rectangle_batches.
Spatial Index: A QuadTree automatically built from the same data as the batches.
Matrices: Shared View and Projection matrices.

title: CorePlotting Library
text: CorePlotting is the foundational library for the WhiskerToolbox plotting stack. It provides unified abstractions for visualizing spatial and temporal data, explicitly separating data & layout from rendering & interaction.

title: CorePlotting Library
text: CorePlotting is the foundational library for the WhiskerToolbox plotting stack. It provides unified abstractions for visualizing spatial and temporal data, explicitly separating data & layout from rendering & interaction.

title: CorePlotting Library
text:
Key Features

Renderer Agnostic: Generates a pure data description of a scene (RenderableScene) consumed by OpenGL, SVG, or other backends.
Zero-Copy Mappers: Uses C++20 ranges to transform data directly into GPU-ready buffers without intermediate allocations.
Unified Layout Engine: Centralized logic for vertical stacking, raster rows, and spatial overlays.
Robust Interaction: Unified hit-testing and interaction controllers for manipulating glyphs (intervals, lines) in world space.

title: CorePlotting Library
text:
The “Big Idea”
The library solves the problem of coupling data structures to specific rendering widgets. Instead of a widget knowing how to draw a DigitalEventSeries, CorePlotting defines a pipeline:

Layout: Determine where a series lives (Y-axis allocation).
Map: Transform data points into world coordinates (x, y).
Build: Assemble geometric batches (RenderablePolyLineBatch, RenderableGlyphBatch).
Render: A thin OpenGL layer consumes the batches.

Key Findings

viewTimeValueRange() is 2.3x slower than direct span or viewValues() access on Vector storage ($$416 M/s vs $$940 M/s). This is the path currently used by the rendering pipeline. The overhead comes from constructing TimeValuePoint structs with virtual dispatch per element.
Vector, TensorColumn, and raw pointer all achieve $$940–980 M/s at 1M samples — effectively memory-bandwidth limited. There is no penalty for using Armadillo column storage vs. std::vector.
BlockCachedMmap degrades catastrophically at scale. At 100K samples with 384 channels, throughput drops to 0.73 M/s — over 1000x slower than contiguous storage. This is caused by per-element mutex acquisition and block-lookup overhead in the access path.
Raw MemoryMapped is 5–7x slower than contiguous storage due to byte offset calculation, memcpy, type switch, and scaling per element.

title: DataViewer Rendering Pipeline Benchmarks
text:
Conclusions and Recommendations

What We Learned

The biggest bottleneck is viewTimeValueRange(). The current rendering pipeline pays a 2.3x penalty using the time+value accessor path instead of direct span access. Switching to a span-based data read would immediately improve vertex generation throughput from $$209 M/s to $$865 M/s — a 4.1x speedup at the data-read stage.
Decimation helps, but mostly for vertex count reduction. The decimation scan itself runs at near-memory-bandwidth speeds ($$880 M/s). The real savings come downstream: fewer vertices to materialize, cache, and upload to GPU. At 384ch × 100K, decimation reduces output from 38.4M to 1.47M vertices — a 26x reduction in GPU upload data.
Pre-allocation and in-place buffers provide no measurable benefit for the compute-side pipeline. Modern allocators handle repeated same-size allocations efficiently. The benefit of pre-allocation would only appear in reducing allocation count (reducing heap fragmentation and GC pressure over long sessions), not in per-frame throughput.
BlockCachedMmap is fundamentally incompatible with real-time rendering. At 70–85x slower than TensorColumn, no amount of algorithmic optimization at the rendering layer can compensate. If mmap data needs real-time visualization, it must be pre-loaded into contiguous memory (either full copy or block-level pre-fetch).
Channel scaling is perfectly linear for contiguous storage. There are no super-linear effects from cache pressure or memory bandwidth saturation up to 384 channels. This means the rendering pipeline can be straightforwardly parallelized if needed.
The cache extraction layer is not truly incremental. Scrolling by 10 samples costs the same as scrolling by 1000 samples — the entire window is re-extracted every frame. A true incremental approach (ring buffer with only-new-data extraction) would reduce scroll costs proportionally to scroll step.



Recommended Optimizations (Priority Order)

Add a span-based fast-path for contiguous storage in the vertex generation pipeline. When the storage backend supports getDataInTimeFrameIndexRange() returning a contiguous std::span, bypass viewTimeValueRange() entirely. Expected improvement: 4x at the data-read stage.
Implement min/max decimation when samples_per_pixel > threshold (e.g., > 4). Output 2 vertices per pixel column (min, max). This reduces vertex count by up to 100x for zoomed-out views and costs essentially nothing beyond the data scan.
Use direct-to-GPU vertex format in the cache. Instead of caching CachedAnalogVertex{x, y, TimeFrameIndex} (24 bytes) and then copying to float[2] (8 bytes), store the GPU-ready format directly. This eliminates the extraction copy entirely — a 4.2x speedup for the cache extraction stage.
Make cache extraction truly incremental. Track the last-extracted range and only extract newly-visible samples on scroll. For small scroll steps, this would reduce extraction cost from \(O(W)\) to \(O(\Delta)\).
Pre-load mmap data into contiguous buffers before rendering. For BlockCachedMmap, perform a bulk read of the visible window into a temporary std::vector<float> and render from that. This converts a 70x-slower per-element path into a single bulk I/O + contiguous render.

title: AnalogTimeSeries View Storage Performance Analysis
text:
Background
A line plot displays continuous analog signals (e.g., LFP, EMG) aligned to trial events. For each alignment event, we need to:

Extract samples within a time window around the alignment point
Transform the data for GPU rendering (populate vertex buffers)

We compared two approaches:

Baseline (Raw Vectors): Use std::vector<std::vector<float>> for windowed signals
View-Based: Use std::vector<shared_ptr<AnalogTimeSeries>> with view storage backend

title: AnalogTimeSeries View Storage Performance Analysis
text:
Key Difference from DigitalEventSeries Views
Unlike DigitalEventSeries views which use index indirection (each access requires looking up an index, then accessing the source), AnalogTimeSeries views provide contiguous span access because:

ViewAnalogDataStorage stores start/end offsets into the source VectorAnalogDataStorage
The source data is always contiguous in memory
Views can return std::span<float const> directly pointing into source memory

This means iteration performance is essentially identical to raw vectors once views are created.

AnalogTimeSeries View Storage Performance Analysis
text:
Architecture: Zero-Copy View Storage

How It Works
The DataStorageWrapper uses shared_ptr internally (fixed from previous unique_ptr bug):
class DataStorageWrapper {
    std::shared_ptr<StorageConcept> _impl;  // Shared ownership of storage
};
When creating a view, we use the aliasing constructor of shared_ptr:
std::shared_ptr<VectorAnalogDataStorage const> getSharedVectorStorage() const {
    if (auto vector_model = std::dynamic_pointer_cast<StorageModel<VectorAnalogDataStorage> const>(_impl)) {
        // Aliasing constructor: shares ownership with _impl but points to inner storage
        return std::shared_ptr<VectorAnalogDataStorage const>(vector_model, &vector_model->_storage);
    }
    return nullptr;
}


View Storage Structure
Each view consists of:

A shared_ptr to the source’s VectorAnalogDataStorage (shared among all views)
Start and end indices defining the view window
A separate TimeIndexStorage for the view’s time indices

Source (1M samples)
    └── _data_storage (DataStorageWrapper)
            └── _impl (shared_ptr<StorageConcept>)
                    └── VectorAnalogDataStorage with float* data

View 1 (window around alignment 0)      ──┐
    └── ViewAnalogDataStorage            │
        ├── _source (shared_ptr) ────────┼── All share same source
        ├── _start_index = 1000          │
        └── _end_index = 2000            │
                                         │
View 2 (window around alignment 1)      ──┤
    └── ViewAnalogDataStorage            │
        ├── _source (shared_ptr) ────────┘
        ├── _start_index = 5500
        └── _end_index = 6500
...

title: AnalogTimeSeries View Storage Performance Analysis
text:
Historical Note: The unique_ptr Bug
The original DataStorageWrapper implementation used std::unique_ptr<StorageConcept>:
// BUG: unique_ptr prevented sharing - had to copy entire storage for views!
std::unique_ptr<StorageConcept> _impl;
This was the same bug found in DigitalEventStorageWrapper. The fix changed to shared_ptr to enable:

Zero-copy view creation via aliasing constructor
Correct lifetime management (source outlives views)
Multiple views sharing one underlying storage

When to Use Views vs. Raw Vectors
Views are now the preferred approach for most use cases:

Zero-copy data sharing (no memcpy)
Faster creation than raw vector extraction for dense time storage
Integration with TimeFrame conversion system
Chaining with lazy transforms
Full AnalogTimeSeries API (getAtTime, elements, etc.)

Raw vectors may still be preferred for:

Sparse time storage sources (where O(n) time materialization is required)
When you need to mutate the extracted data
Integration with external libraries expecting std::vector<float>
