gather() provides cleaner API with no performance penalty - You get ergonomic benefits (source tracking, transform(), intervalAt()) for free.
The transform() helper is very fast - 4µs to compute statistics across 1000 trials.

For most interactive visualization and analysis use cases, the view-based overhead is acceptable. The gather() utility is recommended for trial-aligned operations as it provides the cleanest API. For performance-critical rendering loops requiring maximum throughput, raw vectors remain the better choice.

title: DigitalEventSeries View Storage Performance Analysis
text:
Time Normalization with Transform Pipeline
Building on the gather/view infrastructure, we evaluated the performance of applying value projections (time normalization) to trial-aligned data. This is essential for raster plots and other trial-aligned visualizations where events need to be normalized relative to an alignment point (t=0 at trial start).

Normalization Benchmark Setup
Configuration remains the same: - 100,000 total events - 1,000 alignment events (trials) - Window size: ±500 around each alignment
Three normalization approaches tested:

Baseline + Normalization: Extract events and normalize times in a single pass (manual)
Gather + Value Projection: Use GatherResult with per-trial value projections via NormalizeTimeValue transform
Isolated Normalization: Just the normalization step without buffer population



Full Pipeline Results (With Normalization)



Approach
Time (µs)
Relative to Baseline




Baseline (No Normalization)
367
1.0x


Baseline + Normalization
598
1.6x


Gather (No Normalization)
1,223
3.3x


Gather + Normalization
1,424
3.9x



Key Insight: Adding normalization costs only ~63% more for baseline (231µs), but ~17% more for gather (201µs). The gather approach absorbs normalization overhead more efficiently due to better amortization across the view creation cost.


Isolated Normalization Phase Analysis
Measuring just the normalization step (without buffer population):








Approach
Time (µs)
Description




Baseline Normalization
429
Extract windows + normalize (1000 trials × ~100 events)


Gather + Projection
1,484
Create gather result + build projections + iterate with projection


Difference
+1,055
Gather overhead for normalization


Overhead Factor
3.5x
Gather normalization is 3.5x slower





Phase Breakdown: Where Does the Overhead Come From?
Breaking down the Gather + Normalization pipeline:



Phase
Time (µs)
Notes




Create gather result
~240
View creation (1000 views)


Build projections
~50
Create projection factory for each trial


Apply projections
~1,194
Iterate views + project each event time


Total
1,484




For comparison, Baseline Normalization breakdown:



Phase
Time (µs)
Notes




Extract + normalize
429
Binary search + memory copy + subtract


Total
429






Store-Based Projection Infrastructure
The gather approach uses PipelineValueStore populated by buildGatherRowStore():
ValueProjectionFactoryV2<EventWithId, float> projection_factory =
    [](PipelineValueStore const& store) -> ValueProjectionFn<EventWithId, float> {
        NormalizeTimeParams params;
        int64_t alignment = store.getInt("alignment_time").value_or(0);
        params.setAlignmentTime(TimeFrameIndex{alignment});
        return [params](EventWithId const& event) -> float {
            return normalizeTimeValue(event.time(), params);
        };
    };

for (size_t i = 0; i < gathered.size(); ++i) {
    auto store = buildGatherRowStore(gathered, i);
    projections[i] = projection_factory(store);
}


Why Is Gather Slower for Normalization?
Several factors contribute to the 3.5x overhead:

View Creation Overhead: Creating 1000 views takes ~240µs, amortized across the operation
Lambda Captures: Each trial’s projection captures its bound parameters (NormalizeTimeParams)
Virtual Dispatch: Type-erased storage adds indirection on each event access
Memory Layout: Events accessed via index indirection rather than contiguous array
Cache Locality: Jumping between indices and data arrays reduces cache efficiency



Performance Sweet Spot
Despite the overhead, gather with projections has advantages in certain scenarios:








Scenario
Winner
Reason




Single pass, raw raster
Baseline
No abstraction overhead needed


Multiple analyses on same gather
Gather
Amortize view creation across multiple operations


Trial sorting by metric
Gather
Use reduce() with 4µs overhead per operation


Complex filtering
Gather
View-based filtering is composable and clean


Interactive UI updates
Gather
Cached views make incremental updates cheap



Example: If you need to compute spike counts, first-spike latencies, AND draw raster:
auto gathered = gather(spikes, trials);  // 1,223µs - one-time cost

// Operation 1: Count spikes
auto counts = gathered.transform([](auto v) { return v->size(); });  // 4µs
// Operation 2: Compute latencies  
auto latencies = gathered.reduce(latency_reducer);  // ~50µs
// Operation 3: Draw raster with normalization
auto projections = gathered.project(normalize_factory);  // 50µs
// ... then iterate with projections  // ~1,194µs

// Total: 1,223 + 4 + 50 + 50 + 1,194 = 2,521µs vs. 3× separate baseline runs


Conclusion on Normalization

Baseline normalization is simple and fast - Direct extraction + subtraction takes 429µs
Gather + projection adds abstraction overhead - 3.5x slower in isolation, but provides composability
The cost is reasonable for trial-aligned analysis - Additional 201µs for gather+normalization vs. gather alone is ~2.5% of the gather cost
Transform pipeline infrastructure is ready - PipelineValueStore bindings enable flexible trial-based transformations
Use baseline for performance-critical tight loops - Use gather for analysis pipelines where composability matters more than raw speed

For raster plot generation where you’re only doing visualization, stick with baseline or raw vectors. For interactive analysis dashboards where you compute multiple metrics per trial, gather+transforms provide better code organization and reusability with acceptable performance cost.

title: Profiling and Performance
text: This document describes the local benchmarking infrastructure for Neuralyzer, including how to create benchmarks, run them outside the normal test suite, and analyze performance using profiling tools.

title: Profiling and Performance
text:
Quick Start
# Configure and build the local benchmark preset
cmake --preset my-clang-release
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release

# Heaptrack regression guard (pass/fail, not CTest)
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target record_benchmark_baselines
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target check_benchmark_regressions

# Optional: Google Benchmark JSON (stress executables are excluded)
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target run_benchmarks

# Manual ScatterPlot stress run
./out/build/Clang/Release/benchmark/benchmark_ScatterPlotView

# Manual DataViewer allocation probe (defaults: 1ch, scroll-by-1)
./out/build/Clang/Release/benchmark/benchmark_DataViewerView
Benchmarks are intentionally not registered as CTest tests. A normal command such as ctest --preset my-clang-release runs correctness tests only.

title: Profiling and Performance
text:
Architecture

CMake Infrastructure
The benchmarking system is built on cmake/BenchmarkUtils.cmake, which provides:

add_selective_benchmark() - Create individual benchmark executables and register them with the local benchmark runner
configure_benchmark_for_profiling() - Add profiling tool support
add_benchmark_suite_target() - Create the run_benchmarks target that runs enabled benchmarks and writes JSON results
print_benchmark_summary() - Display configuration summary

Each benchmark can be individually enabled/disabled via CMake options:
# Disable a specific benchmark
cmake --preset my-clang-release -DBENCHMARK_SCATTERPLOTVIEW=OFF

# Only build specific benchmarks
cmake --preset my-clang-release -DBENCHMARK_SCATTERPLOT=ON -DBENCHMARK_OTHER=OFF


Test Data Fixtures
benchmark/fixtures/BenchmarkFixtures.hpp provides fixtures for generating realistic test data:

MaskDataFixture - Generate MaskData with configurable properties
LineDataFixture - Generate LineData for curve/line benchmarks
PointDataFixture - Generate PointData for point-based benchmarks

Presets are available for common scenarios: - Presets::SmallMaskData() - Quick iteration (10 frames) - Presets::MediumMaskData() - Realistic testing (100 frames) - Presets::LargeMaskData() - Stress testing (1000 frames) - Presets::SparseMaskData() - Few masks, large time gaps - Presets::DenseMaskData() - Many small masks per frame
Example usage:
#include "fixtures/BenchmarkFixtures.hpp"

BENCHMARK_F(MyBenchmark, TestCase)(benchmark::State& state) {
    auto fixture = MaskDataFixture(Presets::MediumMaskData());
    auto mask_data = fixture.generate();
    
    for (auto _ : state) {
        // Benchmark code here
    }
}

title: Profiling and Performance
Profiling and Performance
Profiling and Performance
text:
Performance Analysis Tools

1. Perf (CPU Profiling)
Profile CPU usage and generate call graphs:
# Record profile data
perf record -g ./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter=PanZoom

# View interactive report
perf report

# Generate flamegraph
perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg

# View specific functions
perf annotate functionName

# Show hot spots
perf top
Key perf options: - -g - Enable call-graph (stack trace) recording - -e cycles - Profile CPU cycles - -e cache-misses - Profile cache misses - --call-graph dwarf - Use DWARF for more accurate call graphs


2. Heaptrack (Memory Profiling)
Analyze memory allocation patterns:
# Run with heaptrack
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target run_scatterplot_heaptrack

# View results in GUI
heaptrack_gui heaptrack.benchmark_ScatterPlot.*.gz

# View results in terminal
heaptrack_print heaptrack.benchmark_ScatterPlot.*.gz
What heaptrack shows: - Total memory allocated - Peak memory usage - Number of allocations - Call stacks for allocations - Memory leaks - Temporary allocations


3. Valgrind Cachegrind (Cache Analysis)
Analyze cache behavior:
# Run cachegrind
valgrind --tool=cachegrind ./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter=PanZoom

# Visualize results
cg_annotate cachegrind.out.<pid>

# Interactive visualization
kcachegrind cachegrind.out.<pid>
Metrics provided: - L1/L2/L3 cache hits/misses - Instruction cache behavior - Data cache behavior - Branch prediction statistics


4. Assembly Inspection
View generated assembly for optimization:
# Method 1: objdump
objdump -d -C -S ./benchmark_ScatterPlot | less

# Search for specific function
objdump -d -C -S ./benchmark_ScatterPlot | grep -A 50 "updateProjectionOnly"

# Method 2: During compilation (if GENERATE_ASM=ON)
# Assembly files (.s) generated alongside object files
find . -name "*.s" | xargs less
What to look for: - Loop vectorization (SIMD instructions) - Unnecessary branches - Memory access patterns - Inlining decisions - Register usage


5. Time Command (Quick Stats)
Get quick overview of resource usage:
/usr/bin/time -v ./benchmark_ScatterPlot

# Key metrics:
# - Maximum resident set size (peak memory)
# - Page faults (major = disk I/O, minor = memory)
# - Context switches
# - CPU percentage


6. Clang Build Time Analysis
If built with -DENABLE_TIME_TRACE=ON:
# View compilation time breakdown
ClangBuildAnalyzer --all build_trace build_results.bin
ClangBuildAnalyzer --analyze build_results.bin

title: Profiling and Performance
text:
Example Workflows

Workflow 1: Optimize a Hot Function
# 1. Identify hot spots
perf record -g ./benchmark_ScatterPlot
perf report  # Identify slowest function

# 2. View assembly
objdump -d -C -S ./benchmark_ScatterPlot | grep -A 100 "mySlowFunction"

# 3. Check cache behavior
valgrind --tool=cachegrind ./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter=MyFunction

# 4. Make changes and compare
./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter=MyFunction > before.txt
# ... make changes ...
./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter=MyFunction > after.txt
compare.py compare before.txt after.txt  # From Google Benchmark tools


Workflow 2: Fix Memory Issues
# 1. Identify allocation hot spots
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target run_scatterplot_heaptrack

# 2. View in GUI
heaptrack_gui heaptrack.benchmark_ScatterPlot.*.gz
# Look for:
# - Temporary allocations in loops
# - Large peak allocations
# - Memory leaks

# 3. Check for leaks with valgrind
valgrind --leak-check=full ./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter=MyTest

# 4. Verify fix
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target run_scatterplot_heaptrack
# Compare before/after total allocations and peak memory


Workflow 3: Compare Algorithms
# Benchmark different implementations
./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_filter="Algorithm_v1|Algorithm_v2" \
    --benchmark_format=json > comparison.json

# Use benchmark tools to compare
tools/compare.py benchmarks comparison.json baseline.json

# Or export to CSV for plotting
./benchmark_ScatterPlot --benchmark_format=csv > data.csv
# Import into spreadsheet/plotting tool

title: Profiling and Performance
Profiling and Performance
text:
Interpreting Results

Benchmark Output
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Benchmark                         Time             CPU   Iterations
-------------------------------------------------------------------
BM_Pipeline/0                  1.23 ms         1.23 ms          569
BM_Pipeline/1                 12.45 ms        12.43 ms           56
BM_Pipeline/2                124.56 ms       124.12 ms            6

Time: Wall-clock time (includes I/O, system time)
CPU: CPU time (excludes I/O wait)
Iterations: How many times the benchmark ran



What’s Fast Enough?

< 1 microsecond: Excellent for element operations
< 1 millisecond: Good for frame-level processing
< 100 milliseconds: Acceptable for batch operations
> 1 second: Consider optimization or progress reporting



Profiling Result Interpretation
Perf Report: - Focus on functions with >5% of total time - Check for unexpected function calls - Look for optimization opportunities in hot paths
Heaptrack: - Peak memory < 2x working set is good - Allocation count should be O(1) for inner loops - Look for unnecessary temporary allocations
Cachegrind: - L1 miss rate < 5% is excellent - L2 miss rate < 1% is good - Look for cache-unfriendly access patterns

title: Profiling and Performance
text:
Local Performance Monitoring

Save Baseline Results
# Save current performance as baseline
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target run_benchmarks
cp -r out/build/Clang/Release/benchmark-results benchmark-baseline-local

# After changes, compare
cmake --build --preset my-clang-release --target run_benchmarks

# Compare results
benchmark/tools/compare_benchmark_json.py \
    benchmark-baseline-local \
    out/build/Clang/Release/benchmark-results \
    --tolerance 0.30
Keep these baselines local to the machine, compiler, and preset that produced them. Timing numbers are hardware dependent. For memory regressions in interaction paths, run the focused benchmark executable under heaptrack and compare allocation totals and call stacks locally.

title: Profiling and Performance
text:
Troubleshooting

Benchmarks Too Fast
If benchmarks complete in < 1 microsecond:
// Increase work per iteration
for (auto _ : state) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) {  // Amortize overhead
        auto result = fastFunction();
        benchmark::DoNotOptimize(result);
    }
}
state.SetItemsProcessed(state.iterations() * 100);


High Variability
If standard deviation > 10% of mean:

Close other applications
Disable CPU frequency scaling: sudo cpupower frequency-set --governor performance
Pin to specific CPU: taskset -c 0 ./benchmark_ScatterPlot
Increase minimum iteration time: --benchmark_min_time=5



Build Issues
# Benchmarks not building
cmake -DENABLE_BENCHMARK=ON ..

# Specific benchmark disabled
cmake --preset my-clang-release -DBENCHMARK_SCATTERPLOT=ON

# Google Benchmark not found
# (Should auto-fetch with FetchContent, but can install manually)
sudo apt install libbenchmark-dev  # Ubuntu/Debian

title: Keymap System
text: The Keymap System provides configurable, context-aware keyboard shortcuts for WhiskerToolbox. It is heavily inspired by Blender’s keymap architecture, adapted for a Qt6 docked-widget environment.

title: Keymap System
text:
Motivation
All keyboard shortcuts in WhiskerToolbox are currently hardcoded:

Global keys (Space for play/pause, arrows for frame navigation) live in MainWindow::eventFilter().
Per-widget keys (1–9 for group assignment in Media_Widget, Enter/Escape/Backspace for polygon editing in scatter plots) are in individual keyPressEvent() overrides.
Always-routed keys (arrow keys dispatched to TimeScrollBar regardless of focus) are mixed into the global event filter with manual qobject_cast checks.

There is no way for users to reconfigure bindings, no way for a widget to advertise “I provide action X,” and no systematic conflict detection. The Keymap System replaces this ad-hoc approach with a structured, extensible, and user-configurable dispatch layer.

title: Keymap System
text:
Use Cases

Focus switching — Assign a hotkey (e.g., F2) to raise and focus a specific editor, regardless of which widget currently has keyboard focus.
Per-editor shortcuts — When a particular editor is the active editor, its EditorFocused actions take priority (e.g., Media Viewer group assignment on Alt+1–9).
Always-routed commands — Certain actions always dispatch to a specific widget even when it is not focused (e.g., arrow keys always control the timeline scrollbar).

title: Keymap System
Keymap System
text:
Relationship to Existing Systems







System
Relationship




SelectionContext
KeymapManager reads activeEditorId() to determine focused editor for scope resolution


ContextAction
Orthogonal — ContextActions are mouse-driven actions shown in context menus; KeyActions are keyboard-driven. A future unification could share action IDs.


Commands (ICommand)
A KeyActionAdapter handler may internally create and execute an ICommand. The keymap layer handles input binding; the command layer handles data mutation.


EditorRegistry
KeymapManager uses the type registry to enumerate editor types (for auto-generated focus actions) and to look up widget instances for dispatch.


AppPreferencesData
Stores user keybinding overrides. Loaded on startup, saved on change.

These are not planned for initial implementation but the architecture supports them.


QKeySequence natively supports up to 4 key combos (e.g., Ctrl+K then Ctrl+C). The KeymapManager would need a state machine to track partial matches. Data model already supports this — no structural changes needed, only dispatch logic.



Blender also binds mouse buttons (e.g., middle-click for orbit). A parallel MouseActionDescriptor using the same KeyActionScope model could be added. The event filter already handles QEvent::MouseButtonPress.



Blender ships multiple keymap presets (Blender, Industry Compatible). WhiskerToolbox could ship presets for different workflows (e.g., “Labeling”, “Analysis”). Implementation: a KeymapPreset struct containing a complete set of overrides, selectable in the Keybinding Editor.



Some actions might want to fire but not consume the event, allowing it to also reach the focused widget. A bool consuming = true field on KeyActionDescriptor would control this. Not needed for v1.



Currently, an EditorFocused action is available whenever that editor type has focus. A richer version could add a predicate (like ContextAction::is_applicable) — e.g., “polygon_complete only available when polygon tool is active.” This would tie into the existing ContextAction infrastructure.

title: Keymap System — Implementation Roadmap
text:
This roadmap breaks the Keymap System into incremental steps that each produce a working, testable result. Each step can be merged independently — later steps build on earlier ones but the system is functional after any completed step.
Guiding principles:

No existing behavior changes until explicitly migrated (hardcoded keys keep working alongside the new system)
Each step is buildable and testable in isolation
Widget adoption is incremental — unmigrated widgets continue using keyPressEvent() as before

title: Keymap System — Implementation Roadmap
text:
These are not planned for initial implementation but the architecture supports them.


QKeySequence natively supports up to 4 key combos (e.g., Ctrl+K then Ctrl+C). The KeymapManager would need a state machine to track partial matches. Data model already supports this — no structural changes needed, only dispatch logic.



Blender also binds mouse buttons (e.g., middle-click for orbit). A parallel MouseActionDescriptor using the same KeyActionScope model could be added. The event filter already handles QEvent::MouseButtonPress.



Blender ships multiple keymap presets (Blender, Industry Compatible). WhiskerToolbox could ship presets for different workflows (e.g., “Labeling”, “Analysis”). Implementation: a KeymapPreset struct containing a complete set of overrides, selectable in the Keybinding Editor.



Some actions might want to fire but not consume the event, allowing it to also reach the focused widget. A bool consuming = true field on KeyActionDescriptor would control this. Not needed for v1.



Currently, an EditorFocused action is available whenever that editor type has focus. A richer version could add a predicate (like ContextAction::is_applicable) — e.g., “polygon_complete only available when polygon tool is active.” This would tie into the existing ContextAction infrastructure.

title: Python Integration
text: This guide details the internal architecture of Neuralyzer’s Python integration, explaining how the embedded interpreter works, how data is marshaled between C++ and Python, and how to extend the bindings.

title: Python Integration
text:
Architecture Overview
The Python integration is built on three main components:

PythonWidget (Qt UI):

Located in src/WhiskerToolbox/Python_Widget.
Handles the visual interface: Console, Editor, and Properties panel.
Manages the PythonEngine instance.
Connects UI signals (like “Run” button) to the engine’s execute() method.

PythonEngine (Embedded Interpreter):

Located in src/python_bindings/PythonEngine.cpp.
Wraps pybind11::embed.
Manages the Python interpreter lifecycle (initialization, finalization).
Maintains the globals() dictionary to persist state across executions (REPL behavior).
Redirects sys.stdout and sys.stderr to C++ callbacks for display in the UI.

PythonBridge (Data Marshalling):

Located in src/python_bindings/PythonBridge.cpp.
Acts as the bridge between the application’s DataManager and the Python environment.
Injects the dm proxy object into the Python namespace on startup.
Handles the conversion of C++ data types to Python objects and vice-versa.

title: Python Integration
text:
Bindings (whiskertoolbox_python)
The core of the integration is the whiskertoolbox_python PyBind11 module. This module exposes C++ classes to Python. It is embedded directly into the application binary, so there is no separate .pyd or .so file to deploy.
Source location: src/python_bindings/

Key Binding Files

bind_module.hpp: Forward declarations for binding functions.
bindings.cpp: The main PYBIND11_EMBEDDED_MODULE definition. Calls individual init functions.
numpy_utils.hpp: Helper functions for zero-copy NumPy array creation.
bind_datamanager.cpp: Binds the DataManager class and its methods.
bind_analog.cpp: Binds AnalogTimeSeries.
bind_point.cpp: Binds PointData and Point2D.
bind_tensor.cpp: Binds TensorData.

title: Python Integration
text:
Data Types and Zero-Copy Strategy
To ensure high performance with large datasets (e.g., electrophysiology or high-speed video data), we prioritize zero-copy access where possible.

AnalogTimeSeries & TensorData
These types store data in contiguous memory blocks (std::vector or similar). We expose these buffers to Python as read-only NumPy arrays.

C++ Side: std::span<float const>
Python Side: numpy.ndarray (flags: WRITEABLE=False)

This allows users to use libraries like numpy and scipy directly on the data without the overhead of copying millions of samples.


Ragged Data (Points, Lines, Masks)
Data types that are “ragged” (variable number of elements per time point) are more difficult to map directly to NumPy. * Currently, these are exposed via std::vector copies (e.g., getAtTime(t) returns a list of objects). * Future optimization may involve creating custom iterators or structured NumPy arrays.

title: Python Integration
Supervised Robust PCA Operation
text:
SupervisedRobustPCAOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that fits Robust PCA (via ROSL decomposition) exclusively on the labeled subset of observations. The ROSL algorithm decomposes the labeled data into a low-rank component and sparse errors, making the resulting principal components robust to outliers. All observations (labeled and unlabeled) are then projected into the resulting space.
This is useful when the labeled data may contain outliers or corrupted observations, and the user wants the principal components to capture the underlying low-rank variance structure rather than being influenced by sparse noise.

title: Supervised Robust PCA Operation
text:
Architecture

Class Hierarchy
MLModelOperation (interface)
  └── MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (abstract base)
        ├── LogitProjectionOperation
        ├── SupervisedPCAOperation
        └── SupervisedRobustPCAOperation (this class)


Pimpl Pattern
The Impl struct holds:

eigenvectors — \((D \times n\_components)\) projection matrix (from SVD of low-rank component)
eigenvalues — squared singular values / \((N-1)\), sorted descending
mean — per-feature mean (from labeled subset)
total_variance — sum of all eigenvalues (for variance ratio computation)

title: Supervised Robust PCA Operation
text:
Algorithm

fitTransform

Validate inputs (non-empty, matching dimensions, \(\geq 2\) classes, n_components \(\leq D\))
Compute mean from labeled subset
Center labeled data (subtract mean)
Auto-compute lambda if not provided: \(\lambda = 1/\sqrt{\max(m,n)}\)
ROSL decomposition: decompose centered labeled data into low-rank \(A\) + sparse error \(E\)
SVD on low-rank component \(A\) to extract principal directions
Store top n_components left-singular vectors as eigenvectors
Project ALL data (not just labeled subset) onto the learned basis



transform

Center new data using the stored labeled-subset mean
Project: result = eigenvectors.t() * centered



Key Properties

requiresAllClassesForFitting() returns false — the pipeline subsets to the positive class
Output column names use the prefix SRPCA: (e.g., SRPCA:0, SRPCA:1, …)
explainedVarianceRatio() returns the fraction of total variance explained per component

The operation appears in the DimReductionPanel’s supervised algorithm combo box. When selected, it shows the Robust PCA parameter widget (n_components, lambda, max_iter) and hides the class name fields (since it’s non-discriminative, like Supervised PCA).
The default output key suffix is _srpca.

text:
Architecture
models/
├── MLDimReductionOperation.hpp      # Abstract base with fitTransform/transform
└── unsupervised/
    ├── PCAOperation.hpp/.cpp        # Principal Component Analysis (manual eigendecomp)
    ├── RobustPCAOperation.hpp/.cpp  # Robust PCA via ROSL (Armadillo)

MLDimReductionOperation
MLDimReductionOperation extends MLModelOperation with dimensionality-reduction-specific pure virtual methods:







Method
Purpose

Fit model and project data in one call


transform(features, result)

The base class overrides getTaskType() → MLTaskType::DimensionalityReduction and routes the standard fit() method to fitTransform().


Data Convention
MLCore uses the mlpack convention: matrices are (features × observations) — each column is one observation. TensorData uses the opposite: (observations × features). The TransformsV2 wrapper handles the transpose.

Center data by subtracting column means
Compute covariance matrix

Feature scaling (z-score normalization) is the caller’s responsibility and should be applied before calling fitTransform(). PCA only centers internally — it no longer scales internally. See the Feature Scaling Roadmap for rationale.

title: Dimensionality Reduction
text:
TSNEOperation
Implements t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding via the tapkee library. t-SNE is a non-linear, stochastic method well suited for 2D/3D visualization of high-dimensional data.

Backend
Tapkee is a header-only C++ dimensionality reduction library. It is fetched via FetchContent in external/CMakeLists.txt but its own CMakeLists.txt is not processed — instead, a lightweight tapkee_headers INTERFACE target is created manually, linking Eigen3::Eigen and fmt::fmt-header-only.


Implementation

Convert Armadillo matrix (features × observations) → Eigen matrix (same layout, both column-major)
Call tapkee::with(...).embedUsing(eigen_data) with tDistributedStochasticNeighborEmbedding method
Convert Eigen output → Armadillo result (n_components × observations)

The sne_theta parameter controls Barnes-Hut approximation: theta > 0 enables the O(N log N) approximation, theta == 0 uses exact O(N²) computation.


Parameters









Field
Type
Default
Description




n_components
size_t
2
Output dimensions (usually 2 or 3)


perplexity
double
30.0
Effective neighborhood size (5–50 typical)


theta
double
0.5
Barnes-Hut angle (0 = exact, >0 = faster)





Limitations

No out-of-sample projection: transform() always returns false. t-SNE is transductive — it embeds only the data it was fit on.
No explained variance: explainedVarianceRatio() returns empty (not meaningful for t-SNE).
Stochastic: Results vary between runs (no seed parameter exposed yet).
Perplexity auto-clamping: If perplexity ≥ n_observations / 3, it is clamped internally.



Edge Cases

Empty data → returns false
Fewer than 4 observations → returns false
n_components = 0 → returns false
Excessive perplexity → automatically clamped

title: Dimensionality Reduction
text:
RobustPCAOperation
Implements Robust PCA via the ROSL (Robust Online Subspace Learning) algorithm. Unlike standard PCA, Robust PCA decomposes the data matrix into a low-rank component and a sparse error component: X = A + E. This makes it resilient to sparse outliers and gross corruptions that would distort standard PCA.

Backend
Uses the header-only rosl.hpp by Tom Furnival (GPL3 license), which depends only on Armadillo. No additional external dependencies are needed.


Implementation

Center data by subtracting feature means
Run ROSL to decompose: centered = A + E (low-rank + sparse error)
SVD on the low-rank component A to get orthogonal principal directions
Take the top n_components left-singular vectors as eigenvectors
Project: eigenvectors.t() * centered_data

The lambda parameter controls the sparsity penalty on the error matrix. When set to 0 (default), it is auto-computed as 1 / sqrt(max(m, n)), which is the theoretically optimal value for Robust PCA.


Parameters









Field
Type
Default
Description




n_components
size_t
2
Number of components to retain


lambda
double
0.0
Sparsity regularization (0 = auto: 1/sqrt(max(m,n)))


tol
double
1e-5
Convergence tolerance for ALM iterations


max_iter
size_t
100
Maximum ALM iterations





Capabilities

Out-of-sample projection: transform() is supported — new data is centered and projected via the learned eigenvectors.
Explained variance: explainedVarianceRatio() returns per-component variance from the SVD singular values of the low-rank component.
Deterministic: Fixed seed (42) for reproducibility.



Edge Cases

Empty data → returns false
Fewer than 2 observations → returns false
n_components > features → returns false
n_components = 0 → returns false

Uses cereal binary serialization storing eigenvectors, eigenvalues, mean, total variance, and component count.

title: Dimensionality Reduction
text:
ICAOperation
Implements Independent Component Analysis (ICA) via mlpack’s RADICAL (Robust, Accurate, Direct ICA aLgorithm). Unlike PCA, which finds uncorrelated components ordered by variance, ICA finds components that are statistically independent.

Backend
Uses mlpack::Radical, which is included in the mlpack headers already used by the project.


Implementation

Call mlpack::Radical::Apply(features, independent, unmixing) to decompose the input
Store the learned unmixing matrix W for projecting new data: Y = W * X



Parameters









Field
Type
Default
Description

double
0.175
Standard deviation of Gaussian noise added to data


replicates
size_t
30
Number of Gaussian-perturbed replicates per point

size_t
150
Number of angles in brute-force search during 2D RADICAL


sweeps
size_t
0
Number of sweeps (0 = dimensions - 1)


m
size_t
0
Vasicek’s m-spacing estimator parameter (0 = sqrt(dimensions))





Capabilities

Out-of-sample projection: transform() is supported — new data is projected via the learned unmixing matrix.
Explained variance: explainedVarianceRatio() returns empty (not meaningful for ICA).
No dimensionality reduction: Output has the same number of dimensions as the input. Each output dimension is an independent component.



Edge Cases

Empty data → returns false
Fewer than 2 observations → returns false



Save/Load
Uses cereal binary serialization storing the unmixing matrix and feature count.


Performance Notes
RADICAL scales quadratically in the number of input dimensions. For high-dimensional data, consider reducing dimensionality with PCA first.

title: Model Interface & Registry
text:
MLModelOperation (models/MLModelOperation.hpp) is the abstract base class for all ML algorithms. It provides a uniform API for both supervised and unsupervised workflows.


auto model = registry.create("Random Forest");
auto params = model->getDefaultParameters();

model->train(features, labels, params.get());
model->predict(new_features, predictions);
// Optional:
model->predictProbabilities(new_features, probabilities);



auto model = registry.create("K-Means");
auto params = model->getDefaultParameters();

model->fit(features, params.get());
model->assignClusters(new_features, assignments);



All methods operate on armadillo matrices in mlpack convention:

Feature matrices: (features × observations) — each column is one sample
Label rows: (1 × observations) — each element is a class index [0, num_classes)
Probability matrices: (num_classes × observations) — each column sums to 1.0




Feature scaling (z-score normalization) is a pipeline-level concern, not an algorithm-level concern. Individual algorithms do not scale features internally — they only center when mathematically required (e.g., PCA subtracts the mean). Callers are expected to z-score normalize features via FeatureConverter::convertTensorToArma() with zscore_normalize=true before passing data to any operation. See the Feature Scaling Roadmap for the full rationale.

Default implementations of supervised methods return false for unsupervised models (and vice versa), so each concrete model only overrides the methods relevant to its task type.

Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian / GMM)
text:
HiddenMarkovModelOperation wraps mlpack::HMM<Distribution> to provide sequence-aware classification within the MLCore framework. Unlike frame-based classifiers (Random Forest, Logistic Regression) that treat each observation independently, the HMM exploits temporal continuity — the probability of being in state \(s_t\) depends on \(s_{t-1}\).
Four emission distribution variants are supported:

mlpack type
Use case

Unimodal with diagonal covariance (fewer parameters)

Multi-modal emissions with full covariance per component


Diagonal GMM

Multi-modal with diagonal covariance per component

Emission Type Selection
The use_diagonal_covariance and use_gmm_emissions flags combine orthogonally:



use_gmm_emissions
use_diagonal_covariance
Emission type




false
false
Single Gaussian (full covariance)


false
true
Single Gaussian (diagonal covariance)


true
false
GMM (full covariance per component)


true
true
Diagonal GMM (diagonal covariance per component)





GMM Emissions
When use_gmm_emissions is true, each hidden state uses an mlpack::GMM (or mlpack::DiagonalGMM) as its emission distribution instead of a single Gaussian. This allows each state to model multi-modal observation distributions 014 useful when a single hidden state actually encompasses multiple sub-states with distinct emission characteristics.
Each state019s GMM has num_gaussians components. During supervised training, mlpack fits the mixture via EM on the observations assigned to that state. Prediction (Viterbi, Forward-Backward) works identically to the single-Gaussian case; only the emission probability computation changes.
The isGMMEmissions() and numGaussiansPerState() methods report the active configuration after training. Serialization includes the GMM flag and component count, so loaded models correctly reconstruct the matching HMM variant.


Diagonal Covariance
When use_diagonal_covariance is true, the HMM uses mlpack::DiagonalGaussianDistribution<> instead of full covariance. This:

Reduces covariance parameters per state from \(\frac{M(M+1)}{2}\) to \(M\)
Reduces emission evaluation cost from \(O(M^2)\) to \(O(M)\)
Improves numerical stability with limited training data
Assumes features are conditionally independent given the hidden state

The isDiagonalCovariance() method reports the active variant after training. Serialization includes the diagonal flag, so loaded models correctly reconstruct the matching HMM type.

A fourth radio button, “From Events (ideal for HMM)”, enables selection of a DigitalEventSeries from the DataManager. This maps point events to binary state labels (event present → state 1, absent → state 0). State is persisted as label_event_key in MLCoreWidgetStateData.


Results (ResultsPanel)
After training, the results panel detects if the trained model is an HMM via dynamic_cast and displays the learned transition matrix in a monospaced formatted text block. The matrix shows \(P(\text{next state} \mid \text{current state})\) with columns summing to 1.0.

title: Hidden Markov Model (Gaussian / GMM)
text:
Limitations

Supervised only: The current implementation requires labeled sequences. Unsupervised Baum-Welch training (EM) is not exposed, though mlpack supports it.
Gaussian / GMM emissions: Four emission variants are supported (full/diagonal Gaussian, full/diagonal GMM). Discrete emissions are not supported.
Fixed state count: The number of states must be specified before training. Model selection (choosing the optimal state count) must be done manually.
No warm-starting: Each train() / trainSequences() call initializes a fresh HMM. Incremental refinement of an existing model is not supported.
Memory: The Forward-Backward algorithm allocates a (num_states × observations) probability matrix. Very long sequences with many states may consume significant memory.

title: Softmax Regression Operation
text:
SoftmaxRegressionOperation is a supervised multi-class classifier that wraps mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat>. Unlike LogisticRegressionOperation (binary-only), it handles any number of classes \(C \geq 2\) using L2-regularized softmax regression optimized with L-BFGS.
The operation produces calibrated per-class probability estimates via the softmax function, making it suitable as both a classifier and a dimensionality reduction technique that projects features into a \(C\)-dimensional probability simplex.

title: Softmax Regression Operation
text:
Architecture

Pimpl Pattern
The implementation uses the pimpl idiom to isolate mlpack.hpp from consumers:
SoftmaxRegressionOperation.hpp  →  MLModelOperation (public API)
SoftmaxRegressionOperation.cpp  →  mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat> (hidden)
The Impl struct holds:

std::unique_ptr<mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat>> — the trained model
num_classes, num_features — cached training metadata
trained — readiness flag



Training
Training uses the constructor-based API:
ens::L_BFGS optimizer;
optimizer.MaxIterations() = max_iterations;

model = std::make_unique<SRModel>(
    features, labels, num_classes, optimizer, lambda, false);
The number of classes is detected automatically from arma::max(labels) + 1.


Prediction

predict() calls model->Classify(features, predictions) for hard labels.
predictProbabilities() calls model->Classify(features, predictions, probabilities) for a (num_classes × num_observations) matrix where each column sums to 1.0.



Serialization
Uses cereal binary archives. The serialization format stores:

num_classes (size_t)

The mlpack model (via mlpack’s built-in cereal support)

title: HMM Performance Analysis: Whisker Contact Detection at High Sampling Rates
text:
Encoder features (192-dim via ConvNeXt + GlobalAvgPool) are extracted per-frame from video, then an HMM classifies contact intervals. Two experimental configurations show dramatically different performance:










Configuration
Video resolution
Encoder input
Sampling rate
Performance




A (640×480)
640×480
256×256 (resized)
~500 Hz
Good


B (256×256)
256×256
256×256 (native)
~2000 Hz
Poor



Features look similar by visual inspection. No bug was found in the image encoding or resize path.





Supervised HMM training counts state transitions directly from labeled sequences. With the same physical interval duration:

500 Hz: 50-frame block → self-transition \(A_{ii} \approx 49/50 = 0.98\), switch penalty \(\log(0.02) \approx -3.9\)
2000 Hz: 200-frame block → self-transition \(A_{ii} \approx 199/200 = 0.995\), switch penalty \(\log(0.005) \approx -5.3\)

The model becomes far more reluctant to transition. Short intervals get swallowed, and transition boundaries shift.



With \(D = 192\) features and \(K\) states:



Covariance mode
Params per state
Total for K=2




Full
\(192 + 192 \times 193 / 2 = 18{,}720\)
37,440


Diagonal
\(192 + 192 = 384\)
768



At 2000 Hz with ~12,000 samples and 2 states, that’s ~6,000 samples per state—but consecutive frames are nearly identical due to temporal autocorrelation, so the effective independent sample count is much lower. Full covariance estimation at 192 dims requires ~18,528 independent samples per state. This is massively underdetermined.
Fix: Use use_diagonal_covariance = true in HMMParameters, and/or apply PCA to reduce from 192 to 20–30 dimensions before HMM fitting.



Whisker contact involves three behavioral regimes, not two:









Regime
Contact?
Duration at 2000 Hz
Transition behavior




Quiescent
No
Thousands of frames
Very sticky


Whisking, retracted
No
50–100 frames (half-cycle at 10–20 Hz)
Fast oscillation with contact


Whisking, in contact
Yes
50–100 frames
Fast oscillation with retracted



A 2-state HMM forces one transition matrix to explain both the very slow quiescent↔︎whisking transitions AND the fast 10–20 Hz contact oscillations. It compromises on an intermediate transition probability that fits neither regime.
Fix: Use 3 states with combined interval labels (see below).



Different pole positions produce qualitatively different contact patterns:

Anterior pole: Brief contacts at whisk peaks, fast transitions
Posterior pole: Sustained contacts spanning multiple whisk cycles, slow transitions

A single HMM averages these into one compromise transition matrix.
Fix: Train separate HMMs per pole condition (simplest), or use a model with covariate-dependent transitions (see Advanced Models).





Diagonal covariance (use_diagonal_covariance = true)
3-state combined labels from two interval series:

Whisking intervals + Contact intervals → Combined state
(whisking=0, contact=0) → state 0 (quiescent)
(whisking=1, contact=0) → state 1 (whisking, no contact)
(whisking=1, contact=1) → state 2 (whisking, contact)
After prediction, decompose: state 2 → contact, states 0,1 → no contact

Separate HMMs per pole position — each gets its own transition matrix reflecting its actual dynamics
Optional PCA from 192 → 20–30 dimensions before HMM if diagonal covariance alone isn’t sufficient




Given \(N\) binary interval series, produce \(2^N\) combined HMM states. This is a general abstraction:
combined_state = Σ(interval_i × 2^i)  for i in 0..N-1
After HMM prediction, decompose back via the same mapping. This allows encoding complex multi-interval behavioral structure into the HMM state space while maintaining a clean label interface.



For cases where transition dynamics vary by a known continuous covariate (e.g., pole position), several models go beyond standard HMMs:


The transition matrix is a function of observed inputs:
\[P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i, \mathbf{u}_t) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_{ij}^\top \mathbf{u}_t)}{\sum_k \exp(\mathbf{w}_{ik}^\top \mathbf{u}_t)}\]
Each row of the transition matrix is a softmax regression on the covariate. This is the most direct solution to “transition dynamics vary smoothly with pole position.”
Available in: ssm (Python, Linderman lab), dynamax (JAX)



Replaces the implicit geometric dwell-time distribution with explicit duration distributions per state. Can specify that anterior-contact lasts 25–50 ms while posterior-contact lasts 100+ ms.
Available in: pyhsmm (Python), hsmm (R)



Both emissions and transitions are generalized linear models on covariates. Used extensively in systems neuroscience (International Brain Lab, Churchland lab).
Available in: ssm (Python), glm-hmm (Python, Churchland lab)



Combines discrete HMM states with per-state linear dynamics on continuous observations. Naturally handles temporal autocorrelation. Overkill for contact detection, appropriate if modeling whisker kinematics directly.
Available in: ssm (Python), dynamax (JAX)



Nonparametric—automatically infers the number of states. The “sticky” variant adds learned self-transition bias per state, so quiescent states can be sticky while whisking states oscillate.
Available in: pyhsmm (Python), ssm (Python)

The PythonBridge module in WhiskerToolbox could be used to call Python implementations of these models if needed.






A frame-level classifier (SVM, random forest, logistic regression) learns a decision boundary in feature space. Adding “no pole present” frames to the “no contact” class is purely beneficial — it expands the classifier’s understanding of what non-contact looks like. The classifier doesn’t care why there’s no contact. More negative variety = better boundary = fewer false positives.



The HMM jointly estimates three things per state:

Emission distribution: what features look like in this state
Transition probabilities: how long this state lasts and what follows it
Initial distribution: which state the sequence starts in

If “no pole present” frames are added to the “no contact” state:

Emissions get corrupted: The “no contact” distribution becomes a mixture of (a) quiescent with no pole, (b) whisking past where the pole would be, and (c) whisking near the pole but not touching. These have different feature profiles. The emission Gaussian becomes broad and uninformative — it overlaps with genuine contact features.
Transitions get corrupted: “No pole” periods are 100% self-transition for no-contact. Mixing those with whisking periods (which have rapid contact↔︎no-contact oscillations) averages the transition rates toward something that describes neither regime.
Net effect: The HMM becomes less confident about everything. The emission distributions are blurry (high variance from mixing conditions), and the transition matrix is a meaningless average of two very different dynamics.

Takeaway: HMM training data should be condition-matched — only include frames from the same pole condition (or dynamically similar periods). Adding “easy negatives” from no-pole trials dilutes the emission estimates rather than improving them.






In a standard HMM, \(P(z_t \mid z_{t-1})\) is a constant matrix — it doesn’t see the features at all. The model has no mechanism to say “given these features, I should transition.” It can only say “on average across all training data, this is how often state A follows state A.”
This is why diverse negatives hurt: the transition row for “no contact” averages quiescent dynamics (almost never transition) with whisking dynamics (transition every 50 frames). The model can’t distinguish these at transition time because it doesn’t look at the features when deciding to transition.
The IOHMM / GLM-HMM models fix exactly this by replacing:
\[P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i) = A_{ij} \quad \text{(constant)}\]
with:
\[P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i, \mathbf{y}_t) = f(A_{ij}, \mathbf{y}_t) \quad \text{(feature-dependent)}\]
Now the model can learn: “when features look like quiescent, self-transition probability is 0.9999” and “when features look like active whisking, self-transition is 0.95.” A single “no contact” state could accommodate both sub-regimes because the transition function adapts to the current context.



A single Gaussian per state is unimodal — one mean, one covariance. If “no contact” includes both quiescent frames (low-energy features) and active-whisking-no-contact frames (high-energy features), the Gaussian places its mean somewhere in between and inflates its variance to cover both. This produces:

Poor likelihood scores for both sub-populations (both are in the tails)
Overlap with the “contact” emission distribution (the inflated variance bleeds into contact feature space)

Non-parametric or richer emission models help:








Emission model
Multi-modal?
Captures “no contact” diversity?




Single Gaussian
No
No — one mean, one variance


Gaussian Mixture (GMM-HMM)
Yes
Yes — learns sub-clusters automatically


Kernel density
Yes
Yes — but scales poorly to 192 dims


Neural network (deep HMM)
Yes
Yes — most flexible



A GMM-HMM (each state’s emission is a mixture of Gaussians) would let the “no contact” state have one mixture component for quiescent features and another for active-whisking features. mlpack supports mlpack::HMM<mlpack::GMM>, though it is not currently exposed in HiddenMarkovModelOperation.



Even with perfect multimodal emissions, the fixed transition matrix remains the bottleneck. A GMM-HMM can correctly identify “these features are quiescent-no-contact” vs. “these features are whisking-no-contact” and assign high emission probability to both. But when deciding \(P(\text{transition to contact} \mid \text{currently no contact})\), it uses the same transition probability regardless of which mixture component generated the current observation. It still can’t capture “quiescent → never transitions” vs. “whisking → transitions at 10–20 Hz.”
The full solution requires both feature-dependent transitions AND rich emissions — which is what the GLM-HMM provides.




A practical approach that works with the current codebase:

Train a frame-level discriminative classifier on all available data (diverse negatives, all pole positions — heterogeneity helps here)
Produce per-frame contact probabilities (the classifier’s output)
Feed the 1D probability signal into a simple 2-state HMM for temporal smoothing

The classifier handles the emission complexity (multimodal negatives, pole-dependent features). The HMM only needs to learn the temporal dynamics of a 1-dimensional signal with well-calibrated likelihoods. This avoids the Gaussian emission problem entirely and reduces the transition matrix to a simple smoothing role.

title: MLCore Library
text:
MLCore is a static C++ library (src/MLCore/) that provides machine learning algorithms operating directly on WhiskerToolbox core data types. It has zero Qt dependency and is fully testable in isolation.
The library provides:

Supervised classification: Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression
Unsupervised clustering: K-Means, DBSCAN, Gaussian Mixture Model
Dimensionality reduction: PCA (with MLDimReductionOperation base class)
End-to-end pipelines that compose validation, conversion, training/fitting, prediction, metrics, and output writing into single entry points
Feature validation and conversion from TensorData to armadillo matrices
Label assembly from multiple sources (intervals, entity groups, data-entity groups)
Prediction output following the putative group pattern

title: MLCore Library
text:
Architecture
MLCore (static, no Qt)
├── features/          # TensorData validation, conversion, label assembly
├── metrics/           # Binary & multi-class classification metrics
├── preprocessing/     # Class balancing (subsample / oversample)
├── models/            # Abstract interface + concrete implementations
│   ├── supervised/    # Random Forest, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression
│   └── unsupervised/  # K-Means, DBSCAN, Gaussian Mixture
├── output/            # PredictionWriter — putative group pattern output
├── entity_utils/      # Bulk TimeEntity registration & conversion
└── pipelines/         # ClassificationPipeline, ClusteringPipeline

Dependency Graph
MLCore
├── DataManager          # Data storage & retrieval
│   ├── TensorData       # Feature matrices
│   ├── AnalogTimeSeries # Probability output
│   └── DigitalTimeSeries# Interval output
├── Entity               # EntityRegistry & EntityGroupManager
│   ├── EntityRegistry

title: MLCore Library
text:
Key Design Decisions

TensorData as Feature Matrix
Feature assembly is not part of MLCore. Users build feature tensors using the TensorDesigner/TensorColumnBuilders infrastructure. MLCore validates, converts (float→double, NaN handling, z-score normalization), and consumes the result via FeatureConverter.


Pimpl Pattern for Model Isolation
All model operations (Random Forest, K-Means, etc.) use the pimpl idiom to isolate mlpack headers from consumers. This keeps compile times reasonable and prevents mlpack’s transitive includes from leaking.


Putative Group Output Pattern
Predictions never overwrite user labels. Output goes to groups prefixed with the configured prefix (e.g., "Predicted:Contact", "Cluster:0"). This follows the pattern established by LineKalmanGrouping elsewhere in the project.


Three Label Modes
Labels can come from:

DigitalIntervalSeries — binary labeling (inside=positive, outside=negative)
TimeEntity groups — multi-class from entity group membership at each frame
Data-entity groups — multi-class from data object group membership

See Label Assembly for details.

title: Supervised PCA Operation
text:
SupervisedPCAOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that fits PCA exclusively on the labeled subset of observations. The principal components therefore capture variance within the labeled data, not the entire dataset. All observations (labeled and unlabeled) are then projected into the resulting space.
This is useful when the labeled data represents a specific phenomenon of interest (e.g., whisker contact frames), and the user wants the top principal components to reflect variance within that phenomenon rather than variance across the full recording.

title: Supervised PCA Operation
text:
Architecture

Class Hierarchy
MLModelOperation (interface)
  └── MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (abstract base)
        ├── LogitProjectionOperation
        └── SupervisedPCAOperation (this class)


Pimpl Pattern
The implementation uses the pimpl idiom to keep Armadillo matrix members out of the header:
SupervisedPCAOperation.hpp  →  MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (public API)
SupervisedPCAOperation.cpp  →  eigenvectors, eigenvalues, mean, stddev (hidden)
The Impl struct holds:

eigenvectors — \((D \times n\_components)\) projection matrix
eigenvalues — sorted descending
mean — per-feature mean (from labeled subset)
total_variance — sum of all eigenvalues (for variance ratio computation)

title: Supervised PCA Operation
text:
Algorithm

fitTransform

Validate inputs (non-empty, matching dimensions, ≥ 2 classes, n_components ≤ D)
Compute statistics from labeled subset: per-feature mean
Center labeled data (subtract mean)
Covariance matrix from centered labeled data: \(\Sigma = \frac{1}{N-1} X_c X_c^T\)
Eigendecomposition via arma::eig_sym, reversed to descending order
Truncate to top n_components eigenvectors
Project ALL data (not just labeled) using the fitted eigenvectors and mean



transform
Uses the stored eigenvectors and mean to project new data without retraining.

Logit Projection Operation
text:
LogitProjectionOperation is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that trains a softmax regression classifier on labeled feature data and extracts the raw pre-softmax logit activations as a discriminative \(C\)-dimensional projection. The output is a \((C \times N)\) matrix where each column holds the class logit scores for one observation.
Since logits represent the linear decision boundary in feature space, this is equivalent to a supervised linear projection — a data-driven counterpart to PCA that maximizes class separation rather than variance.

title: Logit Projection Operation
text:
Architecture

Class Hierarchy
MLModelOperation (interface)
  └── MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (abstract base)
        └── LogitProjectionOperation (concrete)
MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation parallels MLDimReductionOperation for unsupervised reduction. It adds a labeled fitTransform() method while routing train() to fitTransform() (discarding the output) so the operation is compatible with the standard registry workflow.


Pimpl Pattern
The implementation uses the pimpl idiom to isolate mlpack.hpp from consumers:
LogitProjectionOperation.hpp  →  MLSupervisedDimReductionOperation (public API)
LogitProjectionOperation.cpp  →  mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat> (hidden)
The Impl struct holds:

std::unique_ptr<mlpack::SoftmaxRegression<arma::mat>> — the trained model (used only during fitTransform)
arma::mat weight_matrix — extracted weight matrix \(W\) of shape \((C \times D)\)
arma::vec bias — extracted bias vector \(b\) of shape \((C)\)
num_classes, num_features, col_names — metadata
trained — readiness flag

After fitTransform(), the mlpack model is retained in memory. After load(), the model pointer is null — transform() works without mlpack in both cases because it uses the extracted \(W\) and \(b\) directly.


Training and Weight Extraction
Training uses fitIntercept=true for better model expressiveness:
ens::L_BFGS optimizer;
optimizer.MaxIterations() = max_iterations;

model = std::make_unique<SRModel>(
    features, labels, num_classes, optimizer, lambda, true);  // fitIntercept=true
With fitIntercept=true, Parameters() returns a \((C \times (D+1))\) matrix:

Column 0: bias vector
Columns 1..D: weight matrix

Extraction:
bias = model->Parameters().col(0);           // (C,)
weight_matrix = model->Parameters().cols(1, D);  // (C, D)


Logit Computation
The forward pass for new data \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times N}\):
result = weight_matrix * features;   // (C, N)
result.each_col() += bias;           // broadcast add bias


Serialization
Save/load stores only \(W\) and \(b\) (not the mlpack model), using cereal::BinaryOutputArchive:
[num_classes][num_features][col_names][weight_matrix][bias]
This makes the serialized artifact self-contained for inference without mlpack dependencies.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text: PlottingSVG is a static, Qt-free library that converts CorePlotting::RenderableScene objects into publication-quality SVG documents. It is the SVG counterpart to PlottingOpenGL — both consume the same CorePlotting scene graph but produce different output: OpenGL draw calls vs. SVG strings.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text: PlottingSVG is a static, Qt-free library that converts CorePlotting::RenderableScene objects into publication-quality SVG documents. It is the SVG counterpart to PlottingOpenGL — both consume the same CorePlotting scene graph but produce different output: OpenGL draw calls vs. SVG strings.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text:
Key Features

Symmetric with PlottingOpenGL: Same input (RenderableScene), different output. Widgets that build a scene for OpenGL can export to SVG without a second scene-building path.
No Qt dependency: Pure C++ string output via <sstream> and <fstream>. Usable in headless or batch workflows.
Layered documents: SVGSceneRenderer groups geometry into named <g> layers (rectangles, polylines, glyphs, decorations).
Decoration system: Canvas-space overlays (scalebar, axes) via the SVGDecoration interface.
Legacy flat export: SVGExport.hpp preserves the DataViewer document layout (single element list, no named layers).

title: PlottingSVG Library
text:
Motivation
SVG export previously lived in CorePlotting/Export/SVGPrimitives (removed). OpenGL rendering already had its own library (PlottingOpenGL); embedding SVG in CorePlotting created architectural asymmetry and forced each widget to duplicate document assembly.
PlottingSVG extracts SVG rendering into a dedicated library that any consumer can link.

title: PlottingSVG Library

Architecture

Position in the Stack
CorePlotting (data types, layout, scene building)
    ├── PlottingOpenGL  (RenderableScene → OpenGL draw calls)
    └── PlottingSVG     (RenderableScene → SVG strings)
Both backends depend on CorePlotting but not on each other. Widgets link PlottingOpenGL for live rendering and optionally PlottingSVG for export.

title: PlottingSVG Library
text:
Export APIs
PlottingSVG exposes two paths. New widget integrations should use SVGSceneRenderer.

SVGSceneRenderer (preferred)
Main entry point for layered SVG export. Stores a non-owning pointer to the scene; the scene must remain alive through render(). At render() time the renderer reads scene.view_matrix and scene.projection_matrix and computes MVP = projection * view * batch.model_matrix per batch.
namespace PlottingSVG {

class SVGSceneRenderer {
public:
    SVGSceneRenderer();  // default 1920×1080 canvas, white background

    void setScene(CorePlotting::RenderableScene const & scene);
    void setCanvasSize(int width, int height);
    void setBackgroundColor(std::string const & hex_color);
    void addDecoration(std::unique_ptr<SVGDecoration> decoration);
    void clearDecorations();

    [[nodiscard]] std::string render() const;
    [[nodiscard]] bool renderToFile(std::filesystem::path const & path) const;
};

}
Layer order: rectangles → polylines → glyphs → decorations (only when decoration output is non-empty). If no scene is set, the document still contains XML header, viewBox, and background.
Plot widgets typically copy live OpenGL view/projection matrices onto the cached scene before calling render(), and use the widget’s current pixel dimensions as canvas size.

transformVertexToSVG(vertex, mvp, canvas_width, canvas_height):

ndc = mvp * vertex
Perspective divide when |ndc.w| > 1e-6

title: State Estimation Library
text:
The primary goals of this library are to provide a modular framework for state estimation tasks. The high-level objectives include:

Generate Smooth Estimates: Produce a smooth estimate of a state from raw data.
Compare and Validate: Generate a smooth estimate and compare it against a pre-existing estimate, with the ability to flag potential outliers.
Interpolate Missing Data: Generate smoothed predictions that can fill in gaps where data is missing. This is in contrast to simply refining existing measurements.
Assign Identity to Unlabeled Data: Use predictions to assign identities to measured data points within a time series that has only sparse labels.

title: State Estimation Library
text:
Design Principles and Variation Points
The library should be designed in a modular fashion to accommodate several key points of variation in state estimation problems. The interfaces should be flexible enough to handle significant structural differences between algorithms.

Data Type
The nature of the input data is a primary variation point. The library must handle:

Continuous Data: Analog time series or other continuous state variables.
Discrete Data: Data that exists on a discrete grid or set of points. An example would be making a prediction for a point within an image mask where only certain pixels are available.



Filtering Schemes
The design must support different families of filtering algorithms, which may have different assumptions about data distributions and different methodological considerations.

Kalman Filters:

Standard Kalman Filter
Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for linearized systems
Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)

Particle Filters:

Bootstrap Particle Filter
Sequential Importance Sampling with Resampling (SIR)




Smoothing Operations
Alongside forward-in-time filtering, the library must incorporate smoothing operations, which use the full dataset to refine estimates by making a backward pass through the data. The design should recognize that some smoothers are tightly paired with specific filters, while others may be more general.

Paired Smoother: An example is the Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother, which is specifically paired with the Kalman filter.
Complex Smoothers: For particle filters, smoothing and resampling schemes can be more complicated and may require filter-specific implementations.



Ancillary Tools for Performance
To ensure high performance, especially for complex schemes, the library should incorporate specialized data structures and algorithms.

Example: For particle filters operating on spatial data, a k-d tree could be implemented to accelerate the lookup and resampling of large particle fields based on their location.

The overall goal is to design interfaces that are modular enough to accommodate these major structural variations as new algorithms and techniques are implemented.

title: TensorColumnAnalogStorage
text:
TensorColumnAnalogStorage is a zero-copy CRTP storage backend for AnalogTimeSeries that directly references a column of a TensorData object. It is part of Phase 3 of the multi-channel storage roadmap.
File: src/DataObjects/AnalogTimeSeries/storage/TensorColumnAnalogStorage.hpp

title: TensorColumnAnalogStorage
text:
TensorColumnAnalogStorage is a zero-copy CRTP storage backend for AnalogTimeSeries that directly references a column of a TensorData object. It is part of Phase 3 of the multi-channel storage roadmap.
File: src/DataObjects/AnalogTimeSeries/storage/TensorColumnAnalogStorage.hpp

title: TensorColumnAnalogStorage
text:
Purpose
When multi-channel data is stored as a TensorData (an Armadillo arma::fmat with shape [time × channels]), individual channels need to be exposed as AnalogTimeSeries objects for compatibility with DataViewer_Widget, transforms, and export. TensorColumnAnalogStorage enables this without copying data.

title: TensorColumnAnalogStorage
text:
Memory Model
Armadillo uses column-major layout: each column of an arma::fmat is contiguous in memory. TensorColumnAnalogStorage caches the raw column pointer (arma::fmat::colptr(c)) to provide \(O(1)\) element access and contiguous span access.
arma::fmat(rows=1000, cols=32)  ← column-major

   col 0       col 1       col 2      ...
┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐
│ t0      │ │ t0      │ │ t0      │
│ t1      │ │ t1      │ │ t1      │
│ ...     │ │ ...     │ │ ...     │
│ t999    │ │ t999    │ │ t999    │
└─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘
     ↑            ↑
  _col_ptr     _col_ptr
  (col=0)      (col=1)
Each TensorColumnAnalogStorage holds a std::shared_ptr<TensorData const>, ensuring the underlying matrix stays alive as long as any view exists.

title: TensorColumnAnalogStorage
TensorColumnAnalogStorage
text:
Integration: TensorToAnalog Transform
The TensorToAnalog transform (Phase 1, updated in Phase 3) uses this backend:

Copies the input TensorData into a shared_ptr (self-contained ownership).
Resolves time storage once (shared across all column views).
For each selected column, constructs a TensorColumnAnalogStorage and wraps it in an AnalogTimeSeries via createFromStorage.

The resulting AnalogTimeSeries objects share the same TensorData memory.

title: TensorColumnAnalogStorage
text:
Non-Armadillo Fallback
If the TensorData uses a storage backend other than ArmadilloTensorStorage (e.g. LibTorchTensorStorage), the column pointer cache (_col_ptr) is nullptr. In this case:

isContiguous() returns false
getSpan() / getSpanRange() return empty spans
getValueAt(i) falls back to TensorData::at({i, col}) (per-element virtual dispatch)

This ensures correctness for all backends while preserving zero-copy performance for the common Armadillo case.

title: DigitalIntervalSeries
text:
Storage range queries (getOverlappingRange)
All backends return indices [start_idx, end_idx) where each interval satisfies interval.start <= end && interval.end >= start. Implementation differs by backend and layout:









Backend
Disjoint fast path
Overlapping fallback
Notes




OwningDigitalIntervalStorage
O(log n) binary search when assumeDisjointIntervals() is true
O(n) linear scan when false
Hint set from IntervalLayout via _syncStorageDisjointHint()


ViewDigitalIntervalStorage
O(log n) when source()->assumeDisjointIntervals()
O(n) via filterByOverlappingRangeLinear()
filterByOverlappingRange() picks path from source hint


LazyDigitalIntervalStorage
Not available
Always O(n) linear scan
See limitation below



Doxygen @see links on each getOverlappingRangeImpl() cross-reference the other backends.

Lazy storage limitation
LazyDigitalIntervalStorage::getOverlappingRangeImpl() always uses a linear scan. Unlike owning and view storage, lazy storage does not read assumeDisjointIntervals() and therefore cannot use the binary-search fast path, even when the underlying transform view yields sorted disjoint intervals.
This is acceptable for current use (createFromView() + IntervalLayout::Overlapping intermediates) where overlaps are possible and range queries are infrequent. If disjoint lazy views become hot paths, add an assumeDisjointIntervals() hook to lazy storage mirroring owning storage.


Why the fast path requires disjoint intervals
The O(log n) optimization assumes sorted-by-start intervals are also sorted-by-end (true only when intervals are pairwise non-overlapping). With overlaps such as [0, 100] and [50, 60], binary search on end times can return incorrect index bounds; the linear fallback avoids that.

title: PlotDataExport Library
text:
PlotDataExport is a header-only, Qt-free library in namespace PlotDataExport that serializes plot data to CSV strings. Free functions take core data types (GatherResult, HistogramData, HeatmapRowData, PerTrialHeatmapInput) and return CSV suitable for analysis in Python (pandas/seaborn/matplotlib) and R (readr/ggplot2).
The library handles serialization only. File dialogs, button placement, and user interaction are the responsibility of each plot widget.

title: AnalogIntervalPeak (TransformsV2)
text:
TimeFrame handling
Most transforms do not call setTimeFrame on their output. TimeFrame assignment is normally performed by DataManager::setData (or ElementRegistry propagation for single-input transforms).
AnalogIntervalPeak is an exception. It explicitly attaches a TimeFrame on the output DigitalEventSeries because:

Stored events use analog indices. Peak times written to storage are TimeFrameIndex values from the analog series coordinate system.
Binary registry propagation uses input1 only. ElementRegistry copies the first input’s TimeFrame (DigitalIntervalSeries). When analog and interval series use different time bases, that would make view() resolve the wrong ClockTicks.
The transform therefore prefers the analog TimeFrame, falling back to the interval TimeFrame only when analog has none.

When committing results through the UI or SynthesizeData, still assign the output to the analog time key so DataManager and the transform agree on the time base.

title: MedianFilterMask (TransformsV2)
text:
Algorithm
For each input Mask2D:

Resolve canvas size from MaskMedianFilterParams when both dimensions are positive, otherwise size the canvas to the mask’s axis-aligned point extents plus background border padding (max(1, window_size / 2)).
Rasterize mask points to a binary image on the chosen canvas.
Apply median_filter with the configured odd window size.
Convert filtered pixels back to absolute mask coordinates.
Return empty Mask2D if input is empty or filtering removes all pixels.

Invalid window_size values (even or non-positive) fall back to 3.

title: AnalogDifference (TransformsV2)
text:
Algorithm
Differencing operates on index-adjacent samples in storage order (not raw TimeFrameIndex frame gaps), consistent with TensorCentralDifference.
For sample index i and window w:



Method
Formula




Backward
data[i] - data[i - w]


Forward
data[i + w] - data[i]


Central
(data[i + w] - data[i - w]) / (2 * w)



Each output sample is anchored at the same TimeFrameIndex as input index i. With the default Skip edge policy, samples with incomplete windows are omitted.

title: Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
text:
This document provides a concrete task list for hardening the ObserverData callback system against thread-safety violations. It describes the problem, the patterns that fix it, and step-by-step instructions for applying each pattern to existing code.
For the core ObserverData API and integration patterns, see the Observer Library.
For the broader concurrency architecture — ownership model, write reservations, and staged design — see Concurrency Architecture.

title: Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
text:
This document provides a concrete task list for hardening the ObserverData callback system against thread-safety violations. It describes the problem, the patterns that fix it, and step-by-step instructions for applying each pattern to existing code.
For the core ObserverData API and integration patterns, see the Observer Library.
For the broader concurrency architecture — ownership model, write reservations, and staged design — see Concurrency Architecture.

title: Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
text:
Problem Statement
ObserverData is explicitly not thread-safe: notifyObservers() calls every registered callback synchronously on the calling thread. When DataManager::setData() is called from a background QThread, observer callbacks that manipulate Qt widgets execute on the wrong thread — undefined behavior that causes heap corruption, ASAN crashes, and intermittent segfaults.
This was discovered via a crash in MLCoreWidget: the PipelineWorker (QThread) called writePredictions() → dm.setData() → notifyObservers() on the background thread. Many widget callbacks directly called QComboBox::clear(), QTreeWidget::clear(), and similar — all require the main thread.






NoteRe-entrancy vs. Thread Safety



ObserverData::notifyObservers() copies the observer map to a snapshot before invoking callbacks. Adding or removing observers from within a callback is therefore safe for a single notification round — additions take effect on the next notifyObservers() call. This does not make the library thread-safe: concurrent addObserver, removeObserver, or notifyObservers calls from different threads remain undefined behavior.



Why It Surfaces Intermittently
On the first pipeline run, few observers are registered for the new output keys. On subsequent runs, more widgets have attached observers, increasing the number of unsafe cross-thread callbacks and making the race more likely to manifest.

title: Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
text:
Design Decisions

QTimer::singleShot(0, ...) over Qt::QueuedConnection signals. Both work. QTimer::singleShot is simpler to add to existing lambdas and does not require adding new signals.
Assertion in notifyObservers() instead of individual widgets. Catches the problem at the source (wrong-thread notification) rather than the symptom (wrong-thread widget manipulation). One assertion covers all current and future observers.
Deferred writes as the primary fix for workers, not callback hardening. Hardening callbacks makes them tolerant of wrong-thread calls, but the fundamental design principle is: workers should never call DataManager::setData(). Deferred writes enforce this at the architecture level.
ObserverData stays Qt-free. The assertion uses #ifdef QT_CORE_LIB guards. Non-Qt consumers of ObserverData are not affected.

title: Observer Thread-Safety Roadmap
text:
Relationship to Other Roadmaps



Roadmap
Scope
Relationship




Concurrency Architecture
DataManager ownership, write reservations, borrow tracking
This document addresses the immediate observer problem; the concurrency architecture provides the long-term structural solution (workers never write to DataManager directly)


Threaded Loading Roadmap
Background data loading via fork-join
Data loading is already safe by design (worker returns data, main thread calls setData). No observer hardening needed — but the ASSERT_MAIN_THREAD macro will verify this.



The deferred-writes pattern in this document is the low-cost precursor to Stage 2 (Write Reservations) of the concurrency architecture. It achieves the same thread confinement guarantee without the full reservation infrastructure.
This document              Concurrency Architecture
(immediate fixes)          (long-term design)
─────────────────          ──────────────────────────
Deferred writes      →     Write Reservations (Stage 2)
Callback hardening   →     Eliminated (workers never notify)
notifyObservers()    →     Borrow Tracking (Stage 3)
 assertion                  enforces protocol at compile time

title: TensorToPoint2D
text:
Decode modes

decode() — single peak

Flatten the channel and take the global argmax.
If the peak value is <= 0, return {0, 0} (scaled to target image size when configured).
Otherwise return integer pixel coordinates, optionally refined with parabolic subpixel fitting along each axis when params.subpixel is true.



decodeMultiple() — all local maxima
Returns every pixel that:

exceeds params.threshold, and
is strictly greater than all eight neighbors (local maximum)

Each peak is optionally subpixel-refined and scaled to target image coordinates.
