title: C++ Development Tools Reference
text:
IWYU (Include What You Use)
Version: 0.21 (based on Ubuntu clang version 17.0.6)
Purpose: IWYU analyzes C++ source files to ensure that they directly include all headers they use and do not include unnecessary headers. This helps reduce compilation times and maintain clean dependencies.
Location: /usr/bin/include-what-you-use
Command Line Usage:
Basic usage on a single file (requires compiler flags):
include-what-you-use -I/path/to/includes src/file.cpp
Using with compile_commands.json (recommended):
# Extract compilation command for a specific file from compile_commands.json
# and pass those flags to IWYU
include-what-you-use -Xiwyu --verbose=3 $(jq -r '.[] | select(.file | contains("main.cpp")) | .arguments[]' out/build/Clang/Release/compile_commands.json | grep -v "^clang" | tr '\n' ' ')
Common IWYU options: - -Xiwyu --verbose=3: Increase verbosity - -Xiwyu --check_also=<glob>: Check additional files matching pattern - -Xiwyu --mapping_file=<file>: Use custom mapping file - -Xiwyu --no_default_mappings: Disable default mappings
Validation:
# Verified IWYU is installed and accessible
include-what-you-use --version
# Output: include-what-you-use 0.21 based on Ubuntu clang version 17.0.6
Use Cases: - Reduce compilation times by removing unnecessary includes - Identify missing direct includes - Maintain clean header dependencies - Prevent header inclusion bloat

title: C++ Development Tools Reference
text:
cppcheck
Version: 2.13.0
Purpose: Static analysis tool for C/C++ code that detects bugs, undefined behavior, dangerous coding constructs, and stylistic issues without executing the program.
Location: /usr/bin/cppcheck
Command Line Usage:
Analyze a single file:
cppcheck --enable=warning,performance --suppress=missingIncludeSystem src/file.cpp
Analyze entire source directory:
cppcheck --enable=all --suppress=missingIncludeSystem --project=compile_commands.json
Analyze with specific checks:
# Enable specific check categories
cppcheck --enable=warning,performance,portability,information src/

# Full analysis (slower but more thorough)
cppcheck --enable=all --inconclusive src/
Common options: - --enable=<checks>: Enable specific checks (all, warning, style, performance, portability, information) - --suppress=<id>: Suppress specific warnings - --project=<file>: Use compilation database - --inconclusive: Show inconclusive results - --quiet: Only show errors - --verbose: Show verbose output
Validation:
# Verified cppcheck is installed
cppcheck --version
# Output: Cppcheck 2.13.0

# Test on project file
cppcheck --enable=warning,performance --suppress=missingIncludeSystem src/WhiskerToolbox/main.cpp
# Successfully executed and reported issues
Use Cases: - Static bug detection (null pointer dereferences, memory leaks, etc.) - Code quality checks - Performance issue detection - Portability checks - Pre-commit hook integration

title: MediaProcessingPipeline
text:
Key Components

ProcessingOptionsSchema.hpp
Companion header providing ParameterUIHints<T> specializations for each processing option struct defined in ImageProcessing/ProcessingOptions.hpp. This keeps the rfl dependency out of ImageProcessing while adding UI annotations (tooltips, value ranges) for AutoParamWidget.
Annotated structs:

ContrastOptions — alpha/beta/display range
GammaOptions — gamma value
SharpenOptions — sigma
ClaheOptions — grid size, clip limit
BilateralOptions — diameter, color/spatial sigma
MedianOptions — kernel size
MagicEraserParams — brush size, median filter size
ColormapOptions — colormap type, alpha, normalize



ProcessingStep.hpp
Descriptor struct for a named processing step:

display_name — human-readable name for UI sections
chain_key — key used with MediaData::addProcessingStep() (e.g., "1__lineartransform")
schema — ParameterSchema for auto-generating the parameter UI
apply — type-erased function void(cv::Mat&, nlohmann::json const&) that applies the step



ProcessingStepRegistry
Singleton registry mapping step names to ProcessingStep descriptors. Steps register at static-initialization time via the RegisterStep<Params> RAII helper (same pattern as DataSynthesizer’s RegisterGenerator and TransformsV2’s static registration).
// Example registration
static RegisterStep<ContrastOptions> const reg_contrast{
    "Linear Transform",
    "1__lineartransform",
    [](cv::Mat& m, ContrastOptions const& o) { ImageProcessing::linear_transform(m, o); }
};
Currently registered steps: Linear Transform, Gamma Correction, Image Sharpening, CLAHE, Bilateral Filter, Median Filter. Magic Eraser and Colormap are handled specially due to their state/rendering requirements.

title: MediaProcessingPipeline

Design Rationale
This library exists to support the phased refactoring of MediaProcessing_Widget from hand-written per-filter widgets to AutoParamWidget-driven generic UI.

title: Fuzz Testing
text: Fuzz testing is a way that we can test programs with random inputs. This is a technique that allows us to test many interesting edge cases very efficiently and really harden our program against failing.

title: Fuzz Testing
text: Fuzz testing is a way that we can test programs with random inputs. This is a technique that allows us to test many interesting edge cases very efficiently and really harden our program against failing.

title: Fuzz Testing
text:
Procedure
The procedure might look like this: Imagine we have an input file for some kind of processing. In fuzz testing, we could randomly generate text and feed it to our transformation function, and we could do this many, many times. We consider a success in this case to be if the program doesn’t crash.
In our circumstance with Neuralyzer we could imagine that for loading data, we could randomly generate lots and lots of data and see if those loading functions crash whenever we try to load it. Alternatively, we could randomly generate different specification files or configuration files to load that data and see if it crashes. If we forget a semicolon or something that causes a critical failure, does it crash, or does it fail gracefully and give some kind of useful message to the user?

title: Fuzz Testing
text:
Structured Fuzzing and Corpora
We also can try to add some structure to our fuzzing in what is referred to as a corpus for our fuzz test. In a corpus, we specify a range of parameter values, and we can vary some parameters within that range and see if the output changes. This can help us catch things that are more specific than just random crashes. By changing values to be within the ranges that we would expect and doing this many times over many different parameters, we may be able to catch things that we wouldn’t see otherwise.

title: Fuzz Testing
text:
Neuralyzer and Chaining Transformations
We also might be able to test how we chain together different types of transformations. In Neuralyzer, we have the ability to chain together different types of data transformations. By chaining together data transformations in a random way, we might be able to ensure our processing pipelines are robust in this type of variability.
The goal of Neuralyzer is to be able to have as many of the specifications as we can in a format that can be read from JSON files. This is facilitated with a reflection library known as Reflect CPP. The more things that we have in JSON specifications, the easier it is for us to use a corpus to load those and test them with fuzzing.

title: Fuzz Testing
text:
Implementation
Fuzz testing in this library can be specified with the fuzz test library made by Google: https://github.com/google/fuzztest.
Whenever we use the fuzz testing library for a translation unit, we should specify that library for that file with the name of the translation unit. We can specify a fuzzing file as .fuzz.cpp in our library, and then we can add it to the fuzz test driver. Again, these should be written in such a way that if expectations are not met, it will flag what the state was from the random state there, help us understand why this test may have failed, and repeat it with those more specific parameters.

title: Media Keymap Actions

title: Row Gather Geometry
text:
RowGatherGeometry (src/TransformsV2/extension/gatherResult/RowGatherGeometry.hpp) resolves per-column tensor gather windows before TensorColumnBuilders builds an interval-row provider.
The helper supports identity row geometry and non-identity interval-row pipelines that produce prepared interval windows:

Empty or whitespace row_pipeline_json is identity.
Explicit {"steps": []} is identity.
Non-identity row_pipeline_json is loaded as a TransformPipeline and executed against the original row-source DigitalIntervalSeries.
The output must be a DigitalIntervalSeries with the same row count as the original row source.
Other outputs, including DigitalEventSeries sample times, are rejected until later row-pipeline phases implement the corresponding provider dispatch.

Identity resolution returns the original row-source DigitalIntervalSeries as the prepared gather windows and verifies that the row count remains unchanged. Non-identity interval-window outputs are treated only as per-column gather geometry; the tensor RowDescriptor remains tied to the original row source. interval_property columns bypass this path because they read metadata from the original row source and do not gather source data.
Window-producing transforms should preserve one output interval per original row. If overlap is possible, transforms should return DigitalIntervalSeries::createOverlapping() output so overlapping gather windows remain separate tensor rows.

title: Sinc Interpolation Transform
text:
The SincInterpolation transform performs band-limited Nyquist upsampling on AnalogTimeSeries data using windowed-sinc interpolation. It is a pure data container transform with no TimeFrame awareness — it takes N input samples and produces (N-1) * factor + 1 output samples.
This is the core algorithm for aligning signals recorded at different sampling rates (e.g., 500 Hz camera data → 30 kHz electrophysiology).

title: Sinc Interpolation Transform
text:
Algorithm
For each output sample position \(m \in [0, M-1]\) where \(M = (N-1) \cdot \text{factor} + 1\):

Compute fractional input position: \(x = m / \text{factor}\)
If \(x\) is an exact integer (i.e., \(m \bmod \text{factor} = 0\)), pass through the original sample directly.
Otherwise, compute the windowed-sinc interpolation:

\[
y(m) = \frac{\sum_{n=\lfloor x \rfloor - K + 1}^{\lfloor x \rfloor + K} w(x-n) \cdot \text{sinc}(x-n) \cdot s(n)}{\sum_{n=\lfloor x \rfloor - K + 1}^{\lfloor x \rfloor + K} w(x-n) \cdot \text{sinc}(x-n)}
\]
where:

\(\text{sinc}(t) = \sin(\pi t) / (\pi t)\), with \(\text{sinc}(0) = 1\)
\(w(t)\) is the window function (Lanczos, Hann, or Blackman)
\(K\) is the kernel half-width
\(s(n)\) is the input sample at index \(n\) (with boundary handling)


Kernel Normalization
The denominator in the formula above normalizes the kernel weights to sum to 1. This is essential because the windowed-sinc kernel, when truncated to a finite support \([-K, K]\), does not naturally sum to 1 everywhere. Without normalization, DC signals would exhibit small amplitude errors (~0.7–1.3%).


Window Functions








Window
Formula (for \(|t| < a\))
Properties




Lanczos
\(\text{sinc}(t/a)\)
Best sidelobe suppression-to-width ratio


Hann
\(0.5(1 + \cos(\pi t / a))\)
Smooth, good general purpose


Blackman
\(0.42 + 0.5\cos(\pi t/a) + 0.08\cos(2\pi t/a)\)
Lowest sidelobes, wider main lobe





Boundary Modes







Mode
Behavior




SymmetricExtension
Reflects signal at boundaries (e.g., index -1 maps to index 1). Preserves signal continuity and produces smaller edge artifacts.


ZeroPad
Pads with zeros outside the input range. Simple but introduces edge discontinuities.

title: Event To Interval Transform
text:
The EventToInterval transform expands each event in a DigitalEventSeries into a window interval, producing a DigitalIntervalSeries with IntervalLayout::Overlapping. This is the materialized counterpart to the lazy EventExpanderAdapter used by GatherResult, and is the first step in the GatherResult DigitalIntervalSeries migration.
Each event at TimeFrameIndex T becomes one interval:
[T - pre_expansion, T + post_expansion]
Expansion is performed in TimeFrameIndex space (not absolute clock time). The output preserves the input TimeFrame.

AnalogToTensor & TensorToAnalog
text:
Algorithm

AnalogToTensor

Validate all channels share the same TimeFrame (pointer identity) and sample count.
Build flat row-major data by iterating each channel via viewValues() (mmap-safe).
Return TensorData::createTimeSeries2D(...) preserving the shared TimeFrame and TimeIndexStorage.



TensorToAnalog

Determine columns to extract (all if columns is empty).
For each column, create an AnalogTimeSeries backed by TensorColumnAnalogStorage when the source uses Armadillo storage (zero-copy colptr() access). Otherwise, call TensorData::getColumn(i) for an owning copy.
If the tensor has RowType::TimeFrameIndex, preserve time indices via RowDescriptor::timeStoragePtr()->getAllTimeIndices().
Set the TimeFrame from the source tensor on each output.

To register views in DataManager, use TensorDesign::createTensorColumnViews.

title: TransformsV2
text: TransformsV2 is the second generation data transformation library in WhiskerToolbox, designed for high performance, type safety, and composability.

title: TransformsV2
text:
Key Goals

Type Safety: Leveraging C++20 concepts and strong typing to prevent runtime errors where possible.
Performance: Minimizing allocations through “Fusion” of element-wise operations.
Flexibility: Supporting complex pipelines that can be defined at runtime (e.g., via JSON) or compile-time.
Lifting: Automatically generalizing element-wise operations (like Mask2D -> Point2D) to work on containers (like MaskData).

title: TensorTemporalNeighbors
text:
Time-Alignment Rule
Neighbors are determined by sorted row position in TimeIndexStorage, not by raw frame number ±1. For example, if rows exist at frames [10, 20, 50], offset +1 from frame 10 yields the row at frame 20 (the next stored row), not frame 11 (which has no data).
Both DenseTimeIndexStorage and SparseTimeIndexStorage guarantee sorted indices.

title: TensorTemporalNeighbors
text:
Boundary Policies







Policy
Behavior




NaN
Fill missing neighbor features with NaN. All rows preserved.


Drop
Remove rows where any offset is out-of-range. Output has fewer rows.


Clamp
Clamp to first/last row when an offset goes out-of-range.


Zero
Fill missing neighbor features with 0.0f.

title: TensorTemporalNeighbors
text:
Output Layout
Columns are ordered as: [original cols] [offset_1 cols] [offset_2 cols] ...
Shifted columns are named "{original_col}_lag{offset}", e.g. feat1_lag-1, feat1_lag+1.
If include_original is false, original columns are omitted.

title: Creating Mask Labels
text: Creating mask labels is done through the GrabCut tool. Currently it can be opened through the Tongue Tracking widget.

title: Creating Mask Labels
text:
GrabCut Tool Operation

Selecting ROI
To start creating a mask, left click and drag the mouse over the image to form a green rectangle as the region of interest. The objected intended to be masked should be completely within this rectangle. If a mistake is made the reset button returns the tool to the initial state.
The GrabCut algorithm works as such: the algorithm keeps track of the mask and for each iteration, attempts to refine it. In between iterations, the user can tweak the mask to provide feedback to the algorithm, which will be noted through subsequent iterations.
After drawing an ROI the “Iterate Grabcut” button becomes functional. Using it completes one iteration of the GrabCut algorithm. The first usage of this button will show the initial mask created by the algorithm. Ideally the user should press this button throughout the editing process.

Opacity of the displayed mask can be adjusted with the transparency slider



User Feedback
In between iterations the user has access to a drawing bush whose radius can be adjusted. It is used to paint feedback for the GrabCut algorithm, which it will take into account upon pressing the “Iterate Grabcut” button. The brush has four colors:

“Definite Background”: Tells GrabCut the painted area is definitely not part of the mask.
“Definite Foreground”: Tells GrabCut the painted area is definitely part of the mask.
“Probable Background”: Suggests to GrabCut the painted area may not be part of the mask. GrabCut uses this information to create a better mask but may partially/fully disobey it.
“Probable Foreground”: Suggests to GrabCut the painted area is likely part of the mask. GrabCut uses this information to create a better mask but may partially/fully disobey it.



Saving and Exporting
The GrabCut tool may be exited at any time by pressing the “Exit” button. “Save and Exit” will exit the tool and save the mask into the main application and displayed in the media player. All created masks can be saved to disk using the “Save Drawn Masks” button in the Tongue Tracking widget.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
You have a long video and want to label specific events or behaviors (e.g., whisker contacts, licking bouts, freezing episodes) by inspecting scattered regions of the video. You need to:

Record the intervals where you observed events.
Track which regions of the video you have actually inspected, so that unlabeled frames within inspected regions are correctly treated as “no event” rather than “unknown.”

This distinction matters for training classifiers and computing metrics — frames you never looked at should not count as negative examples.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
You have a long video and want to label specific events or behaviors (e.g., whisker contacts, licking bouts, freezing episodes) by inspecting scattered regions of the video. You need to:

Record the intervals where you observed events.
Track which regions of the video you have actually inspected, so that unlabeled frames within inspected regions are correctly treated as “no event” rather than “unknown.”

This distinction matters for training classifiers and computing metrics — frames you never looked at should not count as negative examples.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
Prerequisites

A video loaded in the Media Viewer.
(Optional) An existing DigitalIntervalSeries or DigitalEventSeries if you want to add labels to a pre-existing data object.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
Concepts
This workflow uses two types of interval data:

Label intervals — The events you are marking (e.g., contact_intervals). Each interval represents a region where the behavior occurred.
Tracked regions — The regions of the video you have inspected. Any frame inside a tracked region that does not have a label is implicitly “no event.” Frames outside all tracked regions are “unknown.”

The Triage Session Widget manages the tracked-regions bookkeeping automatically via the AddInterval command.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
Steps

1. Open the Triage Session Widget
Go to View → Tools → Triage Session to open the widget.


2. Create a Pipeline
A pipeline is a sequence of steps you wish to execute. In the Triage Widget, if you click “Mark”, followed by “Commit”, a pipeline of commands will be applyed to all frames between the Mark and Commit frames. In this scenario with labeling your behavior, you will most likely add the behavioral intervals in a sequence of frames (say between 1 and 1000). At frame 1000, you may wish to skip to another part of the video for more diverse training data. It would be useful to add an interval to signify that you have manually classified all frames in this part of the video. To do this, on frame 1, you can set a Mark, and click Add Command… Select the AddInterval command. The pipeline will now be populated with this command - you can expand the dialogue to see the Interval Key, Start Frame and End Frame options. For Interval Key, type “tracked_regions”. For Start Frame, use ${make_frame} and for End frame use ${current_frame}. You should see this JSON produced below your command:
{
  "name": "Track Inspected Region",
  "commands": [
    {
      "command_name": "AddInterval",
      "description": "Record inspected region",
      "parameters": {
        "interval_key": "tracked_regions",
        "start_frame": "${mark_frame}",
        "end_frame": "${current_frame}",
        "create_if_missing": true
      }
    }
  ]
}
If you also want to copy events from a predicted series into a curated series at the same time, add a CopyByTimeRange command before the AddInterval:
{"commands":
[
  {
    "command_name":"AddInterval",
    "parameters":
      {"interval_key": "tracked_regions",
      "start_frame": "${mark_frame}",
      "end_frame": "${current_frame}",
      "create_if_missing":true},
    "description":"Append an interval to a DigitalIntervalSeries, creating it if needed"
  }
  ]
}
This JSON can be saved and loaded. For trivial pipelines they are easy to create, but as they become more complex, you may wish to re-use them for next time.
Clicking mark, scrolling to another frame, and clicking commit will result in an interval between the mark frame and the current frame being added to a DigitalIntervalSeries named “tracked_regions”.


3. Inspect and Commit Regions
The key insight is that you do not need to inspect the video sequentially. Jump to any region of interest and process it:

Jump to a region you want to inspect (e.g., frame 75000).
Press Mark. The widget records frame 75000 as mark_frame.
Scrub forward through the region (e.g., to frame 76000), watching for events of interest. Use other tools (e.g., the Data Manager or Media Viewer annotation tools) to add labels for events you observe during this stretch.
Press Commit at the end of the inspected region. The pipeline runs:

The interval [75000, 76000] is added to tracked_regions.

Jump to the next region of interest (e.g., frame 150000) and repeat.



4. Interpret the Results
After inspecting several regions, your data has three categories of frames:







Frame Category
How to Identify




Labeled event
Frame has an entry in the label data object (e.g., contact_intervals)


No event (negative)
Frame is inside a tracked_regions interval but has no label


Unknown
Frame is not inside any tracked_regions interval



This three-way distinction is essential for honest evaluation. When computing precision/recall or training a classifier, exclude “unknown” frames from the negative class.


5. Monitor Progress
The Tracked Regions section of the widget shows:

Interval count — How many separate regions you have inspected.
Total frame count — The cumulative number of frames covered by all inspected regions.

Use this to track your progress across the full video.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
Tips

Non-contiguous inspection is the point. You can inspect frames 75000–76000, then 150000–151000, then 10000–12000. The tracked-regions data object records them all.
Overlapping commits are safe. If you accidentally commit an overlapping region, the AddInterval command simply adds another interval. Overlapping intervals can be merged later if needed.
Use CopyByTimeRange instead of MoveByTimeRange when you want to keep the original predictions intact (e.g., for comparison).
Template variables let you reuse the same pipeline JSON across experiments with different data key names. Define defaults in the variables section.

title: How-To: Label Video Intervals
text:
Example: Contact Labeling Workflow
A typical contact-labeling session might look like this:

Load a video and predicted contact intervals (predicted_contacts).
Create a pipeline that copies predicted contacts and tracks inspected regions.
Jump to a predicted contact event.
Mark → scrub through the contact region → visually confirm or correct → Commit.
Jump to the next predicted contact.
Repeat until you have inspected enough regions for your analysis.

After the session, you have:

curated_contacts — confirmed contact intervals.
tracked_regions — every region you inspected, whether or not it contained contacts.

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
This guide walks through fitting an Input-Output HMM (IOHMM) to classify whisker contact frames using deep-learning encoder features and the dynamax library (JAX-based).
A standard HMM models contact/no-contact as hidden states with a fixed transition matrix. At high frame rates this struggles because (1) the transition matrix is overwhelmingly self-transitioning, (2) the transition dynamics cannot adapt to the behavioral context — e.g., whether the animal is actively whisking or quiescent.
A standard GLM-HMM (Ashwood et al., 2022) improves emissions by making them input-dependent, but it still uses a fixed transition matrix. This means the probability of switching between behavioral regimes is constant regardless of what the animal is doing — which is the core limitation.
An Input-Output HMM solves this by making both transitions and emissions depend on the input features:
Input-driven transitions (IOHMM): \[
P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\text{softmax}(\mathbf{V}_i \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{c}_i)_j
\]
Input-driven emissions (GLM): \[
P(y_t = \text{contact} \mid z_t = k,\; \mathbf{u}_t) =
\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{b}_k)
\]
Each state \(k\) has its own transition weights \(\mathbf{V}_k\) and emission weights \(\mathbf{W}_k\), so both when the model transitions between states and how each state maps features to contact labels are learned from data.
Why input-dependent transitions matter: When the animal starts whisking vigorously, the input-dependent transition model can increase the probability of switching to a “contact-prone” state. When it stops whisking, transitions toward a “quiet” state become more likely. This context-sensitivity is impossible with a fixed transition matrix.
Why dynamax? The ssm library does not install on Python 3.12 (required for neuralyzer). dynamax is the JAX-based successor from the same group (probml). While dynamax provides CategoricalRegressionHMM (input-dependent emissions with fixed transitions), we build a custom IOHMM by subclassing its modular HMMTransitions component — following the custom HMM pattern.

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 0: Environment Setup
Create a dedicated conda environment with Python 3.12, then install the dependencies in the correct order. This step only needs to be done once.






Warning



Why the version pins? dynamax has no version constraints on its core dependencies (tensorflow_probability, jax, numpy are all unpinned). Running pip install dynamax pulls the latest of everything, but the latest releases are mutually incompatible:

JAX 0.5+ removes jax.interpreters.xla.pytype_aval_mappings (used by TFP).
NumPy 2.0+ renames np.reshape(newshape=...) to shape= (used by TFP).

The pins below are a known-working combination for dynamax.


# 1. Create the environment (Python 3.12 is required for neuralyzer)
conda create -n dynamax python=3.12 -y
conda activate dynamax

# 2. Install dynamax
pip install dynamax

# 3. Pin dependencies to a known-working combination
pip install jax==0.4.30 jaxlib==0.4.30 numpy==1.26.4 scipy==1.13.0 tensorflow-probability==0.24.0

# 4. Install IPython — required by fastprogress (a dynamax transitive dep)
#    for progress-bar display during EM fitting.
pip install ipython






Tip



GPU users: Replace step 3 with pip install "jax[cuda12]==0.4.30" jaxlib==0.4.30 ... to use an NVIDIA GPU.


Verify the environment is set up correctly:
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model import CategoricalRegressionHMM  # for reference
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.abstractions import HMM, HMMTransitions
import jax, numpy as np
print(f"JAX {jax.__version__}, NumPy {np.__version__}")  # 0.4.30, 1.26.4
print("Environment OK")

Shape \([T, D]\) — encoder features per frame

Training block intervals (in video time coordinates)


contact

Contact intervals (in video time coordinates)









Important



Time base mismatch: Intervals use TimeFrameIndex values (e.g., 37000) but the feature array is indexed by row (e.g., row 0). Each TensorData row has an associated TimeFrameIndex; we use findRowGreaterOrEqual() and findRowLessOrEqual() to convert interval boundaries to row indices. This follows the same pattern as the C++ MLCore classification pipeline.


Output: A new DigitalIntervalSeries written back to DataManager with predicted contact intervals from the GLM-HMM.

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 1: Extract Data from DataManager
import numpy as np

# --- Encoder features: shape (T, D) ---
features_td = dm.getData("features")          # TensorData
X_all = np.array(features_td.values, copy=True)  # writable copy
T_total, D = X_all.shape
print(f"Feature matrix: {T_total} frames × {D} dimensions")
print(f"Row type: {features_td.rowType()}")  # should be 'TimeFrameIndex'

# --- Row ↔ TimeFrameIndex conversion helpers ---
# Each TensorData row has an associated TimeFrameIndex (a plain int in Python).
# We use the TensorData row-index API (same pattern as MLCore's ClassificationPipeline).
row_time_indices = features_td.rowTimeIndices()  # list of int, one per row
print(f"  Row 0 → TimeFrameIndex {int(row_time_indices[0])}")
print(f"  Row {T_total-1} → TimeFrameIndex {int(row_time_indices[-1])}")

def time_to_row(time_val):
    """Convert a TimeFrameIndex value to a feature-array row index (inclusive start)."""
    row = features_td.findRowGreaterOrEqual(int(time_val))
    return row if row is not None else T_total  # past end

def time_to_row_end(time_val):
    """Convert a TimeFrameIndex to the exclusive-end row index for an interval."""
    row = features_td.findRowLessOrEqual(int(time_val) - 1)
    return (row + 1) if row is not None else 0  # before start

def row_to_time(row_idx):
    """Convert a feature-array row index back to a TimeFrameIndex value."""
    return int(row_time_indices[row_idx])

# --- Training block intervals ---
train_intervals = dm.getData("train").toList()
print(f"Training blocks: {len(train_intervals)}")
for iv in train_intervals:
    r_s = time_to_row(iv.start)
    r_e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
    print(f"  TimeFrameIndex [{iv.start}, {iv.end}) → rows [{r_s}, {r_e})  ({r_e - r_s} frames)")

# --- Contact intervals ---
contact_intervals = dm.getData("contact").toList()
print(f"Contact intervals: {len(contact_intervals)}")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
section: Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
text:
Step 2: Build Binary Labels from Intervals
We need a frame-level binary label \(y_t \in \{0, 1\}\) for each training block. dynamax expects a batch dimension: emissions shape is (num_batches, T, ...) and inputs shape is (num_batches, T, D).
import jax.numpy as jnp

def intervals_to_binary(total_frames, intervals):
    """Convert contact intervals to a binary array in feature-row space.

    Each interval's start/end is converted from TimeFrameIndex values to
    feature-array row indices using the TensorData row-index API.
    """
    labels = np.zeros(total_frames, dtype=np.int32)
    for iv in intervals:
        r_s = time_to_row(iv.start)
        r_e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
        labels[r_s:r_e] = 1
    return labels

# Build per-frame binary contact labels over the entire session (in row space)
y_all = intervals_to_binary(T_total, contact_intervals)
print(f"Total contact frames (row space): {y_all.sum()} / {T_total}")

# Standardise features (important for logistic regression convergence)
X_mean = X_all.mean(axis=0)
X_std = X_all.std(axis=0) + 1e-8
X_all_normed = (X_all - X_mean) / X_std

# Split into per-block arrays (converting TimeFrameIndex → row indices)
X_blocks = []  # list of (T_block, D) arrays — inputs
y_blocks = []  # list of (T_block,) arrays — integer class labels

for iv in train_intervals:
    s = time_to_row(iv.start)
    e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
    assert e > s, (
        f"Empty block after conversion: TimeFrameIndex [{iv.start},{iv.end}) → rows [{s},{e}). "
        f"Feature rows span TimeFrameIndex [{int(row_time_indices[0])}, {int(row_time_indices[-1])}]. "
        f"Check that the training interval overlaps the feature range."
    )
    X_blocks.append(X_all_normed[s:e])
    y_blocks.append(y_all[s:e])

print(f"Prepared {len(X_blocks)} training blocks")
for i, (xb, yb) in enumerate(zip(X_blocks, y_blocks)):
    n_contact = int(yb.sum())
    pct = 100 * n_contact / len(yb) if len(yb) > 0 else 0.0
    print(f"  Block {i}: {len(yb)} frames, {n_contact} contact ({pct:.1f}%)")






Important



Padding for batched EM: dynamax’s fit_em requires all sequences in a batch to have the same length. If your training blocks differ in length, either:

Pad shorter blocks (shown below), or
Fit on each block separately with fit_sgd.

We show the padding approach here.


def pad_sequences(arrays, pad_value=0):
    """Pad a list of variable-length arrays to the same length along axis 0."""
    max_len = max(a.shape[0] for a in arrays)
    padded = []
    for a in arrays:
        pad_width = [(0, max_len - a.shape[0])] + [(0, 0)] * (a.ndim - 1)
        padded.append(np.pad(a, pad_width, constant_values=pad_value))
    return np.stack(padded)

# Pad and convert to JAX arrays
batch_emissions = jnp.array(pad_sequences(y_blocks, pad_value=0))   # (B, T_max)
batch_inputs = jnp.array(pad_sequences(X_blocks, pad_value=0.0))    # (B, T_max, D)

print(f"Batched emissions shape: {batch_emissions.shape}")
print(f"Batched inputs shape:    {batch_inputs.shape}")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 3: Create the Input-Output HMM
dynamax does not include an IOHMM out of the box, but its modular architecture makes it straightforward to build one. We create a custom InputDrivenHMMTransitions class (following the custom HMM pattern) and combine it with the existing CategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions.






Note



How dynamax handles input-dependent transitions internally: The base HMMTransitions class already supports inputs in its API — the _compute_transition_matrices() method vmaps over time steps when inputs are provided, producing a (T-1, K, K) tensor of time-varying transition matrices. The gradient-based M-step also passes inputs through. We just need to implement distribution() so it actually uses the inputs.


import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax.random as jr
import optax
import tensorflow_probability.substrates.jax.distributions as tfd

from typing import NamedTuple, Optional, Tuple, Union
from jaxtyping import Float, Array

from dynamax.parameters import ParameterProperties
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.abstractions import (
    HMM, HMMTransitions, HMMParameterSet, HMMPropertySet
)
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.initial import (
    StandardHMMInitialState, ParamsStandardHMMInitialState
)
from dynamax.hidden_markov_model.models.categorical_glm_hmm import (
    CategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions, ParamsCategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions
)
from dynamax.types import IntScalar, Scalar


# ── Input-Driven Transition Parameters ──────────────────────────────
class ParamsInputDrivenTransitions(NamedTuple):
    """Parameters for input-driven transitions.

    weights[i, j, :] are the feature weights for transitioning
    from state i to state j.
    """
    weights: Union[Float[Array, "num_states num_states input_dim"],
                   ParameterProperties]
    biases: Union[Float[Array, "num_states num_states"],
                  ParameterProperties]


# ── Input-Driven Transition Model ───────────────────────────────────
class InputDrivenHMMTransitions(HMMTransitions):
    r"""Transitions whose probabilities depend on external inputs.

    $$P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i, \mathbf{u}_t) =
      \text{softmax}(\mathbf{V}_i \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{c}_i)_j$$

    where $\mathbf{V}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times M}$ and
    $\mathbf{c}_i \in \mathbb{R}^K$.

    The base class `_compute_transition_matrices` and gradient-based
    `m_step` handle all the heavy lifting — we only implement
    `distribution`, `initialize`, and `log_prior`.
    """

    def __init__(self, num_states, input_dim,
                 m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
                 m_step_num_iters=50):
        super().__init__(m_step_optimizer=m_step_optimizer,
                         m_step_num_iters=m_step_num_iters)
        self.num_states = num_states
        self.input_dim = input_dim

    def distribution(self, params, state, inputs=None):
        logits = params.weights[state] @ inputs + params.biases[state]
        return tfd.Categorical(logits=logits)

    def initialize(self, key=None, method="prior",
                   transition_weights=None, transition_biases=None):
        if key is None:
            raise ValueError("key must be provided")

        key1, key2 = jr.split(key)

        if transition_weights is None:
            # Small random weights — features start with weak influence
            transition_weights = 0.01 * jr.normal(
                key1, (self.num_states, self.num_states, self.input_dim))

        if transition_biases is None:
            # Sticky initialisation: self-transitions are initially preferred
            transition_biases = 2.0 * jnp.eye(self.num_states)

        params = ParamsInputDrivenTransitions(
            weights=transition_weights, biases=transition_biases)
        props = ParamsInputDrivenTransitions(
            weights=ParameterProperties(),
            biases=ParameterProperties())
        return params, props

    def collect_suff_stats(self, params, posterior, inputs=None):
        # Override: pass full inputs to M-step. The base class slices
        # inputs[1:] here, but _compute_transition_matrices also slices
        # inputs[1:] internally — causing a double-slice shape mismatch.
        return posterior.trans_probs, inputs

    def log_prior(self, params):
        """Gaussian prior on weights (L2 regularisation)."""
        return -0.5 * jnp.sum(params.weights ** 2)


# ── Full IOHMM Parameter Set ───────────────────────────────────────
class ParamsIOHMM(NamedTuple):
    initial: ParamsStandardHMMInitialState
    transitions: ParamsInputDrivenTransitions
    emissions: ParamsCategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions


# ── Input-Output HMM ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(HMM):
    r"""HMM with input-driven transitions AND input-driven emissions.

    **Transitions (IOHMM):**
    $$P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i, \mathbf{u}_t) =
      \text{softmax}(\mathbf{V}_i \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{c}_i)_j$$

    **Emissions (Categorical GLM):**
    $$P(y_t \mid z_t = k, \mathbf{u}_t) =
      \text{Cat}(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{u}_t + \mathbf{b}_k))$$

    Unlike `CategoricalRegressionHMM`, the transitions are **not** a fixed
    matrix — they depend on the input features at each time step.
    """

    def __init__(self, num_states, num_classes, input_dim,
                 initial_probs_concentration=1.1,
                 transition_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
                 transition_m_step_num_iters=50,
                 emission_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
                 emission_m_step_num_iters=50):
        self.input_dim = input_dim

        initial_component = StandardHMMInitialState(
            num_states,
            initial_probs_concentration=initial_probs_concentration)

        transition_component = InputDrivenHMMTransitions(
            num_states, input_dim,
            m_step_optimizer=transition_m_step_optimizer,
            m_step_num_iters=transition_m_step_num_iters)

        emission_component = CategoricalRegressionHMMEmissions(
            num_states, num_classes, input_dim,
            m_step_optimizer=emission_m_step_optimizer,
            m_step_num_iters=emission_m_step_num_iters)

        super().__init__(num_states, initial_component,
                         transition_component, emission_component)

    @property
    def inputs_shape(self):
        return (self.input_dim,)

    def initialize(self, key=jr.PRNGKey(0), method="prior",
                   initial_probs=None,
                   transition_weights=None, transition_biases=None,
                   emission_weights=None, emission_biases=None):
        key1, key2, key3 = jr.split(key, 3)
        params, props = dict(), dict()

        params["initial"], props["initial"] = \
            self.initial_component.initialize(
                key1, method=method, initial_probs=initial_probs)
        params["transitions"], props["transitions"] = \
            self.transition_component.initialize(
                key2, method=method,
                transition_weights=transition_weights,
                transition_biases=transition_biases)
        params["emissions"], props["emissions"] = \
            self.emission_component.initialize(
                key=key3, method=method,
                emission_weights=emission_weights,
                emission_biases=emission_biases)

        return ParamsIOHMM(**params), ParamsIOHMM(**props)


num_states = 3     # K: number of hidden behavioral states
num_classes = 2    # binary outcome: contact / no-contact
input_dim = D      # encoder feature dimensionality

model = InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(
    num_states=num_states,
    num_classes=num_classes,
    input_dim=input_dim,
)

# Initialize parameters
params, props = model.initialize(key=jr.PRNGKey(0))
print(f"IOHMM: {num_states} states, {input_dim}-dim inputs, {num_classes} categories")
print(f"Transition weights shape: {params.transitions.weights.shape}")
print(f"Transition biases shape:  {params.transitions.biases.shape}")
print(f"Emission weights shape:   {params.emissions.weights.shape}")
print(f"Emission biases shape:    {params.emissions.biases.shape}")

Choosing the number of states

K=2 is the minimum: one state for “contact-responsive” frames and one for “non-responsive”.
K=3 is recommended: adds a transition/ambiguous state that absorbs boundary uncertainty.
Higher K may overfit; use cross-validation (see Cross-Validation) to select.



Tuning the M-step
The transition and emission components each use gradient descent for their M-step. You can tune the optimizer and number of iterations independently:
model_tuned = InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(
    num_states=num_states,
    num_classes=num_classes,
    input_dim=input_dim,
    transition_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-3),  # slower LR for transitions
    transition_m_step_num_iters=100,                # more iterations
    emission_m_step_optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
    emission_m_step_num_iters=50,
)

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
section: Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
text:
Step 4: Fit the Model with EM
num_iters = 100

params, log_probs = model.fit_em(
    params,
    props,
    emissions=batch_emissions,
    inputs=batch_inputs,
    num_iters=num_iters,
)
print(f"Final log-probability: {log_probs[-1]:.2f}")

Multiple initialisations
EM finds a local optimum. Run several random initialisations and keep the best:
best_lp = -jnp.inf
best_params = None

for seed in range(5):
    cand_params, cand_props = model.initialize(key=jr.PRNGKey(seed))
    cand_params, lps = model.fit_em(
        cand_params, cand_props,
        emissions=batch_emissions,
        inputs=batch_inputs,
        num_iters=num_iters,
    )
    if lps[-1] > best_lp:
        best_lp = lps[-1]
        best_params = cand_params

params = best_params
print(f"Best log-probability across initialisations: {best_lp:.2f}")


Alternative: SGD fitting
If EM is slow or you want mini-batch training, use SGD instead:
import optax

params_sgd, losses = model.fit_sgd(
    params,
    props,
    emissions=batch_emissions,
    inputs=batch_inputs,
    optimizer=optax.adam(1e-3),
    num_epochs=100,
)


Print convergence
lps = np.array(log_probs)
print(f"Log-probability: {lps[0]:.2f} → {lps[-1]:.2f} over {len(lps)} iterations")
if len(lps) > 5 and abs(lps[-1] - lps[-5]) < 0.1:
    print("  ✓ Converged (last 5 iterations changed < 0.1)")
else:
    print("  ⚠ May not have converged — consider increasing num_iters")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 5: Inspect the Fitted Model

Viterbi decoding (most likely state sequence)
Decode each training block using its unpadded data:
for i, (yb, xb) in enumerate(zip(y_blocks, X_blocks)):
    emissions_i = jnp.array(yb)      # (T_block,)
    inputs_i = jnp.array(xb)         # (T_block, D)
    states = model.most_likely_states(params, emissions_i, inputs=inputs_i)
    states_np = np.array(states)
    unique, counts = np.unique(states_np, return_counts=True)
    print(f"Block {i}: states = {dict(zip(unique, counts))}")


Inspect learned transition weights
Unlike a standard HMM, the IOHMM has no single transition matrix — transitions are recomputed at every time step from the features. To understand the learned dynamics, inspect the transition weight norms and biases:
trans_W = np.array(params.transitions.weights)   # (K, K, D)
trans_b = np.array(params.transitions.biases)     # (K, K)

print("Transition biases (act as baseline log-odds for each transition):")
print(np.around(trans_b, decimals=3))
print()
for i in range(num_states):
    for j in range(num_states):
        w = trans_W[i, j, :]
        print(f"  State {i+1}→{j+1}: ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, "
              f"bias = {trans_b[i,j]:.3f}")


Evaluate mean transition matrix on training data
To get an intuitive summary, compute the average transition matrix over the training features:
def mean_transition_matrix(params, X_normed):
    """Average the input-dependent transition matrix over all frames."""
    W = np.array(params.transitions.weights)   # (K, K, D)
    b = np.array(params.transitions.biases)     # (K, K)
    logits = np.einsum("ijd,td->tij", W, X_normed) + b[None, :, :]  # (T, K, K)
    exp_logits = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    trans_mats = exp_logits / exp_logits.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return trans_mats.mean(axis=0)

avg_A = mean_transition_matrix(params, X_all_normed)
print("Mean transition matrix (averaged over all features):")
print(np.around(avg_A, decimals=3))


Inspect per-state GLM weights
weights = np.array(params.emissions.weights)   # (K, C, D)
biases = np.array(params.emissions.biases)     # (K, C)
for k in range(num_states):
    # For binary classification, the "contact" class weight is weights[k, 1, :]
    w = weights[k, 1, :] - weights[k, 0, :]   # contrast: contact vs no-contact
    print(f"State {k+1}: ||Δw|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.3f}, "
          f"top-5 features = {np.argsort(np.abs(w))[-5:][::-1]}")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
section: Step 6: Apply Model to Training Data
text:
Step 6: Apply Model to Training Data
We compute per-frame contact probability on the training region and write the results back to DataManager as two objects:

AnalogTimeSeries — continuous P(contact) for each frame (viewable in DataViewer)
DigitalIntervalSeries — thresholded contact intervals (viewable in DataViewer)

This lets you visually compare the model’s output against the ground-truth contact intervals directly in WhiskerToolbox.
import whisker_toolbox as wt


def emission_probs(params, X_normed):
    """Compute P(y=c | z=k, u_t) for all frames, states, and classes.

    Returns
    -------
    probs_all : np.ndarray, shape (T, K, C)
    """
    W = np.array(params.emissions.weights)   # (K, C, D)
    b = np.array(params.emissions.biases)    # (K, C)
    logits = np.einsum("kcd,td->tkc", W, X_normed) + b[None, :, :]  # (T, K, C)
    exp_logits = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return exp_logits / exp_logits.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)


def transition_matrix_at(params, u_t):
    """Compute the K×K transition matrix for a single input vector.

    Returns
    -------
    A_t : np.ndarray, shape (K, K) — row i is P(z_next | z_prev=i, u_t)
    """
    W = np.array(params.transitions.weights)  # (K, K, D)
    b = np.array(params.transitions.biases)   # (K, K)
    logits = np.einsum("ijd,d->ij", W, u_t) + b  # (K, K)
    exp_logits = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return exp_logits / exp_logits.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)


def predict_contact_labeled(model, params, y_block, X_block):
    """Evaluate P(contact) on data where labels are available.

    Uses the smoother to get posterior state probabilities
    P(z_t | y_{1:T}, u_{1:T}), then marginalises:
    P(y_t=1) = sum_k P(y_t=1 | z_t=k, u_t) * P(z_t=k | all data).

    This conditions on the observed labels to infer the hidden state.
    """
    posterior = model.smoother(params, jnp.array(y_block), inputs=jnp.array(X_block))
    state_probs = np.array(posterior.smoothed_probs)               # (T, K)
    p_contact = emission_probs(params, X_block)[:, :, 1]           # (T, K)
    return np.sum(p_contact * state_probs, axis=1)                 # (T,)


def predict_contact_unlabeled(params, X_normed):
    """Predict P(contact) on data without labels using input-driven transitions.

    Forward-propagates the state belief using the input-dependent transition
    model. At each frame:

      1. Marginalise over states to get P(y_t=1).
      2. Propagate state belief to the next frame via the input-dependent
         transition matrix A(u_{t+1}).

    No pseudo-observations or autoregressive feedback is needed because the
    input-driven transitions naturally track the behavioral context through
    the features. With a fixed transition matrix, the state belief would
    collapse to the stationary distribution; with input-dependent transitions,
    it adapts at every time step.
    """
    K = len(np.array(params.initial.probs))
    T = X_normed.shape[0]

    pi0 = np.array(params.initial.probs)
    probs_all = emission_probs(params, X_normed)  # (T, K, C)

    alpha = pi0.copy()
    contact_prob = np.zeros(T)

    for t in range(T):
        alpha /= alpha.sum()
        contact_prob[t] = np.dot(probs_all[t, :, 1], alpha)

        if t + 1 < T:
            A_t = transition_matrix_at(params, X_normed[t + 1])
            alpha = alpha @ A_t

    return contact_prob


def prob_to_intervals(contact_prob, threshold=0.5):
    """Threshold a probability array into contiguous (start_row, end_row) pairs."""
    binary = (contact_prob >= threshold).astype(int)
    intervals = []
    in_iv = False
    start = 0
    for t in range(len(binary)):
        if binary[t] == 1 and not in_iv:
            start = t; in_iv = True
        elif binary[t] == 0 and in_iv:
            intervals.append((start, t)); in_iv = False
    if in_iv:
        intervals.append((start, len(binary)))
    return intervals


def predict_full_session(model, params, X_all_normed, y_all, train_intervals,
                         time_to_row, time_to_row_end):
    """Predict P(contact) for the full session (hybrid approach).

    The timeline is split into labeled segments (covered by training
    intervals) and unlabeled gaps between them:

    - **Labeled segments** use the smoother conditioned on actual labels,
      giving high-quality state inference.
    - **Unlabeled gaps** use forward propagation with input-dependent
      transitions — no pseudo-observations needed because the features
      drive the state evolution directly.
    """
    T = X_all_normed.shape[0]
    contact_prob = np.zeros(T)

    pi0 = np.array(params.initial.probs)
    probs_all = emission_probs(params, X_all_normed)  # (T, K, C)

    # Convert intervals to sorted row ranges
    labeled_ranges = []
    for iv in train_intervals:
        s = time_to_row(iv.start)
        e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
        if e > s:
            labeled_ranges.append((s, e))
    labeled_ranges.sort()

    def fill_unlabeled(start, end, alpha_init):
        """Forward propagation for an unlabeled gap."""
        alpha = alpha_init.copy()
        for t in range(start, end):
            alpha /= alpha.sum()
            contact_prob[t] = np.dot(probs_all[t, :, 1], alpha)
            if t + 1 < end:
                A_t = transition_matrix_at(params, X_all_normed[t + 1])
                alpha = alpha @ A_t
        return alpha

    def fill_labeled(start, end):
        """Smoother-based prediction for a labeled segment."""
        posterior = model.smoother(
            params, jnp.array(y_all[start:end]),
            inputs=jnp.array(X_all_normed[start:end]),
        )
        state_probs = np.array(posterior.smoothed_probs)  # (T_block, K)
        p_contact = probs_all[start:end, :, 1]            # (T_block, K)
        contact_prob[start:end] = np.sum(p_contact * state_probs, axis=1)
        return state_probs[-1]  # terminal state distribution

    # Process the timeline in order: gap → labeled → gap → labeled → ...
    alpha = pi0.copy()
    cursor = 0

    for (s, e) in labeled_ranges:
        if cursor < s:
            alpha = fill_unlabeled(cursor, s, alpha)
        terminal_state = fill_labeled(s, e)
        if e < T:
            A_next = transition_matrix_at(params, X_all_normed[e])
            alpha = terminal_state @ A_next
        cursor = e

    # Trailing unlabeled segment
    if cursor < T:
        fill_unlabeled(cursor, T, alpha)

    return contact_prob

Apply to training blocks
On training data we have labels, so we use the smoother to condition the state inference on the actual observations — matching how a standard HMM evaluates its training fit.
# Evaluate contact probability on training blocks (using labels)
for iv in train_intervals:
    s = time_to_row(iv.start)
    e = time_to_row_end(iv.end)
    X_block = X_all_normed[s:e]
    y_block = y_all[s:e]
    contact_prob = predict_contact_labeled(model, params, y_block, X_block)

    # --- AnalogTimeSeries: P(contact) per frame ---
    times = [row_time_indices[r] for r in range(s, e)]
    prob_analog = wt.AnalogTimeSeries(contact_prob.tolist(), times)

    time_key = dm.getTimeKey("features")
    dm.setData("glm_hmm_prob", prob_analog, time_key)
    print(f"Wrote 'glm_hmm_prob': {len(contact_prob)} frames, "
          f"mean P(contact) = {contact_prob.mean():.3f}")

    # --- DigitalIntervalSeries: thresholded predictions ---
    threshold = 0.5
    pred_intervals_rows = prob_to_intervals(contact_prob, threshold)
    result = wt.DigitalIntervalSeries()
    for s_row, e_row in pred_intervals_rows:
        s_time = int(row_time_indices[s + s_row])
        e_time = int(row_time_indices[s + min(e_row, e - s) - 1])
        result.addInterval(s_time, e_time)

    dm.setData("glm_hmm_contact", result, time_key)
    print(f"Wrote 'glm_hmm_contact': {len(pred_intervals_rows)} intervals "
          f"(threshold={threshold})")






Tip



Visualise in WhiskerToolbox: Open the DataViewer widget and add:

glm_hmm_prob as an analog channel — shows the continuous P(contact) curve
glm_hmm_contact as a digital channel — shows predicted contact intervals
contact as a digital channel — shows ground-truth contact intervals

Overlaying these lets you see where the model agrees/disagrees with your labels.

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Step 7: Predict on Full Session
The full session is a mix of labeled training regions and unlabeled gaps. With a standard HMM (fixed transitions), the state belief would collapse to the stationary distribution in unlabeled regions, making predictions meaningless. With the IOHMM, the input-dependent transitions naturally track the behavioral context through the features, so forward propagation alone produces informative predictions.
predict_full_session uses a hybrid strategy:

Labeled segments (training intervals) → smoother conditioned on actual labels, identical to Step 6.
Unlabeled gaps → forward propagation with input-dependent transitions, initialised from the terminal state distribution of the preceding labeled block. No pseudo-observations needed.

# Predict on the full session (hybrid: smoother on labeled, forward on gaps)
contact_prob_all = predict_full_session(
    model, params, X_all_normed, y_all, train_intervals,
    time_to_row, time_to_row_end,
)

# --- Write full-session probability ---
all_times = [int(t) for t in row_time_indices]
prob_analog_all = wt.AnalogTimeSeries(contact_prob_all.tolist(), all_times)

time_key = dm.getTimeKey("features")
dm.setData("glm_hmm_prob", prob_analog_all, time_key)
print(f"Updated 'glm_hmm_prob': {T_total} frames (full session)")

# --- Write full-session thresholded intervals ---
threshold = 0.5
pred_intervals_rows = prob_to_intervals(contact_prob_all, threshold)
result_all = wt.DigitalIntervalSeries()
for s_row, e_row in pred_intervals_rows:
    s_time = int(row_time_indices[s_row])
    e_time = int(row_time_indices[min(e_row, T_total) - 1])
    result_all.addInterval(s_time, e_time)

dm.setData("glm_hmm_contact", result_all, time_key)
print(f"Updated 'glm_hmm_contact': {len(pred_intervals_rows)} intervals (full session)")

title: Input-Output HMM for Whisker Contact Detection Using dynamax
text:
Cross-Validation
To select \(K\) and evaluate prediction quality, hold out one training block at a time:
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score


def cross_validate(K, X_blocks, y_blocks, input_dim, n_init=5, n_iters=100):
    """Leave-one-block-out cross-validation for IOHMM."""
    cv_model = InputDrivenCategoricalRegressionHMM(
        num_states=K,
        num_classes=2,
        input_dim=input_dim,
    )

    f1_scores = []
    for held_out in range(len(X_blocks)):
        X_train = [X_blocks[i] for i in range(len(X_blocks)) if i != held_out]
        y_train = [y_blocks[i] for i in range(len(y_blocks)) if i != held_out]

        # Pad training sequences
        train_emissions = jnp.array(pad_sequences(y_train, pad_value=0))
        train_inputs = jnp.array(pad_sequences(X_train, pad_value=0.0))

        best_lp = -jnp.inf
        best_p = None
        for seed in range(n_init):
            p, pr = cv_model.initialize(key=jr.PRNGKey(seed * 100 + held_out))
            p, lps = cv_model.fit_em(
                p, pr,
                emissions=train_emissions,
                inputs=train_inputs,
                num_iters=n_iters,
            )
            if lps[-1] > best_lp:
                best_lp = lps[-1]
                best_p = p

        # Predict on held-out block (use unlabeled predictor for honest eval)
        prob = predict_contact_unlabeled(best_p, X_blocks[held_out])
        y_pred = (prob >= 0.5).astype(int)
        y_true = y_blocks[held_out]
        f1_scores.append(f1_score(y_true, y_pred))

    return np.mean(f1_scores), np.std(f1_scores)


for K in [2, 3, 4]:
    mean_f1, std_f1 = cross_validate(K, X_blocks, y_blocks, D)
    print(f"K={K}: F1 = {mean_f1:.3f} ± {std_f1:.3f}")

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
The Triage Session Widget provides a structured workflow for reviewing and curating data across video frames. It implements a Mark / Commit / Recall pattern: you mark a starting frame, scrub through the video to review a region, then either commit (execute a batch operation on that region) or recall (abort and return to the mark point).
This widget is especially useful for:

Line triage — reviewing deep-learning predictions and moving correct outputs to a ground-truth dataset.
Interval labeling — inspecting scattered regions of a video and recording which frames have been reviewed.
Multi-step workflows — chaining several operations (move data, record intervals, run transforms) into a single atomic commit.

The Triage Session Widget is accessed via the menu: View → Tools → Triage Session.

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
Widget Layout
The widget is divided into four sections:

Status
Displays the current state of the triage session:

Idle — No marking in progress. Shows the current frame number.
Marking (from X) — Marking is active from frame X. Shows the current frame number.



Controls
Three buttons control the triage workflow:








Button
Enabled When
Action




Mark
Idle
Begin a triage range at the current frame


Commit
Marking (with valid pipeline)
Execute the pipeline for [mark_frame, current_frame]


Recall
Marking
Abort marking and return to Idle without executing anything





Pipeline
The pipeline section defines what happens when you press Commit. A pipeline is a sequence of commands that operate on your data. You can configure the pipeline in two ways:

Load JSON — Load a pre-written pipeline from a .json file.
Guided Editor — Visually build a pipeline by adding commands from a dropdown and filling in parameters with form widgets.

A collapsible Raw JSON section shows the underlying JSON representation and can be edited directly.
See Pipeline Configuration below for details.


Tracked Regions
Shows the number of intervals and total frame count in the tracked-regions DigitalIntervalSeries. This lets you see at a glance how much of the video has been triaged.

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
The Mark / Commit / Recall Workflow
┌───────┐   Mark    ┌─────────┐   Commit   ┌───────┐
│ Idle  │ ────────► │ Marking │ ──────────► │ Idle  │
└───────┘           └─────────┘             └───────┘
                         │
                         │ Recall
                         ▼
                    ┌───────┐
                    │ Idle  │
                    └───────┘

Navigate to the start of a region you want to process.
Press Mark. The widget records the current frame as mark_frame and transitions to the Marking state.
Scrub through the video to the end of the region you want to process.
Press Commit. The pipeline executes with two runtime variables automatically set:

${mark_frame} — the frame where you pressed Mark.
${current_frame} — the frame where you pressed Commit.

The widget returns to Idle. The tracked-regions counter updates to reflect the committed range.

If you change your mind, press Recall to abort and return to Idle without executing anything.

title: Triage Session Widget
text:
Pipeline Configuration
A pipeline is a CommandSequenceDescriptor — a JSON document listing commands to execute in order. Each command has a command_name and a parameters object.

Available Commands







Command
Description




MoveByTimeRange
Move entities in a frame range from one data object to another


CopyByTimeRange
Copy entities in a frame range (source unmodified)


AddInterval
Add an interval to a DigitalIntervalSeries


ForEachKey
Iterate a list and execute sub-commands for each item





Variable Substitution
Parameters can reference variables using the ${variable} syntax:

Runtime variables — ${mark_frame} and ${current_frame} are automatically populated by the triage session when you commit.
Template variables — Define your own in the variables section of the pipeline JSON. These are substituted before execution.



Example Pipeline JSON
{
  "name": "Line Triage Pipeline",
  "version": "1.0",
  "commands": [
    {
      "command_name": "MoveByTimeRange",
      "description": "Move correct predictions to ground truth",
      "parameters": {
        "source_key": "predicted_whisker",
        "destination_key": "ground_truth_whisker",
        "start_frame": "${mark_frame}",
        "end_frame": "${current_frame}"
      }
    },
    {
      "command_name": "AddInterval",
      "description": "Record triaged region",
      "parameters": {
        "interval_key": "tracked_regions",
        "start_frame": "${mark_frame}",
        "end_frame": "${current_frame}",
        "create_if_missing": true
      }
    }
  ]
}


Using the Guided Editor
Instead of writing JSON by hand, you can build a pipeline visually:

Click Add Command… to open the command picker.
Select a command from the list (e.g., MoveByTimeRange).
Fill in the parameter form — text fields for data keys, number fields for frame indices. You can type ${mark_frame} or ${current_frame} in text fields to use runtime variables.
Repeat to add more commands.
Use the arrow buttons to reorder commands, or the × button to remove one.

The guided editor and raw JSON stay synchronized — edits in one are reflected in the other.

title: Media Viewer Overview
text:
The Media Viewer Widget provides a unified display for neuroscience videos or images.
It is the central place where behavioral, microscopic, and event data can be inspected visually, and in addition, you can also process video or images as well as manipulate or modify extracted features such as mask or keypoint data.
In essence, the widget is designed to:

title: Media Viewer Overview
text:
Main Components

Media Window
This is the main display area. All visual data and overlays will appear here.
Feature Table
A table showing all available data streams. Each entry lists its name, type, and visibility.
Visibility can be toggled on or off.
Subwidgets
Specialized panels for interacting with particular types of data. Only the relevant panel is active at a time, when selected.

title: Media Viewer Overview
text:
Supported Data Types
The widget supports multiple kinds of data. Each type has its own controls and visualization style.







Data Type
Description




Keypoints (Points)
Individual locations, e.g. positions of body parts.


Lines
Linear features, e.g. traces of movement or signals.


Masks
Regions of interest in an image or video frame.


Digital Intervals
Time periods when a signal or event is active.


Tensors
Multi-dimensional data, often from machine learning.


Media (Video/Images)
Raw recordings or still frames.


Text Overlays
Labels, annotations, or other text displayed on media.

title: Media Viewer Overview
text:
Feature Table
The feature table lists all available data sources.

Feature — the name of the data stream.

Type — the category of the data (e.g. Mask, Point, Line).

Enabled — whether the data is visible in the media window.

Enabling a feature makes it visible in the media window; disabling it hides it.

title: Media Viewer Overview
text:
Subwidgets
Each data type provides its own subwidget.

Point Widget — shows and manages keypoints.

Line Widget — displays traces or line data.

Mask Widget — handles binary masks or segmented regions.

Interval Widget — manages time-based event data.

Tensor Widget — provides tools for visualizing complex arrays.

Text Widget — adds and edits text overlays.

Processing Widget — applies filters or transformations to media.

title: Media Processing
text:
The Media Processing Widget provides a collection of tools to adjust, enhance, and transform media data (images or video) within the viewer.
Each processing option can be enabled by checking the Active box, and its effect will be applied directly in the media viewer.
This guide introduces each option, its background, and how to use each effectively.
When media is selected in the feature table within the media widget, you will be presented with the following actions:

title: Media Processing
text:
Linear Transform
A linear transform modifies pixel intensity values by applying a simple linear function:
\[
I_{out}(x, y) = \alpha \cdot I_{in}(x, y) + \beta
\]

Alpha (Contrast): Controls contrast. Values >1 increase contrast, values between 0 and 1 decrease contrast.

Beta (Brightness): Adjusts brightness by shifting all pixel values up or down.

Minimum / Maximum: Sets intensity clipping or scaling boundaries. Pixels outside this range are clamped. This is often used for rescaling pixel intensities into a normalized display range.

Use case: Brightening dark images, increasing contrast, or standardizing pixel intensity ranges.

title: Media Processing
text:
Gamma Correction
Gamma correction is a nonlinear intensity adjustment:
\[
I_{out}(x, y) = I_{in}(x, y)^\gamma
\]

Gamma: The power-law exponent.

γ < 1: Brightens images (boosts darker regions).

γ > 1: Darkens images (suppresses bright regions).


This compensates for human visual perception, which is more sensitive to relative changes in darker tones.
Use case: Making hidden details in dark or bright regions more visible.

title: Media Processing
text:
Image Sharpening
Sharpening highlights edges by enhancing high-frequency details. This method uses an unsharp mask:
\[
I_{out} = I_{in} + \lambda \cdot (I_{in} - G_\sigma(I_{in}))
\]
Where \(G_\sigma\) is a Gaussian blur applied with standard deviation σ.

Sigma: Controls the blur radius used before sharpening. Small values sharpen fine details; larger values enhance broader structures.

Use case: Highlighting boundaries, edges, and fine structures in images.

title: Media Processing
text:
CLAHE (Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization)
CLAHE improves local contrast by redistributing pixel intensities based on local histograms. Unlike global histogram equalization, CLAHE works in small tiles (grid regions).

Clip Limit: Prevents noise amplification by limiting the contrast enhancement.

Grid Size: Defines the size of the local regions used for histogram equalization.

Use case: Bringing out local details in images with varying illumination, e.g., microscopy or medical images.

title: Media Processing
text:
Bilateral Filter
The bilateral filter smooths images while preserving edges. It considers both spatial proximity and intensity similarity:
\[
I_{filtered}(x) = \frac{1}{W_p} \sum_{x_i \epsilon \Omega} I(X_i) \cdot f_r(||I(x_i)-I(x)||) \cdot g_s(||x_i - x||)
\]

Diameter: Size of the filter kernel (neighborhood).

Color Sigma (σr): How much intensity differences are preserved; large values allow smoothing across intensity changes, small values preserve edges.

Space Sigma (σs): How far pixels influence each other in space.

Use case: Noise reduction while keeping edges sharp (useful for video or structural microscopy data).

title: Media Processing
text:
Median Filter
The median filter replaces each pixel with the median value of its neighborhood.

Kernel Size: Defines the neighborhood size. Larger kernels smooth more but may lose detail.

Use case: Removing salt-and-pepper noise or impulse noise.

title: Media Processing
text:
Magic Eraser
The magic eraser provides an interactive editing tool for masking unwanted regions.

Brush Size: Size of the drawing tool when marking regions.

Median Filter Size: Strength of smoothing applied to the mask.

Start Drawing Button: Enables drawing mode inside the media viewer.

Clear Mask Button: Resets the mask.

Use case: Manually erasing artifacts, covering distracting elements, or excluding regions from processing.

title: Media Processing
text:
Colormap
A colormap maps grayscale intensity values to colors using a lookup table (LUT). This improves visibility and interpretation of data.

Lookup Table (LUT): Defines the mapping (e.g., Jet, Hot, Cool). Each intensity is assigned a unique color.

Alpha (Blend): Controls transparency of the colormap overlay (0 = fully transparent, 1 = fully opaque).

Normalize Checkbox: Rescales intensity values into a normalized range before applying the colormap, ensuring full use of the LUT range.

Use case: Enhancing interpretability of microscopy, behavior, or heatmap-like data.

title: Contrast and Brightness Adjustment
text:
These two filters are implemented with a single linear transform taking parameters “alpha” (\(\alpha\)) and “beta” (\(\beta\)). Pixel values are multiplied by \(\alpha\) to adjust contrast, then have \(\beta\) added to adjust brightness: \[
g(x) = \alpha f(x) + \beta
\] In effect the magnitude of \(\alpha\) corresponds to the amount of contrast and the magnitude of \(\beta\) corresponds to the amount of brightness.
